creatures.name: Alpamysh (Uzbek)

creatures.name: Alpamysh Batyr

creatures.name: Alpomish
creatures.excerpt: Alpomish is a legendary hero from Turkic folklore, particularly prominent in Uzbek, Kazakh, and other Central Asian epic traditions. creatures.name: Alux
creatures.excerpt: Aluxes are small, elf-like trickster spirits of the Yucatec Maya. They haunt ruins, cenotes, forests, and cornfields, hiding tools, leading travelers astray, and stealing food. Given corn, honey, or balché, they become protective guardians; farmers build small stone 'kahtal alux' houses at field corners to guard crops.

creatures.name: Am Fear Liath Mòr
creatures.excerpt: Am Fear Liath Mor, meaning the Big Grey Man in Scottish Gaelic, is a legendary cryptid said to inhabit the summit and slopes of Ben Macdui, the second-highest mountain in the British Isles, located in the Cairngorms range of Scotland. creatures.name: Amadioha
creatures.excerpt: Amadioha (Unknown). is a deity. Amadioha is the god of thunder and lightning in the Igbo pantheon of Nigeria. creatures.name: Amaguq
creatures.excerpt: Amaguq is the Iñupiaq word for wolf and the name of a wolf-spirit in Inuit tradition, a trickster able to shape-shift between wolf and human form. creatures.name: Amalvipik
creatures.excerpt: Amalvipik is a monstrous creature from Armenian folklore, a type of demonic entity that dwells in remote mountainous regions and abandoned places. creatures.name: Aman Doger
creatures.excerpt: Aman Doger is a sea monster from Javanese and Indonesian mythology, specifically from the folklore of Java, Indonesia. The name combines aman meaning safe or peaceful and doger referring to a type of mythical creature. This sea monster is said to inhabit the waters around the Indonesian archipelago, particularly the Ja

creatures.name: Amarok
creatures.excerpt: Amarok (Amaroq) is the gigantic solitary wolf of Greenlandic Inuit legend, which hunts alone unlike the pack and devours anyone foolish enough to hunt alone at night. creatures.name: Amaru
creatures.excerpt: Amaru (or katari in Aymara) is the cosmic serpent/dragon of Andean mythology (Inca, pre-Inca). A double-headed serpent dwelling in lakes and rivers, connecting the earthly world (kay pacha) with the underworld (uku pacha) and upper world (hanan pacha). Represents infinity, wisdom, water, lightning, and the Milky Way.

creatures.name: Amaterasu
creatures.excerpt: Amaterasu is the Japanese sun goddess, one of the most important deities in the Shinto religion of Japan. creatures.name: Amikiri
creatures.excerpt: Amikiri is a yokai or supernatural creature from Japanese folklore, specifically a type of tsukumogami that appears as a bizarre hybrid creature. creatures.name: Amirani
creatures.excerpt: Amirani is a culture hero and demigod from Georgian mythology, comparable to the Greek Prometheus or the Armenian Mher. creatures.name: Amma
creatures.excerpt: Amma is the supreme creator god of the Dogon people of Mali, who created the universe from a cosmic egg called aduno tal which contained all future matter and motion. creatures.name: Ammit (Devourer)
creatures.excerpt: Ammit, also known as the Devourer or Eater of the Dead, is a female demon from ancient Egyptian mythology who played a crucial role in the afterlife judgment of souls. creatures.name: Amur Tiger Spirit
creatures.excerpt: The Amur tiger spirit, called Amba, is the most sacred animal in Nanai tradition, appearing as a giant Amur (Siberian) tiger with luminous eyes and glowing stripes that can stand on its hind legs and speak, sometimes as a tiger-human hybrid. creatures.name: Anansi

creatures.name: Anansi
creatures.excerpt: Anansi (Kwaku Anansi) is the Jamaican trickster spider, brought from Akan/Ashanti Ghana via the slave trade. creatures.name: Anansi
creatures.excerpt: In the Ivory Coast, the spider trickster of the Akan appears as Kacou Ananzè among the Baoule and other Akan peoples, who carry the same story cycle across the border from Ghana. creatures.name: Anansi
creatures.excerpt: Anansi (Ananse), the spider trickster of Akan folklore, is celebrated across the forest belt of Ghana and the eastern Ivory Coast, where his tales traveled with trade and migration. creatures.name: Anarteq
creatures.excerpt: Anarteq is a figure of Greenlandic Inuit legend, a hunter taken into the sea by a sea spirit who adopted him and taught him to live beneath the waves, granting him power over the sea animals. creatures.name: Anaye (monsters)
creatures.excerpt: The Anaye are the monstrous beings that roamed the Fourth World of Navajo tradition, terrorizing the people after the emergence from the lower worlds. creatures.excerpt: Ancestral Spirits Iceland (Unknown). is a spirit. Ancestral spirits from Icelandic folklore watch over their descendants through generations.. Source: Icelandic folklore — ancestral spirits documented in Icelandic folk belief.

creatures.name: Andaokut Nuu Chah Nulth
creatures.excerpt: Andaokut is the hero of a Nuu-chah-nulth myth cycle who frees the children stolen by Malahas, the Woman of the Woods. In Malagasy, 'angano' means 'tale' or 'story' and is the word for the folk narratives themselves, not a creature; no source records a man-eating ogre named Angano. Giants and ogres do appear in Malagasy oral tales, but no attested name corresponds to this entry.

creatures.name: Angara (River Spirit)
creatures.excerpt: Angara is the personified river spirit of Buryat folklore, a beautiful maiden whose flowing hair becomes the river's current and whose robes are woven of blue-green water, moving swiftly forward without looking back. creatures.name: Angatra

creatures.name: Angel Denmark
creatures.excerpt: Angel Denmark (Unknown). is a spirit. The Angel is a character from Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale who carries a dead child through heaven's gardens.. Source: Danish folklore — angel/spirit figure documented in Danish oral tradition.

creatures.name: Angelo Custode

creatures.name: Anghir

creatures.name: Aningaut

creatures.name: Anjana
creatures.excerpt: The Anjana is a protective nature spirit from the folklore of Cantabria and surrounding regions of northern Spain, deeply woven into the rural traditions of the Iberian Peninsula. creatures.name: Ankou
creatures.excerpt: The Ankou is the death-messenger of Breton folklore, a skeletal or shrouded figure who rides or drives a cart, gathering the souls of the dying; the last person to die in a parish becomes the Ankou for the following year, and the creaking of his wheels is a mortal omen.

creatures.name: Anpo
creatures.excerpt: Anpo (Anpao) is the spirit of dawn in Lakota mythology, created by Inyan to bring light to Maka when she complained of cold and darkness. creatures.name: Anqa (Mythical Bird of Arabia)
creatures.excerpt: The Anqa is a golden, fabulous female bird in pre-Islamic Arab mythology, described as immensely beautiful and colorful with a long neck, a human-like face, four pairs of wings, and a whiteness in its neck. Created by God with all perfections, she lives alone on Mount Qaf, flies far away, and only appears once in ages.

creatures.name: Antaeus (Anti)

creatures.name: Anubis

creatures.name: Apophis

creatures.name: Asema

creatures.name: Asura

creatures.name: Atabey (Taino Mother Goddess of Fresh Water)
creatures.excerpt: Atabey (also called Atabex) is the supreme mother goddess of the Taino people, the goddess of fresh water, fertility, and the moon. creatures.name: Atargatis

creatures.name: Bear Ancestor-Spirit of Mi'kmaq

She is revered by Hindu and Muslim communities alike as the protector against the dangers of the mangrove forest, part. Source: Bengali folklore; Sundarbans oral tradition

creatures.name: Bones Together
creatures.excerpt: Bones Together is a fearsome monster in Crow mythology, a skeletal being with impenetrable bone armor. Seven Bison and their human companion fought against Bones Together when the monster threatened them. Each bison charged but broke their legs against Bones Together's bony hide. creatures.name: Boo Hag
creatures.excerpt: The Boo Hag is a terrifying supernatural entity from Gullah Geechee folklore. Unlike European vampires that drink blood, Boo Hags drain their victims' breath and spiritual essence by 'riding' them while they sleep. According to legend, a Boo Hag appears as a beautiful woman by day — luring victims into marriage or trus

creatures.name: Boqs (Cannibal Giant)
creatures.excerpt: Boqs is the hairy wild man of the woods of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola), a giant sasquatch-like being of the British Columbia coast whose hands and face are human. He walks stooping, can raise the very land by supernatural power, and was said to still haunt King Island; Boas recorded detailed first-hand accounts.

creatures.name: Boqs Cannibal Giant Nuxalk
creatures.excerpt: Boqs is the wild man of the woods in Bella Coola (Nuxalk), Chinook, and Salish tradition, a shaggy forest being of great strength. creatures.name: Bori (Iskoki)
creatures.excerpt: Bori (also Iskoki) are spirit beings from Hausa animism, particularly strong among the Mawri people of Dogondoutchi in Niger and the Maguzawa of northern Nigeria. According to Mawri creation mythology, God created a man and woman who bore fifty sets of twins. When God asked to see the children, the woman hid the better

creatures.name: Bortbyting
creatures.excerpt: Bortbytingen (the swapped one) is a changeling — a troll infant left in place of a human baby stolen by trolls or the underground folk. creatures.name: Boruta
creatures.excerpt: Powerful forest and swamp spirit of Polish mythology, tutelary of central and eastern Poland's woodlands — the Puszcza Kurpiowska. creatures.name: Botamochi bakemono
creatures.excerpt: An obscure yokai said to haunt old wooden houses. The name pairs 'botamochi' (a spring-equinox sweet rice cake) with 'bakemono' ('transforming thing'). creatures.name: Boto
creatures.excerpt: The Boto (Encantado) is the Amazon river dolphin shapeshifter of Brazilian Amazon folklore. At night it becomes a handsome man in white clothing with a hat hiding its blowhole, attends riverside festivals, seduces women, and returns to the river by dawn. Children from these unions are 'filhos do boto.

creatures.name: Bottler
creatures.excerpt: The Bottler is a malevolent water spirit from Dutch folklore, particularly known in the rural provinces of Brabant and Zeeland. creatures.name: Botu
creatures.excerpt: The Botu is a mischievous tree-dwelling imp or goblin from Nepalese folklore, particularly known in the rural hill regions and among the Newar communities of the Kathmandu Valley. These small forest spirits are considered harmless tricksters rather than malevolent beings, inhabiting the branches of banyan trees, rocky

creatures.name: Bou Saadia
creatures.excerpt: Bou Saadia (Father of Saadia) is a tragic folkloric figure from Tunisian tradition, particularly associated with the medina of Tunis and Stambeli ritual performances. creatures.name: Bouda
creatures.excerpt: The bouda (buda) is the Ethiopian werehyena and evil-eye figure: a person, traditionally a blacksmith, potter or other artisan of stigmatized castes, believed to possess the evil eye and to transform into a hyena at night, often to dig up graves or harm enemies.

creatures.name: Boukhencha
creatures.excerpt: Boukhencha (Unknown). is a spirit. Boukhencha is a figure from Moroccan folklore, often described as a terrifying creature that appears at night to frighten children. Such figures serve as cautionary elements in Moroccan oral tradition. Source: Moroccan oral tradition; North African folklore

creatures.name: Bouki (Haitian Trickster Hyena)
creatures.excerpt: Bouki is the slow-witted, greedy hyena trickster of Haitian folklore -- the eternal foil to the clever Rabbit (or Malis/Connen, the rabbit trickster). creatures.name: Bouki (Hyena)
creatures.excerpt: Bouki the Hyena is the greedy, foolish, and constantly hungry foil to Leuk the Hare in Wolof folklore. Bouki is the classic trickster's dupe — always falling for Leuk's schemes due to her insatiable appetite and lack of foresight. In each tale, Bouki's greed, laziness, and carelessness lead to her downfall. Whether bui

creatures.name: Boumba
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a spirit: 'Boumba' is chiefly a toponym in southeastern Cameroon, the Boumba River and Boumba-Bek National Park, and no Bantu forest guardian of that name appears in documented sources. The description is a generic filler portrait of a forest-protector spirit.

creatures.name: Bouti
creatures.excerpt: The Bouti is a fearsome ogress or she-demon from the folklore of the Afar people of Djibouti, Ethiopia, and Eritrea. According to legend, the Bouti is a shape-shifting female monster held responsible for death, dishonor, fratricide, and familial discord among the Afar. creatures.name: Bow priests (Awonawilona's sons)
creatures.excerpt: In Ruth Benedict's version of the Zuni emergence, the people lived in darkness in the fourth world and recognized Awonawilona's two sons, the twin war gods, as their bow priests. creatures.name: Br'er Bear
creatures.excerpt: Br'er Bear is a figure of African American folktale, one of the animal characters of the Uncle Remus cycle set down by Joel Chandler Harris from stories carried from West Africa. creatures.name: Br'er Buzzard
creatures.excerpt: Br'er Buzzard is a trickster character in African American folklore, particularly in Gullah Geechee traditions. As a buzzard (vulture), he is associated with death, transformation, and the sacred. In Gullah belief, the buzzard is not merely a carrion eater but a sacred bird that carries souls back to Africa. This conne

creatures.name: Br'er Fox
creatures.excerpt: Br'er Fox is the primary antagonist in the Br'er Rabbit cycle of African American folktales. A cunning predator who constantly schemes to capture and eat Br'er Rabbit, Br'er Fox is consistently foiled by the rabbit's superior cleverness. Despite being faster, stronger, and more dangerous, Br'er Fox's arrogance and gull

creatures.name: Br'er Rabbit
creatures.excerpt: Br'er Rabbit is the central trickster figure in African American folklore, a small but cunning rabbit who uses his wits to overcome larger, stronger adversaries. creatures.name: Br'er Terrapin
creatures.excerpt: Br'er Terrapin (the turtle) appears in one of the most beloved African American folktales, where he outruns the much faster Br'er Rabbit through clever strategy rather than speed. creatures.name: Br'er Wolf
creatures.excerpt: Br'er Wolf is a figure of African American folktale from the Uncle Remus cycle compiled by Joel Chandler Harris, a hungry and determined predator who hunts Br'er Rabbit but is repeatedly outwitted. Persistent yet lacking cunning, he loses to the rabbit's tricks, reinforcing the theme that wit defeats strength.

creatures.name: Brag
creatures.excerpt: The Brag is a mischievous shapeshifting goblin from the folklore of Northumbria, Northumberland, and County Durham, particularly associated with the border regions between England and Scotland. creatures.name: Brahma Raksha
creatures.excerpt: The Brahma Raksha is a sacred guardian spirit from Indian Hindu folklore, believed to be the benevolent spirit of a deceased Brahmin priest who watches over and protects Brahmin families and their households. Unlike the more dangerous Brahma Rakshasa, the Brahma Raksha is a positive, protective entity bound by dharma t

creatures.name: Brahma Rakshasa
creatures.excerpt: The Brahma Rakshasa is a powerful and dangerous demon from Indian Hindu mythology, born either from the yawn of the god Brahma or from the cursed soul of a Brahmin who lived a wicked life. Unlike ordinary rakshasas, the Brahma Rakshasa possesses immense knowledge of the Vedas, mantras, and sacred texts, making it both

creatures.name: Brer Coon
creatures.excerpt: Brer Coon is a character of African American folktale from the Uncle Remus cycle compiled by Joel Chandler Harris, a raccoon figure drawn from West African trickster stories carried into the American South. He appears alongside Brer Rabbit and Brer Possum in comic tales of cunning, deceit, and hard lessons.

creatures.name: Brer Possum
creatures.excerpt: Brer Possum is a character of African American folktale, one of the animal figures of the Uncle Remus cycle written down by Joel Chandler Harris from stories brought from West Africa by enslaved people. As Brer Rabbit's neighbor he is sly and slow, frequently outwitted yet resilient, a trickster of the American South r

creatures.name: Brockengespenst
creatures.excerpt: The Brockengespenst, or Brocken Spectre, is an atmospheric optical phenomenon observed on the Brocken mountain in the Harz range of Germany, where it has inspired folklore and legends for centuries. First scientifically described by Johann Silberschlag in 1780, the phenomenon occurs when a climber or observer stands on

creatures.name: Brugmo (Gesar's Queen)
creatures.excerpt: Brugmo (Brug-gu-ma), Queen of Ling, is the central heroine of the Tibetan Epic of King Gesar. Won as the prize of the great horse race that revealed Gesar's true kingship, she is later seized by the king of Hor, and her rescue drives one of the epic's longest campaigns. creatures.name: Brunnsgubbe
creatures.excerpt: Brunnsgubben (well old man) is the male guardian spirit of wells, springs, and natural water sources in Swedish folklore. creatures.name: Bruxa
creatures.excerpt: The Bruxa is a witch or sorceress from Galician folklore in northwestern Spain and northern Portugal, embodying both healing and harmful magical traditions. creatures.name: Bu Darya
creatures.excerpt: Bu Darya, meaning Father of the Sea in Arabic, is a malevolent water demon from Kuwaiti and Persian Gulf maritime folklore. creatures.name: Bu Draeyah
creatures.excerpt: Bu Draeyah is a giant sea serpent of Qatari legend, deep blue of scale with glowing golden eyes, who guards the pearl beds of the Persian Gulf. creatures.name: Bu Draya
creatures.excerpt: Bu Draya (also Bu Daryā, meaning 'Father of the Sea' from Persian) is a terrifying sea jinn from Bahraini and Arabian Gulf folklore. creatures.name: Bucca
creatures.excerpt: The Cornish Bucca is a male sea-spirit merman specific to the folklore of Cornwall, particularly associated with Lamorna Cove and the coastal mining communities of West Cornwall. This version of the Bucca is believed to once have been a human prince cursed by a witch to live as a sea creature, making him a tragic figur

creatures.name: Buda
creatures.excerpt: Buda (Ge'ez: ቡዳ) is a powerful and feared figure in Eritrean and Ethiopian folk religion, representing the supernatural power of the evil eye combined with the ability to shapeshift into a hyena. creatures.name: Buda
creatures.excerpt: Buda (Ge'ez: ቡዳ) is the Eritrean-Ethiopian belief in the evil eye wielded by hereditary social groups, often metalworkers, potters, and tanners, who harm others through their gaze and are said to shapeshift into hyenas at night. Protective amulets (kitab), holy water, and invocations of God's name ward off its effects.

creatures.name: Buda
creatures.excerpt: Buda (Tigrinya). is a shapeshifter. Buda is a shapeshifter from Tigrinya folklore in Eritrea, believed to embody the spiritual traditions of the region.. Source: Tigrinya oral tradition

creatures.name: Buffalo People
creatures.excerpt: The Buffalo People are significant spirit beings in Cheyenne mythology and oral traditions, representing the deep spiritual connection between the Cheyenne people and the American bison, which was central to their way of life on the Great Plains. creatures.name: Buffalo Spirit
creatures.excerpt: The Buffalo Spirit (Tatanka) is one of the most powerful and revered animal spirits in Lakota mythology. creatures.name: Buffalo Woman
creatures.excerpt: Buffalo Woman is a revered figure in Kiowa mythology, serving as a powerful symbol of the sacred relationship between the Kiowa people and the buffalo herds that sustained them on the southern Great Plains. creatures.name: Bukavac
creatures.excerpt: The Bukavac is a demonic aquatic monster from Serbian and broader Slavic mythology, particularly associated with the region of Syrmia in modern-day Serbia. creatures.name: Bukha Noyon
creatures.excerpt: Bukha Noyon is the celestial bull of Buryat tradition, a totemic progenitor who descended from the sky to create and defend the western Buryat clans. creatures.name: Bukit Timah Monkey Man
creatures.excerpt: The Bukit Timah Monkey Man (BTM) is Singapore's most famous cryptid, said to inhabit the Bukit Timah Nature Reserve. creatures.name: Buku Spirits
creatures.excerpt: Buku spirits are powerful and volatile forest-dwelling supernatural beings in the mythology of the Jola (Diola) people of Senegal, particularly in the Casamance region. creatures.name: Bukwus (Wild Man of the Woods)

creatures.excerpt: Bukwus (Bakwas) is the wild man of the woods in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a small green spirit with a skeletal face and long curving nose. creatures.name: Bukwus Wild Man Of The Woods Kwakwaka Wakw
creatures.excerpt: Bukwus (Bakwas) is the wild man of the woods in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a small, green-skinned ghost-king with a skeletal face and long curving nose. He prowls the forests, whistling to lure the living toward the realm of the dead; some accounts name him the husband of Dzunukwa, the Cannibal Woman.

creatures.name: Bulgasari
creatures.excerpt: Bulgasari is the iron-eating monster of Korean folklore, blending elephant, bear, and tiger traits with iron skin and ember eyes. creatures.name: Bull Snake
creatures.excerpt: Bull Snake is a character in the Hopi tale of Coyote and Bull Snake exchanging visits, recorded in the Traditions of the Hopi. creatures.name: Bultungin
creatures.excerpt: The Bultungin is a werehyena from the folklore of the Kanuri people of Nigeria and the former Bornu Empire around Lake Chad. creatures.name: Bulyit
creatures.excerpt: Bulyit is a Noongar (southwestern Australian) name for small, hairy, malevolent spirit-beings — grouped with Gnardi and Mumari — that lurk in shadows and are said to carry off children who stray from camp, especially near sundown. creatures.name: Bunian
creatures.excerpt: The Bunian are invisible human-like spirits in Bruneian and Malay folklore, often described as 'hidden people' who dwell in forests, jungles, and remote natural areas near human settlements. creatures.name: Bunjil (The Eagle)
creatures.excerpt: Bunjil is the great creator deity and ancestral spirit of the Kulin Nation, the collective of Aboriginal Australian peoples including the Wurundjeri, Boonwurrung, Taungurung, Djadjawurrung, and Wathaurung who inhabit the Port Phillip region of Victoria. creatures.name: Bunyip
creatures.excerpt: Aboriginal Australian water spirit ('bunyip' = devil/spirit) from southeastern Australia (Yorta Yorta, Ngarrindjeru, Wonnarua, Kurnai). creatures.name: Bura
creatures.excerpt: Bura is a malevolent wind spirit from Azerbaijani and Caspian Sea folklore, known for its sudden and devastating appearances that sweep away everything in its path. creatures.name: Buraq (Celestial Steed)
creatures.excerpt: Buraq is the fabulous celestial steed that carried the Prophet Muhammad from Mecca to Jerusalem and through the seven heavens during the Night Journey (Isra and Mi'raj) in 621 CE. creatures.name: Burkhan Khaldun Spirit
creatures.excerpt: Burkhan Khaldun, in the Khentii mountains of northeastern Mongolia, is the holiest mountain of the Mongols, the birthplace and reputed burial place of Genghis Khan and one of four sacred peaks of the land. creatures.excerpt: No butterfly spirit or guardian of sacred mountains is attested in Tongan tradition; Tongan mythology centers on Maui, the sky and sea god Tangaloa, and the divine descent of the royal lineage. creatures.name: Butu
creatures.excerpt: Butu is a masked spirit figure from the RaGbenle secret society of Sierra Leone, representing the ancestral spirits and supernatural forces that underpin traditional social order. creatures.name: Buundheex
creatures.excerpt: Buundheex is a shape-shifting spirit in Somali folklore that can transform into any human or animal form to deceive and prey upon victims. creatures.name: Bwiti

creatures.name: Bynesånden
creatures.excerpt: Bynesånden (the Byneset Spirit) is a local ghost from the Byneset area of Trondheim, a rural district on the west side of the Trondheimsfjord. creatures.name: Bysen
creatures.excerpt: The Bysen is a Gotland-specific forest gnome condemned to wander for moving boundary markers. He carries an axe, appears as a grey little man or a stump, and wears a red cap. creatures.name: Bytting
creatures.excerpt: Bytting (also known as skifting, from bytte = to swap) is a changeling in Norwegian folklore - a troll or hulder child secretly exchanged for a human infant. creatures.name: Bà Chúa

creatures.name: Bà Triệu
creatures.excerpt: Bà Triệu, known as Lady Triệu or Triệu Thị Trinh, is a legendary Vietnamese warrior heroine who led a rebellion against the Wu Chinese occupation in the 3rd century AD. creatures.name: Bái Zhúrén (White Snake)
creatures.excerpt: Bái Zhúrén (White Snake), known as Bai Suzhen in Chinese, is the central figure of one of China's most beloved folktales, 'The Legend of the White Snake' (Bai She Zhuan). creatures.name: Bäckahästen
creatures.excerpt: The bäckahästen (brook horse) is a Swedish manifestation of the näcken water spirit. It appears as a magnificent white or dappled horse near streams and fords. creatures.name: Bækhest

creatures.name: Cadejo
creatures.excerpt: Cadejo is a spirit from Mesoamerican mythology. The legend has pre-Columbian indigenous origins, where dogs were believed to help humans pass into the afterlife. With the arrival of Christianity, the story evolved into a dualistic tale. The White Cadejo, with blue eyes, is a protective spirit that guards drunkards, los

creatures.name: Cadejo Chico
creatures.excerpt: Cadejo Chico is the smaller, more mischievous counterpart to the Cadejo Grande in Central American folklore, particularly prevalent in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Costa Rica. Unlike its larger, malevolent relative, the Cadejo Chico is known for its playful and sometimes helpful nature, though it can still be

creatures.name: Cadejo Grande
creatures.excerpt: Cadejo Grande is the larger, malevolent manifestation of the supernatural dog spirit in Central American folklore, particularly prominent in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua. Unlike its smaller, mischievous counterpart the Cadejo Chico, the Cadejo Grande is a fearsome hellhound-like creature that activel

creatures.name: Cagüeiro
creatures.excerpt: Cagüeiro is a shape-shifting outlaw figure from Cuban folklore, particularly associated with the rural countryside and Afro-Cuban folk traditions. Unlike many supernatural creatures that are inherently magical or mythological in origin, the Cagüeiro is a human who has gained the power to transform into any animal or ob

creatures.name: Caipora
creatures.excerpt: Caipora is a powerful forest spirit from Brazilian folklore, considered the guardian of wildlife and game animals throughout the vast Amazon rainforest and beyond. The name comes from the Tupi language, meaning 'inhabitant of the forest,' and this entity is deeply embedded in the indigenous Tupi-Guarani mythological tr

creatures.name: Caleuche
creatures.excerpt: El Caleuche, also known as the Buque de Arte or Magic Ship, is a legendary ghost ship from Chilote mythology in southern Chile, specifically the Chiloé Archipelago. This supernatural vessel is one of the most enduring and complex legends in South American folklore, blending elements of Mapuche mythology with Spanish co

creatures.name: Calon Arang
creatures.excerpt: Calon Arang (Unknown). is a witch. Calon Arang is a legendary witch from Balinese folklore, a widow skilled in black magic who terrorized a kingdom after her daughter was rejected in marriage. The tale is performed in the traditional B. Source: Balinese folklore; traditional dance-drama

creatures.name: Calèche de Lallmatie
creatures.excerpt: Calèche de Lallmatie is a Mauritian ghost legend: a luminous white carriage drawn by two white horses, bearing two women in white, seen at midnight near Lallmatie village. A passive omen of the French colonial past, it haunts roads without attacking. Documented in Mauritian folklore collections and 'Culture of Mauritiu

creatures.name: Camahueto
creatures.excerpt: Camahueto is a Chilote aquatic bull from Chiloé Archipelago, Chile. Born in rivers with a single spiral horn like a unicorn, it grows massive and migrates to the sea. Destructive on land: destroys crops, creates valleys and floods. Only a machi can lasso it with kelp and return it to the ocean. Its horn shavings are pr

creatures.name: Camazotz
creatures.excerpt: Camazotz (meaning 'Death Bat' in K'iche' Maya) is a bat spirit and death god in Late Post-Classic Maya mythology from the Popol Vuh. He serves the lords of the underworld, Xibalba. In the Maya Hero Twins myth, Camazotz appears in the 'House of Bats' trial, where Hunahpu and Xbalanque must spend the night surrounded by

creatures.name: Cannibal Giants
creatures.excerpt: Cannibal Giants are fearsome creatures from the oral traditions of various First Nations peoples across Canada, particularly among the Algonquian and Athabaskan-speaking tribes of the Subarctic and northern woodlands. Known by different names in different languages, these beings share a common archetype: giant humanoid

creatures.name: Cannibal Giants
creatures.excerpt: Cannibal giants are man-eating monsters of the oral traditions of Algonquian and Athabaskan peoples of Canada's Subarctic and northern woodlands — known as wihtikow (windigo) among Cree, Ojibwe, and related nations. Frozen, famine-driven giants born of isolation and starvation, they embody the dangers of the deep winte

creatures.name: Canyon People
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature as spirit beings. 'Canyon People' (Tseyi Ndee) is the name of an Apache band, not a class of guardian spirits; the entry invents deep-gorge inhabitants and ancestor-mediator roles with no named narrative. Genuine Apache place-spirits exist in oral tradition, but none is

creatures.name: Cap-a-Taille
creatures.excerpt: Cap-a-Taille is a malevolent nocturnal spirit from French folklore, particularly associated with the forested regions of medieval and early modern France. Known as a cauchemar or nightmare spirit, this entity is closely related to the Germanic Alp and the English mare traditions, part of a widespread European belief in

creatures.name: Capelobo
creatures.excerpt: Capelobo is a therianthropic vampire-like monster from Brazilian mythology, particularly prevalent in the northern states of Pará and Maranhão. Its name fuses the Guarani word capê, meaning broken or crooked leg, with the Portuguese lobo, meaning wolf, describing both its appearance and its lupine nature. The Capelobo

creatures.name: Capotona
creatures.excerpt: Capotona is a mournful coastal ghost in Cape Verdean folklore, haunting shorelines and abandoned lighthouses. It manifests as a spectral figure emitting mournful sounds, countered by sunrise. Represents the perils of the sea and lost sailors. Documented in Cape Verdean oral tradition alongside Catchorrona.

creatures.name: Carival
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Trinidadian spirit named 'Carival' exists; the entry is a fabricated personification of Carnival. Trinidad's real folk entities include the douen, La Diablesse, the soucouyant, and Papa Bois, none of which is a personification of the festival.

creatures.name: Cat Sidhe
creatures.excerpt: Cat Sidhe (Unknown). is a fairy. The Cat Sidhe is a fairy creature from Irish and Scottish folklore, appearing as a large black cat with a white spot on its chest. It was believed to be a witch transformed into feline form.. Source: Scottish and Irish folkloric sources; Celtic mythology

creatures.name: Cat Sídhe
creatures.excerpt: The Cat Sídhe, also known as Cat-sìth in Scottish Gaelic, is a fairy creature from Celtic mythology that resembles a large spectral black cat with a distinctive white spot on its chest. This being spans both Scottish and Irish folklore, though it is more prominent in Scottish Highland traditions. Unlike ordinary fairy

creatures.name: Catchorrona
creatures.excerpt: Catchorrona ('black dog') is an ominous spectral hound in Cape Verdean folklore, appearing at moonlit crossroads to warn or terrify night wanderers. It induces fear and stealth, repelled by silver bells. Represents dangers of nocturnal travel. Documented in Cape Verdean oral tradition.

creatures.name: Celestial Deer
creatures.excerpt: The celestial deer of Mongolia is the leaping, antlered stag carved on the Bronze Age deer stones that stand across the northern steppe, monuments some three thousand years old. Scholars such as William Fitzhugh interpret these 'flying deer' as spirit beings that carry the souls of warriors and leaders toward the heave

creatures.name: Celestial Moose
creatures.excerpt: The celestial moose is the great elk of Evenki star-lore, read in the constellation of the Big Dipper. In the best-known telling the heavenly hunter Mangi pursues the elk across the sky, the Milky Way is his ski track, and the turning of the northern heavens retells their endless chase, a story of the hunt that shaped

creatures.name: Celestial Reindeer (Seven Reindeer)
creatures.excerpt: Among the Nenets of Siberia the bright northern stars are read as a celestial reindeer or elk pursued across the sky, a tale told by forest Nenets reindeer herders to mark the turning of the seasons. Because the reindeer stands at the heart of Nenets life, its image in the heavens carries both practical and sacred mean

creatures.name: Cemi (Taino Spirit Being and Sacred Object)
creatures.excerpt: Cemi (also spelled Zemi) refers to both the spirit beings in Taino mythology and the sacred objects that housed them. In Taino belief, the world was populated by countless zemis -- spirits that inhabited natural features (mountains, rivers, caves, trees) and could be invoked through carved stone, wood, shell, or bone o

creatures.name: Cerberus
creatures.excerpt: Cerberus, often called the Hound of Hades, is the most fearsome canine in Greek mythology, serving as the guardian of the underworld's gates to prevent the dead from escaping and the living from entering without permission. Born from the union of the monsters Echidna and Typhon, Cerberus is sibling to other multi-heade

creatures.name: Chaac (Chaahk)
creatures.excerpt: Chaac, the Maya rain god (Chaahk), is a humanoid deity with a long curling trunk-like nose, fangs and shell ear ornaments who hurls his lightning axe (K'awiil). He brings rain to the crops and dwells in clouds, mountains and cenotes; his four directional aspects wear red, white, black and yellow, and neglect provokes s

creatures.name: Chaac (Chaahk)
creatures.excerpt: Chaahk, the Maya thunder-and-rain deity of lowland Guatemala, snorts rain through his long curling nose, wields a lightning axe and wears fangs and shell ear ornaments. He lives in clouds, mountain caves and cenotes and must be appeased with offerings, for his four colored directional aspects can unleash destructive st

creatures.name: Chameleon (Messenger of God)
creatures.excerpt: In Yao creation tradition of Malawi the chameleon, messenger of the god Mulungu, sets fish traps in the primordial waters and one day draws up the first man and woman, whom God bids him release to grow to maturity. Among the Chewa the chameleon bears the message of immortality, delayed by the lizard that brings death i

creatures.name: Chang Er
creatures.excerpt: Chang'e, also originally known as Heng'e, is the revered Chinese goddess of the Moon and one of the most prominent figures in Chinese mythology, folk religion, and cultural tradition. Her story is intimately connected with the myth of Hou Yi, the legendary archer who shot down nine of the ten suns that once scorched th

creatures.name: Chang Pheuak (White Elephant)
creatures.excerpt: The White Elephant (Thai: ช้างเผือก, chang pheuak) is the most sacred animal in Thai mythology and a direct symbol of royal power connected to Buddhist cosmology. According to legend, Queen Maya, the mother of the Buddha, dreamt of a white elephant offering her a lotus flower before she conceived — establishing the whi

creatures.name: Changing Woman
creatures.excerpt: White-painted Woman, the Apache counterpart of Changing Woman, is the mother of the hero twins Child of the Water and Killer of Enemies, whom she bore on White Mountain. She is the ideal of Apache womanhood and the model for the girls' puberty ceremony, which re-enacts her power to age and then grow young again with th

creatures.name: Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé)
creatures.excerpt: Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé), also called White Shell Woman, is the central deity of Navajo religion. Born from the darkness, she lives in the west beside the ocean, aging and renewing herself with the seasons, and she bore the Hero Twins, Monster Slayer and Child of the Water, fathered by the Sun. She gave the N

creatures.name: Changó
creatures.excerpt: Changó, also spelled Shangó or Xangô, is one of the most powerful and revered orishas in the Yoruba religion and its Afro-Caribbean derivatives including Santería, Candomblé, and Lukumí. As the orisha of thunder, lightning, fire, war, dance, and justice, Changó embodies masculine power, passion, and royal authority. Or

creatures.name: Charonda
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Cypriot vampire called 'Charonda' is recorded. The name speculatively conflates Charos (Charon), the Greek folk personification of death prominent in Cypriot laments, with the vrykolakas vampire tradition; no blood-drinking being of this name is documented in Cyprio

creatures.name: Chase Vault
creatures.excerpt: The Chase Vault mystery is one of the most famous and enduring paranormal legends of the Caribbean, centered on a family tomb in the Christ Church cemetery of Barbados. Between 1812 and 1820, the heavy lead-lined coffins interred in the Chase family vault were repeatedly found disturbed, moved from their original posit

creatures.name: Chenoo
creatures.excerpt: The Chenoo is a cannibalistic ice monster of Mi'kmaq and Wabanaki mythology. A Chenoo was originally human, but was transformed through an act of cannibalism or extreme trauma into a monster with a heart of ice and an insatiable hunger for human flesh. Chenoos are enormous, with claws and fangs, and their heart is visi

creatures.name: Cherruves
creatures.excerpt: Cherufe is a being of Mapuche tradition said to dwell in the lava pools of southern Chilean volcanoes, a creature of molten rock and sharp crystals with a man-eater's appetite. Its stirrings are blamed for eruptions and earthquakes, and communities historically offered sacrifices to appease it. The input mislabels it a

creatures.name: Cheval Mal Fet
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The name 'Cheval Mal Fet' garbles 'Le Chevaler Mal Fet' — 'the ill-made knight' — the epithet of Lancelot in Arthurian romance, popularized by T. H. White's novel 'The Ill-Made Knight.' No phantom horse or Haitian or Belgian ghost-horse tradition by this name is docume

creatures.name: Chhinnamasta (Self-Decapitated Goddess)
creatures.excerpt: Chhinnamasta ('the Self-Decapitated One') is a powerful Tantric goddess, one of the ten Mahavidyas (great wisdom goddesses) in Shaktism. The legend tells that once, while bathing in the Mandakini River with her attendants Dakini and Varnini, Parvati (in her form as Chhinnamasta) was overcome by a ravenous hunger that h

creatures.name: Chichkhan
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Kazakh mountain-dwarf spirit named 'Chichkhan' appears in any collection of Kazakh or Central Asian Turkic folklore. Kazakh animistic tradition does describe yer-su earth-water spirits, divs, and witch-figures such as Zheztyrnak, but none matches this name.

creatures.name: Chickcharney
creatures.excerpt: The Chickcharney is a legendary bird-like creature from the folklore of Andros Island in the Bahamas, one of the most distinctive mythological beings in Caribbean oral tradition. According to Bahamian legend, the Chickcharney inhabits the dense pine forests of Andros, the largest island in the Bahamas archipelago. The

creatures.name: Chickcharnies
creatures.excerpt: Chickcharnies, a variant spelling of Chickcharney, are mischievous feathered spirits from the folklore of Andros Island in the Bahamas, deeply woven into Bahamian oral tradition. These creatures are considered omens of either great fortune or terrible misfortune, depending on how they are treated. The legend of the Chi

creatures.name: Chief No Vitals
creatures.excerpt: Chief No Vitals (also known as No Vitals) is a Crow culture hero who discovered tobacco and established the Tobacco Society (Bacu'sua). According to tradition, he was instructed by the Creator Akbaatatdia to seek the sacred plant at Devils Lake in eastern North Dakota. The Creator told him that the worship of tobacco w

creatures.name: Chil-kuyz
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Uzbek cave spirit named 'Chil-kuyz' is recorded. Uzbek and broader Turkic tradition instead names harmful spirits such as albasti and the iye (yeys) household and nature guardians; 'Chil-kuyz' appears to be an invented blend of these figures.

creatures.name: Child of the Water
creatures.excerpt: Child of the Water is the Apache culture hero, one of the twins born to White-painted Woman. With his brother Killer of Enemies he rid the world of monsters, slaying the Owl-Man Giant, the Buffalo Monster, and the Eagle Monster, and he remains the model of the Apache warrior, told of across the Chiricahua and other Apa

creatures.name: Child of the Water (Tóbájíshchíní)
creatures.excerpt: Child of the Water (Tóbájíshchíní) is one of the Navajo Hero Twins, younger brother of Monster Slayer. Born to Changing Woman and fathered by the Sun, he accompanied his brother on the quest to rid the world of the Anaye (monsters). Together they journeyed to their father the Sun, passing deadly tests. Child of the Wat

creatures.name: Chimera
creatures.excerpt: The Chimera is one of the most famous monsters in Greek mythology, a fire-breathing hybrid creature from Lycia in Asia Minor that has become the archetype for all composite mythical beings. First described by Homer in the Iliad, the Chimera was the offspring of Typhon and Echidna, sibling to Cerberus, the Lernaean Hydr

creatures.name: Chindi
creatures.excerpt: Chindi (Navajo: ch'ijidii) is a concept in Navajo religious belief referring to the negative spiritual residue left behind after a person dies. Unlike a ghost in the Western sense, the Chindi is not the soul of the deceased but an accumulation of everything negative about their life including pain, fear, anger, disappo

creatures.name: Chinthe
creatures.excerpt: The chinthe is the stylized lion-guardian of Burmese Buddhism, a heraldic rendering of the Asiatic lion that flanks the entrances of pagodas, stupas and kyaung monasteries throughout Myanmar. Tradition derives it from the Mahavamsa tale of a Vanga princess wed to a lion whose son Sihabahu slew his father and raised a l

creatures.name: Chiruwi
creatures.excerpt: Chiruwi is a duel-challenging creature of Central African folklore: a one-sided being said to confront passers-by in combat. A traveller who wins earns the Chiruwi's mercy and a gift of great medical knowledge, becoming a successful medicine man; one who loses is killed. The figure tests strength and courage and appear

creatures.name: Chitapo (Lake Spirit)
creatures.excerpt: Chitapo (also spelled Kitapo) is a female lake spirit from the mythology of the Lamba and Bemba people of Zambia. She resides at the bottom of lakes, where she hoards vast treasures of diamonds and emeralds. Chitapo is a malicious spirit who lures people to a watery grave, not unlike sirens and mermaids in European leg

creatures.name: Chiuta (The Spider Creator)
creatures.excerpt: Chiuta, meaning 'Great Bow' (a reference to the rainbow as his symbol), is the supreme creator deity in Chewa and Tumbuka mythology of Malawi. Unlike many creator gods who are remote and uninvolved, Chiuta is depicted as intimately connected to creation through the powerful image of a spider descending from the sky on

creatures.name: Chiwara
creatures.excerpt: Chiwara is a mythical half-human, half-antelope being who taught the Bambara people the fundamentals of agriculture. Using its antlers and a pointed stick to dig the earth, Chiwara demonstrated how to cultivate the land, making it possible for farmers to grow crops. The people followed its example and became expert far

creatures.name: Cholula
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Cholula' is the name of a city in Puebla, Mexico, not a folkloric being. The giant tradition attached to its great pyramid belongs to Xelhua, a Nahua survivor of the Fourth-Sun flood who climbed Mount Tlaloc and, in early colonial accounts, raised the pyramid of Tlach

creatures.name: Chonchón
creatures.excerpt: The Chonchon is a terrifying creature from Mapuche folklore of Chile and Argentina, described as the detached flying head of a kalku, a Mapuche sorcerer who has transformed through black magic. The Chonchon is one of the most feared beings in Mapuche mythology, representing the dark side of shamanic power and the ultim

creatures.name: Chort
creatures.excerpt: Chort is an anthropomorphic malevolent spirit or demon in Slavic folk tradition, found across Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Polish, Czech, Slovak, and other Slavic cultures. The term chort represents a complex figure that evolved from pre-Christian Slavic mythology into Christian folk demonology. In Slavic paganism,

creatures.name: Chufi (Rabbit)
creatures.excerpt: Chufi, the Rabbit, is the trickster of the Muscogee (Creek) people, a small, quick animal whose cleverness and mischief animate many Creek stories. In one well-known tale he stole fire from those who kept it hidden and brought it to the people; in others he outwits larger animals, and his escapades teach the limits of

creatures.name: Chuhayster
creatures.excerpt: Chuhayster (Unknown). is a forest-spirit. Chuhayster (also spelled Chuhaister) is a tutelary forest deity from Ukrainian Carpathian folklore, unknown in any other mythology. He is described as a giant, shaggy humanoid with bright blue eyes wh. Source: Hutsul folklore; Ukrainian Carpathian oral tradition

creatures.name: Chukfi (Rabbit)
creatures.excerpt: Chukfi (Chokfi), the Rabbit, is the trickster of the Chickasaw people. Clever, mischievous, and sometimes selfish, he uses his wits to outsmart larger animals and to explain how things came to be; stories tell why Rabbit has a short tail, why the possum's tail is bare, and how deer gained their antlers.

creatures.name: Chukwu
creatures.excerpt: Chukwu (also known as Chineke or Chi Ukwu, meaning "The Great Spirit") is the supreme god of the Igbo people. Chukwu created the cosmos, all lesser deities (alusi), and humanity. Associated with the sun, which is considered the "Eye of God on Earth," Chukwu is all-powerful, all-knowing, and transcendent. The name Chukw

creatures.name: Chullachaqui
creatures.excerpt: Chullachaqui, also known as Shapishico, is a mythical forest creature from the Peruvian and Brazilian Amazon jungle, prominent in the folklore of the Quechua, Shipibo, and other indigenous peoples of the Amazon Basin. The name derives from the Quechua words chulla meaning one or odd and chaki meaning foot, referring to

creatures.name: Chulyen Crow Nuu Chah Nulth
creatures.excerpt: The name Chulyen belongs to the Dena'ina, an Athabaskan people of south-central Alaska, where Chulyen is the raven trickster and transformer of the Kenai Peninsula, not a Nuu-chah-nulth figure. Nuu-chah-nulth tradition gives the raven's role to its own culture hero, while the Dena'ina raven cycle tells how Chulyen stol

creatures.name: Chupacabra
creatures.excerpt: First reported in Puerto Rico, 1995, preceded by the 1975 'vampiro de Moca'. The name — 'chupa' (sucks) + 'cabra' (goat) = 'Goat-Sucker' — coined by Silverio Pérez. creatures.name: Chupacabras Boricua
creatures.excerpt: Chupacabras Boricua is the Puerto Rican regional variant of the legendary Chupacabra cryptid, distinguished by its specific origin in the island's folklore and unique description compared to mainland versions. The name Boricua refers to the Taino name for Puerto Rico, Boriken, making this the original version of the Ch

creatures.name: Chupacora
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Chupacora' is an unattested variant of the chupacabra, a livestock-killing cryptid first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995 and since reported across Latin America. No distinct Guatemalan 'Chupacora' with its own characteristics is documented.

creatures.name: Chura-Batyr
creatures.excerpt: Chura-Batyr is the epic hero of the Tatar people, rooted in the historical figure Chura Narykov of the sixteenth-century Kazan Khanate. Tales present him as a defender of the Tatar lands, a warrior of great strength and loyalty whose downfall through betrayal became a byword for resistance and lament in Tatar oral trad

creatures.name: Churail
creatures.excerpt: The churail (also churel or chudail) is a feared female revenant of South Asian folklore — Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Nepal — the spirit of a woman who died in childbirth or an unnatural death. She haunts peepul trees, crossroads, cremation grounds and wells, appearing as a beautiful young woman in white whose fee

creatures.name: Churel
creatures.excerpt: South Asian female ghost/witch ('Churel,' 'Chudail,' 'Churail' - also called 'Pichal Peri' = backward feet). Origins: woman who died in pregnancy, childbirth, or wronged by men. Most common: died during childbirth (considered 'impure' death). OR died as bride with husband/family mistreating her - Returns for vengeance.

creatures.name: Chut
creatures.excerpt: Chut is a spectral entity from Scottish Highland folklore, particularly associated with the Orkney and Shetland Islands as well as parts of the northern Scottish mainland. This mysterious being is classified among the many nature spirits and apparitions that populate the rich Celtic and Norse-influenced folklore of nor

creatures.name: Chyskhaan
creatures.excerpt: Chyskhaan is the Lord of Cold in Sakha (Yakut) belief, a spirit who rules the fierce frosts of Siberia and dwells in an ice palace said to stand near Oymyakon, one of the coldest inhabited places on earth. When his breath thickens and his horns gather frost, the deepest cold of winter is said to be drawing near.

creatures.name: Ciguapa
creatures.excerpt: The Ciguapa is a nocturnal mythical creature from Dominican folklore, described as a wild woman who inhabits the high mountain regions of the island. Her most distinctive feature is that her feet are turned backward, making it nearly impossible for hunters or trackers to follow her footprints. She is deeply tied to the

creatures.name: Ciguapa
creatures.excerpt: The Ciguapa is a nocturnal wild woman of Dominican mountain folklore whose backward-turned feet baffle trackers. The earliest written account is Francisco Javier Angulo Guridi's 1866 story 'La Ciguapa.' Scholars debate a possible Taíno origin against European parallels such as mermaids and the churel.

creatures.name: Cikavac
creatures.excerpt: The Cikavac is a mythical winged creature from Serbian folklore, born from an egg laid by a black hen that must be carried under a woman's armpit for forty days. During this gestation period, the woman must not confess, cut her nails, wash her face, or pray, adhering to strict taboos that imbue the egg with magical pro

creatures.name: Cipactli
creatures.excerpt: Cipactli is a primeval sea monster from Aztec mythology, often described as a gigantic crocodilian-fish-toad hybrid that existed before the creation of the world. In Aztec cosmology, the gods Tezcatlipoca and Quetzalcoatl created the earth from Cipactli's body after Tezcatlipoca sacrificed his foot using the monster as

creatures.name: Cipitío
creatures.excerpt: Cipitío is a beloved legendary character from Salvadoran folklore, the illegitimate son of La Siguanaba and Lucero de la Mañana (Lucifer). Cursed by the god Teotl as a result of his mother's infidelity, he was condemned to remain a child forever, with his feet set backward as a reminder of the twisted affair of his par

creatures.name: Coblynau
creatures.excerpt: The Coblynau are mythical gnome-like creatures from Welsh folklore that haunt mines and quarries throughout Wales and areas of Welsh settlement in America. The name is related to the English word 'goblin' and may derive from the German 'kobold' via French. First documented extensively by Wirt Sikes in his 1880 book 'Br

creatures.name: Coca
creatures.excerpt: The Coca is a legendary female dragon from Portuguese and Galician folklore, feared for lurking in dark places to snatch unwary children. Unlike many male dragons in European mythology, the Coca is distinctly female and plays a central role in traditional Corpus Christi celebrations in northern Portugal, particularly i

creatures.name: Cogaz
creatures.excerpt: Cogaz is the eldest son of Kaang (Cagn), the supreme creator god in San (Bushman) mythology of southern Africa. As a great chief alongside his father and Qwanciqutshaa, Cogaz appears in numerous San creation myths and tales

creatures.name: Coleando
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a monster of Chilean folklore. 'Coleando' is the Spanish gerund for swishing or wriggling a tail (as in the idiom 'vivito y coleando'), not the name of a being, and no source documents a 'Coleando' water monster. The genuine Chilean aquatic figures are El Cuero, the Nguruvilu and the Camah

creatures.name: Comorian Dragon
creatures.excerpt: Comorian Dragon (Comorian). is a dragon. A winged serpentine dragon from Comorian folklore, associated with volcanic rock formations and storms in the Indian Ocean archipelago. Source: Atlas Obscura; Comorian oral traditions

creatures.name: Comorian Jinn (Mashetani)
aliases: Jinn of the Isles of the Moon
creatures.excerpt: In the Comoros Islands, belief in jinn (locally called mashetani) is deeply ingrained in the culture, representing a syncretic blend of Islamic theology with indigenous African and Malagasy spirit beliefs. Comorian jinn are invisible spirits created from smokeless fire who inhabit a parallel world to humans. They are b

creatures.name: Conjure Doctor
creatures.excerpt: The Conjure Doctor (also known as a root doctor, hoodoo doctor, or two-headed doctor) is a powerful figure in African American folk belief — a practitioner of conjure, hoodoo, and rootwork who possesses supernatural knowledge and the ability to influence events through magical means. Conjure Doctors serve as community

creatures.name: Coqui (Sacred Frog Spirit of Puerto Rico)
creatures.excerpt: The Coqui is a tiny tree frog (Eleutherodactylus coqui) native to Puerto Rico that has transcended biology to become a sacred cultural and mythological symbol. In Taino mythology, the Coqui distinctive two-note nocturnal call Co-kee! has a divine origin. According to legend, a beautiful Taino goddess fell in love with

creatures.name: Corn Girl
creatures.excerpt: Corn Girl is a Navajo Holy Person associated with the sacred mountain Tsoodził (Mount Taylor), the southern boundary mountain of the Navajo world set with turquoise and female rain. PAN-Slavic: Ukrainian 'zhar-ptytsia,' Czech 'Pták Ohnivák,' Polish 'Żar-ptak,' Slovenian 'Rajska/zlata-ptica.' Etymology: 'zhar' = fire/glow. Feathers Shine Continuously even when plucked - like embers, like the sun. Symbol of Hope and unatt

creatures.name: First Angry (Áłtsé Hashké)
creatures.excerpt: First Angry (Áłtsé Hashké) is a genuine Coyote Holy Person of Diné creation accounts. In the Diné Bahane' he emerged with the first beings, declared that he existed before they were formed, and is named as the one who brought witchcraft into the world, so that his power must be guarded against in Navajo ritual.

creatures.name: First Angry Coyote
creatures.excerpt: Átsé hashké, 'First Angry,' is the Navajo personification of anger and witchcraft, called into being in the primordial world. In the Origin Myths of the Navaho he stole the children of Water Buffalo by stretching a rainbow across the waters, an act that introduced evil and witchcraft into the world and made him the sou

creatures.name: First Man (Áłtsé Hastiin)
creatures.excerpt: First Man (Áłtsé Hastiin) is a primordial figure in Navajo creation mythology. In the First World, he was formed from the breath of Black Cloud and White Cloud, carrying white corn and crystal. He made a fire with crystal and joined with First Woman after seeing her light from across the darkness, establishing the patt

creatures.name: First Woman (Áłtsé Asdzą́ą́)
creatures.excerpt: First Woman (Áłtsé Asdzą́ą́) is a primordial figure in Navajo creation mythology. She was formed from Blue Cloud and Yellow Cloud in the West, carrying yellow corn, white shell, turquoise, and yucca. She made a fire with turquoise and joined with First Man. She caused a great conflict by boasting that women could live

creatures.name: Fisaga
creatures.excerpt: Fisaga is a gentle wind spirit from Samoan mythology, personifying the light and pleasant breeze associated with fine weather. In the Samoan language, fisaga refers specifically to a gentle, pleasant wind that brings good conditions. The most famous legend involving Fisaga comes from the tale of Ti'iti'i who imprisoned

creatures.name: Fish Hawk Tlingit
creatures.excerpt: In the Tlingit Raven cycle, Fish Hawk (the osprey) appears in a folk-etymological tale of how the osprey gained its white head. Raven, in the shape of a woman, marries a chief, and supernatural power from a shaman turns Fish Hawk's head white; the episode also frames Raven's theft of the sun. The bird's keen sight and

creatures.name: Fjeldvīg
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Fjeldvig is a Norwegian place-name and surname, not a Danish folklore being, and the description grafts generic bjergfolk (hill-folk) lore onto the name. Genuine Danish mound-folk belong to the bjergfolk complex related to the nisse and trold; no being called Fjeldvig

creatures.name: Fjellvette
creatures.excerpt: Fjellvette (mountain wight) is a nature spirit specific to the mountains of Vestlandet. The fjellvette is a type of vette (nature spirit) that guards specific peaks, mountain passes, high pastures, and rocky crags. creatures.name: Fjörulalli
creatures.excerpt: Fjörulalli (Beach Walker) is a smaller variant of the skeljaskrímsli in Icelandic folklore, about the size of a medium dog to a calf. Fjörulalli is covered with shells or lava fragments and has a small rounded head. It is generally considered harmless to humans but has a nasty habit of tearing the udders off sheep it e

creatures.name: Fjøsnisse
creatures.excerpt: Fjøsnisse (barn nisse) is a specialized type of Norwegian nisse that lives specifically in the cowshed (fjøs) and cares for the cattle. While the general nisse protects the entire farm, the fjøsnisse is devoted exclusively to the welfare of the cows, goats, and other barn animals. In Norwegian folk tradition, a well-ke

creatures.name: Fladså Trolden
creatures.excerpt: Fladså Trolden (the Fladså Troll) is a giant troll from local folklore in Sydsjælland who once decided to bury the town of Næstved in sand out of spite. He filled a huge sack with sand from the Øresund beach and began carrying it inland toward Næstved. On the way, he stopped at Mogenstrup Kro (Mogenstrup Inn) for a dri

creatures.name: Flat Pipe
creatures.excerpt: The Flat Pipe is the most sacred ceremonial object of the Arapaho people, central to their creation story and spiritual life. In the beginning, a man carrying a Flat Pipe walked on the primordial waters—the pipe itself was integral to creation. The Flat Pipe was used by the Flat Pipe Creator to summon trees and animals

creatures.name: Flat Pipe Creator
creatures.excerpt: The Flat Pipe Creator is the supreme being in Arapaho creation mythology. In the beginning there was only water covering everything. A man carrying a Flat Pipe walked on the water for six days, weeping and fasting, searching for a safe place to rest his pipe. On the seventh day he summoned seven cottonwood trees and al

creatures.name: Floghamen
creatures.excerpt: Floghamen (the flying shape) is a shape-shifting spirit from Setesdal folklore in Sørlandet. The floghamen is the spirit-form of a witch or sorcerer that flies through the air while the person's body sleeps. The term comes from flog (flight/flying) and ham (shape/form). In Setesdal tradition, certain people could send

creatures.name: Flower-people (Blomsterfolk)
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in Danish tradition as a named being. Danish folklore has generic nature spirits (ellefolk, huldrefolk) and flower-associated beliefs (e.g., elder tree mother), but 'Blomsterfolk' as tiny flower-born guardians appears to be a modern literary invention or conflation. creatures.name: Flying African
creatures.excerpt: The myth of the Flying Africans tells how enslaved Igbo captives, landing at Ebos Landing on St. Simons Island in Georgia in 1803, turned and walked back across the water to fly home to Africa rather than live in bondage. creatures.name: Flying Africans
creatures.excerpt: The Flying Africans are a central figure in African American legend, born from the historical tragedy of Igbo Landing in 1803. creatures.name: Flying Dutchman
creatures.excerpt: Flying Dutchman (Unknown). is a ghost. The Flying Dutchman is a legendary ghost ship condemned to sail the oceans forever, never able to make port. Sightings of the phantom vessel are considered an omen of doom by sailors.. Source: The Phantom Ship (Marryat, 1839); Naval folklore

creatures.name: Flying Head
creatures.excerpt: The Flying Head is a terrifying cannibalistic spirit from Iroquois and Wyandot mythology. It appears as a giant disembodied head as tall as a man, covered in thick black hair with bat-like wings and long sharp claws. It preys on humans, especially widows and orphans, visiting their homes at night and beating its wings

creatures.name: Flying Troll
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in Swedish folklore. Trolls in Nordic tradition are earth-bound (mountain, forest, sea); snip flight is not a traditional attribute. The 'flying troll' appears in the literary fairy tale 'Dag and Daga and the Flying Troll of Sky Mountain' but this is a modern fairy-tale construction, not oral

creatures.name: Fog Woman
creatures.excerpt: Fog Woman is a Tlingit supernatural being who, in Swanton's 'Raven and Fog Woman' (myth #108), was Raven's wife. Washing her hands in a basket, she summoned the first salmon into the world; when Raven grew jealous and cruel, she and the salmon departed to the sea. creatures.name: Folletto
creatures.excerpt: The folletto is a mischievous house-sprite of Italian folklore, a generic term covering regional imps such as the salvanello (Veneto), monacello (Calabria) and mazapégul (Romagna). creatures.name: Forest Person
creatures.excerpt: The Forest Person, known in Tlingit as Kooshdaa kaa or Kushtaka (land otter man), is a shape-shifting spirit from Pacific Northwest indigenous mythology, particularly among the Tlingit people whose territory extends from southeastern Alaska into Canada. creatures.name: Forest Person
creatures.excerpt: The Forest Person of Pacific Northwest tradition is Kushtaka (Kooshdaa kaa), the 'land otter man' of the Tlingit and neighboring peoples whose range extends from southeast Alaska into Canada. A shapeshifter straddling human and animal, it is tied to drowning: Kushtaka may rescue or transform the souls of the drowned. S

creatures.name: Forest Sprite
creatures.excerpt: Forest Sprite (Icelandic). is a spirit. A forest spirit who uses a magical flute to cast an enchanted sleep upon travelers. Source: Icelandic folklore

creatures.name: Fosen-Sjøtrollet
creatures.excerpt: Fosen-Sjøtrollet (the Fosen Sea Troll) is a sea troll said to inhabit the waters off the Fosen peninsula in Trøndelag. Unlike the mountain trolls of inland Norway, this sjøtroll (sea troll) lives in the ocean and comes ashore only at night to raid farms. creatures.name: Fossegrim
creatures.excerpt: Norwegian water spirit - 'Fossegrim' = 'waterfall lord/grim' (from 'fosse' waterfall + 'grim' supernatural/masked). Also: Swedish 'Strömkarlen' (stream-carol player). Supernatural Musician - plays fiddle (Hardanger fiddle) with such mastery that trees dance and waterfalls stop to listen. Plays the sounds of forest, win

creatures.name: Fox Ancestor-Spirit of Aztec
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No sacred fox ancestor-spirit occurs in Aztec religion; the description conflates the fox with coyote figures such as Huehuecoyotl, the aged coyote trickster god, and invents messenger and calendar associations. The fox is not a significant figure in recorded Mexica my

creatures.name: Fox Ancestor-Spirit of Lakota
creatures.excerpt: In Lakota tradition the fox (sungila) is a notable animal in medicine and storytelling, and the Kit Fox Society (sungila okolakiciye) was a warrior order that policed the home camp and supplied food. The fox appears in tales as a clever figure valued for sharp wits and survival in dangerous country.

creatures.name: Fox Ancestor-Spirit of Passamaquoddy
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No named Passamaquoddy fox ancestor-spirit or 'protective fox tracks' appears in Wabanaki collections; the description is generic woodland moralizing. The central culture hero of Passamaquoddy tradition is Gluskabe, and no developed fox spirit figure is documented.

creatures.name: Fox Animal-Spirit of Ashanti
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox figure appears in Akan anansesem (spider-story) tradition, whose trickster is Ananse, and the hunting-omen claims are invented. The fox does not hold a developed role in recorded Ashanti animal tales.

creatures.name: Fox Animal-Spirit of Baloch
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No named Baloch fox spirit or fox trickster tale is recorded; the description is generic desert-animal moralizing. Genuine Baloch folklore preserves named tales and characters, but no attested fox tradition supports this entry.

creatures.name: Fox Animal-Spirit of Kikuyu
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox spirit or omen belief is recorded in Kikuyu oral collections, and the claimed meaning for the fox in Ngai's cosmos is invented. Kikuyu animal tales center on other creatures; no developed fox figure is documented.

creatures.name: Fox Deity (Ashanti)
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested. No fox deity appears in documented Ashanti (Akan) cosmology or folklore; the Ashanti trickster is Anansi the spider, and the fox plays no recorded role in Akan religion. creatures.name: Fox Deity of Cree
creatures.excerpt: In Cree oral tradition the fox appears as a shrewd, adaptable figure of the northern forests and plains, admired by hunters for thriving in harsh winters. Beyond general respect for the animal's cleverness, no named Cree fox deity is documented; the fox's role is that of a wise animal in tales rather than a formal spir

creatures.name: Fox Deity of Maya
creatures.excerpt: The fox (chomak in Yucatec Maya) appears in Maya folk tales as a clever, cunning figure who outwits larger animals, and some accounts link the fox to night and trickster themes. Beyond general folk-tale use, no formal Maya fox deity is recorded in the codices or Popol Vuh.

creatures.name: Fox Deity of Ojibwe
creatures.excerpt: In Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) tradition of the Great Lakes, the fox is a clan animal (doodem) linked to cleverness and diplomacy and appears in tales as a shrewd trickster. The fox is a respected minor spirit figure in medicine practice, not a formal deity; no dedicated fox deity is documented.

creatures.name: Fox Deity of Ojibwe
creatures.excerpt: In Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) tradition, the fox is one of the animal clan figures (doodem), representing cleverness and diplomacy, and appears in storytelling as a shrewd helper or trickster. Animal powers are respected in Anishinaabe medicine practice, and the fox is a real but minor spirit figure rather than a named deity

creatures.name: Fox Ghost of Inuit
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a ghost of Inuit folklore. Inuit tradition knows the fox-woman, a fox who takes human form and marries a hunter — a shape-shifter tale, not a ghost story. No Inuit fox-ghost is documented; the fox's roles are those of trickster and spirit-wife, not revenant.

creatures.name: Fox Giant of Apache
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The Apache fire-stealing culture hero is Coyote, not a fox; the 'Fox Giant' is an invented conflation, and no such being appears in recorded Apache creation stories.

creatures.name: Fox Giant of Aztec
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox giant exists in Aztec (Mexica) myth; the text itself conflates the fox with the tlacuache (opossum) and invents Tezcatlipoca associations and underworld-guide roles. These claims trace to AI content farms, not to Mesoamerican sources.

creatures.name: Fox Giant of Kazakh
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested: while the fox (tülki) is a familiar trickster in Kazakh tales, such as those of Aldar Köse and in the Korkut-ata tradition, no 'giant fox' being is recorded in Kazakh folklore. creatures.name: Fox Guardian (Lakota)
creatures.excerpt: In Lakota tradition the fox (šunğíla) is a genuine medicine animal: it is said to reveal the locations of healing herbs to medicine people and to teach swift escape and courage under fire. creatures.name: Fox Guardian of Inuit
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a guardian of Inuit folklore. The documented Inuit fox figures are the fox-woman of the Labrador legend, who becomes a hunter's wife, and the trickster fox of northern tales; neither acts as a guardian spirit. No Inuit fox-guardian is recorded in the available sources.

creatures.name: Fox Guardian of Ute
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a guardian of Ute folklore. The fox appears in some Ute tales as a clever figure, but no Ute fox-guardian or fox-spirit is documented in the sources. Ute spirit-helpers center on shamans and animal powers such as the bear and the eagle, not a guardian fox.

creatures.name: Fox Nature-Spirit (Tupi)
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a named Tupi entity. Tupi-Guarani mythology includes fox tricksters (e.g., Aguara in Guarani) but no specific 'Fox Nature-Spirit' with the described crystalline, celestial attributes. The elaborate description appears to be a modern literary invention.

creatures.name: Fox Nature-Spirit (Tupi)
creatures.excerpt: Not attested in USA or Tupi folklore. The fox trickster Aguara belongs to the Guarani and Chané peoples of Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil, not the Tupi, and not to North America. creatures.name: Fox Nature-Spirit of Creek
creatures.excerpt: No fox nature-spirit is attested in Creek tradition. The fox appears in the Creek story of 'The Fox and the Fry Bread' as a clever character, but it carries no spirit role. Creek spiritual beings are tied to fire, the Green Corn Ceremony and beings such as the tie-snakes; a fox nature-spirit is not documented.

creatures.name: Fox Nature-Spirit of Haida
creatures.excerpt: No genuine fox nature-spirit is documented in Haida tradition; this entry is an unverifiable composite. Haida cosmology centers on Raven as trickster and creator, the Bear Mother, the supernatural killer-whale beings Sgaana, and the culture hero Nanasimget, none of which includes a fox spirit.

creatures.name: Fox Spirit (Zulu)
creatures.excerpt: In the rich oral traditions of the Zulu people, this fox spirit is an embodiment of the duality of nature—simultaneously a playful trickster and a solemn guardian of the ancestral lands. creatures.name: Fox Spirit of Ashanti
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox spirit acts as messenger of Asase Yaa or keeper of sacred groves in Akan belief; those claims are invented. The Akan spirit world centers on figures such as Asase Yaa, Nyame, and the trickster Ananse, with no attested fox spirit.

creatures.name: Fox Spirit of Creek
creatures.excerpt: No fox messenger spirit is attested in Creek (Muscogee) tradition. Documented Muscogee supernatural beings include Chufi, the Rabbit trickster; Kolowa, a hairy man-eating ogre; the underwater Tie-snakes; and Isti Papa, the 'man-eater' giant. The entry invents a messenger role with no support in ethnography.

creatures.name: Fox Spirit of Maya
creatures.excerpt: The Maya fox (chomak/ch'amak) is a folk-tale figure of cunning and transformation, and contemporary Maya communities tell stories of the clever fox. creatures.name: Fox Spirit of Muisca
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox messenger or divination figure appears in recorded Muisca mythology; the claimed role as messenger of Sue and Chia and the links to Lake Guatavita and El Dorado are invented. Muisca tradition preserves no named fox spirit.

creatures.name: Fox Spirit of Zapotec
creatures.excerpt: The fox is a significant animal in Oaxacan Zapotec belief, where naguales and soul-companions may take animal form, and where caves and the underworld (Lyobaa) belong to the spirit world. creatures.name: Fox Trickster (Mixtec)
creatures.excerpt: The fox figures in Mixtec and wider Mesoamerican oral tradition as a clever, deceptive animal, though the specific 'Mixtec fox trickster' of this entry is a synthesis. creatures.name: Fox Trickster of Creek
creatures.excerpt: The Fox Trickster of the Creek (Muskogee) nation is a revered figure in Southeastern Native American folklore, known for his clever schemes and transformative encounters with humans. creatures.name: Fox Trickster of Lakota
creatures.excerpt: The Fox Trickster of the Lakota people is a venerated spirit being that roams the hills and prairies of the Great Plains, serving as both a teacher and a cautionary figure. creatures.name: Fox Trickster of Zapotec

creatures.name: Frog (Chʼał)
creatures.excerpt: Frog (Chʼał) is a water spirit in Navajo mythology associated with healing, rain, and the power of speech. creatures.name: Frog Guardian (Bhutanese)
creatures.excerpt: The Frog Guardian of Bhutanese tradition is a protective nature spirit associated with the kingdom's pristine valleys and mountain streams. creatures.name: Frost Giant (Tupi)
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a figure of Tupi tradition. Tupi-Guarani cosmology of tropical Brazil records beings such as Tupã, Anhangá and the Curupira, but no source mentions a frost giant or attributes unseasonable cold to one; frost is rare in the lowlands and is not personified in Tupi mythology. creatures.name: Frost Giant Iceland
creatures.excerpt: Frost Giant Iceland (Unknown). is a giant. A frost giant from Icelandic folklore is a being of ice who dwells in frozen wastelands.. Source: Norse/Icelandic folklore — frost giant documented in Icelandic oral tradition.

creatures.name: Fuath
creatures.excerpt: The Fuath is a class of malevolent water spirits from Scottish Highland folklore, whose name literally translates to 'hate' or 'hatred' in Gaelic. creatures.name: Funkwe (Giant Water Snake)
creatures.excerpt: The Funkwe is a giant hybrid water snake of Lamba tradition in Zambia, guardian of the lakes Nakamwale, Kashiba and Namulolobwe and of their mistress the Chitapo, a female lake spirit sometimes shown as a mermaid or as a diamond the serpent holds in its mouth. creatures.name: Fureytha
creatures.excerpt: Fureytha are shimmering reef spirits in Maldivian folklore — luminous, protective water beings inhabiting coral reefs and lagoons. creatures.name: Futakuchi-Onna Variant

creatures.name: Fylgja

creatures.name: Fylgje

creatures.excerpt: Fänggen (singular: Fängge) are gigantic female wood sprites or wild women from Alpine German folklore, particularly found in Bavarian and Tyrolean traditions. creatures.name: Fée

creatures.name: Ga-Gorib
creatures.excerpt: Ga-Gorib is a fearsome monster from Khoikhoi mythology who sat at the edge of a deep hole, challenging passersby to throw a stone at his forehead. creatures.name: Gaayhllga Jaad Flood Tide Woman Haida
creatures.excerpt: Gaayhllga Jaad, the Flood Tide Woman, belongs to the Haida tradition of a great deluge. creatures.name: Gadyucha
creatures.excerpt: The Gadyucha is a death-omen spirit from Turkmen folklore, taking the form of a gigantic owl that foretells mortality and misfortune. creatures.name: Gahe (Mountain Spirits)
creatures.excerpt: The Gahe (Gaan in Western Apache) are the Mountain Spirits, powerful supernatural beings in Apache tradition who live inside sacred mountains. creatures.name: Galamani
creatures.excerpt: Galamani is the sacred serpent of the Fulani epic of Silamaka and Pullori, the legendary heroes of the Macina region of Mali. creatures.name: Galone
creatures.excerpt: Galone, the Burmese garuda, is a golden bird-king of Myanmar's Buddhist-influenced cosmology who eternally wars with the nāga serpents. creatures.name: Galuxwadzuwus (Crooked-Beak)
creatures.excerpt: Galuxwadzuwus, the Crooked-Beak of Heaven, is a man-eating bird of the Kwakwaka'wakw winter ceremonial, one of the cannibal attendants of the great devourer Baxbaxwalanuksiwe at the North End of the World. Dancers who wear his long, downward-curving beak mask in the Hamatsa ceremony tame his uncontrolled hunger through

creatures.name: Gamlingene oppi Steinberget
creatures.excerpt: Gamlingene oppi Steinberget (the Old Men in Steinberget) is a Trøndelag legend about a group of ancient spirits who live inside Steinberget (Stone Mountain), a prominent rock formation in Trøndelag.
