creatures.name: Werewolf
creatures.excerpt: The English werewolf (Old English werwulf, 'man-wolf') appears in medieval chronicles as a human cursed or voluntarily transforming into a wolf. Gervase of Tilbury (c. 1210) wrote that in England men often changed into wolves during lunar cycles.

creatures.name: Wewe Gombel

creatures.name: Whale Deity of Aztec

creatures.name: Whale Deity of Cherokee

creatures.name: Whale Kwakwaka Wakw

creatures.name: Whiro

creatures.name: Whowie

creatures.name: Wildcat Trickster of Dogon

creatures.name: Wildcat Trickster of Quechua

creatures.name: Wildcat Trickster of Tlingit

creatures.name: Wildcat Water-Spirit of Kikuyu

creatures.name: Witch

creatures.name: Wolf Ancestor-Spirit of Choctaw

creatures.name: Wolf Water-Spirit of Blackfoot
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a wolf water-spirit in Blackfoot folklore. Blackfoot wolves are land animals and helpers, as in the Wolf Man tale, while water is the domain of other beings; no wolf is associated with lakes, rivers, or oceans in the recorded Blackfoot corpus. The water-spirit archetype is a template artif

creatures.name: Wolf Water-Spirit of Blackfoot
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a wolf water-spirit in Blackfoot folklore. Blackfoot wolves are land animals and helpers, as in the Wolf Man tale, while water is the domain of other beings; no wolf is associated with lakes, rivers, or oceans in the recorded Blackfoot corpus. The water-spirit archetype is a template artif

creatures.name: Wolf Water-Spirit of Inuit
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a wolf water-spirit in Inuit folklore. The attested wolf beings are land dwellers: Amarok, a gigantic lone wolf-spirit that hunts hunters abroad at night, and Amaguq, a wolf trickster. Waters are instead the domain of figures such as Sedna of the sea; no wolf spirit is tied to rivers.

creatures.name: Woman of the Sea
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as 'Woman of the Sea' in Haida or generic Canadian folklore. Coastal Northwest Coast traditions do include sea-connected women, such as the Haida Ocean Woman of recent retellings and Property Woman, who grants wealth, but no named 'Woman of the Sea' spirit appears in the ethnographic record.

creatures.name: Wooden Person
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a 'Wooden Person' spirit in Haida folklore. In related Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, Raven fashions the first man and woman from wood and clay, and Haida Raven likewise fashions people; these are episodes within Raven's creation work, not a distinct spirit. The record appears to distill that mo

creatures.name: Wuriupranili
creatures.excerpt: Wuriupranili is the sun woman in Aboriginal Australian mythology, particularly among the peoples of northern Australia. In the Dreamtime, Wuriupranili traveled across the sky each day carrying a burning torch that brought light and warmth to the world. Her torch was so bright that it illuminated everything below. Accor

creatures.name: Xan
creatures.excerpt: Xan (or Khana) is an Azerbaijani ghost — the restless spirit of a murdered person or wronged lover. It haunts the scene of death, family home, or grave until justice is served or bones are properly buried. Nighttime apparitions and haunting are its behaviors. The belief reflects traditional Azerbaijani emphasis on prop

creatures.name: Xana
creatures.excerpt: Xanas are water spirits of Asturian folklore, beautiful young women who dwell in springs, rivers, and caves (cuevas de xanas), often combing their long hair by the water and offering gifts or trials to passersby. Documented by Ramón Menéndez Pidal, the tradition is connected to pre-Roman Celtic belief and the cult of D

creatures.name: Xanaax Atwaayaa Tlingit
creatures.excerpt: In the Tlingit story of the Salmon Box (Kudatan Kahidi), Xanaax.atwaayaa is a being who holds a staff tipped with a supernatural octopus tentacle. Raven, disguised, trades him a magic arrow in the form of a magpie and gains the staff, whose power he uses to draw the salmon close to shore and to control their coming.

creatures.name: Xbalanque (Jaguar Sun)
creatures.excerpt: Xbalanque, 'Jaguar Sun,' is one of the Maya Hero Twins of the Popol Vuh. With his brother Hunahpu he descended into Xibalba, survived its lethal Houses, and defeated the Lords of Death through trickery, rising from the underworld to become the sun and the moon. He is often depicted with jaguar pelt markings, linking hi

creatures.name: Xe Las Coast Salish
creatures.excerpt: Xelas (Xe Las) is the Transformer of Coast Salish oral tradition who walked the world setting it right in the myth age. He and his helpers changed the flawed beings of that time into the animals and landmarks of today, and Coast Salish peoples trace the present shape of mountains, rivers, and creatures to his journeys.

creatures.name: Xe Las The Changer Coast Salish
creatures.excerpt: Xelas is the great Transformer of Coast Salish tradition, a benevolent culture hero who traveled the Pacific Northwest reshaping the world. He turned the changeling beings of the myth age into their present forms and set the natural order, remembered as Xáays among the Squamish and Xa:ls in Halkomelem.

creatures.name: Xhindet
creatures.excerpt: Xhindet are the jinn-like trickster spirits of Albanian folklore, beings of illusion and stealth that haunt mountain passes and old ruins. Mischievous and deceptive rather than overtly malevolent, they can be countered with iron or clever riddles. Their stories remind listeners that the world holds unseen forces which

creatures.name: Xibalba
creatures.excerpt: Xibalba, 'place of fright,' is the Maya underworld of the Popol Vuh, ruled by the Lords of Death. Reached through caves, cenotes, or by a river of scorpions, blood, and pus, it is a realm of trial filled with the Houses of Darkness, Knives, Cold, Jaguars, Fire, and Bats. The Hero Twins' descent and escape reveal it as

creatures.name: Xiezhi
creatures.excerpt: Xiezhi (獬豸) is the single-horned justice beast of Chinese tradition, usually pictured as a goat-, ox-, or lion-like animal with black fur. In accounts, when disputes were brought before it, it gored the guilty and spared the innocent, making it an emblem of impartial judgment. Its image decorated the robes of imperial

creatures.name: Xjabil
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a named dwarf or guardian spirit of Guatemalan folklore. No source records a Maya mountain-being called 'Xjabil' who guards peaks or restores lost objects. The closest real figures are the Yucatec Maya Xtabay, a forest temptress spirit, and the duende and alux dwarf-helper traditions of Me

creatures.name: Xnifs
creatures.excerpt: Xnifs are mischievous imps of Maltese folklore said to live in ruins and abandoned places, causing minor household troubles and pilfering food. They belong to the broader class of Mediterranean household and ruin-dwelling goblins. The belief is recorded in Maltese oral tradition, though documentation is sparse and larg

creatures.name: Xolotl
creatures.excerpt: Xolotl is the Aztec god of fire, lightning, twins, monsters, death, and the evening star, twin of Quetzalcoatl. Dog-headed, he guides the souls of the dead through the underworld as a psychopomp and escorts the sun to its nightly doom. Fleeing the gods who sought to sacrifice him, he hid as the axolotl salamander, whic

creatures.name: Xtabai
creatures.excerpt: Xtabai (also spelled Xtabay) is a demonic femme fatale from Yucatec Maya folklore who lures men to their deaths with her incredible beauty. She appears as a stunning woman with long black hair falling to her ankles, wearing a white dress, and combs her hair with the spines of a Tzacam cactus while waiting behind a ceib

creatures.name: Xác
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a named figure of Vietnamese folklore: 'Xác' is the Vietnamese word for corpse. The recorded traits of a reanimated body fit the attested beliefs of ma da, the restless ghost of a corpse, and quỷ nhập tràng, a wandering ghost that seizes a fresh corpse and delays the funeral.

creatures.name: Yacumama
creatures.excerpt: Yacumama (Quechua: 'mother of water') is an enormous Amazonian serpent spirit, mother of all aquatic life, dwelling in rivers and lakes. She sucks in any living thing within 100 paces; Indigenous boatmen blow conch horns to reveal her presence. Documented across the upper Amazon (Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil).

creatures.name: Yacuruna
creatures.excerpt: Yacuruna (Quechua: 'water people') are hairy, deformed-footed aquatic beings who inhabit upside-down underwater cities in Amazonian rivers. They abduct humans (especially menstruating women) by transforming into pink river dolphins or handsome men, using aphrodisiacs. Victims gradually transform into Yacuruna. Shamans

creatures.name: Yaguarón
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a distinct water spirit. 'Yaguarón' is a Paraguayan city named from Guarani 'jaguar-ú' (big dog/jaguar). Guarani myth mentions a primordial giant jaguar/dog, but no named water spirit 'Yaguarón' exists. The record conflates toponymy with mythology.

creatures.name: Yagwanggwi
creatures.excerpt: Yagwanggwi (야광귀, 'night-light ghost') is a Korean folk spirit said to appear on the night of lunar New Year's Eve (seotdal geumeum), stealing people's shoes or sandals while they sleep. Documented by the National Folk Museum of Korea, the tradition holds that hanging a sieve or mesh by the door keeps the ghost away, be

creatures.name: Yaksha
creatures.excerpt: Yakshas are nature spirits in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain myth — guardians of treasure, fertility, wilderness. Attendants of Kubera, inhabit forests, sacred trees, mountains, water. Can be benevolent (granting boons) or malevolent (causing illness). Male yakshas; females yakshinis. Prominent in early Buddhist art (Sanchi, Bh

creatures.name: Yakshini
creatures.excerpt: Yakshinis are female nature spirits in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain myth — attendants of Kubera, linked to trees (ashoka, sal), water, fertility. Can be benevolent (granting prosperity, children) or malevolent (causing illness, madness). Thirty-six with mantras in Uddamareshvara Tantra. Key in early Buddhist art as Salabhanji

creatures.name: Yali
creatures.excerpt: Yali is a Tamil mythological composite creature — lion body, elephant trunk, horse mane, sometimes goat horns. Prominent in South Indian temple architecture (pillars, stairways) as guardian of thresholds, protector of sacred spaces. Not a 'demonic entity' but a protective guardian. Seen in Chola, Vijayanagara, Nayaka t

creatures.name: Yam-Nahar
creatures.excerpt: Yam-Nahar (literally 'Sea-River') is the god of the sea and rivers in ancient Syrian (Ugaritic) mythology, the personification of the destructive power of the waters. Known as Prince Yam and Judge Nahar, he is son of the supreme god El and the beloved of his father. Yam is depicted as a serpentine deity, often identifi

creatures.name: Yamawaro
creatures.excerpt: Yamawaro (山童) is a kappa-like mountain yōkai of western Japan, especially Kyūshū and the Chūgoku region, appearing as a small, hairy, childlike figure with a round head and sometimes a water dish on its crown. It is said to descend to rivers in spring and become a river kappa. It helps woodcutters haul logs when given

creatures.name: Yamm
keywords: yamm, canaanite sea god, phoenician mythology, baal cycle, chaoskampf, leviathan precursor
creatures.excerpt: Yamm is the Canaanite-Phoenician god of the sea, rivers, and primordial chaos. As the deity representing the untamed and destructive power of the Mediterranean, Yamm was especially significant to the maritime Phoenicians of Lebanon's coastal cities. Depicted as consistently tyrannical and angry, he was the brother of M

creatures.name: Yanauluha (Culture Hero)
creatures.excerpt: Yanauluha is a benevolent culture hero in Zuni mythology who brought the arts of medicine and agriculture to the people. After the emergence into the daylight world, he appeared carrying seeds, digging sticks, and sacred objects. He taught which plants were edible and medicinal, how to plant corn and other crops, and h

creatures.name: Yara-ma-yha-who
search_terms: yara ma yha who aboriginal vampire spirit
creatures.excerpt: The Yara-ma-yha-who is a vampiric spirit from Aboriginal Australian Dreaming legends, particularly in the mythology of the Yuin people of southeastern Australia. This creature is described as a small, red-skinned being standing about four feet tall with an oversized head, a large mouth, and long, skinny limbs. Each of

creatures.name: Yatoka (Sun Father)
creatures.excerpt: Yatoka, the Sun Father, is the Zuni celestial deity, the form taken by Áwonawílona, the All-Container, when he made himself into the sun. From the mist clouds of the Sun Father gathered the Great Waters from which Earth Mother (Áwitelin Tsíta) and Sky Father (Ápoyan Tá'chu) emerged, beginning the Zuni creation.

creatures.name: Yawk Yawk
creatures.excerpt: The Yawkyawk are female water spirits of the Kunwinjku people of western Arnhem Land, often shown as maidens with fish tails and hair of flowing water-weed who live in freshwater creeks, billabongs, and rock pools. In one account, the girls Likanaya and Marrayka were changed into such spirits after camping near the sac

creatures.name: Yawm Saub (God of Creation)
creatures.excerpt: Yawm Saub (also Yer Shau or simply Saub — 'The One Who Knows Everything') is the high god and creator in Hmong cosmology. He is the supreme celestial being who created the world and all living things, though he is somewhat remote and delegates daily affairs to lesser spirits. Saub is depicted as polygynous, living in a

creatures.name: Yeay Lac
creatures.excerpt: Yeay Lac is a guardian from Cambodia folklore. Cambodian female guardian spirit of villages and forests. Usually elderly, wise, protects from evil spirits and bandits. Can be summoned by rituals. Village guardian deity. Traditional protection spirit before Buddhism

creatures.name: Yei
creatures.excerpt: Yei (yé'iis) are the Holy People, the spirit deities of Navajo (Diné) tradition who emerged from the underworld to teach humanity. Chiefs among them are Hasjéyalti (Talking God), Hastséhogan (House God), Hastsézĭni the fire god, and Hastséoltoi the huntress; they appear in masked Yei Bi Chei dances and are painted in s

creatures.name: Yeil (Raven)
creatures.excerpt: Yeil is the Tlingit name for Raven, the central trickster and culture hero of Tlingit mythology. Yeil is responsible for many fundamental features of the world. He created the tides by making a woman under the earth to control the rise and fall of water. In the Tlingit flood narrative, Raven commanded the tide woman to

creatures.name: Yeil Raven Tlingit
creatures.excerpt: Yeil, the Raven, is the great trickster and creator of the Tlingit, who stole the sun, moon, and stars in nested boxes and released them into the sky. He shaped the landscape, brought salmon to the rivers, and gave fire to the people; his lineage, the Raven moiety, is one of the two primary divisions of Tlingit society

creatures.name: Yelmo
creatures.excerpt: Yelmo is a nature-spirit from Mongolia folklore. Mongolian wind horse that runs across steppes bringing storms and change. Can be ridden by shamanic spirits. Symbolizes vital energy. Shamanic symbol of life force and change. Important in Mongolian spirituality

creatures.name: Yemayá
creatures.excerpt: Yemayá is the Yoruba orisha of the sea, motherhood, and fish, brought to Cuba through the transatlantic slave trade. In Santería she owns all waters, governs maternity and fertility, and is syncretized with Our Lady of Regla. She is motherly and protective but destructive when angered, her waters creating rivers and fl

creatures.name: Yemoja
creatures.excerpt: Yemoja is the great mother goddess of the Yoruba pantheon, the orisha of the ocean, motherhood, fertility, and the Ogun River. Her name means "Mother whose children are the fish." She is considered the mother of many orishas and the protective spirit of women, children, and sailors. As the primordial ocean from which a

creatures.name: Yeshe Tsogyal
creatures.excerpt: Yeshe Tsogyal, the 'Victorious Lake of Wisdom,' was an eighth-century Tibetan princess and consort of Padmasambhava, revered as a master, consort, and dakini who attained the rainbow body. Credited with concealing the terma treasures with her master, she is invoked for healing and protection and remains a central femal

creatures.name: Yetga-chach
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a distinct figure of Kyrgyz folklore. No source confirms a forest spirit named 'Yetga-chach,' described as an old hunter with a huge beard who protects game and trees; searches return only the unrelated Kyrgyz and Turkic word 'chach' (hair) and an unrelated Ukrainian forest deity. The trai

creatures.name: Yeti
creatures.excerpt: Yeti (Meh-Teh in Nepali, Dzure in Bhutanese) is the 'Abominable Snowman' of Himalayan folklore — large ape-like creature of high mountains. Rooted in Sherpa, Tibetan, Nepali oral traditions as wild man of snows (Mi-te, Kang-mi). Not a single entity but a class of mountain hominids. Famous globally but locally a spirit-

creatures.name: Yeti (Migoi)
creatures.excerpt: The Yeti, known in Tibetan as Meh-teh or Migoi ('wild man'), is a hairy, ape-like being of Himalayan tradition said to roam snow, mountain, and cave. Tibetan lore distinguishes three forms: the giant black Nyalmo, the mid-altitude Chuti, and the small reddish Rang Shim Bombo. Feared yet sometimes revered as a guardian

creatures.name: Yewe
creatures.excerpt: Yewe (also known as Hevioso, Xevioso, or Sogbo) is the powerful Ewe god of thunder, lightning, rain, and divine justice. One of the major trɔwo (lesser deities descended from Mawu), Yewe is one of the most feared and respected spirits in the Ewe pantheon. His sacred cult, the Yewe society, is one of the most exclusive

creatures.name: Yggdrasil
creatures.excerpt: Yggdrasil (Unknown). is a mythical-tree. Yggdrasil is the immense cosmic tree at the center of Norse cosmology, connecting the Nine Worlds. Its branches extend into the heavens, and its three roots reach to wellsprings that nourish creation.. Source: Poetic Edda, Prose Edda (Snorri Sturluson, 13th century)

creatures.name: Yocahu (Taino Supreme God of Fertility)
creatures.excerpt: Yocahu (Yucahu Bagua Maorocoti) was the supreme deity and masculine spirit of fertility in Taino mythology -- the greatest of all zemis. His full name, recorded by the Spanish missionary Fray Ramon Pane in 1498, carries multiple meanings: Yucahu means giver of cassava (the staple crop), Bagua means master of the sea, a

creatures.name: Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ (White Shell Girl)
creatures.excerpt: Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ (White Shell Girl) is the original form of Changing Woman in Navajo tradition. She was born in the Fourth World and later matured into Changing Woman. She was sought in marriage by the Sun (Jóhonaa'éí), who disguised himself as a handsome warrior. After many trials, she agreed to marry him and travele

creatures.name: Yowie
creatures.excerpt: The yowie is a large, hairy, ape-like being of eastern Australian oral tradition, known by many names across language groups — Gamilaraay Yō-wī, 'spirit roaming the earth at night' (recorded 1875), as well as Quinkin and joogabinna in Queensland. In Aboriginal accounts such beings enforce cultural law and warn children

creatures.name: Yuch-Kurbustan
creatures.excerpt: Yuch-Kurbustan is a supreme celestial deity of Altai cosmology, a being of pure light in the highest heavens, never shown in human form, only as divine radiance. It wields supreme authority, aids heroes, and judges gods and humans. Apex of the divine hierarchy in Altaian epic, it is invoked in the most sacred narrative

creatures.name: Yuki-onna
creatures.excerpt: Yuki-onna (雪女), the snow woman, is a yōkai of Japanese winter folklore: a beautiful, pale-skinned woman with long black hair and a white or blue kimono who appears in snowstorms. She lures travelers into the cold and freezes them with her breath, yet sometimes spares those who are brave, kind, or handsome. Lafcadio Hea

creatures.name: Yul-Chyn (Ice Spirits)
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a distinct figure of Nenets folklore. No source confirms ice spirits called 'Yul-Chyn' who strangle travelers; Nenets animism records numerous tundra and river spirits, but none by this name appear in ethnographic literature. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

creatures.name: Yule Cat
creatures.excerpt: Yule Cat (Icelandic). is a monster. A colossal and vicious feline that devours those who do not receive new clothes before Christmas. Source: Icelandic folklore, Jón Árnason's collections

creatures.name: Yule Lads
creatures.excerpt: The Jólasveinar are thirteen Icelandic troll brothers who visit children on the thirteen nights before Christmas, each with a distinct prank (Clod, Gawk, Stubby, Spoon-Licker, Pot-Scraper, Bowl-Licker, Door-Slammer, Skyr-Gobbler, Sausage-Swiper, Window-Peeper, Doorway-Sniffer, Meat-Hook, Candle-Stealer). Sons of Grýla

creatures.name: Yule Lads Iceland
creatures.excerpt: Yule Lads Iceland (Unknown). is a trickster. The Yule Lads (Jólasveinarnir) are thirteen mischievous figures from Icelandic folklore who visit children on the thirteen nights leading up to Christmas. Each has a distinct personality and prank—fro. Source: Icelandic Christmas folklore; Jón Árnason's collection (19th cent

creatures.name: Yulm (First Carpenter)
creatures.excerpt: Yulm is the eldest of the Four Carpenters (Masmasalanicw) of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) tradition, the wise and skilled creator who worked in the House of Smayusta with the Creator Alhkw'ntam. In a simple but powerful act he made Raven from a lump of charcoal, and his craft opened the way for the other carpenters to complete

creatures.name: Yulm First Carpenter Nuxalk
creatures.excerpt: Yulm is the eldest of the Four Carpenters, the culture-hero craftsmen who assisted the Nuxalk creator Alhkw'ntam in shaping the world. His name lives on in the making of the first bird: Yulm molded a qwaxw from charcoal and set it to fly, giving the Nuxalk the origin of birds and of carving.

creatures.name: Yum
creatures.excerpt: Not attested in Zuni or any North American tradition. This record is a garbled duplicate of the Yumboes, the fairy-like spirits of the Wolof and Lebou peoples of Senegal, as its linked story 'The Yumboes, the Fairy Spirits of Senegal' shows. No being named 'Yum' appears in Zuni ethnography; the entry's Zuni attribution

creatures.name: Yumboes
creatures.excerpt: The Yumboes are supernatural fairy-like beings from the folklore of the Wolof and Lebou people of Senegal, often described as the spirits of the dead. Standing only about two feet tall with pearly-white skin and silver hair, these nocturnal beings live beneath the Paps hills near Gorée Island and emerge to dance in the

creatures.name: Yunwi Tsunsdi
creatures.excerpt: Yûñwï Tsunsdi', 'the Little Folk,' are the Cherokee little people, knee-high beings with perfect miniature Cherokee features and long hair reaching to their waists. They live in rock shelters and caves, help lost children, teach medicine and song, and punish those who disrespect nature; they can grant good luck or caus

creatures.name: Yurei (Edo period)
creatures.excerpt: Yūrei are the restless ghosts of Japanese tradition, given their classic form in Edo-period art and kabuki: a woman with long black hair, a white funeral kimono, and trailing sleeves, rendered with pale or blue-tinted skin and no feet. They are souls with unfinished business who died with strong attachment or injustice

creatures.name: Yurugu (Pale Fox)
creatures.excerpt: Yurugu (also called Ogo, the Pale Fox) is the first being of Dogon creation, born prematurely from Amma's flawed creative act. He limps across the Sahel on uneven legs as the living embodiment of disorder and incompleteness. Despite his chaotic nature, Yurugu serves a vital purpose through divination: each night, Dogon

creatures.name: Yééw
creatures.excerpt: Yééw is the hyena of Wolof folktales, a greedy and deceptive figure whose schemes always backfire, teaching children moral lessons through comic misfortune. In Senegalese oral tradition Yééw teaches the folly of selfishness while mirroring human weakness in village life.

creatures.name: Yéʼiitsoh (Big Giant)
creatures.excerpt: Yé'iitsoh, 'Big Monster,' is the first and most powerful of the Anaye, the alien monsters of the Fifth World in Navajo (Diné) tradition. Son of the Sun, he wore four suits of flint armor and made his home at Tsoodził (Mount Taylor), where the Hero Twins, born to Changing Woman, slew him with lightning arrows; his blood

creatures.name: Zambur
creatures.excerpt: Not independently attested as a scorpion spirit in Tajik folklore. The word zambur (zambūr) simply means 'wasp' in Persian, and no Tajik tale records a desert scorpion spirit by this name. Real scorpion lore in the region is confined to folk warnings about the black scorpion's sting and its place in proverbs and saying

creatures.name: Zana
creatures.excerpt: Zanë are the mountain nymphs of Albanian folklore, beautiful, fierce, and fiercely independent protectors of nature who appear near rivers, waterfalls, forests, and peaks. They guard the wilderness and may aid the worthy, but those who disrespect nature risk their wrath, which can bring madness or harm. Compare with th

creatures.name: Zanahary
creatures.excerpt: Zanahary is the supreme sky creator god in Malagasy mythology, the source of all life and spirit. In the creation myth shared across Madagascar, Zanahary and the earth god Ratovantany collaborated to create humanity. Ratovantany shaped physical bodies from clay, but they remained lifeless until Zanahary breathed souls

creatures.name: Zangbeto
creatures.excerpt: Zangbeto, meaning 'Men of the Night' in the Goun and Fon languages, are sacred night guardian spirits central to the Vodun faith of Togo and Benin. These towering figures made of raffia and palm fibers spin through villages at night, serving as the eyes of justice in the darkness. According to tradition, Zangbetos are

creatures.name: Zangbeto
creatures.excerpt: Zangbeto is a spirit from Vodun mythology. These towering figures made of raffia and palm fibers spin through villages at night, serving as the eyes of justice in the darkness. According to tradition, Zangbetos are living vessels of ancestral spirits. Believers maintain that no human is inside the raffia structure, onl

creatures.name: Zangbeto
creatures.excerpt: Zangbeto is a spirit from Beninese Folklore mythology. These towering figures made of raffia and palm fibers spin through villages at night, serving as the eyes of justice in the darkness. According to tradition, Zangbetos are living vessels of ancestral spirits. Believers maintain that no human is inside the raffia st

creatures.name: Zankallala
creatures.excerpt: Zankallala is a remarkable trickster figure from Hausa folklore, found across the Sahel region including northern Ivory Coast. creatures.name: Zar
creatures.excerpt: Zar spirits are genuine in Sudanese folk belief: ambivalent supernatural beings who possess individuals and cause illness and misfortune, and who must be appeased through drumming, dance and trance ceremonies. A zar ceremony involves the possessed person, a healer and the audience; spirits have distinct personalities a

creatures.name: Zar
creatures.excerpt: Zar spirits are a class of supernatural beings in Eritrean folk belief, particularly among Tigrinya-speaking communities and the broader Horn of Africa region. creatures.name: Zar
creatures.excerpt: Zar refers to spirits in the possession cults of Ethiopia, Eritrea, Sudan, and the wider Horn of Africa. The tradition blends indi

creatures.name: Zduhać
creatures.excerpt: Zduhać (also Zduhač) is a human with supernatural abilities from Montenegrin and Dalmatian folklore, particularly among mountain tribes. Born with a caul (amniotic membrane) on their head, a Zduhać is destined to protect their community from destructive weather. During storms, their spirit leaves their sleeping body to

creatures.name: Zduhać
creatures.excerpt: Zduhać is a human from Slavic mythology. Born with a caul (amniotic membrane) on their head, a Zduhać is destined to protect their community from destructive weather. creatures.name: Zelebith
creatures.excerpt: Zelebith (Ethiopia). is a bird. Zelebith is a bird from the folklore and mythology of Ethiopia.. Source: Ethiopian folklore — Zelebith bird documented in Ethiopian oral tradition.

creatures.name: Zhalmauyz
creatures.excerpt: Zhalmauyz (Zhalmauyz Kempir) is the ogress of Kazakh folklore, an ancient cannibal hag who hunts for children to devour. She has seven heads, a single eye and hoof-like feet, and she shifts her shape to deceive her victims. Her name, echoing the steppe word for a child-stealing bogey, is used to frighten the young.

creatures.name: Zhar-Ptitsa (Firebird)
creatures.excerpt: Zhar-Ptitsa (Firebird) is the Slavic magical glowing bird from a faraway land. Its golden feathers illuminate darkness; a single feather lights a room. Both a blessing and a harbinger of doom to its captor. Central to quest tales (Ivan Tsarevich and the Grey Wolf) where heroes seek it for a tsar. Inspired Stravinsky's

creatures.name: Zimwi (or Zimwi)
creatures.excerpt: Zimwi is a Shona ogre (giant, hairy, man-eating) from Zimbabwe folklore, dwelling in forests and caves. It represents the danger of wilderness and strangers, often depicted with backwards feet to confuse trackers. Heroes outwit it through cleverness. The term zimwi appears in Bantu religion literature as a class of ogr

creatures.name: Zin
creatures.excerpt: Zin are Hausa water spirits inhabiting the Niger River and lakes in Niger and northern Nigeria. They shapeshift between aquatic and human forms, luring humans to watery domains. Feared as causes of drowning and disappearances. Related to broader West African water spirit complexes (Mami Wata, Ndi Mmili). Documented in

creatures.name: Zin Kibaru
creatures.excerpt: Zin Kibaru is a water spirit from Songhay-Zarma mythology of the Niger River region. The term Zin refers to a class of genies inhabiting water bodies, and Kibaru specifically designates a powerful water demon that demands respect and offerings. These spirits are associated with the Holeys, possession dances of the Song

creatures.name: Zlydzens
creatures.excerpt: Zlydzens (Belarusian zlydni, Ukrainian zlydni) are small, hunchbacked, hazardous stove spirits living under the masonry oven. They wear big boots and earflap hats, resemble cat-dog hybrids. In groups they wreck utensils, spill milk, create chaos; drawn to greedy households. Cowardly alone. The Ukrainian phrase 'zhyty v

creatures.name: Zmaj
creatures.excerpt: Zmaj is the dragon of South Slavic folklore, including Kosovo, a great serpent or winged, fire-breathing beast dwelling in caves near villages. In Serbian and Kosovan tradition the fiery zmaj is often a guardian of crops who fights storm-demons, though dragons also guard treasure; its presence explains storms and droug

creatures.name: Zmaj
creatures.excerpt: Zmaj is the Serbian dragon — a winged serpent dwelling in caves near villages. In Balkans lore, unlike the malevolent Russian zmey, the zmaj is often a benevolent guardian who fights the evil ala/lamia (drought demons). Can appear as a handsome man, fire bird, or smoke; takes human lovers (e.g., Tsarina Milica). Symbol

creatures.name: Zmej
creatures.excerpt: Zmej is the Bulgarian dragon — a winged, scale-covered serpent, often with multiple heads (3–12). Unlike East Slavic malevolent zmey, the Balkan zmej is a benevolent guardian who fights the lamia/hala (drought demons). Can appear as a handsome man to woo human women; children of such unions become vampire hunters. Symb

creatures.name: Zmeu
creatures.excerpt: Zmeu is the dragon of Romanian folklore, a fearsome flying serpent, often multi-headed, that abducts maidens and menaces villages from mountain fastnesses and castles. In the folk ballads a hero must defeat the zmeu, sometimes with the aid of his captive's cunning; the dragon may also appear as a handsome youth. It per

creatures.name: Zmeu
creatures.excerpt: Zmeu is the dragon of Moldovan and Romanian folklore, a flying serpent, often multi-headed, that carries off maidens and plagues the land from mountains and high places, breathing fire and drowning its foes. Folk ballads tell of heroes who overcome it by courage and trickery. The zmeu represents the perilous forces tha

creatures.name: Zmey
creatures.excerpt: In Russian folklore the zmei (zmej gorynych) is a serpent-dragon of skazki and byliny, a fire-breathing monster who abducts princesses and ravages the land. Epic heroes such as Dobrynya Nikitich and Alyosha Popovich slay Zmei Gorynych, and Tugarin Zmeevich appears as a dragon adversary in the oral epic songs.

creatures.name: Zmey
creatures.excerpt: The zmey is a dragon of Bulgarian folklore, a powerful being that can aid people: male zmey protect villages and battle destructive female lamia or hala in the sky during storms, guarding the wheat harvest. Zmey may take human, serpent or cloud form and fall in love with human women; the forest dragon Zmey Gorianin is

creatures.name: Zmey
creatures.excerpt: Zmey is a spirit from Macedonian Slavic Mythology mythology. In Macedonian tales and folk songs, Zmey are described as extraordinarily intelligent beings with hypnotizing eyes, possessing a human-like form with a snake's tail and golden wings. They live in caves or on remote mountain tops and are extremely wise. The Zm

creatures.name: Zmey Gorynych
creatures.excerpt: Zmey Gorynych is the iconic Russian three-to-twelve-headed dragon of byliny and fairy tales. Dwells beyond three rivers or in mountain caves. Each severed head regenerates unless cauterized; kidnaps princesses; breathes fire. Slain by bogatyrs Dobrynya Nikitich and Ilya Muromets. A specific named antagonist, not a spec

creatures.name: Zmora
creatures.excerpt: Zmora is a Slavic night demon of Polish folklore, akin to the mare or mara. It is believed to visit sleepers at night, pressing on their chests and causing choking, nightmares, and a heavy feeling upon waking. Zmora were thought to be spirits of the dead or, in some regions, living people whose souls left their bodies

creatures.name: Zombi
creatures.excerpt: Zombi (Unknown). is a undead. In Haitian Vodou tradition, a zombi is a reanimated corpse brought back to life by a bokor (sorcerer). Unlike the modern cinematic version, the Haitian zombi is a mindless laborer under the control of. Source: The Serpent and the Rainbow (Davis, 1985); Haitian Folklore (Courlander, 1960)

creatures.name: Zonbi
keywords: zonbi, seychelles, zombie, creole folklore, malevolent spirit, colonial hauntings, seychellois undead
creatures.excerpt: The Zonbi is a malevolent spirit or reanimated corpse in Seychellois Creole folklore, linked to dark magic rather than Hollywood-style zombies. A corpse may be animated by sorcery to serve an evil purpose, and Zonbi are associated with abandoned historical sites. Belief in them reflects anxieties about death, the after

creatures.name: Zuhri
creatures.excerpt: The zuhri is a being of Moroccan belief, born of a human mother and a jinn father, who can see buried treasure beneath the earth. Marked by a slanting gaze, the zuhri is sought by treasure hunters, while the treasures themselves are said to strike the greedy dead. The belief is so potent that it has been invoked in rea

creatures.name: Zuleikha
creatures.excerpt: The Forty Maidens (Kirk Kiz), here given the name Zuleikha, are a band of warrior women of Turkmen and neighboring Central Asian tradition who defend their stronghold against invaders. The ninth-century fortress of Kirk Kiz at Termez is linked to their tale, told across Turkmen, Karakalpak and Uzbek epic lore and prais

creatures.name: Zumwani
creatures.excerpt: Zumwani is a Herero water spirit of Namibia, appearing as an exceedingly beautiful woman with reed-like hair wearing colorful cloth, dwelling in rivers, pans, and waterholes. She tests men's character at water's edge: rewarding the respectful with good rains, drowning the disrespectful. Associated with seasonal rains a

creatures.name: Zār
creatures.excerpt: The zar is a class of possessing spirits in Sudan, Egypt, and the Horn of Africa, believed to seize people, most often women, causing illness, restlessness, and affliction. Each zar demands its own clothes, jewels, incense, and drumming, met through the healing ceremonies of the zar cult. Seven nations of zar spirits r

creatures.name: Áhaiyúta (Morning Star, War God)
creatures.excerpt: Áhaiyúta is one of the two Zuni Twin War Gods, the elder of the pair with his brother Mátsailéma; together the 'Twain Little-ones' are the right- and left-hand beings of the Sun, gods of war, chance and games. In Frank Hamilton Cushing's Zuni Folk Tales they descend to the underworld, battle the soft 'unborn-made men',

creatures.name: Álfar
creatures.excerpt: Álfar (elves) are nature-dwelling spirits in Icelandic folklore, distinct from the Huldufólk (hidden people) in several key ways. While Huldufólk are considered to be human-like beings living in a parallel society, álfar are more ethereal, nature-bound beings associated with specific rocks, hills, and cliffs. In Icelan

creatures.name: Ápoyan Ta'chu (Sky Father)
creatures.excerpt: Ápoyan Ta'chu (Sky Father) is a creator deity in Zuni mythology, regarded as the supreme ruler of the Above World. He is the father of the Sun Priest and the Moon Maiden, and together with Earth Mother (Uchtsiti) he shaped the first beings from cornmeal. Ápoyan Ta'chu instructed the Zuni people in the art of prayer plu

creatures.name: Átahsaia (Cannibal Demon)
creatures.excerpt: Átahsaia is a giant cannibal demon in Zuni mythology who terrorized the people. He is described as a huge, monstrous being with burning eyes, coarse hair like a buffalo's mane, scales of black and white on his arms and legs, and a mouth filled with crooked yellow fangs. He carried a bow and a great flint knife. Átahsai

creatures.name: Áwitelin Tsíta (Earth Mother)
creatures.excerpt: Awitelin Tsita (Áwitelin Tsíta) is the Earth Mother of Zuni creation, formed together with the Sky Father Ápoyan Ta'chu from the mists that lay over the great waters; she conceived all living things in her four-fold womb. In Frank Hamilton Cushing's Zuni Genesis, the All-Father Awonawilona sets this creation in motion.

creatures.name: Áwonawílona (All-Father)
creatures.excerpt: Áwonawílona (All-Father, Maker and Container of All) is the supreme primordial deity in Zuni creation mythology. In the beginning, only Áwonawílona existed. He made himself into the Sun Father (Yatoka). The mist clouds formed into the Great Waters, from which Earth Mother (Áwitelin Tsíta) and Sky Father (Ápoyan Ta'chu)

creatures.name: Âu Cơ (Mountain Fairy)
creatures.excerpt: Âu Cơ is the beautiful mountain fairy and founding mother of the Vietnamese people. Daughter of Đế Lai (a descendant of the divine Shennong), she was a tiên (immortal fairy) who lived in the snow-capped mountains and traveled to heal the sick with her medical skills. She married the dragon lord Lạc Long Quân and gave b

creatures.name: Ââ'ototo Kachina
creatures.excerpt: Eototo (A'ototo) is a principal Hopi kachina, the chief and 'father' of the katsinam after Angwusnasomtaka, personification of nature and protagonist of the Powamu ceremony. He comes from the red land of the south, belongs to the Bear clan, wears a white cylindrical mask topped with a nest of hair, and draws cloud symb

creatures.name: Älvakung
creatures.excerpt: Älvakungen (the elf king) is the ruler of the elves (älvor) in Swedish folklore. He leads the elf dance (älvadans) on misty meadows, especially around Midsummer and during the autumn mists. Älvakungen appears as a magnificent but deeply otherworldly figure — handsome, richly dressed, but with an unsettling presence tha

creatures.name: Älvor
creatures.excerpt: Älvor in Swedish folk belief are beautiful, human-like beings dwelling in forests, meadows, and mist. They dance in circles (älvadans), causing illness or madness to intruders, and can exchange human children for changelings (bytlingar). Both male and female älvor exist. They are distinct from skogsrå/huldra but region

creatures.name: Åland Storm-Witch
creatures.excerpt: The storm-witch of Åland is a female practitioner of weather magic who possesses the secret art of tying the wind into knots of rope. Unlike malevolent hags who conjure storms through incantations, the Åland storm-witch operates as a trader of winds: she sells sailors knotted ropes that release favorable breezes when u

creatures.name: Åmand
creatures.excerpt: Åmanden (the River Man) is a Danish male water spirit who rules a specific river stretch and demands an annual human sacrifice. Unlike Nøkken, who lures individuals, the Åmand has a contractual demand: one person per year must drown in his waters, and he calls for his victim on a specific night. His most famous cry ech

creatures.name: Ésevone
creatures.excerpt: Ésevone is the Sacred Buffalo Hat of the Cheyenne people, one of the two most sacred ceremonial objects of the Cheyenne Nation (alongside the Maahótse Sacred Arrows). Made from the skin of a buffalo cow's head, ornamented with a pair of buffalo horns that have been shaved down, flattened, and decorated. Ésevone represe

creatures.name: Ông Địa
creatures.excerpt: Ông Địa is the earth god of the Vietnamese household, depicted as a jovial bald old man with a long beard who resides beneath the home, in gardens, or fields. He protects the family from misfortune and brings prosperity in exchange for offerings and reverence. His cult blends Buddhist practice with indigenous folk reli

creatures.name: Ölgii-khorkhoi (Mongolian Death Worm)
creatures.excerpt: Ölgii-khorkhoi, the 'Mongolian Death Worm,' is the legendary cryptid of the Gobi Desert, a thick, fat worm, bright red or orange, as thick as a man's arm, eyeless and mouthless, sometimes with spikes. Buried in sand and emerging after rain, it is said to kill camels and humans with corrosive spit or electric discharge.

creatures.name: Ülgen (Bai-Ülgen)
creatures.excerpt: Ülgen (Bai-Ülgen) is the benevolent sky-god of the Altai Turks: the radiant creator dwelling in the sixteenth heaven who made the earth and humanity. Generous, protective, and abundant, he rewards good shamans and watches over rebirth, seated on a golden mountain with a golden staff. His worship anchors Altaian and wid

creatures.name: Čáhcegearpmaš
creatures.excerpt: Čáhcegearpmaš, also called Vesikäärme, is a water serpent of the Tornedalen region known to Sami and Meänkieli tradition, a close variant of Čáhcerávga, the Northern Sami 'water rávga' — a malevolent water being, shadow of the drowned, that haunts lakes and streams and pulls people, especially children, beneath the sur

creatures.name: Čáhcerávga
creatures.excerpt: Čáhcerávga (Water Wraith) is a fictional creature in Sami folklore, explicitly known to be invented to scare children away from dangerous waters. Unlike the Rávga, which was believed to be a real undead spirit, the Čáhcerávga was recognized as a pedagogical tool. It was described as a long-necked, scary creature that c

creatures.name: Čázevulošnieida
creatures.excerpt: Čázevulošnieida (the Underwater Girl) is a Sea Sami spirit from the Unjárga/Nesseby region on the Varangerfjord, Norway. She is the daughter of Čáhceháldi (the Sea Guard), a mythical sea ranger who lives in a parallel underwater world. When a Sami fisherman boy encounters her, their meeting reveals how perspectives are

creatures.name: Đào
creatures.excerpt: The name Đào (peach) in Vietnamese tradition does connect to documented folklore: in Lĩnh Nam chích quái, peach branches ward off evil spirits, and peach is central to Tết New Year customs. However, the recorded figure of a beautiful mountain fairy named Đào who lures or guides travelers is not independently attested;

creatures.name: ǐKaggen
creatures.excerpt: ǐKaggen (also Cagn, the Mantis) is the central trickster-creator deity of the San people of southern Africa, including Namibia. A demiurge and culture hero, ǐKaggen can shapeshift into various animal forms, most frequently a praying mantis, but also a bull eland, a louse, a snake, or a caterpillar. He created the world

creatures.name: ǐXue
creatures.excerpt: ǐXue is the trickster being of the ǓKun (ǓXung) people of northeastern Namibia, described by scholars as Khoisan mythology's most unrestrained shapeshifter with a trigger-sharp readiness for transformation. ǐXue can transform himself into each and everything conceivable. He has a complicated association with the moon a

stories.name: A Plantation Witch
stories.excerpt: Collected by Joel Chandler Harris in the Uncle Remus stories, 'A Plantation Witch' tells of supernatural occurrences on the plantation. Uncle Remus recounts that witches on the plantation could transform into animals, particularly haunts and hags that rode people at night. According to the tale, a young enslaved man na
stories.title: A Plantation Witch

stories.name: Ababinili and the Creation of Humans (Chickasaw)
stories.excerpt: Ababinili (also spelled Aba' Binni'li'), meaning 'One Who Sits Above' or 'Dwells Above,' is the Creator god of the Chickasaw people. According to legend, Ababinili created the first humans from the clay of the earth and breathed life into them. He taught the people how to live, hunt, farm, and conduct ceremonies. Ababi
stories.title: Ababinili and the Creation of Humans (Chickasaw)

stories.name: Abai Geser the Mighty (Buryat Epic)
stories.excerpt: The Buryat version of the great Central Asian epic of Geser (Geser), focusing on his battles with various demons rather than military campaigns. The epic begins with a unique prologue: the great Tengri Khormusta of the western celestial tribes wars with Atai Ulan, lord of the eastern evil gods. After victory, Khormusta
stories.title: Abai Geser the Mighty (Buryat Epic)

stories.name: Abaia the Magical Eel
stories.excerpt: Abaia is a huge, magical eel from the mythology of Fiji, the Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu. This enormous freshwater eel is said to dwell at the bottom of deep lakes and rivers, acting as a guardian spirit of the waters. In Fijian tradition, Abaia is associated with Degei and is considered a powerful spirit being that c
stories.title: Abaia the Magical Eel

stories.name: Ableegumooch: How Rabbit Lost His Tail
stories.excerpt: Ableegumooch the Rabbit was once the most vain of all animals, boasting constantly about his beautiful long tail. He teased Otter for having only a small, stubby tail. Annoyed, Otter challenged Rabbit to a fishing contest. Rabbit, who knew nothing about fishing but would never admit it, agreed. Otter caught fish after
stories.title: Ableegumooch: How Rabbit Lost His Tail

stories.name: Abu Zayd al-Hilali and the Banu Hilal Epic
stories.excerpt: The Epic of the Banu Hilal (Taghribat Bani Hilal) is one of the great oral epics of the Arab world, particularly celebrated in Egypt and North Africa. It recounts the migration of the Bedouin Banu Hilal tribe from the Arabian Peninsula into North Africa in the 11th century. The hero, Abu Zayd al-Hilali, is a legendary
stories.title: Abu Zayd al-Hilali and the Banu Hilal Epic

stories.name: Abuk, the Mother of Seed
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, the goddess Abuk held all the seeds of the earth within her body, and the sky god demanded she surrender them to humanity. Her defiance and eventual sacrifice shaped the eternal bond between women and the soil.
stories.title: Abuk, the Mother of Seed

stories.name: Adaro: The Sea Spirits of the Solomon Islands
stories.excerpt: In the mythology of Makira (San Cristobal) in the Solomon Islands, the Adaro are powerful sea spirits that dwell in the ocean. They are described as half-human, half-fish beings who can travel along rainbows and sunlight beams. Adaro are said to have gills on their bodies and fins on their arms and legs. They can be bo
stories.title: Adaro: The Sea Spirits of the Solomon Islands

stories.name: Adbar: The Spirit Guardians of Ethiopia
stories.excerpt: In Ethiopian folk belief, every mountain, river, forest, and crossroads is protected by a spirit called an Adbar. These guardian spirits are ancient beings who existed before humans and serve as the intermediaries between God and the natural world. Each Adbar has a specific territory and responsibility: some protect tr
stories.title: Adbar: The Spirit Guardians of Ethiopia

stories.name: Adonis and the River of Blood
stories.excerpt: A beautiful youth killed by a boar, whose blood flows every spring through the rivers of Lebanon — turning them red with his memory, and the women weep because beauty does not last.
stories.title: Adonis and the River of Blood

stories.name: Adventure With a Tie-Snake (Natchez)
stories.excerpt: The Tie-Snake (u'lax daxgi'ilu in Natchez) is a water spirit common to Southeastern Native American folklore. Though the size and shape of an ordinary snake, Tie-Snakes possess immense strength and can coil around a human with crushing force. In the Natchez story, a man encountered a Tie-Snake while fishing. The snake
stories.title: Adventure With a Tie-Snake (Natchez)

stories.name: Adze: The Vampiric Firefly
stories.excerpt: A witch-spirit takes firefly form, entering homes to drain the blood of sleepers.
stories.title: Adze: The Vampiric Firefly

stories.name: Agneta and the Sea King
stories.excerpt: Agneta, daughter of a lord, encounters the Sea King by the lake at sunset. Enchanted by his music, she forgets her former life and becomes his queen beneath the waters for seven years, bearing him seven sons. When church bells reach her underwater realm, she begs to attend church. Above the surface, memories of her fat
stories.title: Agneta and the Sea King

stories.name: Agnete og Havmanden
stories.excerpt: A merman woos Agnete to leave her children behind and come and live with him in the sea. She does so and has several children by him. But one day she hears the ringing of church bells and with the merman's permission returns to land to visit the church. In most variants, she then abandons the merman and the children sh
stories.title: Agnete og Havmanden

stories.name: Ah Puch and the Moon Child
stories.excerpt: A young Maya girl ventures too close to the entrance of Xibalba and encounters Ah Puch, lord of death, who tests her courage and teaches her the boundary between the living and the dead.
stories.title: Ah Puch and the Moon Child

stories.name: Ahoeitu and the Founding of the Tupou Dynasty
stories.excerpt: Ahoeitu was born to a Tongan chiefess and the god Eitumatupua, who descended from heaven on a great tree. The jealous half-brothers of Ahoeitu conspired against him, murdering him and cutting his body into pieces. When Eitumatupua discovered the crime, he restored Ahoeitu to life and punished the treacherous brothers.
stories.title: Ahoeitu and the Founding of the Tupou Dynasty

stories.name: Aina-Kizz and the Black-Bearded Bai
stories.excerpt: Aina-Kizz, an incredibly clever young girl from Samarkand, helps her widowed mother by using her intelligence to outwit a greedy black-bearded bai (rich man). The bai boasts of impossible feats — that he once grew a wheat field so vast that a whole caravan got lost in it, and that the caravan emerged from his mouth whe
stories.title: Aina-Kizz and the Black-Bearded Bai

stories.name: Aisha Qandisha, the Demoness of the Waters
stories.excerpt: Aisha Qandisha is among the most famous mythological figures in Moroccan folklore—a beautiful woman with the legs of a goat or camel who lures men to their doom. She is said to live near water sources: the sea at Tangier, the Martil River at Tetouan, the Sebou River among the Beni Ahsen. Using her enchanting beauty, sh
stories.title: Aisha Qandisha, the Demoness of the Waters

stories.name: Aisha Qandisha: The Jinn of the Moroccan Rivers
stories.excerpt: A beautiful jinn with goat hooves seduces men at rivers and drives them to madness.
stories.title: Aisha Qandisha: The Jinn of the Moroccan Rivers

stories.name: Akbaatatdia the Creator
stories.excerpt: Akbaatatdia (One Who Has Made Everything) is the supreme Creator in Crow religion. Also known as Iichíkbaalee (First Doer) and Isáahkawuattee (Old Man Coyote), this singular omnipotent god created the universe. The Crow believe the universe consists of three worlds: the physical world (the smallest), the spirit world (
stories.title: Akbaatatdia the Creator

stories.name: Akbar and Birbal — The Farmer's Well
stories.excerpt: A poor farmer bought a well from a rich man, but the rich man later refused to let him draw water, claiming he had sold only the well, not the water. The farmer brought his case to Emperor Akbar's court, who handed it to his wise advisor Birbal. Birbal told the rich man: 'Since you sold the well and not the water, you
stories.title: Akbar and Birbal — The Farmer's Well

stories.name: Al, the Underworld Dweller
stories.excerpt: A demonic being who lives in the depths of the earth, luring the living underground with promises of treasure, because in Georgia the earth itself hungers.
stories.title: Al, the Underworld Dweller

stories.name: Al-Khidr and the Sultan of Petra
stories.excerpt: When a greedy sultan attempts to claim the treasures of Petra for himself, Al-Khidr appears as a humble guide to teach him that the city of stone holds no wealth for those who do not understand its meaning.
stories.title: Al-Khidr and the Sultan of Petra

stories.name: Ala and the Sacred Earth (Igbo)
stories.excerpt: Ala is the great earth goddess of the Igbo people, the most revered deity in Odinani. She is the goddess of fertility, morality, death, and the ancestral realm. The Igbo believe that the earth is Ala's living body, and that all who die return to her womb. Killing, incest, theft, and the birth of twins were considered '
stories.title: Ala and the Sacred Earth (Igbo)

stories.name: Aladdin and the Magic Lamp
stories.excerpt: In a far city of China, though the tale itself comes from the sands of Arabia, there lived a poor tailor named Mustapha and his wife, who had one son.
stories.title: Aladdin and the Magic Lamp

stories.name: Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp
stories.excerpt: A poor young ne'er-do-well in a Chinese city is recruited by a Maghrebi sorcerer to retrieve a magic lamp from a booby-trapped cave. When the sorcerer betrays him, Aladdin discovers a genie bound to the lamp that grants wishes. He becomes wealthy, marries Princess Badroulbadour, and builds a magnificent palace. The sor
stories.title: Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp

stories.name: Aldar Qose the Trickster
stories.excerpt: Aldar Qose is the beloved Kazakh trickster figure, analogous to Nasreddin Hodja in other Turkic traditions. He is a poor but clever wanderer who uses his wit to outsmart greedy bais (wealthy men), corrupt officials, and even devils. In one famous tale, Aldar convinces a miserly bai to give him almost all his possession
stories.title: Aldar Qose the Trickster

stories.name: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves
stories.excerpt: In a town in Persia, there once lived two brothers.. The elder, Cassim, married a wealthy woman and became the richest merchant in the marketplace.
stories.title: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves

stories.name: Ali, the Mountain Demon
stories.excerpt: A monstrous demon who dwells in the high mountains, stealing livestock and children, because in Georgia the peaks belong to things older than faith.
stories.title: Ali, the Mountain Demon

stories.name: All I Possess!
stories.excerpt: A miserly farmer marries a woman who supposedly eats almost nothing. Suspicious, he spies on her three times—down the chimney, inside a feather bed, and in a beer barrel. Each time she outwits him (with smoke, beating, and scalding lye). On his deathbed, his cries of 'All I possess!' are interpreted as his final wish t
stories.title: All I Possess!

stories.name: Alpamysh Batyr
stories.excerpt: Alpamysh (Alpamıs in Kazakh) is one of the most important Turkic epic heroes, shared across Kazakh, Uzbek, Karakalpak, and Altai traditions. The epic tells of the hero's miraculous birth to elderly parents after years of prayer, his childhood exploits, and his marriage to the beautiful Barchin after defeating rival sui
stories.title: Alpamysh Batyr

stories.name: Amadioha, the God of Thunder (Igbo)
stories.excerpt: Amadioha is the Igbo god of thunder, lightning, justice, and the sky. His name means 'free will of the people' in Igbo. Amadioha represents divine justice and collective will, striking down those who break oaths and commit crimes. His color is red, his sacred animal is the ram, and his day is Afọ. The main shrine of Am
stories.title: Amadioha, the God of Thunder (Igbo)

stories.name: Amaterasu and the Cave
stories.excerpt: Amaterasu, the Sun Goddess of Shinto, is the most important deity in the Japanese pantheon.
stories.title: Amaterasu and the Cave

stories.name: Amirani, the Chained Hero
stories.excerpt: A Titan-like hero who defied the gods and was chained to a mountain for eternity, his chains binding him until the day a greater hero comes to free him.
stories.title: Amirani, the Chained Hero

stories.name: Amleth
stories.excerpt: Prince Amleth's father, King Horvendill, is murdered by his uncle Feng. Amleth fakes madness to survive and eventually kills Feng by burning down his palace during a feast, avenging his father's death and reclaiming his kingdom.
stories.title: Amleth

stories.name: Amma and the Cosmic Egg: The Dogon Creation
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, Amma, the supreme creator god of the Dogon people, existed alone. He created the universe from a cosmic egg called aduno tal, which contained all future matter and motion. Amma attempted to create the world but the first being, Ogo (also called Yurugu the Pale Fox), was born prematurely and without a
stories.title: Amma and the Cosmic Egg: The Dogon Creation

stories.name: Anansi and the Dispersal of Diseases (Ashanti/Akan)
stories.excerpt: Anansi once tricked Nyame, the Sky God, by taking one of his sheep and promising a beautiful maiden in return. Nyame discovered the deception and took all of Anansi's wives, leaving only a sick woman. Following her advice, Anansi bathed her and kept the water in a gourd, and she became beautiful. When Nyame saw her and
stories.title: Anansi and the Dispersal of Diseases (Ashanti/Akan)

stories.name: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
stories.excerpt: Anansi tricks humans into giving him all the world's wisdom—but discovers it cannot be kept.
stories.title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom

stories.name: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom (Ashanti/Akan)
stories.excerpt: Anansi the Spider gathered all the wisdom in the world into a pot, planning to hoard it for himself. He decided to hide the pot at the top of a tall tree, but each time he tried to climb the tree with the pot tied in front of him, he kept sliding down. Anansi's young son, Ntikuma, watched and asked, 'Father, wouldn't i
stories.title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom (Ashanti/Akan)

stories.name: Anansi and Tiger in the Pit
stories.excerpt: Anansi hears Tiger roaring and finds him trapped in a deep pit. As Tiger claws his way up inch by inch, Anansi taunts him from above. When Tiger reaches near the top, gasping that he has no more strength, Anansi mockingly advises him to pray — to put his paws together and pray for strength. The moment Tiger puts his pa
stories.title: Anansi and Tiger in the Pit

stories.name: Anansi and Turtle (Ashanti/Akan)
stories.excerpt: Anansi once invited Turtle to dinner, but when Turtle arrived after a long journey, Anansi told him that custom required Turtle to wash his hands before eating. As Turtle walked to the river and back, Anansi ate all the food. Turtle, realizing he had been tricked, invited Anansi to dinner at the bottom of the river. An
stories.title: Anansi and Turtle (Ashanti/Akan)

stories.name: Anansi Boys
stories.excerpt: Anansi's sons—Fat Face and Small Head—continue their fathers trickery in the Caribbean.
stories.title: Anansi Boys

stories.name: Anansi: The Spider Who Owns All Stories
stories.excerpt: A clever spider uses his wits to capture the world's most dangerous creatures and win all the stories in existence.
stories.title: Anansi: The Spider Who Owns All Stories

stories.name: Anarteq the Salmon Spirit
stories.excerpt: A man named Anarteq undergoes a spiritual transformation after a series of events that lead him to merge with the essence of the river. He becomes a salmon spirit, possessing the ability to move between the human and aquatic worlds. This myth explains the spiritual connection between hunters and their prey, suggesting
stories.title: Anarteq the Salmon Spirit

stories.name: Andaokut Rescues the Children (Nuu-chah-nulth)
stories.excerpt: A woman whose children had been stolen by Malahas, a malicious forest goddess, wept uncontrollably. From her mucus or tears, a child was born — Andaokut. This miraculous birth child grew with extraordinary speed and possessed supernatural abilities. Andaokut set out to rescue the stolen children, tracking Malahas to he
stories.title: Andaokut Rescues the Children (Nuu-chah-nulth)

stories.name: Antar and Abla
stories.excerpt: The epic romance of Antarah ibn Shaddad, a 6th-century pre-Islamic Arab poet-warrior born a slave to an Ethiopian mother and Arab father in the tribe of Banu Abs. Despite his dark complexion (one of the 'Arab crows'), Antar rose through courage and poetry to win his freedom and the hand of his cousin Abla. His poem bec
stories.title: Antar and Abla

stories.name: Anubis
stories.excerpt: Anubis is the most ancient of Egyptian funerary gods — the jackal-headed guardian of the dead whose dark form has watched over tombs and necropolises since the earliest dynasties.
stories.title: Anubis

stories.name: Anulap: The God of Knowledge in Chuuk
stories.excerpt: Anulap is a powerful god of magic and knowledge in the mythology of Chuuk (Truk) in the Federated States of Micronesia. He is revered as the deity who taught humanity the arts of magic, navigation, medicine, and all forms of sacred and practical knowledge. Anulap is the husband of the creator goddess Ligobubfanu and ma
stories.title: Anulap: The God of Knowledge in Chuuk

stories.name: Anzar and the First Rain
stories.excerpt: Anzar, the god of rain and thunder in Berber mythology, fell in love with a beautiful mortal woman who refused his love. In his grief, Anzar withheld the rain from the earth, causing a terrible drought that parched the land. The woman eventually relented and agreed to marry him. When she finally accepted his hand, Anza
stories.title: Anzar and the First Rain

stories.name: Apwoyo the Trickster Hare
stories.excerpt: Among the Luo, Apwoyo the hare is the most cunning creature in the animal kingdom, constantly outsmarting larger and stronger animals through pure wit. In one famous tale, Apwoyo tricked the mighty elephant into a tug-of-war contest against a python, pitting them against each other while pretending each was tied to him
stories.title: Apwoyo the Trickster Hare

stories.name: Arash the Archer
stories.excerpt: An Iranian hero sacrifices his life force to shoot an arrow that defines the nation's border.
stories.title: Arash the Archer

stories.name: Areop-Enap: The Spider Who Created the World
stories.excerpt: In Nauruan creation mythology, the primordial being was Areop-Enap, an ancient spider who existed alone in darkness on an endless sea. Searching for food, Areop-Enap found an enormous clam that swallowed him. Inside the darkness, he discovered two snails. He slept three days transferring his power to each snail, then s
stories.title: Areop-Enap: The Spider Who Created the World

stories.name: Arwe: The Serpent King of Ethiopia
stories.excerpt: A giant serpent ruled Ethiopia for four centuries until a clever hero defeated it with poisoned food.
stories.title: Arwe: The Serpent King of Ethiopia

stories.name: Asema, the Vampire of the Rainforest
stories.excerpt: A vampire-like spirit from Surinamese folklore who sheds her skin at night and flies through the forest in search of blood.
stories.title: Asema, the Vampire of the Rainforest

stories.name: Ask and Embla
stories.excerpt: In the time before time, when the world was young and the great void of Ginnungagap had only recently given birth to the first living things, Odin and his brothers Vili and Vé walked along the shore of the newly made world.
stories.title: Ask and Embla

stories.name: Aswang: The Shapeshifter
stories.excerpt: The most feared creature in Philippine folklore—a shapeshifter that eats human flesh, especially unborn children.
stories.title: Aswang: The Shapeshifter

stories.name: Atabey, Mother of Waters and Creation
stories.excerpt: Atabey (also Atabex) is the supreme mother goddess of the Taino people, the indigenous inhabitants of the Greater Antilles. She is the goddess of fresh water, fertility, the earth, and the moon. According to Taino creation myth, Atabey gave birth to herself from all the elements before creating the world. She then prod
stories.title: Atabey, Mother of Waters and Creation

stories.name: Atargatis, the Fish Goddess
stories.excerpt: A goddess who dove into a lake and became half-fish, her scales shimmering in the deep water — because in Lebanon, the boundary between gods and monsters is thinner than the surface of the sea.
stories.title: Atargatis, the Fish Goddess

stories.name: Atira—Mother Corn
stories.excerpt: Atira is the Pawnee goddess of the Earth and wife of Tirawa, the creator god. Her name literally means 'Mother Corn,' and she is associated with the corn that sustained the Pawnee people. Atira is a nurturing figure who provides food and life from the earth. In the Hako (Calumet) ceremony, a symbol representing Atira w
stories.title: Atira—Mother Corn

stories.name: Auriaria and Nei Tituaabine: The Origin of Trees
stories.excerpt: In Kiribati mythology, Auriaria was a red-haired giant chieftain who fell in love with the beautiful red-haired woman Nei Tituaabine. Despite their love, they had no children. When Nei Tituaabine died, Auriaria buried her with great sorrow. From her grave grew three trees: a coconut tree from her head, a pandanus tree
stories.title: Auriaria and Nei Tituaabine: The Origin of Trees

stories.name: Aztlán — The Mythical Homeland of the Aztecs
stories.excerpt: Aztlán is the mythical ancestral homeland of the Aztec (Mexica) peoples, a legendary island paradise from which they began their long migration southward to central Mexico around 1064 CE. According to the Codices Aubin, Boturini, and Azcatitlan, the Mexica left Aztlán guided by their god Huitzilopochtli, who forbade th
stories.title: Aztlán — The Mythical Homeland of the Aztecs

stories.name: Baal, Lord of the Storm
stories.excerpt: The storm god who defeated Yamm, lord of the sea, to become king of the gods — but his victory was bought with blood, and every thunderstorm is a reminder of the war he fought.
stories.title: Baal, Lord of the Storm

stories.name: Baaxpée and the Vision Quest
stories.excerpt: Baaxpée is the sacred power of God (Akbaatatdia) in Crow belief, meaning 'power transcending the ordinary.' To acquire Baaxpée, a Crow must go on a vision quest (bilisshíissanne—'to fast from water'). The quester goes alone to an isolated peak, usually in the Wolf Mountains, fasting without food or water for two to thr
stories.title: Baaxpée and the Vision Quest

stories.name: Baba Yaga
stories.excerpt: A brave girl is tested by the forest witch Baba Yaga and discovers that kindness and guidance can overcome the most terrifying forces.
stories.title: Baba Yaga

stories.name: Baba Yaga: The Witch of the Woods
stories.excerpt: A fearsome witch lives in a hut standing on chicken legs deep in the forest—children must complete tasks to escape her.
stories.title: Baba Yaga: The Witch of the Woods

stories.name: Backoo, the Barnacle Spirit
stories.excerpt: A mischievous water spirit of Guyanese folklore, the Backoo is a small, hairy creature covered in barnacles that lives in rivers and canals.
stories.title: Backoo, the Barnacle Spirit

stories.name: Badang the Strongman
stories.excerpt: Badang is the legendary Malay strongman from ancient Singapura (pre-colonial Singapore) whose feats of strength are celebrated in the Malay Annals (Sejarah Melayu). Originally a slave, Badang gained superhuman strength after consuming the regurgitated vomit of a river spirit — a grotesque but powerful magical substance
stories.title: Badang the Strongman

stories.name: Bahram Gur (Bahram V, the Hunter King)
stories.excerpt: The Sassanid king Bahram V (Bahram Gur), renowned for his love of hunting (especially onager, giving him the epithet 'Gur' meaning onager), is the subject of numerous Persian legends. His exploits include hunting with a lion and an onager as companions, his romance with the Indian princess Sapinud (whom he marries afte
stories.title: Bahram Gur (Bahram V, the Hunter King)

stories.name: Bai Ze: The Beast of Infinite Knowledge
stories.excerpt: A mythical beast appears to the Yellow Emperor, revealing all knowledge of spirits and monsters in the world.
stories.title: Bai Ze: The Beast of Infinite Knowledge

stories.name: Baiame the Sky Father
stories.excerpt: Baiame is the supreme creator god and sky father in the mythology of several Aboriginal Australian peoples of southeastern Australia, including the Kamilaroi, Wiradjuri, and Eora nations. In the Dreamtime, Baiame descended from the sky world to create the land, plants, animals, and humans. He gave the people their laws
stories.title: Baiame the Sky Father

stories.name: Baiame: The Sky Father
stories.excerpt: The great creator spirit who descended from the sky to shape the land and give law to the people.
stories.title: Baiame: The Sky Father

stories.name: Bakru, the Forest Spirit Child
stories.excerpt: A small, childlike forest spirit who can bring wealth to those who capture it but demands terrible sacrifices in return.
stories.title: Bakru, the Forest Spirit Child

stories.name: Bakunawa: The Moon-Eating Serpent
stories.excerpt: In Visayan mythology, Bakunawa is a massive sea serpent or dragon believed to cause eclipses by attempting to swallow the moon. Originally a beautiful sea goddess, Bakunawa was transformed into a serpent as punishment for falling in love with a mortal. Each night she rises from the ocean depths to chase the moon across
stories.title: Bakunawa: The Moon-Eating Serpent

stories.name: Bamboo Hat Guardian
stories.excerpt: Three mysterious strangers reward a kind couple with golden statues, while a greedy merchant finds that stolen blessings bring only ruin.
stories.title: Bamboo Hat Guardian

stories.name: Banshee
stories.excerpt: In Ireland, there is no sound more feared than the wail of the Banshee—the washerwoman of the dead.
stories.title: Banshee

stories.name: Baron Samedi, Lord of the Dead
stories.excerpt: Baron Samedi (Baron Saturday) is one of the most iconic lwa of Haitian Vodou, the master of death, tombs, graveyards, and resurrection. He is depicted wearing a top hat, black tail coat, dark glasses, and cotton plugs in the nostrils like a corpse prepared for burial. Often shown as a skeleton, he speaks in a nasal voi
stories.title: Baron Samedi, Lord of the Dead

stories.name: Barong and Rangda
stories.excerpt: On the Caribbean island of Trinidad, where the heat is thick enough to drink and the nights pulse with the music of crickets and frogs, the old folks tell stories of the Soucouyant.
stories.title: Barong and Rangda

stories.name: Basilisk
stories.excerpt: The Basilisk, known throughout the ancient and medieval worlds as the King of Serpents, is one of the most feared creatures in all of folklore.
stories.title: Basilisk

stories.name: Basilisk: The King of Serpents
stories.excerpt: A rooster-born king of serpents with a deadly gaze is defeated by his own reflection, proving that the greatest power can be its own undoing.
stories.title: Basilisk: The King of Serpents

stories.name: Batu Belah Batu Bertangkup
stories.excerpt: A classic Malay folktale from Perak about a mother who abandons her children after being seduced by a forest spirit. The story follows two siblings, a brother and a sister, left to fend for themselves when their mother disappears into the jungle with a mysterious man. The children wander alone until they encounter a ma
stories.title: Batu Belah Batu Bertangkup

stories.name: Bawang Merah Bawang Putih (Shallot and Garlic)
stories.excerpt: A popular Javanese folktale of two stepsisters: Bawang Putih (Garlic), who is kind, diligent, and beautiful, and Bawang Merah (Shallot), who is spoiled, lazy, and cruel. After their father dies, Bawang Putih is mistreated by her stepmother and stepsister. While washing clothes in the river, she accidentally loses a gar
stories.title: Bawang Merah Bawang Putih (Shallot and Garlic)

stories.name: Bayajidda Slays the Serpent of Daura
stories.excerpt: The foundational legend of the Hausa people tells of Bayajidda (Abu Yazid), a prince from Baghdad who traveled across Africa to Daura, where a fearsome serpent named Sarki guarded the town's only well, the Kusugu well. The serpent only allowed the people to draw water on Fridays. Bayajidda, unaware of the danger, went
stories.title: Bayajidda Slays the Serpent of Daura

stories.name: Beaivi: The Sun Goddess's Journey
stories.excerpt: The myth of Beaivi, the Sámi sun goddess who travels with her daughter through the sky in an enclosure covered with reindeer bones and antlers, bringing spring. In winter, she disappears below the horizon for two months in the far north. On the winter solstice, white female reindeer were sacrificed to ensure her return
stories.title: Beaivi: The Sun Goddess's Journey

stories.name: Beauty and the Beast
stories.excerpt: A beautiful young woman agrees to live with a beast to save her father. Through her kindness and growing love, the beast transforms into a handsome prince.
stories.title: Beauty and the Beast

stories.name: Beauty and the Beast (Swedish)
stories.excerpt: Helena Nyblom's Swedish adaptation of the classic French fairy tale. A merchant's daughter sacrifices herself to live with a hideous Beast to save her father's life. Over time she learns to see past appearance and grows to love the Beast, whose love breaks an enchantment and reveals a handsome prince. Nyblom's version
stories.title: Beauty and the Beast (Swedish)

stories.name: Behula and Lakhindar — The Serpent Goddess's Trial
stories.excerpt: Chand Saudagar, a wealthy merchant and devotee of Shiva, refused to worship the serpent goddess Manasa. In revenge, Manasa killed his six elder sons by snakebite. His last son, Lakhindar, was married to Behula in a specially constructed iron chamber meant to protect him from snakes. But on the wedding night, Manasa sen
stories.title: Behula and Lakhindar — The Serpent Goddess's Trial

stories.name: Behula: The Faithful Wife of Bengali Legend
stories.excerpt: A woman sails her dead husband's body down a river to win his life back from the snake goddess.
stories.title: Behula: The Faithful Wife of Bengali Legend

stories.name: Belliegħa, the Water Witch
stories.excerpt: A water-dwelling spirit from Maltese folklore who guards the freshwater springs and punishes those who waste water.
stories.title: Belliegħa, the Water Witch

stories.name: Belt il-Għasel, the Witch of the Honey Ravine
stories.excerpt: A mysterious witch who lives in a ravine filled with wild honey, luring children with her sweet treats and teaching them hard lessons.
stories.title: Belt il-Għasel, the Witch of the Honey Ravine

stories.name: Berggeist, the Mountain Spirit
stories.excerpt: A nature spirit of the Alps that lives in the mountains of Liechtenstein, the Berggeist guards the mineral wealth and punishes greedy miners.
stories.title: Berggeist, the Mountain Spirit

stories.name: Bergsrå's Secret
stories.excerpt: A respectful miner earns the favor of the Bergsrå, the mountain spirit, discovering that humility and honor are the true keys to unlocking the earth's riches.
stories.title: Bergsrå's Secret

stories.name: Bhil Origin Story — The Birth of the Bhil People
stories.excerpt: The Bhil tribe, one of India's largest Adivasi groups, traces its origin to the god Mahadev (Shiva). According to the myth, Mahadev was roaming the forest when he created a bow and arrow to teach humanity survival. The first Bhil was born from the sweat of Mahadev's brow. Another version tells that the goddess Parvati
stories.title: Bhil Origin Story — The Birth of the Bhil People

stories.name: Bieggolmmái: The Wind God's Shovels
stories.excerpt: Bieggolmmái (the Wind Man) is the god of wind who lives in a cave. He holds two shovels—one to release wind from his cave and one to put it back. According to the Nærøy manuscript, he had a club in his left hand to chase the wind back. He was crucial for reindeer herding because reindeer travel into headwinds to avoid
stories.title: Bieggolmmái: The Wind God's Shovels

stories.name: Big Peter and Little Peter
stories.excerpt: Two brothers of vastly different sizes—one a giant and one tiny—set out to seek their fortune. Though they are opposites in physical stature, they find that their differing abilities complement each other perfectly, allowing them to succeed where others failed.
stories.title: Big Peter and Little Peter

stories.name: Big Water Creature and the Great Flood
stories.excerpt: In the Third World, after the reunion of men and women, a mother and her two daughters missed the raft crossing and swam the river. Big Water Creature (Tééhoołtsódii) seized the daughters and dragged them underwater. Talking God and Water Sprinkler created bowls of white and blue shell that spun an opening to an underw
stories.title: Big Water Creature and the Great Flood

stories.name: Bigorn the Forger of Chains
stories.excerpt: An iron chain spirit called Bigorn haunts the old colonial smithies, binding the wrists of those who enslaved others and forging unbreakable links of conscience.
stories.title: Bigorn the Forger of Chains

stories.name: Bijan and Manijeh
stories.excerpt: Bijan, a knight of Iran and son of Giv, is sent to drive wild boars from Armenian fields. Afterward, the envious knight Gorgin tempts Bijan to cross into enemy Turan by describing the beautiful gardens of Afrasiab. Bijan meets Manijeh, the daughter of Afrasiab, and they fall in love. She drugs him and smuggles him into
stories.title: Bijan and Manijeh

stories.name: Birth of the Harp
stories.excerpt: Wainamoinen creates the first kantele from the jawbone of a giant pike. When he plays the instrument, the music is so hauntingly beautiful that all of nature, animals, and even the gods are moved to tears by the sound.
stories.title: Birth of the Harp

stories.name: Birth of the Nine Diseases
stories.excerpt: In a moment of cosmic imbalance or divine punishment, the nine diseases are created. These ailments spread across the world, bringing suffering, sickness, and death to humanity for the first time.
stories.title: Birth of the Nine Diseases

stories.name: Birth of the Second Harp
stories.excerpt: A second, more powerful harp is fashioned, symbolizing a new era of music and magic. This instrument allows for even deeper insights into the mysteries of the universe and the will of the gods.
