stories.title: Birth of the Second Harp

stories.name: Birth of Wainamoinen
stories.excerpt: In primeval times, the Daughter of the Ether descends to the ocean. A duck nests on her knee, laying six golden eggs and one iron egg. These eggs break, forming the earth, sky, sun, moon, and stars. Wainamoinen is born and spends years in the womb before emerging as an old, wise singer and enchanter who shapes the earl
stories.title: Birth of Wainamoinen

stories.name: Bishop Svedberg and the Devil
stories.excerpt: Bishop Svedberg's wagon loses a wheel on the way to Brunsbo but he calmly continues the journey. Upon arrival he reveals the devil himself had been serving as the missing wheel. The devil later burns down Brunsbo in revenge and the bishop banishes him to hell.
stories.title: Bishop Svedberg and the Devil

stories.name: Blockhead Hans
stories.excerpt: A story about a man who is considered a fool by society, but whose simple, honest nature and unwavering kindness lead to an unexpected positive outcome and the realization of his true worth.
stories.title: Blockhead Hans

stories.name: Blue Jay Finds a Wife (Chinook)
stories.excerpt: Ioi decided it was high time for Blue Jay to quit his playful trickery and settle down with a wife. She told him he must select a wife from the land of the dead, from the Supernatural People. Ioi recommended that Blue Jay choose an old woman and suggested the recently deceased wife of a chief. Blue Jay went to the ghos
stories.title: Blue Jay Finds a Wife (Chinook)

stories.name: Blue Jay Visits Ghost Town (Chinook - Ioi and Blue Jay)
stories.excerpt: Blue Jay's sister Ioi was bought by ghosts as a wife and disappeared to the land of the dead. After a year, Blue Jay went searching for her. He asked all the trees and birds where people go when they die. He journeyed to the ghost town, which appeared to him as a place of bones and decay, but the ghosts saw it as beaut
stories.title: Blue Jay Visits Ghost Town (Chinook - Ioi and Blue Jay)

stories.name: Bluebeard
stories.excerpt: Once there lived a man of immense wealth who owned fine houses in town and country, with silver and gold plate, embroidered furniture, and gilded coaches.
stories.title: Bluebeard

stories.name: Bodu Naga: The Serpent Spirit of the Lagoon
stories.excerpt: Bodu Naga is a great serpent spirit in Maldivian folklore inhabiting lagoons, reefs, and deep channels between islands. In pre-Islamic Maldives, Nagas were revered as powerful nature spirits associated with the waters that surrounded the atolls. Fishermen offered prayers and small offerings before venturing into waters
stories.title: Bodu Naga: The Serpent Spirit of the Lagoon

stories.name: Bonbibi – The Lady of the Sundarbans Forest
stories.excerpt: Bonbibi is the guardian spirit of the Sundarbans mangrove forest, worshipped by both Hindus and Muslims in Bengal and Bangladesh. According to legend, she was sent by Allah to protect forest-dwellers from the demon-king Dakkhin Rai, who ruled the forest in the form of a tiger and demanded human sacrifices. Bonbibi, acc
stories.title: Bonbibi – The Lady of the Sundarbans Forest

stories.name: Bonbibi: The Guardian of the Sundarbans
stories.excerpt: A goddess revered by both Hindus and Muslims protects the people of the Sundarbans from the tiger demon.
stories.title: Bonbibi: The Guardian of the Sundarbans

stories.name: Boots and His Brothers
stories.excerpt: Three brothers try to win a princess by felling a magical oak and digging a well. The older brothers fail and are exiled, but the youngest, Boots, uses magical tools to succeed.
stories.title: Boots and His Brothers

stories.name: Boots and the Troll
stories.excerpt: A poor boy who is ridiculed for wearing oversized boots discovers that the footwear possesses magical properties that allow him to outsmart a greedy troll. Through wit and the strange power of his boots, he manages to secure a fortune and prove his worth to the community that once mocked him.
stories.title: Boots and the Troll

stories.name: Boots Who Made the Princess Say 'That's a Story'
stories.excerpt: A king offers his daughter's hand to anyone who can make her admit a story is a lie. Boots wins by telling an increasingly absurd tale of exaggeration that eventually forces the princess to concede.
stories.title: Boots Who Made the Princess Say 'That's a Story'

stories.name: Boukhencha: The Ogre of the Moroccan Mountains
stories.excerpt: In the villages of the Rif and the Atlas Mountains, where the Berber traditions run deep and the night air carries the scent of mint and cedar, parents tell their children about Boukhencha.
stories.title: Boukhencha: The Ogre of the Moroccan Mountains

stories.name: Bouki the Hyena's Greed (Wolof)
stories.excerpt: Bouki the Hyena found a field of ripe watermelons and decided to eat them all. But each time he took a bite, the vine made a creaking sound that terrified him because he thought it was a farmer approaching. Bouki became so paranoid that he refused to eat alone and begged Leuk the Hare to join him. Leuk agreed on one co
stories.title: Bouki the Hyena's Greed (Wolof)

stories.name: Bouti, the Red Sea Demon
stories.excerpt: A malevolent sea demon of Djiboutian folklore, Bouti rises from the depths during storms to capsize boats and drown sailors.
stories.title: Bouti, the Red Sea Demon

stories.name: Brer Cooter (Terrapin) and the Deer: The Great Race
stories.excerpt: In this Gullah Geechee variant of the classic trickster race tale, Brer Cooter (the terrapin) and Brer Deer are both courting the same young lady. She declares she will marry whichever one wins a ten-mile race. Brer Deer laughs at the slow-moving terrapin, but Brer Cooter is clever. He stations nine members of his fami
stories.title: Brer Cooter (Terrapin) and the Deer: The Great Race

stories.name: Brer Rabbit and the Briar Patch (Bred and Bawn)
stories.excerpt: After Brer Fox captures Brer Rabbit using the Tar-Baby, he declares his intent to kill and eat him. Brer Rabbit pleads for his life, begging not to be thrown into the briar patch, suggesting instead that he be roasted, hanged, drowned, or skinned. The more Brer Rabbit begs to avoid the briar patch, the more determined
stories.title: Brer Rabbit and the Briar Patch (Bred and Bawn)

stories.name: Brer Rabbit and the Moon in the Millpond
stories.excerpt: A classic African American trickster tale in which Brer Rabbit, feeling thirsty, goes to the millpond to drink and sees the moon reflected in the water. Mistaking it for a golden cheese wheel, he tries to retrieve it. Unable to reach it from the bank, he tricks Brer Fox into helping him by claiming there is a valuable
stories.title: Brer Rabbit and the Moon in the Millpond

stories.name: Brer Rabbit Finds His Match at Last
stories.excerpt: Brer Rabbit, overconfident after countless successful tricks, encounters a creature he cannot outsmart. In some versions, it is Old Man Tarrypin (the terrapin) who turns the tables on Brer Rabbit; snip in others, it is a wise old woman or a young girl who matches wits with him. Brer Rabbit tries every trick in his repe
stories.title: Brer Rabbit Finds His Match at Last

stories.name: Brer Rabbit Nibbles Up the Butter
stories.excerpt: Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox, Brer Possum, and Brer Coon together churn butter and set it aside to share later. Brer Rabbit grows hungry and secretly eats all the butter. When the friends discover the butter is gone, Brer Rabbit blames Brer Possum and suggests they test who is guilty by having each lie down in the sun and see
stories.title: Brer Rabbit Nibbles Up the Butter

stories.name: Brer Rabbit Rides Brer Fox
stories.excerpt: Brer Rabbit, seeking to prove his superiority, convinces Miss Meadows and the girls that he can ride Brer Fox like a horse. Brer Fox overhears this boast and vows revenge. The next day, Brer Rabbit pretends to be sick and asks Brer Fox to carry him to Miss Meadows's house. Once on Brer Fox's back, Brer Rabbit digs in h
stories.title: Brer Rabbit Rides Brer Fox

stories.name: Brer Rabbit's Laughing Place
stories.excerpt: Brer Fox catches Brer Rabbit and declares he will finally kill him. Brer Rabbit, always quick-witted, says he does not care about dying but begs to be allowed to visit his 'laughing place' one last time to die happy. Curious, Brer Fox agrees and follows Brer Rabbit into the woods. Brer Rabbit leads him to a hollow tree
stories.title: Brer Rabbit's Laughing Place

stories.name: Brer Terrapin Outruns Brer Rabbit
stories.excerpt: Brer Rabbit, proud of his speed, mocks Brer Terrapin for his slow, plodding pace. Brer Terrapin challenges Brer Rabbit to a race. Knowing he cannot win on speed alone, Brer Terrapin stations his wife and several family members at intervals along the race course. At each mile marker, Brer Rabbit calls out 'Brer Terrapin
stories.title: Brer Terrapin Outruns Brer Rabbit

stories.name: Briar Rose (Sleeping Beauty)
stories.excerpt: In times long past, a king and queen ruled a prosperous kingdom. Centers on Fairy, from Europe. nature-spirit associated with forest and meadow..
stories.title: Briar Rose (Sleeping Beauty)

stories.name: Brother Martin
stories.excerpt: Set during Sweden's Christianization, Brother Martin, a monk from Sigtuna, travels into the remote Bergslagen region to missionize among pagan forest dwellers. The deep woods are still ruled by the old beliefs, and he finds himself unable to convert the stubborn, idolatrous people. As he pushes deeper into the wilderne
stories.title: Brother Martin

stories.name: Bruin and Reynard
stories.excerpt: A series of encounters between Bruin the Bear and Reynard the Fox, where the fox's superior intelligence and deceptive nature allow him to repeatedly outsmart the stronger but slower-witted bear, often leading the bear into ridiculous and embarrassing situations.
stories.title: Bruin and Reynard

stories.name: Bu Darya, the Father of the Sea
stories.excerpt: A powerful sea demon who rules the waters of the Arabian Gulf, demanding respect and tribute from every sailor who ventures into his domain.
stories.title: Bu Darya, the Father of the Sea

stories.name: Bu Draya of the Deep Channel
stories.excerpt: A fleet of pearl divers encounters the Bu Draya, a massive sea creature that guards the deepest channel between Bahrain and the mainland, and must negotiate safe passage.
stories.title: Bu Draya of the Deep Channel

stories.name: Bukha Noyon the Bull God
stories.excerpt: A Buryat myth about Bukha Noyon, the sacred bull god who descended from the sky to create the world. In the beginning, the sky god sent Bukha Noyon, a massive celestial bull, down to the primordial waters. The bull dredged up mud from the bottom with his horns, which the creator used to form the earth. Bukha Noyon then
stories.title: Bukha Noyon the Bull God

stories.name: Bukit Shahbandar (The Warning Hill)
stories.excerpt: A Bruneian legend about Datu Mansur, a corrupt Shahbandar (harbor master) who abused his authority by overtaxing merchants and stealing from the Sultan's treasury. The people suffered under his greed, but none dared speak against him. An elderly village bomoh (shaman) named Nenek Fatimah warned him that the ancestors w
stories.title: Bukit Shahbandar (The Warning Hill)

stories.name: Bukwus the Wild Man of the Woods (Kwakwaka'wakw)
stories.excerpt: Bukwus is the male counterpart of D'Sonoqua, the Wild Man of the Woods in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology. He is a hairy, giant being who lives in the deep forests and is associated with the spirits of those who died by starvation or exposure. Bukwus roams the woods calling out in a hollow voice, trying to lure humans into the
stories.title: Bukwus the Wild Man of the Woods (Kwakwaka'wakw)

stories.name: Bunyip
stories.excerpt: In the billabongs, swamps, and deep waterholes of Australia, there dwells a creature of ancient legend—the Bunyip.
stories.title: Bunyip

stories.name: Bushy Bride
stories.excerpt: A man marries a woman who appears bushy and strange in form, much to the surprise of his family. However, her outward appearance hides a magical nature and a virtuous heart, which eventually bring prosperity and joy to the household.
stories.title: Bushy Bride

stories.name: Buttercup
stories.excerpt: A plump and fond-of-good-things boy named Buttercup is captured by a wicked witch. Despite her terrifying nature, Buttercup uses his quick wit and appetite to outmaneuver her, eventually escaping her clutches to find wealth and freedom.
stories.title: Buttercup

stories.name: Butu, the Sierra Leonean Spirit
stories.excerpt: A forest spirit of Sierra Leone, Butu is a mysterious being that haunts the dense jungles, punishing those who harm the sacred groves.
stories.title: Butu, the Sierra Leonean Spirit

stories.name: Buzz Buzz, the Modern Spirit
stories.excerpt: A mysterious spirit of the modern era, Buzz Buzz is said to manifest through electronic devices, a digital-age counterpart to traditional nature spirits.
stories.title: Buzz Buzz, the Modern Spirit

stories.name: Bwiti, the Sacred Path
stories.excerpt: Bwiti is a central spiritual tradition of Gabon, a sacred practice involving the iboga plant that connects initiates to the spirit world.
stories.title: Bwiti, the Sacred Path

stories.name: Bárðar Saga - The Guardian of Snæfell
stories.excerpt: Bárðr, born of a human mother and a father who was half-giant and half-troll, settles in Snæfellsnes. After a series of family conflicts involving his brother and children, Bárðr gives away his land and vanishes into the Snæfellsjökull ice cap. He becomes the guardian spirit of the region, appearing in a grey cowl to h
stories.title: Bárðar Saga - The Guardian of Snæfell

stories.name: Bárðar Saga - The Mound of King Raknarr
stories.excerpt: Gestr, the son of Bárðr, journeys to the far north to challenge the undead King Raknarr. With the help of a priest and a magic candle, Gestr enters Raknarr's burial mound and beheads the king and his 500 undead crew. However, the magic candle fails, and Gestr is only saved by the divine light of King Olaf, who drains t
stories.title: Bárðar Saga - The Mound of King Raknarr

stories.name: Calon Arang the Witch
stories.excerpt: Before the Maori arrived in New Zealand, the islands were already inhabited by mysterious beings whose stories predate human memory. Calon Arang is one such tale — a story of dark magic and the terror it unleashed upon an ancient kingdom.
stories.title: Calon Arang the Witch

stories.name: Capture of the Fire-fish
stories.excerpt: To restore light and warmth, the heroes embark on a perilous journey to the depths of the ocean to capture a magical fire-fish, which is the only source of fire remaining in the world.
stories.title: Capture of the Fire-fish

stories.name: Capture of the Sampo
stories.excerpt: The heroes of Kalevala successfully infiltrate Pohjola and steal the Sampo. A thrilling and dangerous chase ensues as Louhi, the Mistress of Pohjola, pursues them with all her might to reclaim the magical mill.
stories.title: Capture of the Sampo

stories.name: Cedar Woman (Ts'uu Jaas) and the Cedar Tree (Haida)
stories.excerpt: In Haida worldview, the Cedar Tree is considered an Ancient Sister called Ts'uu Jaasas. She is a SGaana Kiidads (Supernatural Being) and a physical manifestation of the Haida people's interconnected relationship with the land and sea. The cedar tree is regarded as every woman's older sister, known as Ts'uu K'waayGa. Th
stories.title: Cedar Woman (Ts'uu Jaas) and the Cedar Tree (Haida)

stories.name: Cerberus
stories.excerpt: At the gates of the Underworld, where the River Styx flows black and cold and the souls of the dead drift like shadows in the mist, there stands a guardian that has never been bribed, never been tricked, and never been defeated.
stories.title: Cerberus

stories.name: Chang Er on the Moon
stories.excerpt: A very long time ago, in the age when gods still walked among mortals, there were ten suns in the sky.
stories.title: Chang Er on the Moon

stories.name: Changer and the Creation of the World (Coast Salish)
stories.excerpt: In Coast Salish tradition, dukʷibəɬ the Changer (also known as Xe'las or Xelas) walked the earth when the world was not yet as it is today. Sometimes he appeared as a brilliant light from the East, sometimes as a young man, sometimes as several young men, and sometimes as an invisible old person who knew everything. Th
stories.title: Changer and the Creation of the World (Coast Salish)

stories.name: Changó, the Lord of Thunder and Fire
stories.excerpt: Changó (Shangó) is the powerful orisha of thunder, lightning, fire, and war in Cuban Santería/Lucumí, syncretized with Saint Barbara in Catholic tradition. According to myth, Changó was once a king of the Yoruba city of Oyo who was deified after death. He wields a double-headed axe and dances with fiery intensity. Chan
stories.title: Changó, the Lord of Thunder and Fire

stories.name: Charcoal Nils and the Troll-Woman
stories.excerpt: A Swedish tale of Nils, a charcoal burner, who encounters a troll-woman in the forest. He outwits her through cleverness and escapes her supernatural traps.
stories.title: Charcoal Nils and the Troll-Woman

stories.name: Charonda the Blood-Drinker
stories.excerpt: In the villages of the Karpas Peninsula, the Charonda rises each night to drain the vitality of the living, leaving only hollow shells where people once stood.
stories.title: Charonda the Blood-Drinker

stories.name: Chata and Chicksah: The Separation of the Choctaw and Chickasaw (Choctaw/Chickasaw)
stories.excerpt: Two brothers named Chata and Chicksah led their people from the west, following a sacred pole. Each night they planted the pole in the ground, and each morning they traveled in the direction it leaned. After an immensely long journey, they finally reached a place where the pole stood perfectly upright. There, they laid
stories.title: Chata and Chicksah: The Separation of the Choctaw and Chickasaw (Choctaw/Chickasaw)

stories.name: Cheval Mal Fet, the Cursed Steed
stories.excerpt: A ghostly black horse that appears on the roads of Wallonia, carrying a demonic rider who tempts travelers into deadly bargains.
stories.title: Cheval Mal Fet, the Cursed Steed

stories.name: Cheyenne Creation Story
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, all was water and nothing existed but the Creator Ma'heo'o and aquatic birds. The Creator sent various waterbirds—the loon, otter, beaver, and turtle—to dive to the bottom of the endless water to bring up mud. After several failures, the turtle succeeded in bringing up the primordial mud. From this mu
stories.title: Cheyenne Creation Story

stories.name: Chhinnamasta — The Self-Decapitated Goddess
stories.excerpt: Goddess Chhinnamasta (the 'Self-Decapitated One') is a powerful Tantric deity worshipped primarily in Bengal and parts of eastern India. The legend tells that once, while bathing in the Mandakini River with her attendants Dakini and Varnini, Parvati (in her form as Chhinnamasta) was overcome by a ravenous hunger that h
stories.title: Chhinnamasta — The Self-Decapitated Goddess

stories.name: Chickasaw Creation and the Sacred Pole (Chickasaw)
stories.excerpt: The Chickasaw creation story tells of their emergence as a people guided by a sacred pole. According to tradition, the Chickasaw and Choctaw were originally one people who migrated from the west. They carried a sacred pole (sometimes described as a dogwood pole) which they planted each night. Each morning, they would t
stories.title: Chickasaw Creation and the Sacred Pole (Chickasaw)

stories.name: Chickasaw Flood Myth (Chickasaw)
stories.excerpt: The Chickasaw flood myth tells of a time when the earth was covered by a great deluge. As the waters rose, the people climbed to the highest ground, but the water continued to rise. Ababinili, the Creator, instructed a man and a woman to build a raft and take on board pairs of all the animals. The flood covered even th
stories.title: Chickasaw Flood Myth (Chickasaw)

stories.name: Chimera
stories.excerpt: The Chimera was not one monster but three, all wrapped into one terrible form.. Its head was the head of a lion—the king of beasts—but wrong, changed.
stories.title: Chimera

stories.name: Chimi Lhakhang and the Divine Madman Drukpa Kunley
stories.excerpt: Chimi Lhakhang (the Fertility Temple) in Punakha district, Bhutan, is associated with Drukpa Kunley (1455–1529), the 'Divine Madman' — a Buddhist monk famous for his outrageous methods of teaching. When three demonesses terrorized the Dochula Pass, Drukpa Kunley pursued them to Lobesa Hill, where the chief demoness Lor
stories.title: Chimi Lhakhang and the Divine Madman Drukpa Kunley

stories.name: Chinthe: The Lion Guardians of the Burmese Pagodas
stories.excerpt: Half-lion half-dragon guardians protect the entrances of pagodas across Myanmar.
stories.title: Chinthe: The Lion Guardians of the Burmese Pagodas

stories.name: Chitapo of the Silent Lake
stories.excerpt: A woman grieving the loss of her child wanders to a lake in the Bangweulu wetlands and encounters Chitapo, a lake spirit who offers to return what was taken but demands a price measured in memory.
stories.title: Chitapo of the Silent Lake

stories.name: Chiuta, the Spider Who Wove the World
stories.excerpt: Before the world had form, Chiuta the Spider sat upon the void and spun the first web — and from that web, the rivers, the mountains, and the people were born.
stories.title: Chiuta, the Spider Who Wove the World

stories.name: Chiwara: The Antelope Spirit Who Taught Agriculture
stories.excerpt: The Bambara people of Mali revere Chiwara, a mythical half-human, half-antelope being who taught humans the fundamentals of agriculture. Chiwara used its antlers and a pointed stick to dig into the earth, making it possible for humans to cultivate the land. The people watched the antelope and followed its example to cr
stories.title: Chiwara: The Antelope Spirit Who Taught Agriculture

stories.name: Choctaw Creation: The Emergence from Nanih Waiya (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, there was a great mound called Nanih Waiya. The Creator fashioned the first people from the earth within this mound. These first Choctaw emerged from a long, dark cave that led from the center of the mound into daylight. After emerging, they scattered across the land to populate the earth. When a grea
stories.title: Choctaw Creation: The Emergence from Nanih Waiya (Choctaw)

stories.name: Chuhayster: The Windy Grandfather of the Carpathians
stories.excerpt: A cheerful forest spirit protects travelers from the dangerous mavkas in the Carpathian Mountains.
stories.title: Chuhayster: The Windy Grandfather of the Carpathians

stories.name: Chupacabra: The Goat Sucker
stories.excerpt: A creature that drains the blood of livestock, appearing after strange lights in the Puerto Rican night.
stories.title: Chupacabra: The Goat Sucker

stories.name: Chura-Batyr: The Hero of Kazan
stories.excerpt: Chura-Batyr is the heroic epic of the Tatar people, set in the mid-16th century during the Kazan Khanate's struggle against the expanding Moscow state. Chura is a batyr (hero) who defends Kazan against Russian invasion. The epic contains ancient motifs including Chura's miraculous birth to elderly parents after years o
stories.title: Chura-Batyr: The Hero of Kazan

stories.name: Chyskhaan, the Snow Spirit
stories.excerpt: The Yakut legend of Chyskhaan, the powerful spirit of winter and cold who rules over the frozen landscape of Siberia. Chyskhaan is depicted as a towering figure with icy breath that can freeze anything instantly and a heart made of permafrost. He is both feared and respected by the Sakha people, as he governs the long,
stories.title: Chyskhaan, the Snow Spirit

stories.name: Cinderella
stories.excerpt: A mistreated girl goes to the ball with magic help. Centers on Fairy, from Europe. nature-spirit associated with forest and meadow..
stories.title: Cinderella

stories.name: Comanche Creation: The Dust People
stories.excerpt: The Great Spirit collected swirls of dust from the four directions—north, south, east, and west—and molded them into strong, powerful figures. He breathed life into them, and the Comanche people were born from the earth itself, infused with the strength of mighty storms and the spirit of the wind. However, a shape-shif
stories.title: Comanche Creation: The Dust People

stories.name: Corn Woman (Creek)
stories.excerpt: Corn Woman is a central figure in Muscogee Creek mythology. Her origin story varies across traditions: in one version, corn fell from a woman's feet after she rubbed them together; in another, corn poured from her thigh after she scratched it. Many legends end with Corn Woman sacrificing herself to allow corn crops to
stories.title: Corn Woman (Creek)

stories.name: Corn Woman and the Origin of Corn (Natchez)
stories.excerpt: The Natchez legend of Corn Woman (also known as Corn-Woman's Son) tells how agriculture came to the people. According to the story, Corn Woman gave birth to a son and from her body came the first corn. In one version, corn poured from her thigh when she scratched it. In another, she sacrificed herself so that corn woul
stories.title: Corn Woman and the Origin of Corn (Natchez)

stories.name: Coviella
stories.excerpt: In the sun-drenched hills of the Italian countryside, where olive groves stretch across terraced slopes and the scent of rosemary and thyme drifts on the warm breeze, there once lived a young woman named Coviella.
stories.title: Coviella

stories.name: Coyote and Eagle Steal the Sun and Moon
stories.excerpt: A Zuni story explaining the origin of day and night and the changing seasons. In the beginning, the Sun and Moon were kept locked in boxes by a powerful being who would not release them. The world was in perpetual twilight. Coyote and Eagle, two of the most clever animals, devised a plan. Eagle flew to the being's home
stories.title: Coyote and Eagle Steal the Sun and Moon

stories.name: Coyote and the Creation of the Tribes (Chinook/Chelan)
stories.excerpt: Long ago, the Great Chief Above made the world, then the animals and birds. After twelve moons, the animal people gathered. Bluejay, Meadowlark, and Coyote complained about their names, but the Creator declared that names would stay as given. The Creator told Coyote he would be the head of all creatures and given power
stories.title: Coyote and the Creation of the Tribes (Chinook/Chelan)

stories.name: Coyote Helps Decorate the Night
stories.excerpt: In this Hopi story about the origins of the night sky, the animals were decorating the darkness. Various animals placed stars and patterns in the sky, but Coyote, growing impatient with the slow, careful work, grabbed a handful of stars and threw them carelessly across the sky. This explains why some stars are scattere
stories.title: Coyote Helps Decorate the Night

stories.name: Coyote the Comanche Trickster
stories.excerpt: Coyote is the central trickster figure in Comanche folklore. Unlike the spider tricksters of other Plains tribes, Coyote is a clever but flawed creature who often helps humans while constantly getting into trouble due to greed, dishonesty, and recklessness. Many Comanche storytellers refer to Coyote affectionately as t
stories.title: Coyote the Comanche Trickster

stories.name: Crab Water-Spirit of the Mangroves
stories.excerpt: A water spirit in crab form guards the mangrove forests and coral reefs, dragging fishermen who poison the water into the tides to learn the sea's lessons firsthand.
stories.title: Crab Water-Spirit of the Mangroves

stories.name: Crane and Changer (Coast Salish)
stories.excerpt: As told by Snoqualmie Charlie, this story recounts how dukʷibəɬ the Changer came upon a man with very long legs standing by the shore, getting hit over the head by rocks. The Changer asked what he was doing, and the man explained he was trying to get food but the rocks kept hurting him. The Changer took the rocks, decl
stories.title: Crane and Changer (Coast Salish)

stories.name: Creation of the Sun and Moon
stories.excerpt: In the Fourth World of Navajo tradition, First Man, First Woman, and Great Coyote planned the creation of the sun and moon. They summoned Black God (Fire God) from beneath the earth along with Water Sprinkler, House God, and Talking God. Turquoise Boy agreed to become the Sun and White Shell Girl the Moon, but demanded
stories.title: Creation of the Sun and Moon

stories.name: Crow Morning Star
stories.excerpt: In Crow belief, the Morning Star (Aapisowaahs) is a heroic figure who lights the night sky. He is the son of Naato'si (the Sun) and Ko'komiki'somm (the Moon), created by the first being Apistotoke. Old Man Coyote traveled to the sky world and brought knowledge of the Morning Star back to the people. The Morning Star is
stories.title: Crow Morning Star

stories.name: Cunjah Maum and the Healing Roots
stories.excerpt: On a rice plantation along the South Carolina coast, an old Gullah woman named Cunjah Maum was known as the most powerful rootworker in the Lowcountry. When the master's daughter fell ill with a mysterious fever that no doctor could cure, the master reluctantly sent for Cunjah Maum. She came to the big house and asked
stories.title: Cunjah Maum and the Healing Roots

stories.name: Curupira: The Forest Guardian of Brazil
stories.excerpt: A forest spirit with backward-facing feet protects the Amazon from those who would destroy it.
stories.title: Curupira: The Forest Guardian of Brazil

stories.name: Cú Chulainn and the Salmon of Knowledge
stories.excerpt: In the green, rolling hills of ancient Ireland, beside the silver waters of the River Boyne, there lived a poet named Finegas.
stories.title: Cú Chulainn and the Salmon of Knowledge

stories.name: D'Sonoqua (Dzunukwa) and the Children (Kwakwaka'wakw)
stories.excerpt: D'Sonoqua, also known as Dzunukwa or Tsonokwa, is the Wild Woman of the Woods, a giant cannibal ogress in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition. She is black in color with messy hair, pendulous breasts, pursed red lips, and carries a huge basket on her back. She wanders the forests calling 'Hu! Hu!' - a sound that children are told
stories.title: D'Sonoqua (Dzunukwa) and the Children (Kwakwaka'wakw)

stories.name: Dag and Daga, and the Flying Troll of Sky Mountain
stories.excerpt: Dag and Daga are orphaned siblings who live alone in a forest cottage after their parents die. Despite being young, they manage to survive through their own resourcefulness: Dag hunts with his bow, and Daga gathers herbs, berries, and mushrooms. They live happily until one day Dag goes hunting and does not return. Daga
stories.title: Dag and Daga, and the Flying Troll of Sky Mountain

stories.name: Dakuwaqa the Shark God
stories.excerpt: Dakuwaqa is a fearsome shark deity in Fijian mythology who appears as a fierce sea monster guarding the islands. He was greatly respected by fishermen for protecting them from danger at sea. In one creation myth, Dakuwaqa attempted to conquer Kadavu Island by swimming up a river, but the goddess Rokobakaniceva challeng
stories.title: Dakuwaqa the Shark God

stories.name: Dame Soåsan
stories.excerpt: A powerful female troll named Dame Soåsan lives in the hills near Eksjö. She punishes those who insult her and rewards those who show kindness. A poor woman who spins yarn for her grows rich but becomes greedy, cheats the trolls, and loses everything. A servant girl who is kind to troll children is rewarded with cows t
stories.title: Dame Soåsan

stories.name: Dangun: The Founder of Korea
stories.excerpt: A divine being descends from heaven and marries a bear to found the first Korean kingdom.
stories.title: Dangun: The Founder of Korea

stories.name: Davy Crockett
stories.excerpt: The legendary king of the wild frontier, folk hero of American expansion and tall-tale tradition.
stories.title: Davy Crockett

stories.name: Death of Lemminkainen
stories.excerpt: While attempting to kill the swans in the river of the underworld (Tuonela), Lemminkainen is ambushed and killed. His body is brutally torn to pieces and scattered across the river, symbolizing the ultimate price of his hubris and reckless ambition.
stories.title: Death of Lemminkainen

stories.name: Degei the Serpent God
stories.excerpt: The creator god who brought humans from the mountains. Centers on Degei, from Fiji. deity associated with Polynesian heavens and Polynesian sacred sites..
stories.title: Degei the Serpent God

stories.name: Degei the Serpent God and the Creation of Fiji
stories.excerpt: Degei, the supreme god of Fijian mythology, is a great serpent who created the world, fruits, and the first humans. He hatched an egg from which the first human couple emerged. Degei lives in a cave near the summit of Mount Uluda in the Nakauvandra Range. Earthquakes and thunder are caused by his uneasy turnings within
stories.title: Degei the Serpent God and the Creation of Fiji

stories.name: Departure of Changing Woman
stories.excerpt: In Navajo tradition, after the monsters were defeated and the world was made safe, Changing Woman decided to leave the earth. She gathered the Holy People and announced her departure to the West. She created a beautiful floating house made of turquoise, abalone shell, white shell, and jet, located on an island in the w
stories.title: Departure of Changing Woman

stories.name: Devi, the Mountain Giant
stories.excerpt: A race of giants who once ruled the mountains of Georgia before humans drove them into the deep caves, where they still wait to reclaim the surface.
stories.title: Devi, the Mountain Giant

stories.name: Dharumavantha Rasgefaanu: First Convert to Islam
stories.excerpt: Dharumavantha Rasgefaanu (Sultan Dhovemi) was the king of the Maldives who converted to Islam in 1153 CE, marking the nation's transformation from Buddhism to Islam. According to Maldivian tradition, the king's conversion was triggered by the miracle of Abu'l-Barakat al-Barbari, who vanquished the sea demon Rannamaari
stories.title: Dharumavantha Rasgefaanu: First Convert to Islam

stories.name: Dhegdheer: The Cannibal Woman with Long Ears
stories.excerpt: Dhegdheer ('Long-Ears') was once a normal woman whose selfishness and greed cursed her into a monstrous form. Her ears grew enormous, granting her supernatural hearing — she could detect the faintest heartbeat from miles away. She developed an insatiable hunger for human flesh, particularly children, and would creep si
stories.title: Dhegdheer: The Cannibal Woman with Long Ears

stories.name: Didibri, the Rainbow Dragon
stories.excerpt: A great dragon-like serpent associated with the rainbow, sometimes a bringer of destruction and other times a protector of hidden treasure.
stories.title: Didibri, the Rainbow Dragon

stories.name: Diné Bahaneʼ: The Four Worlds
stories.excerpt: The Navajo creation epic describes four worlds through which the Diyin Dineʼé (Holy People) journeyed. The First World (Niʼ Hodiłhił, Black World) was small with a floating island in four seas, inhabited by Air-Spirit People, insect people, and the four rulers of the seas. First Woman (Áłtsé Asdzą́ą́) and First Man (Áł
stories.title: Diné Bahaneʼ: The Four Worlds

stories.name: Ditaolane Slays the Devourer Khanyapa
stories.excerpt: In Basotho mythology, the monstrous Khanyapa (also called Kholumolumo or Kgodumodumo) went about swallowing every living thing in its path, devouring entire villages until only one pregnant woman survived by hiding in a stable, her scent masked by ashes. She prayed to Modimo and gave birth to a son named Ditaolane, who
stories.title: Ditaolane Slays the Devourer Khanyapa

stories.name: Div (Daeva), the Demon of the Waste
stories.excerpt: A powerful demon from Zoroastrian tradition who brings drought, disease, and despair to the people of the Afghan highlands.
stories.title: Div (Daeva), the Demon of the Waste

stories.name: Div-e Sepid, the White Demon
stories.excerpt: A legendary white demon from Persian epic tradition, the Div-e Sepid is a monstrous being of immense strength who terrorized the heroes of old.
stories.title: Div-e Sepid, the White Demon

stories.name: Djinn
stories.excerpt: Before humans, before the world was made as it is now, there were beings made of smokeless fire—beings that did not burn, because they were the fire itself.
stories.title: Djinn

stories.name: Doll i' the Grass
stories.excerpt: A tiny, fairy-like girl discovered in the grass is initially seen as a curiosity. Through her bravery, intelligence, and helpfulness, she becomes indispensable to the royal family, demonstrating that even the smallest among us can possess the greatest strength of character.
stories.title: Doll i' the Grass

stories.name: Don Pedrito Jaramillo — The Healer of Los Olmos
stories.excerpt: Don Pedro Jaramillo (1829–1907) is the most famous curandero (traditional healer) and folk saint of South Texas. Born to Purépecha parents in Guadalajara, Mexico, he received his healing calling after a vision during a three-day treatment for a nose ailment with mud and water. He moved to the Los Olmos Creek area near
stories.title: Don Pedrito Jaramillo — The Healer of Los Olmos

stories.name: Doña Sebastiana — The Skeleton in the Cart
stories.excerpt: Doña Sebastiana is a folk figure from New Mexican Hispano culture, depicted as a skeleton riding a wooden cart or chariot, carrying a bow and arrow. She is the northern New Mexican variant of the Grim Reaper, brought by Spanish colonists and merged with Indigenous death imagery. Unlike the anonymous European Death, Doñ
stories.title: Doña Sebastiana — The Skeleton in the Cart

stories.name: Drakaina of the Copper Mines
stories.excerpt: Beneath the ancient copper mines of Skouriotissa, a dragon守护 the veins of ore and punishes those who take more than the earth can spare.
stories.title: Drakaina of the Copper Mines

stories.name: Draugar of the Barrow
stories.excerpt: A wicked Viking warrior is cursed to remain as an undead draugr, haunting his burial barrow and punishing those who seek his stolen silver.
stories.title: Draugar of the Barrow

stories.name: Draugur (Faroese Revenant Legends)
stories.excerpt: In Faroese folklore, the draugur (dreygur) is a malevolent undead being or revenant, akin to the Norse draugr. Draugar are described as large in build, wearing grey clothes with black hair—the same description given for Huldufólk in Faroese tradition. They are said to inhabit graves, mounds, and coastal areas, often gu
stories.title: Draugur (Faroese Revenant Legends)

stories.name: Drukpa Kunley Subduing the Demoness of the Pass
stories.excerpt: The most famous legend of the Divine Madman Drukpa Kunley recounts his confrontation with the three demonesses of Dochula La. Two lesser demonesses merged into the body of the chief demoness Loro Duem and fled to Punakha. When Loro Duem reached the hillock of Lobesa, she disguised herself as a red dog. Drukpa Kunley, u
stories.title: Drukpa Kunley Subduing the Demoness of the Pass

stories.name: Duende of the Ceiba Cathedral
stories.excerpt: A young boy who befriends a forest Duende learns that the small spirits of the Belizean jungle guard the ancient ceiba trees, and their friendship comes with a duty to protect what cannot protect itself.
stories.title: Duende of the Ceiba Cathedral

stories.name: Duende, the Forest Guardian
stories.excerpt: A small, dwarf-like forest spirit who protects the animals and trees of the Ecuadorian highlands.
stories.title: Duende, the Forest Guardian

stories.name: Dukher Boro — The Great Sorrow of Bengal
stories.excerpt: Dukher Boro (literally 'Elder Brother of Sorrow') is a tragic figure from the Maimansingha Gitika, a collection of Bengali folk ballads from the Mymensingh region of Bangladesh. The ballad tells of a virtuous man who experiences immense suffering and loss through no fault of his own — losing his family, property, and s
stories.title: Dukher Boro — The Great Sorrow of Bengal

stories.name: Dullahan
stories.excerpt: The headless rider of Irish folklore who heralds death with his grim procession.
stories.title: Dullahan

stories.name: Dullahan: The Headless Horseman
stories.excerpt: A headless warrior who rides at night, carrying his own head—and anyone who watches is marked for death.
stories.title: Dullahan: The Headless Horseman

stories.name: Duppy: The Restless Spirits of Jamaica
stories.excerpt: Duppies are restless spirits in Jamaican folklore, believed to be the souls of the dead who have not found peace. Good duppies appear in dreams (called 'dream you') to give advice or information from deceased family and friends. Bad duppies can cause harm and may be set on someone through obeah (sorcery). Duppies are s
stories.title: Duppy: The Restless Spirits of Jamaica

stories.name: Durga
stories.excerpt: Long before the age of men, when the cosmic forces of good and evil were locked in an eternal struggle, there arose a demon unlike any the universe had seen before.
stories.title: Durga

stories.name: Dutchman, the Guyanese Phantom
stories.excerpt: The ghost of a Dutch colonist who wanders the plantations and canals of Guyana, forever searching for the treasure he buried and never reclaimed.
stories.title: Dutchman, the Guyanese Phantom

stories.name: Dwen and the Spirit of the Hidden Valley
stories.excerpt: A grieving mother is led by a mysterious spirit into a hidden valley where the boundaries between the living and the dead grow thin, and learns that love does not end at death.
stories.title: Dwen and the Spirit of the Hidden Valley

stories.name: Dwenn: The Stone That Remembers
stories.excerpt: A stonemason building a church in the hills above St. David's encounters the Dwenn, a spirit of the land itself, and learns that some stones hold the memory of everything that has ever happened upon them.
stories.title: Dwenn: The Stone That Remembers

stories.name: Dybbuk, the Clinging Spirit
stories.excerpt: A dybbuk is a restless spirit in Jewish folklore that possesses the living to resolve unfinished business, clinging to its host until exorcised.
stories.title: Dybbuk, the Clinging Spirit

stories.name: Dze-temi, the Night Hunter
stories.excerpt: A spectral hunter who rides through the night sky, chasing the souls of the dead, because in Georgia the hunt never ends.
stories.title: Dze-temi, the Night Hunter

stories.name: Dzudzerume, the Mountain Witch
stories.excerpt: A mountain witch who steals children and replaces them with changelings, because in Georgia the mountains take what they want.
stories.title: Dzudzerume, the Mountain Witch

stories.name: Džambas, the Macedonian Demon
stories.excerpt: A demonic creature of North Macedonian folklore, Džambas haunts the forests and mountains, leading travelers astray with eerie lights.
stories.title: Džambas, the Macedonian Demon

stories.name: Each Uisge
stories.excerpt: In the Scottish Highlands, the water spirits called Each Uisge haunt the fords and bridges of the wild rivers.
stories.title: Each Uisge

stories.name: East of the Sun and West of the Moon
stories.excerpt: A courageous girl journeys to the ends of the earth to rescue her love from a cruel enchantment.
stories.title: East of the Sun and West of the Moon

stories.name: Ebbe Skamelson
stories.excerpt: Knight Ebbe Skamelson betroths the beautiful Malfred before departing for the Crusades for seven years. Believing him dead, Malfred's mother betroths her to another. Ebbe returns during the wedding feast and in rage kills Malfred, her mother, and the bridegroom. He seeks papal absolution but cannot find peace, and is s
stories.title: Ebbe Skamelson

stories.name: Egle: The Queen of Serpents
stories.excerpt: A young woman marries a serpent king and must choose between her husband and her family in Lithuania's greatest folk tale.
stories.title: Egle: The Queen of Serpents

stories.name: El Aro, the Spectral Ring
stories.excerpt: A ghostly apparition in Honduran folklore, El Aro is a spectral ring that rolls through the streets at night, foretelling death or disaster.
stories.title: El Aro, the Spectral Ring

stories.name: El Bacá: The Demonic Familiar of Dominican Folklore
stories.excerpt: A shapeshifting demon brings wealth to its master in exchange for blood sacrifices.
stories.title: El Bacá: The Demonic Familiar of Dominican Folklore

stories.name: El Boyo: The Mournful Ghost
stories.excerpt: El Boyo is a sorrowful ghost haunting the rivers and swamps of Nicaragua, the restless spirit of a drowned man whose eerie wailing warns travelers away from dangerous waters.
stories.title: El Boyo: The Mournful Ghost

stories.name: El Cadejo and the Drunkard
stories.excerpt: A drunkard who mocked the Cadejo and was found dead on the road the next morning, because in Panama the things you laugh at are the things that laugh last.
stories.title: El Cadejo and the Drunkard

stories.name: El Cadejo, the Dog of the Night
stories.excerpt: A large spectral dog that appears at night, sometimes white and protective, sometimes black and deadly, because in Panama every traveler needs a guardian or a grave.
stories.title: El Cadejo, the Dog of the Night

stories.name: El Cadejo, the Honduran Spirit Dog
stories.excerpt: A legendary spirit dog of Honduras, El Cadejo appears as a large shaggy beast with glowing eyes, alternately a protector and a portent of doom.
stories.title: El Cadejo, the Honduran Spirit Dog

stories.name: El Caleuche: The Ghost Ship of Chiloé
stories.excerpt: A brilliantly lit ghost ship crewed by witches and demons sails the canals of southern Chile, luring sailors to their doom.
stories.title: El Caleuche: The Ghost Ship of Chiloé

stories.name: El Chupacabra
stories.excerpt: The goat-sucking creature of Puerto Rican legend, blamed for mysterious livestock deaths.
stories.title: El Chupacabra

stories.name: El Chupacabra in the Texas Borderlands
stories.excerpt: Throughout the 2000s and 2010s, dozens of alleged Chupacabra carcasses were reported across Texas, particularly in San Antonio, Cuero, Hood County, and Coleman County. Ranchers described finding livestock with puncture wounds and drained of blood, often attributing the attacks to a strange, hairless creature. In Cuero
stories.title: El Chupacabra in the Texas Borderlands

stories.name: El Chupacabra — The Goat-Sucker
stories.excerpt: The Chupacabra is a legendary cryptid that first appeared in Puerto Rico in 1995, blamed for mysterious livestock killings in which animals were found drained of blood. Descriptions vary: in Puerto Rico and Latin America it is often depicted as a reptilian, alien-like creature with spines along its back, standing 3-4 f
stories.title: El Chupacabra — The Goat-Sucker

stories.name: El Coco — The Boogeyman of the Spanish-Speaking World
stories.excerpt: El Coco, also known as El Coco Man or El Hombre del Costal (the Sack Man), is a bogeyman figure used throughout the Spanish-speaking world to frighten children into good behavior. The figure likely has Moorish origins, derived from the Arabic word for 'fear.' In the Mexican-American and Chicano communities of the South
stories.title: El Coco — The Boogeyman of the Spanish-Speaking World

stories.name: El Cuchubo, the Shadow Thief
stories.excerpt: A small hairy creature that steals shadows, leaving its victims alive but without a shadow, because in Panama even your shadow can be taken.
stories.title: El Cuchubo, the Shadow Thief

stories.name: El Cucuy — The Monster Under the Bed
stories.excerpt: El Cucuy is a distinctly Mexican and Mexican-American variant of the bogeyman legend, particularly prevalent in the US Southwest among Chicano families. Unlike the more generic El Coco, El Cucuy is specifically described as a small, hairy, goblin-like creature who lives under children's beds or in dark closets, waiting
stories.title: El Cucuy — The Monster Under the Bed

stories.name: El Cuellado, the Long Neck
stories.excerpt: A creature with an impossibly long neck that peers into windows at night, watching families sleep, because in Panama even the walls have eyes.
stories.title: El Cuellado, the Long Neck

stories.name: El Dorado
stories.excerpt: High in the cold, windswept plateau of the Colombian Andes, there lies a lake of dark, still water, ringed by ancient mountains and shrouded in mist.
stories.title: El Dorado

stories.name: El Duende — The Gnomelike Trickster
stories.excerpt: El Duende is a small, gnomelike creature from Spanish and Latin American folklore who has a prominent place in Mexican-American oral tradition. Described as a tiny old man or child-like figure wearing a large hat and often carrying a walking stick, El Duende lives in forests, caves, or abandoned buildings. He is known
stories.title: El Duende — The Gnomelike Trickster

stories.name: El Duende, the Costa Rican Trickster
stories.excerpt: A small, mischievous forest spirit of Costa Rica, El Duende leads travelers astray and plays pranks on those who wander into his domain.
stories.title: El Duende, the Costa Rican Trickster

stories.name: El Jinete Sin Cabeza del Valle — The Headless Horseman of the Valley
stories.excerpt: While the headless horseman is a figure known in many cultures, the Hispanic version from the Rio Grande Valley and northern Mexico has unique characteristics. Known as El Jinete Sin Cabeza, this specter is said to be the ghost of a Spanish conquistador or a Mexican rancher who lost his head in battle — either during t
stories.title: El Jinete Sin Cabeza del Valle — The Headless Horseman of the Valley

stories.name: El Lobizón: The Argentine Werewolf
stories.excerpt: In the vast plains of Argentina, where the pampas stretch to the horizon and the cattle graze beneath a sky that seems too large for the world, there is a curse so deeply believed that the government passed a law to protect its victims.
stories.title: El Lobizón: The Argentine Werewolf

stories.name: El Nahual — The Shapeshifting Witch
stories.excerpt: El Nahual (or Nagual) is a shapeshifting witch or sorcerer in Mesoamerican and Hispanic folklore, with a strong presence in Mexican-American tradition. The belief, originating with the Aztecs and other Nahua peoples, holds that certain individuals have the spiritual power to transform into animals — most commonly jagua
stories.title: El Nahual — The Shapeshifting Witch

stories.name: El Niño Fidencio — The Child Healer of Espinazo
stories.excerpt: El Niño Fidencio (José de Jesús Fidencio Sintora, 1898–1938) is a Mexican folk saint and curandero whose cult center is in Espinazo, Nuevo León, and whose devotion extends into Mexican-American communities in Texas and California. Orphaned at a young age, Fidencio began performing healings at age 14 and gained fame for
stories.title: El Niño Fidencio — The Child Healer of Espinazo

stories.name: El Pacto con el Diablo — Faustian Legends of the Borderlands
stories.excerpt: Pact-with-the-devil legends are widespread in Hispanic folklore of the US Southwest and northern Mexico, reflecting the deep Catholic influence on borderlands culture. These stories typically involve a desperate or ambitious person who sells their soul to the devil in exchange for wealth, power, love, or musical talent
stories.title: El Pacto con el Diablo — Faustian Legends of the Borderlands

stories.name: El Pombero: The Goblin of the Argentine Forest
stories.excerpt: A nocturnal forest spirit punishes those who harm nature and rewards those who show respect.
stories.title: El Pombero: The Goblin of the Argentine Forest

stories.name: El Silbón — The Whistling Specter of the Plains
stories.excerpt: El Silbón (The Whistler) is a terrifying specter from the folklore of Mexico's northern plains and the US Southwest borderlands. He is described as a tall, thin figure dressed in white, carrying a bundle of bones on his back. His most distinctive feature is his whistle — a melody that begins softly and grows increasing
stories.title: El Silbón — The Whistling Specter of the Plains

stories.name: El Sombrerón — The Goblin with the Big Hat
stories.excerpt: El Sombrerón is a small, mischievous goblin figure from Guatemalan and southern Mexican folklore who also appears in Mexican-American storytelling. He is described as a tiny man — no taller than a child — wearing an enormous hat, a red tie, and riding a tiny horse or mule. El Sombrerón is known for braiding the manes a
stories.title: El Sombrerón — The Goblin with the Big Hat

stories.name: El Tesoro de los Jesuitas — The Jesuit Gold of the Border
stories.excerpt: The legend of the Jesuit Treasure is one of the most enduring treasure myths of the US Southwest and northern Mexico. When the Spanish Crown expelled the Jesuits from New Spain in 1767, the order was said to have hidden vast stores of gold and silver throughout the Sonoran Desert rather than let it fall into royal hand
stories.title: El Tesoro de los Jesuitas — The Jesuit Gold of the Border

stories.name: El Tigrillo, the Spirit of the Jungle Cat
stories.excerpt: A spirit animal of the Costa Rican jungles, El Tigrillo is a spectral ocelot that guards sacred places and guides the worthy through the forest.
stories.title: El Tigrillo, the Spirit of the Jungle Cat

stories.name: El Trauco — The Cursing Dwarf of the Forest
stories.excerpt: El Trauco is a legendary figure from the folklore of Chiloé, Chile, but his legend has traveled through Latin American diaspora communities into the US Southwest. Described as a small, ugly, deformed dwarf — no more than three feet tall — who wears a hat made of a type of vine, has no teeth, and carries a wooden club o
stories.title: El Trauco — The Cursing Dwarf of the Forest

stories.name: El Trauco: The Forest Dwarf of Chiloé
stories.excerpt: A grotesque dwarf-like creature with powers of irresistible seduction haunts the forests of Chiloé.
stories.title: El Trauco: The Forest Dwarf of Chiloé

stories.name: Eleggua, the Trickster Messenger
stories.excerpt: Eleggua (Elegbara) is the trickster orisha of crossroads, doors, opportunities, and fate in Cuban Santería. He is the messenger between humanity and the other orishas, syncretized with the Holy Child of Atocha. Eleggua opens and closes paths, and no ceremony can begin without his permission. He is depicted as a mischie
stories.title: Eleggua, the Trickster Messenger

stories.name: Elvehøj
stories.excerpt: A young man falls asleep beside an elf-mound and is wooed by elf-maidens who sing beautifully. He resists their enchantments, grasping his sword, and is ultimately rescued by the crowing of a cock at dawn, which awakens him from the spell.
stories.title: Elvehøj

stories.name: Encantada, the Andorran Fairy
stories.excerpt: A beautiful fairy of Pyrenean lore, the Encantada of Andorra appears at mountain springs and punishes those who betray promises of love.
stories.title: Encantada, the Andorran Fairy

stories.name: Enkai and the Gift of Cattle
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, Enkai, the supreme god of the Maasai, lived on earth with the first people. One day, Enkai decided to give the Maasai a gift more precious than any other — cattle. He lowered them from the sky on a leather thong, and they landed on the green plains below. Enkai instructed the Maasai that they were to
stories.title: Enkai and the Gift of Cattle

stories.name: Enkai and the Rainbow Serpent
stories.excerpt: In the time when Enkai still walked among the people, a great drought struck the land. Rivers dried up, grass turned to dust, and the cattle began to die. The Maasai begged Enkai for rain, but their prayers went unanswered. One day, a young girl saw a magnificent rainbow serpent emerge from a dry riverbed. The serpent
stories.title: Enkai and the Rainbow Serpent

stories.name: Epic of Gesar of Ling
stories.excerpt: The great Tibetan epic of King Gesar, the longest living epic in the world with over one million verses and 120 volumes. The story recounts the miraculous birth of Gesar, son of deities sent to earth to vanquish demons, depose the powerful, and aid the weak. He has a despised childhood where he appears as an ugly, snot
stories.title: Epic of Gesar of Ling

stories.name: Er Sogotokh (The Lonely Man)
stories.excerpt: A foundational Yakut Olonkho epic about Er Sogotokh, the first human hero created by the supreme deity. Born alone in the Middle World, he must contend with the hostile Abaasy spirits from the Lower World who seek to destroy him. After achieving victory over the evil forces, he finds a wife from the Upper World and est
stories.title: Er Sogotokh (The Lonely Man)

stories.name: Erdlaveersissok the Entrail-Seizer
stories.excerpt: Erdlaveersissok is a terrifying spirit who haunts the celestial path leading to the moon. She targets travelers who lack composure or discipline. Her most disturbing trait is her habit of stealing the entrails of anyone she can trick into laughing. She serves as a guardian of emotional restraint and a symbol of the per
stories.title: Erdlaveersissok the Entrail-Seizer

stories.name: Erect Horns and the Sacred Buffalo Hat
stories.excerpt: Erect Horns (Tomȯsévėséhe) was the prophet of the Só'taeo'o people who later merged with the Cheyenne. He received the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat) at Tȯhóonévose (Stone Hammer Mountain) near the Great Lakes in Minnesota. The sacred hat represents female power, while the Sacred Arrows represent male power—together they
stories.title: Erect Horns and the Sacred Buffalo Hat

stories.name: Erkei-Mergen and the Seven Suns
stories.excerpt: Long ago, seven suns rose in the sky simultaneously, drying up all rivers and vegetation on earth. Men and animals struggled to survive in the unbearable heat. A famous archer named Erkei-Mergen stepped forward to save the world. Using his divine bow, he shot down the extra suns one by one, restoring balance to the wor
stories.title: Erkei-Mergen and the Seven Suns

stories.name: Erlig Khan and the Palace of the Dead
stories.excerpt: Erlig Khan (also Erlik Khan) is the Mongol and Turkic god of death and ruler of the underworld. In one of the most famous Mongol tales, 'The Woman Who Sought Her Husband in the Palace of Erlik Khan,' a brave woman descends into the underworld to rescue her dead husband. She navigates past guardian spirits and offers tr
stories.title: Erlig Khan and the Palace of the Dead

stories.name: Esben and the Witch
stories.excerpt: Esben is captured by a witch who intends to cook him. Using his wit and bravery, he manages to escape her clutches and outsmart her, eventually returning home safely.
stories.title: Esben and the Witch

stories.name: Eshu the Trickster and the Two Friends (Yoruba)
stories.excerpt: Eshu, the divine messenger and trickster, once walked between two farmers who were best friends, wearing a hat that was red on one side and white on the other. The two friends saw him from opposite fields and later argued about the color of the passerby's hat, each insisting on what they had seen. Their argument escala
stories.title: Eshu the Trickster and the Two Friends (Yoruba)

stories.name: Excalibur
stories.excerpt: In the time of kings, there was a boy named Arthur who pulled a sword from a stone—proving he was the rightful ruler of Britain.
stories.title: Excalibur

stories.name: Eyrbyggja Saga - The Guest Thorgunna
stories.excerpt: The wealthy and sickly Thorgunna is buried with a specific request that her bedding be burned. When a friend, Thorodd, keeps her bed sheets as a gift for his wife, Thorgunna returns as a ghost. She appears in the middle of the night at a farmstead, setting the table and preparing a meal for the living before vanishing
stories.title: Eyrbyggja Saga - The Guest Thorgunna

stories.name: Eyrbyggja Saga - The Haunting of Thorolf Halt-Foot
stories.excerpt: Thorolf Halt-Foot returns as a malevolent draugr after his death, terrorizing the area around Þórsnes. He is buried, reburied, and even burned, yet he continues to return, even manifesting as a bull. Eventually, his son Arnkel manages to lay him to rest by building a high stone wall around his grave to prevent him from
stories.title: Eyrbyggja Saga - The Haunting of Thorolf Halt-Foot

stories.name: Eyrbyggja Saga - The Seal of Frodis-water
stories.excerpt: The house at Frodis-water is haunted by a group of undead fishermen and their leader, Thorir Wooden-leg. The hauntings escalate until a seal's head begins to emerge from the floorboards. Despite the inhabitants' attempts to smash it back down, the seal keeps rising until a young man uses a sledgehammer to drive it back
stories.title: Eyrbyggja Saga - The Seal of Frodis-water

stories.name: Faithful and Unfaithful
stories.excerpt: Two brothers — one faithful, one unfaithful — set out into the world; the faithful brother wins a princess through kindness while the unfaithful one schemes and falls to ruin. This tale is a distant offshoot of the Tristan legend cycle.
stories.title: Faithful and Unfaithful

stories.name: Falak, the Serpent of Purgatory
stories.excerpt: A colossal serpent that guards the bridge between life and death, biting the souls that try to cross — because in Lebanon, the journey to the afterlife is not a gift, but a test.
stories.title: Falak, the Serpent of Purgatory

stories.name: Falcone, the Sammarinese Winged Guardian
stories.excerpt: A monstrous winged creature said to inhabit Mount Titano, Falcone is a guardian of San Marino who protects the republic from invasion.
stories.title: Falcone, the Sammarinese Winged Guardian

stories.name: Farmer Weathersky
stories.excerpt: Farmer Weathersky possesses a unique ability to interact with the weather. When opportunistic neighbors try to exploit his gift or cheat him out of his land, he uses his cleverness to turn the tide in his favor, ensuring justice and prosperity.
stories.title: Farmer Weathersky

stories.name: Faroese Chain Dance and Kvæði (Ballad Tradition)
stories.excerpt: The Faroese chain dance (Føroya Dansur) accompanied by kvæði (ballads) is the national dance and a living tradition that preserves folklore. Dancers form a circle holding hands, moving rhythmically while a kvæðamaður (ballad singer) recites verses recounting tales of legendary heroes, folklore figures, and historical e
stories.title: Faroese Chain Dance and Kvæði (Ballad Tradition)

stories.name: Father Bruin in the Corner
stories.excerpt: A humorous tale about Father Bruin, a bear who believes himself to be superior but is repeatedly tricked by the cunning Reynard the Fox. The story highlights the contrast between Bruin's strength and Reynard's intelligence.
stories.title: Father Bruin in the Corner

stories.name: Finkingo: The Stickball Game (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: The Choctaw game of stickball, known as Finkingo or kabocha, is featured in many Choctaw legends. According to tradition, the game was given to the Choctaw by the spirits to resolve conflicts without warfare. Stickball is played with two small rackets and a ball, and it is extremely fast and violent. The game was often
stories.title: Finkingo: The Stickball Game (Choctaw)

stories.name: Finn, the Giant, and the Minster of Lund
stories.excerpt: A giant named Finn builds Lund Cathedral in exchange for Saint Lawrence's eyes, but the saint overhears Finn's name in a lullaby and Finn turns to stone in the crypt. This world-famous master-builder legend is connected to several European cathedrals; Finn's petrified form can still be seen grasping a pillar in the cry
stories.title: Finn, the Giant, and the Minster of Lund

stories.name: Finnur hin Fróði and Faroese Wizard Legends
stories.excerpt: Faroese folklore includes tales of powerful wizards and cunning folk (wise men and women) who could control weather, heal sickness, and ward off trolls. One of the most famous is Finnur hin Fróði (Finn the Wise), a legendary figure associated with magical knowledge and runic wisdom. These wizard legends blend Norse pag
stories.title: Finnur hin Fróði and Faroese Wizard Legends

stories.name: First Born, First Wed
stories.excerpt: A king's son and a queen's daughter, promised to each other at birth, must overcome separation, enchantment, and a wicked stepmother before they can fulfill their destiny. This is a purely Swedish treatment of the redemption motif.
stories.title: First Born, First Wed

stories.name: First Man and First Woman
stories.excerpt: In the First World, Black Cloud and White Cloud came together in the East, and from their breath First Man (Áłtsé Hastiin) was formed, carrying white corn and crystal. Blue Cloud and Yellow Cloud came together in the West, forming First Woman (Áłtsé Asdzą́ą́) with yellow corn, white shell, turquoise, and yucca. First W
stories.title: First Man and First Woman

stories.name: Flat Pipe and the Arapaho Creation
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, there was nothing but water covering everything. A man carrying a Flat Pipe walked on the water for six days, weeping and fasting, searching for a safe place to rest his pipe. On the seventh day, he called to the four directions and summoned seven cottonwood trees and all the creatures. One by one, va
stories.title: Flat Pipe and the Arapaho Creation

stories.name: Foam Woman and Ice Woman (Haida)
stories.excerpt: Among the SGaana Kiidads (Supernatural Beings) of Haida tradition are Kalga Jaad (Ice Woman) and GaayhllGa Jaad (Flood-Tide-Woman). These female supernatural beings are part of the Raven Traveling narratives, also known as Xuuya Kaagang.ngas, which tell of Raven traveling the earth and transforming it to make it suitab
stories.title: Foam Woman and Ice Woman (Haida)

stories.name: Food for Kings: Oatcake and Herring
stories.excerpt: When King Charles XI confiscated most noble properties in the Great Reduction of 1680, his aunt Countess Maria Eufrosyna of Höjentorp was affected. When the king came to visit, she greeted him with a box on the ear, then served him nothing but a herring's tail and an oatcake. When the king offered to return her propert
stories.title: Food for Kings: Oatcake and Herring

stories.name: Found-in-the-Grass
stories.excerpt: Found-in-the-Grass is a rags-to-riches hero of Arapaho folklore. In some versions, he is an orphan abandoned as an infant and found by villagers in the tall grass. In others, he is the magical twin Spring-Boy grown older. Despite his humble beginnings, Found-in-the-Grass rises to become a great warrior and leader throu
stories.title: Found-in-the-Grass

stories.name: Friar Tuck
stories.excerpt: Of all Robin Hood's Merry Men, none was more surprising than the holy man who could fight like a soldier and laugh like a drunkard.
stories.title: Friar Tuck

stories.name: Friends in Life and Death
stories.excerpt: Two inseparable friends swear to remain loyal even after death. When one passes away, the other visits the grave and journeys into the afterlife. There, he observes the symbolic representations of human greed and contentment, learning a profound lesson about the soul.
stories.title: Friends in Life and Death

stories.name: Fumo Liongo: The Warrior Poet of the Swahili Coast
stories.excerpt: Liongo Fumo was a legendary Swahili prince, warrior, and poet who lived on Pate Island sometime between the 9th and 13th centuries. He was a giant of a man, nearly invulnerable except for his navel, and a master archer whose bow no other man could draw. Despite being the rightful heir, his brother Mringwari usurped the
stories.title: Fumo Liongo: The Warrior Poet of the Swahili Coast

stories.name: Funkwe the Devourer of Rivers
stories.excerpt: When a Tonga village's river begins to vanish overnight, a young girl discovers that the Funkwe, a giant water serpent, has been drinking the river dry as punishment for the village chief's arrogance.
stories.title: Funkwe the Devourer of Rivers

stories.name: Gamarala: The Foolish Farmer of Sri Lankan Folktales
stories.excerpt: A simple village farmer is constantly outwitted by his clever wife and the animals around him.
stories.title: Gamarala: The Foolish Farmer of Sri Lankan Folktales

stories.name: Ganesha
stories.excerpt: Ganesha, the elephant-headed god of wisdom, remover of obstacles, lord of beginnings, is one of the most beloved deities in the Hindu pantheon.
stories.title: Ganesha

stories.name: Garang of the Reed Weapon
stories.excerpt: A mortal hero named Garang forged a weapon from river reeds and bone, then ventured into the spirit marsh to rescue his village's stolen cattle from the water spirits who guarded the flood plain.
stories.title: Garang of the Reed Weapon

stories.name: Garcis, the Giant Who Built the Hills
stories.excerpt: Garcis, a colossal giant of Latvian legend, shaped the rolling hills and river valleys of the Baltic countryside before retreating into the earth as the age of men began.
stories.title: Garcis, the Giant Who Built the Hills

stories.name: Gashadokuro: The Giant Skull
stories.excerpt: A massive skeleton fifteen times bigger than a human appears at night, searching for living people to bite.
stories.title: Gashadokuro: The Giant Skull

stories.name: Gbahali, the Liberian Sea Monster
stories.excerpt: A fearsome sea monster said to inhabit the waters off Liberia's coast, the Gbahali drags unwary fishermen and swimmers to a watery grave.
stories.title: Gbahali, the Liberian Sea Monster

stories.name: Genghis Khan and the Golden Whip
stories.excerpt: According to Mongol legend, the young Temüjin (later Genghis Khan) was riding alone in the steppe when he discovered a golden whip lying on the ground. When he picked it up, the sky thundered and Tengri spoke, telling him that this whip was a sign that he would unite all the Mongol tribes under one banner. The whip had
stories.title: Genghis Khan and the Golden Whip

stories.name: Gertrude's Bird
stories.excerpt: A young girl named Gertrude receives a mysterious bird that possesses the ability to speak and provide guidance. The bird helps her navigate a series of trials and obstacles, leading her toward a destiny of happiness and nobility through kindness and perseverance.
stories.title: Gertrude's Bird

stories.name: Ghost of the White Deer (Chickasaw)
stories.excerpt: The Ghost of the White Deer is a Chickasaw legend explaining why the white deer is considered sacred. A young hunter once encountered a pure white deer in the forest. The deer spoke to him, revealing itself as a spirit sent by Ababinili to test the hunter's character. The hunter chose not to kill the deer, showing merc
stories.title: Ghost of the White Deer (Chickasaw)

stories.name: Ghoul, the Desert Devourer
stories.excerpt: A shape-shifting desert demon that feasts on the flesh of the dead and leads travelers astray in the wilderness of Palestine.
stories.title: Ghoul, the Desert Devourer

stories.name: Gikuyu and Mumbi: The First Parents
stories.excerpt: Ngai, the supreme god who dwells on Mount Kenya (Kirinyaga), created the first man, Gikuyu, and placed him at the center of the land beneath the mountain. Ngai showed Gikuyu a place where a magnificent fig tree (Mukuyu) grew and told him to build his homestead there, naming it Mukurwe wa Gathanga. To Gikuyu, Ngai gave
stories.title: Gikuyu and Mumbi: The First Parents

stories.name: Gizo the Spider Trickster and the Wisdom Bird
stories.excerpt: Gizo is the spider trickster of Hausa folklore, a clever but overconfident schemer whose plans often backfire. In one well-known tale, Gizo tries to outwit the Wisdom Bird but fails spectacularly, teaching that intelligence without humility leads to ruin. Another story tells of him building a luxury lagoon home through
stories.title: Gizo the Spider Trickster and the Wisdom Bird

stories.name: Glooscap and the Evil Frog Monster
stories.excerpt: In the days of the Mi'kmaq ancestors, a monstrous frog spirit had swallowed all the water in the world. Rivers dried up, lakes vanished, and people and animals were dying of thirst. The great being Glooscap took pity on his people. He tracked the enormous frog to its lair and engaged it in a titanic struggle. He struck
stories.title: Glooscap and the Evil Frog Monster

stories.name: Glooscap and the Great Beaver: The Five Islands
stories.excerpt: Glooscap once transformed himself into a giant beaver to create a safe haven for his people. Swimming in the Bay of Fundy, he slapped his enormous tail against the water with such tremendous force that it churned up the earth from the seabed, creating the Five Islands of Nova Scotia. When Glooscap slept, Nova Scotia wa
stories.title: Glooscap and the Great Beaver: The Five Islands

stories.name: Gluskabe and Dzeedzeez (The Baby Who Outmatched the Hero)
stories.excerpt: Gluskabe, the great culture hero, was resting in his lodge after his many labors when he heard a baby crying. The baby was Dzeedzeez (Wasis in Passamaquoddy), whose mother had left him alone while she gathered firewood. Gluskabe, confident in his powers, decided to quiet the baby himself. He tried using his magic, but
stories.title: Gluskabe and Dzeedzeez (The Baby Who Outmatched the Hero)

stories.name: Gluskabe and the Monster Frog
stories.excerpt: A devastating drought struck the land of the Wabanaki. Rivers dried to dust, the lakes shrank, and the people were dying. A giant frog monster had swallowed all the water and held it captive in its bloated body. The people called to Gluskabe for help. Gluskabe found the giant frog sunning itself on a rock, swollen with
stories.title: Gluskabe and the Monster Frog

stories.name: Gluskabe and the Wind Eagle
stories.excerpt: Gluskabe (Glooscap) was annoyed by the constant wind that made life difficult for his people. He traveled to the great mountain where the Wind Eagle — a colossal bird whose wingbeats created all the wind in the world — was perched. Gluskabe climbed the mountain and captured the Wind Eagle, tying its wings together so t
stories.title: Gluskabe and the Wind Eagle

stories.name: Gluskonba and the Four Wishes
stories.excerpt: Gluskonba (Glooscap) offered four Abenaki men a single wish each. The first man wished to be powerful and rich, and was turned into a great pine tree — tall and strong, but rooted in one place forever. The second man wished to be feared by everyone, and was turned into a bear — powerful but alone. The third man wished
stories.title: Gluskonba and the Four Wishes

stories.name: Golden Treasure
stories.excerpt: A story focusing on the pursuit of wealth and the moral lessons learned through the acquisition or loss of a legendary golden treasure, emphasizing that true value is not material.
stories.title: Golden Treasure

stories.name: Golem, the Creature of Clay
stories.excerpt: A being of mud and clay animated by Kabbalistic magic, the Golem of Prague is the most famous artificial creature in Jewish tradition.
stories.title: Golem, the Creature of Clay

stories.name: Gond Creation Myth — The Lizard That Made the World
stories.excerpt: According to the Gond tribe of central India, in the beginning there was only water. The supreme god Bhagavan created a tortoise and a lizard to work together to create land. The tortoise dived deep into the waters and brought up mud on its back. The lizard spread this mud across the surface, forming the first solid gr
stories.title: Gond Creation Myth — The Lizard That Made the World

stories.name: Goosey Grizzel
stories.excerpt: A housekeeper named Grizzel is made to look like a monster by her employer. She joins a band of thieves and uses her frightening appearance to scare others, eventually encountering a priest who tries to 'bind' her.
stories.title: Goosey Grizzel

stories.name: Goubet Monster, the Red Sea Cryptid
stories.excerpt: A fearsome sea monster said to dwell in the Gulf of Tadjoura off the coast of Djibouti, dragging fishermen to their doom.
stories.title: Goubet Monster, the Red Sea Cryptid

stories.name: Grandmother Spider Steals the Fire (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, the only fire belonged to the Thunders in the sky world. The animals held a council to decide who would bring fire to the people. Many brave animals volunteered but failed: Raven tried to carry an ember but his feathers turned black; Screech Owl's eyes were burned red; Hooting Owl's eyes were singed w
stories.title: Grandmother Spider Steals the Fire (Cherokee)

stories.name: Grettis Saga - The Fight with Glámr
stories.excerpt: Grettir Ásmundarson, a man of extraordinary strength, is hired to protect a farm haunted by a wight. He eventually faces the undead shepherd Glámr in a brutal battle. Although Grettir triumphs, Glámr uses his final breath to curse him, leaving Grettir forever unlucky and terrified of the dark, which leads to his eventu
stories.title: Grettis Saga - The Fight with Glámr

stories.name: Gryphon
stories.excerpt: In the distant lands of Scythia, beyond the borders of the known world, there lived creatures of such terrible beauty that they became legend even before Greeks reached them.
stories.title: Gryphon

stories.name: Grímur Kamban (The First Settler)
stories.excerpt: Grímur Kamban is recorded in the Færeyinga Saga as the first Scandinavian settler in the Faroe Islands, arriving around 825 AD—decades before the main Norse colonization of Iceland. He settled at Funningur on Eysturoy. The name 'Kamban' may be of Gaelic origin, suggesting he was a Norse-Gael from the British Isles (pos
stories.title: Grímur Kamban (The First Settler)

stories.name: Gudbrand on the Hill-side
stories.excerpt: Gudbrand, a poor and humble youth, embarks on a journey and helps various animals and spirits along the way. His kindness and selflessness are rewarded when he is guided to a hidden treasure and the heart of a beautiful princess, proving that a good heart is the greatest asset.
stories.title: Gudbrand on the Hill-side

stories.name: Guinevere at the Trial by Fire
stories.excerpt: Accused of treason, Queen Guinevere faces the ordeal by fire at the court of King Arthur, where her innocence must be proven by divine judgment or consumed by flame.
stories.title: Guinevere at the Trial by Fire

stories.name: Guri Kunna: The Sea Witch of Hitra
stories.excerpt: A dangerous sea witch lures fishermen to their doom along the Hitra and Fosen coast.
stories.title: Guri Kunna: The Sea Witch of Hitra

stories.name: Göroglu: The Son of the Grave (Turkmen Version)
stories.excerpt: The Turkmen epic of Göroglu ('Son of the Grave') — also known as Köroğlu — is the national epic of Turkmenistan, recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Unlike the western versions, the Turkmen Göroglu was born miraculously in his mother's grave after she died, giving him his name. He was raised by his gr
stories.title: Göroglu: The Son of the Grave (Turkmen Version)

stories.name: Güije: The River Goblin of Cuba
stories.excerpt: Small black-skinned goblins haunt Cuban rivers, playing tricks on those who disturb their waters.
stories.title: Güije: The River Goblin of Cuba

stories.name: Haggs: The Twilight Wanderer
stories.excerpt: A schoolteacher new to the island dismisses the village warnings about the Haggs, a malevolent spirit of the twilight hours, until she finds her classroom filled with the scent of burning herbs and the chalk has written itself on the board.
stories.title: Haggs: The Twilight Wanderer

stories.name: Hanako-San: The Bathroom Ghost
stories.excerpt: A ghost girl haunts school bathrooms in Japan. Knock three times and ask if she is there—if she answers, you are marked.
stories.title: Hanako-San: The Bathroom Ghost

stories.name: Hansel and Gretel
stories.excerpt: Children abandoned in the forest discover a witch's gingerbread house and must use their wits to survive.
stories.title: Hansel and Gretel

stories.name: Hanuman
stories.excerpt: Hanuman was born to the wind god Vayu and the celestial nymph Anjana.. According to the Ramayana, his mother was a vanara — a divine monkey being — who had been blessed with a son possessing the strength of the gods.
stories.title: Hanuman

stories.name: Hatim al-Tai: The Legend of Generosity
