stories.excerpt: Hatim ibn Abdallah of the Tai tribe, a pre-Islamic Arab chief in 6th-century Yemen, became the enduring symbol of Arab generosity and chivalry. Countless legends recount his extreme hospitality: slaughtering his prized horse when no other food was available for guests, giving away his possessions until left with nothin
stories.title: Hatim al-Tai: The Legend of Generosity

stories.name: Hatuibwari: The Dragon God of the Solomon Islands
stories.excerpt: Hatuibwari is a powerful dragon-like being from the mythology of the Solomon Islands, particularly among the people of Guadalcanal. Described as a massive serpent with the features of a dragon, Hatuibwari is a creator and cultural hero who shaped the islands and taught humans essential skills. In some accounts, Hatuibw
stories.title: Hatuibwari: The Dragon God of the Solomon Islands

stories.name: Hatupatu and the Bird-Woman
stories.excerpt: Hatupatu was a young Maori warrior who was captured by Kurangaituku, a fearsome bird-woman with sharp claws and a taste for human flesh. She kept him in her cave dwelling, but clever Hatupatu bided his time. When Kurangaituku relaxed her guard, he escaped, running across the rugged landscape of the central North Island
stories.title: Hatupatu and the Bird-Woman

stories.name: He Who Could Ride in All Weathers
stories.excerpt: A castle-dwelling daughter is brought home by her father to the castle in Tyrol. She does not give her hand to the richest or most handsome suitor, but instead chooses the one who defies all dangers and makes his way through all weathers. The tale carries a feminist message about a woman's right to choose her partner b
stories.title: He Who Could Ride in All Weathers

stories.name: Heer Ranjha — The Tragic Lovers of Punjab
stories.excerpt: Heer, the beautiful daughter of a wealthy Jatt family in Jhang, fell deeply in love with Ranjha, a youngest son who tended cattle and played the flute. They met secretly for years until Heer's jealous uncle Kaido exposed them. Heer's family forcibly married her to another man. The heartbroken Ranjha became a wandering
stories.title: Heer Ranjha — The Tragic Lovers of Punjab

stories.name: Heitsi-Eibib Defeats the Ga-Gorib
stories.excerpt: Heitsi-Eibib, the ancestral hero and trickster of the Khoikhoi people, confronted the fearsome monster Ga-Gorib who sat at the edge of a deep hole, challenging passersby to throw a stone at his forehead. The stone would bounce back and kill the thrower. Unlike his predecessors, Heitsi-Eibib refused the challenge and in
stories.title: Heitsi-Eibib Defeats the Ga-Gorib

stories.name: Helhest
stories.excerpt: A three-legged horse associated with the goddess Hel. It is seen in churchyards as a harbinger of death and illness, often appearing before a person dies. Legend says a living horse was interred in every churchyard before human burial, returning as the Hel-horse.
stories.title: Helhest

stories.name: Heloha and Melatha: Thunder and Lightning Birds (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: In Choctaw mythology, Heloha (Thunder) and Melatha (Lightning) are two enormous birds responsible for the dramatic thunderstorms that sweep across the Mississippi region. Heloha, the female, lays her giant eggs high in the clouds, and the eggs rumble and roll around atop the clouds, creating the sound of thunder. Her m
stories.title: Heloha and Melatha: Thunder and Lightning Birds (Choctaw)

stories.name: Hi'iaka's Journey to Bring Lohiau to Pele
stories.excerpt: Pele fell in love with Lohiau, a chief of Kauai, during a spirit dream. She sent her beloved youngest sister Hi'iaka to retrieve him. Hi'iaka agreed on the condition that Pele protect her sacred lehua groves and friend Hopoe. On Kauai, Hi'iaka found Lohiau had died of heartbreak and spent thirty days chanting to revive
stories.title: Hi'iaka's Journey to Bring Lohiau to Pele

stories.name: Hi-nun and the Niagara Legend
stories.excerpt: The Seneca tell of Hi-nun, the Thunderer, who fought a great battle with a monstrous serpent living in the Niagara River. The serpent had grown so large that it blocked the flow of the river, causing devastating floods. Hi-nun descended from the sky with his thunderbolt and struck the serpent, whose thrashing body carv
stories.title: Hi-nun and the Niagara Legend

stories.name: Hiawatha and the Invention of Wampum
stories.excerpt: When Hiawatha's three daughters were killed by the evil Tadodaho, he was consumed by grief and wandered the wilderness. The Great Peacemaker found him and taught him the Condolence Ceremony to ease his grief. As part of this ceremony, Hiawatha invented wampum — strings of purple and white shell beads — to record the la
stories.title: Hiawatha and the Invention of Wampum

stories.name: High John the Conqueror and the Devil's Daughter
stories.excerpt: High John the Conqueror, an African prince sold into slavery who became a legendary trickster, falls in love with the Devil's beautiful daughter. The Devil, enraged, sets John a series of impossible tasks to keep them apart: John must clear sixty acres of forest in half a day, plow the land, plant it with corn, and har
stories.title: High John the Conqueror and the Devil's Daughter

stories.name: High John the Conqueror Brings Freedom
stories.excerpt: According to the lore collected by Zora Neale Hurston, High John the Conqueror was more than a trickster—he was a spirit of liberation who moved invisibly among the enslaved. Born an African prince, John was captured and sold into slavery, but his spirit could never be broken. When the whip fell, John would 'take the s
stories.title: High John the Conqueror Brings Freedom

stories.name: Hikule'o, Tangaloa, and Maui Divide the Cosmos
stories.excerpt: In Tongan creation myth, after the primordial god Taufulifonua fathered Hikule'o with his sister Havea Lolofonua, the three great powers divided the universe. Hikule'o received Pulotu, the underworld realm of spirits and the afterlife. Tangaloa took the vast sky and heavens, becoming ruler of the celestial domain. Maui
stories.title: Hikule'o, Tangaloa, and Maui Divide the Cosmos

stories.name: Hina: The Woman in the Moon
stories.excerpt: Hina (also called Sina or Ina across different Polynesian cultures) was a mortal woman who became the moon goddess. In the Maori version, Hina went to fetch water at night and cursed the moon when she stumbled in darkness. The moon descended, caught her, and lifted her into the sky. In Hawaiian tradition, Hina was the
stories.title: Hina: The Woman in the Moon

stories.name: Hinemoa and Tutanekai
stories.excerpt: Hinemoa, a high-born maiden from the shores of Lake Rotorua, fell in love with Tutanekai, a younger son of a chief who lived on Mokoia Island. Her family disapproved of the match. Tutanekai would play his flute across the lake each night, and Hinemoa listened from the shore. One night, spurred by her love, Hinemoa tied
stories.title: Hinemoa and Tutanekai

stories.name: Hinnon, the Thunder Spirit
stories.excerpt: The Huron believe in the Thunders, a group of powerful storm spirits who live in the sky and look like a cross between men and giant turkeys. Their leader is Hinnon, whom they call Grandfather. Hinnon and his warriors pursue and destroy the great horned serpents and other monsters that threaten the world. When lightnin
stories.title: Hinnon, the Thunder Spirit

stories.name: Hiro the Trickster and the Magic Canoe
stories.excerpt: Hiro, the Tahitian trickster god of thieves and the son of the god Ta'aroa, built a magical canoe that could sail faster than the wind. Using his cunning and his enchanted vessel, Hiro traveled across the Society Islands performing daring thefts and outsmarting chiefs and gods alike. He stole fish from the markets, foo
stories.title: Hiro the Trickster and the Magic Canoe

stories.name: Hlakanyana: The Zulu-Xhosa Trickster Born from the Womb
stories.excerpt: Hlakanyana (Uhlakanyana) is a cunning trickster figure in Zulu and Xhosa folklore, of weasel-like size and nature, who speaks from his mother's womb demanding to be born because the cattle of his father are being devoured. After birth, he embarks on a series of adventures: he tricks a cannibal by cooking the cannibal's
stories.title: Hlakanyana: The Zulu-Xhosa Trickster Born from the Womb

stories.name: Hoklonote: The Shape-Shifting Spirit (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: Hoklonote is a malevolent Choctaw spirit who can assume any shape it desires. This bad spirit is believed to be able to read people's thoughts, making it nearly impossible to hide from. Hoklonote takes different forms to deceive and harm humans — appearing as a loved one, an animal, or even an inanimate object. The spi
stories.title: Hoklonote: The Shape-Shifting Spirit (Choctaw)

stories.name: Holy Boy Makes the Sun and Moon
stories.excerpt: In Apache tradition, Holy Boy was unhappy with the darkness in the underworld and decided to create a sun. He tried many materials without success. Cyclone, spying on the Hactcin, told Holy Boy that White Hactcin had the sun. Holy Boy went to White Hactcin who gave him the sun, and to Black Hactcin who gave him the moo
stories.title: Holy Boy Makes the Sun and Moon

stories.name: Hotu Matu'a Discovers Rapa Nui
stories.excerpt: King Hotu Matu'a lived in the mythical land of Hiva, which was sinking beneath the ocean. A prophet named Hau Maka appeared in Hotu Matu'a's dream and told him to search for a new island called Rapa Nui. Seven explorers were sent ahead in a canoe, finding the uninhabited island. They returned to report its location. Ho
stories.title: Hotu Matu'a Discovers Rapa Nui

stories.name: Hotuiyi (Antelope) and the Warning
stories.excerpt: A Comanche hunting party was pursuing a herd of antelope across the plains when a strange antelope with glowing eyes appeared. The lead hunter recognized it as a spirit messenger and halted the chase. The antelope led the party to a hidden spring where they found water, then traced a path around a dangerous canyon wher
stories.title: Hotuiyi (Antelope) and the Warning

stories.name: Hou Yi and the Arrows
stories.excerpt: Before there were emperors or dynasties, before history was written in bronze and bone, the world was ruled by gods, and among those gods were the ten suns.
stories.title: Hou Yi and the Arrows

stories.name: How Anansi Got His Stories
stories.excerpt: Long ago, all stories in the forest belonged to Tiger, and were called Tiger Stories. Anansi, tired of being mocked as the weakest creature, demanded that stories be named after him. Tiger set an impossible task: capture Snake. After failing with a noose, a pit trap, and a cage, Anansi tricked Snake by challenging his
stories.title: How Anansi Got His Stories

stories.name: How Brer Rabbit Lost His Fine Bushy Tail
stories.excerpt: In this pourquoi tale explaining why rabbits have short tails, Brer Rabbit once had a long, beautiful, bushy tail that he showed off constantly. Brer Fox grew tired of Brer Rabbit's vanity and devised a plan. During a cold winter, Brer Fox went ice fishing and called out to Brer Rabbit, showing him a string of fish he
stories.title: How Brer Rabbit Lost His Fine Bushy Tail

stories.name: How Death Came to Humanity (Yoruba/Benin)
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, humans did not experience death. When they grew old, the god Olorun would rejuvenate them. A man named Iku (Death) was sent to test humanity. Iku appeared as an old man begging for food, but only one woman, a poor widow, shared her meal with him. Iku rewarded her by warning her that a plague would com
stories.title: How Death Came to Humanity (Yoruba/Benin)

stories.name: How Fisher Went to the Skyland (The Big Dipper)
stories.excerpt: Long ago, the giant lynx Mishipeshu had imprisoned all the summer birds in a cave beneath the earth, plunging the world into endless winter. The animals held a council and decided to free the birds. Fisher, the swiftest of them, led a band of animals to the cave. While the others distracted Mishipeshu, Fisher slipped i
stories.title: How Fisher Went to the Skyland (The Big Dipper)

stories.name: How Fox Saved the People
stories.excerpt: During a catastrophic famine, the cunning Fox discovers a hidden source of food. While Raven tries to take credit through tricks, Fox's genuine assistance saves the community. The tale serves as a lesson in humility and the value of practical wisdom over empty boasting.
stories.title: How Fox Saved the People

stories.name: How Glooscap Found the Summer
stories.excerpt: In the long-ago time, there was no summer — only endless winter. The earth was covered in snow and ice, the people were freezing, and the animals suffered. Glooscap decided to find the spirit of summer and bring it back. He traveled to the far north where Winter, a powerful giant, held Summer captive in his ice lodge.
stories.title: How Glooscap Found the Summer

stories.name: How Gluskabe Stole Tobacco
stories.excerpt: In the early days, tobacco was guarded jealously by Grasshopper (or a giant), who kept it hidden from humanity. The people prayed for tobacco to use in their ceremonies, as it was the sacred plant that carried their prayers to the Creator. Gluskabe heard their pleas and devised a plan. He transformed himself into a sma
stories.title: How Gluskabe Stole Tobacco

stories.name: How Medicine Man Resurrected Buffalo
stories.excerpt: During a terrible famine, all the buffalo had disappeared from the plains. The Arapaho people were starving. A powerful medicine man went into the mountains to seek a vision. After four days of fasting, the spirit of the Earth came to him and told him that the buffalo had gone underground because the people had been wa
stories.title: How Medicine Man Resurrected Buffalo

stories.name: How One Went Out to Woo
stories.excerpt: A clumsy but well-meaning man attempts to find a wife, encountering a series of absurd obstacles and eccentric characters. Through sheer luck and a refusal to be discouraged, he eventually finds a partner who appreciates his oddities.
stories.title: How One Went Out to Woo

stories.name: How Pieraš Ánde Learned Noaidi Skills
stories.excerpt: The initiation story of a Sámi noaidi named Pieraš Ánde who learned shamanic arts. The noaidi's calling often came through dreams, where an ancestor or ancient drum would call the initiate. The initiation involved withdrawal into solitude, metaphorical death and rebirth, and learning to navigate the three levels of the
stories.title: How Pieraš Ánde Learned Noaidi Skills

stories.name: How Rabbit Brought Fire to the People (Creek)
stories.excerpt: In this Muscogee Creek legend, the animals possessed fire but kept it hidden from humans. Rabbit, the trickster figure Chufi, decided to steal fire for the people. Rabbit crept to where the animals were guarding the fire and tricked them. He challenged them to a game and, while they were distracted, grabbed a burning e
stories.title: How Rabbit Brought Fire to the People (Creek)

stories.name: How Smaland and Schonen Came to Be
stories.excerpt: An etiological tale explaining why Småland is rocky and barren while Skåne is flat and fertile — because the Devil tried to create land but was foiled at every turn by God. This humorous origin legend was also used by Selma Lagerlöf in her writings.
stories.title: How Smaland and Schonen Came to Be

stories.name: How the Buffalo Were Released on Earth
stories.excerpt: Long ago, all the buffalo were kept hidden in a cave deep beneath the earth by a powerful spirit who did not want to share them with humans. A young Comanche warrior, guided by a wolf spirit, discovered the cave entrance. Following the wolf's advice, he transformed into a buffalo calf and entered the herd. When the kee
stories.title: How the Buffalo Were Released on Earth

stories.name: How the Coyote Joined the Dance of the Burrowing-Owls
stories.excerpt: A Zuni trickster tale about Coyote who stumbled upon a sacred dance of the Burrowing-owls. The owls were performing a ceremonial dance in the moonlight, and Coyote, ever the opportunist, wanted to join. At first the owls were suspicious, but Coyote insisted he could dance as well as they. He joined their circle, but hi
stories.title: How the Coyote Joined the Dance of the Burrowing-Owls

stories.name: How the Moai Walked
stories.excerpt: According to Rapanui oral tradition, the great stone moai statues were carved at the Rano Raraku quarry and then walked to their final ahu (ceremonial platforms) across the island. The moai walked at night, powered by mana from the ancestors channeled through the kahuna (priests). Using a system of ropes and rocking mo
stories.title: How the Moai Walked

stories.name: How the Rattlesnakes Came to Be What They Are
stories.excerpt: A Zuni story explaining the origin of rattlesnakes and their relationship with humans. In the days of the ancients, rattlesnakes did not have their distinctive rattle or their dangerous venom. A man who had been saved by a rattlesnake or had made a pact with one became the founder of the Rattlesnake Society. The snake
stories.title: How the Rattlesnakes Came to Be What They Are

stories.name: How the Sky-God's Stories Became Anansi's (Ashanti/Akan)
stories.excerpt: Anansi the Spider wanted to buy the stories of Nyame, the Sky God, who owned all the stories in the world. Nyame set a nearly impossible price: Anansi must bring him Onini the python, Mmoboro the hornets, Osebo the leopard, and Mmoatia the invisible dwarf. Through clever trickery, Anansi succeeded. He caught the python
stories.title: How the Sky-God's Stories Became Anansi's (Ashanti/Akan)

stories.name: How the Stálos Were Tricked
stories.excerpt: A classic Stállu trickster tale where a clever Sámi outwits one or more Stállu giants through cunning rather than strength. The story exemplifies the core pattern of Sámi Stállu narratives: a small, clever Sámi hero uses intelligence and knowledge of the landscape to defeat the much larger, stronger, but stupider Stáll
stories.title: How the Stálos Were Tricked

stories.name: How the Summer Birds Came
stories.excerpt: A Zuni myth explaining the origin of small summer birds. In the days of the ancients, there were no little birds — only large birds like eagles, crows, and hawks. A Zuni man discovered a magical bundle of feathers left by the spirits. When he walked into a field of flowers, the bundle began to flutter, and small wings
stories.title: How the Summer Birds Came

stories.name: How Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma Stole the Thunder-Stone and Lightning-Shaft
stories.excerpt: In this Zuni myth, the twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma acquired the powerful weapons of thunder and lightning. The thunder-stone and lightning-shaft were kept by powerful beings who did not want to share their power. The twins, known for their cunning and bravery, devised a plan to steal these sacred weapons. Usi
stories.title: How Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma Stole the Thunder-Stone and Lightning-Shaft

stories.name: Huldra's Tail
stories.excerpt: A skilled hunter falls for a beautiful Huldra, accepting her secret animal tail in a rare display of unconditional love that challenges the nature of forest spirits.
stories.title: Huldra's Tail

stories.name: Huldufólk (The Hidden People)
stories.excerpt: Huldufólk are supernatural beings in Faroese folklore described as large-built, grey-clad, dark-haired people who live in mounds, rocks, and cliffs—invisible to humans unless they choose to be seen. They are tricksters who dislike electricity, technology, crosses, and churches. According to legend, they left Suðuroy wh
stories.title: Huldufólk (The Hidden People)

stories.name: Huldufólk Captured by a Priest at Sørvágsvatn
stories.excerpt: At Sørvágsvatn Lake on Vágar (the lake that famously appears to hang over the ocean), there is a stone mound where, according to legend, a priest trapped several Huldufólk (Hidden People). The priest used his spiritual authority to imprison the supernatural beings within the mound. Visitors to the area claim they can s
stories.title: Huldufólk Captured by a Priest at Sørvágsvatn

stories.name: Hushang Discovers Fire (Sadeh Feast)
stories.excerpt: The second king of the Pishdadian dynasty in Persian myth, Hushang, grandson of the first man Gayomard, one day hurls his flint axe at a serpent blocking his path. He misses the snake but the axe strikes a rock, producing a spark. Curious, the king strikes two flints together and creates fire deliberately — the first c
stories.title: Hushang Discovers Fire (Sadeh Feast)

stories.name: Hóu-koô-pô, the Tiger Spirit
stories.excerpt: A protective tiger spirit who guards the mountains of Taiwan, appearing to those who are lost or in danger.
stories.title: Hóu-koô-pô, the Tiger Spirit

stories.name: Iara: The River Mother of Brazil
stories.excerpt: In the rivers of Brazil, where the water runs dark as tea and the piranhas flash silver in the sun, there is a voice sweeter than any bird.
stories.title: Iara: The River Mother of Brazil

stories.name: Ibong Adarna (The Adarna Bird)
stories.excerpt: The Ibong Adarna is a legendary magical bird from Philippine epic poetry whose song has the power to heal any sickness and whose droppings turn anyone they fall upon into stone. The tale follows three princes — Pedro, Diego, and Juan — who are sent by their dying king to capture the elusive Adarna Bird. Each prince fal
stories.title: Ibong Adarna (The Adarna Bird)

stories.name: Ibonia: The Epic Hero of Madagascar
stories.excerpt: A legendary hero conceived by magic undertakes a quest to rescue his betrothed from a stone monster.
stories.title: Ibonia: The Epic Hero of Madagascar

stories.name: Icarus: Wings Too Close to the Sun
stories.excerpt: In the city of Athens, during the age of legends, there lived a master craftsman named Daedalus.
stories.title: Icarus: Wings Too Close to the Sun

stories.name: Iele, the Dancing Spirits of the Meadow
stories.excerpt: Beautiful but dangerous fairy spirits who dance in moonlit meadows, luring travelers to join their fatal dance.
stories.title: Iele, the Dancing Spirits of the Meadow

stories.name: Ifrit
stories.excerpt: The powerful djinn of the underground. Centers on Ifrit, from Arabia. jinn associated with ruin..
stories.title: Ifrit

stories.name: Igbo Landing: The Flying Africans
stories.excerpt: In May 1803, a group of 75 Igbo people from what is now Nigeria were captured and transported to Georgia. After surviving the Middle Passage, they were loaded onto a small vessel at Savannah and shipped to St. Simons Island to be sold at the slave market. Rather than submit to a life of bondage, the Igbo captives—led b
stories.title: Igbo Landing: The Flying Africans

stories.name: Ijapa and the Sky Feast
stories.excerpt: A clever Yoruba tortoise tries to attend a sky feast by tricking birds into carrying him, but his greed leads to a cracked shell.
stories.title: Ijapa and the Sky Feast

stories.name: Ikenga, the Horned God of Achievement (Igbo)
stories.excerpt: Ikenga is the Igbo deity of achievement, success, war, and the right hand. He is depicted as a horned figure, often holding a sword and a severed human head, representing his power and victory. Every Igbo man traditionally owned a personal Ikenga shrine representing his individual chi (personal god) and his right to ac
stories.title: Ikenga, the Horned God of Achievement (Igbo)

stories.name: Ikkyu: The Monk Child
stories.excerpt: A precocious child monk uses his wit to outsmart greedy merchants and teach a lesson about the subjective nature of value.
stories.title: Ikkyu: The Monk Child

stories.name: Iktomi and the Boulder
stories.excerpt: Iktomi the spider trickster wrapped himself in a fine robe and went walking. He came upon a large boulder and, feeling generous, offered it his robe. The boulder declined, but Iktomi insisted and placed the robe upon it. Later, when Iktomi wanted his robe back, the boulder refused. Iktomi grew angry and insulted the bo
stories.title: Iktomi and the Boulder

stories.name: Iktomi the Spider Trickster
stories.excerpt: Iktomi is the spider trickster of Lakota mythology, born fully grown with the body of a spider and the cunning of a man. He is known for his clever schemes and predictions, but his selfishness and mischievous nature often backfire. In one tale, Iktomi tried to keep a pot of fish soup for himself rather than share with
stories.title: Iktomi the Spider Trickster

stories.name: Ilmarinen Forges the Sampo
stories.excerpt: Louhi, the powerful Mistress of Pohjola, demands that Ilmarinen forge the Sampo—a mythical mill that automatically produces salt, meal, and gold—in exchange for her daughter's hand in marriage. Ilmarinen succeeds in this monumental task, bringing immense wealth and prosperity to the land of Pohjola.
stories.title: Ilmarinen Forges the Sampo

stories.name: Ilmarinen's Bride of Gold
stories.excerpt: Driven by loneliness, Ilmarinen forges a bride out of pure gold. However, he discovers that while she is physically perfect, she is cold and emotionless, lacking a human soul. This results in a hollow marriage and deep dissatisfaction.
stories.title: Ilmarinen's Bride of Gold

stories.name: Ilmarinen's Fruitless Wooing
stories.excerpt: Ilmarinen attempts to find a real human bride to replace his golden creation. However, his efforts are consistently thwarted by fate and his own inability to form a genuine emotional connection with the women he pursues.
stories.title: Ilmarinen's Fruitless Wooing

stories.name: Ilmarinen's Wedding-feast
stories.excerpt: Ilmarinen eventually marries the Daughter of Pohjola. The resulting wedding is a grand and opulent affair, but the celebration is overshadowed by the deep-seated tensions and long-standing rivalry between the peoples of Kalevala and Pohjola.
stories.title: Ilmarinen's Wedding-feast

stories.name: Ilmarinen's Wooing
stories.excerpt: Ilmarinen attempts to woo the Daughter of Pohjola, bringing his skills as a master smith to the table. Like the other suitors, he is subjected to the capricious demands of Louhi, the Mistress of Pohjola, who tests his resolve and his abilities.
stories.title: Ilmarinen's Wooing

stories.name: Imana and the First Rain
stories.excerpt: When the world was dry and the rivers were empty, Imana struck the sky with his staff and the first rain fell — but the rain was a gift, not a right, and it can be taken back.
stories.title: Imana and the First Rain

stories.name: Imana Who Shaped the Land
stories.excerpt: Imana, the supreme creator deity, sculpts the lakes and hills of Rwanda from raw earth and water, then breathes life into the first people, only to discover that free will brings both beauty and sorrow.
stories.title: Imana Who Shaped the Land

stories.name: Imana, God of the Hills
stories.excerpt: The supreme creator god who shaped the hills of Burundi with his hands, placing rivers in the valleys and forests on the slopes — and when the people forgot his name, the hills began to erode.
stories.title: Imana, God of the Hills

stories.name: In the House of Ulda
stories.excerpt: A young Sámi boy from Heahttá went cloudberry picking and took shelter from rain under a rock overhang. The earth opened and he found himself in the underground world of the Ulda. A beautiful Ulda girl with long hair offered him cloudberries on a gold-edged plate. The boy refused the food, remembering his parents' warn
stories.title: In the House of Ulda

stories.name: Ina and the Shark
stories.excerpt: The beautiful maiden Ina longed to reach the island of her lover Tinirau, the god of the ocean. A great shark offered to carry her across the sea. During the journey, Ina grew thirsty and cracked open a coconut, drinking its milk. Later, she struck a second coconut directly onto the shark's head to open it, hurting the
stories.title: Ina and the Shark

stories.name: Inkarri and the Return
stories.excerpt: The last Inca king, beheaded by the Spanish, regrows his body underground and will one day rise to restore the empire and reverse the world.
stories.title: Inkarri and the Return

stories.name: Innocence's Journey
stories.excerpt: Princess Bella sets out on a solitary journey through the deep forest, a passage that strips away the trappings of civilization. A raven steals her crown for its nest. Undeterred, she continues deeper into the woods, shedding her garments as she becomes one with the wild. The story builds to a confrontation with a grea
stories.title: Innocence's Journey

stories.name: Inzoka the Serpent of the Lake
stories.excerpt: A fisherman named Mugabo encounters Inzoka, the great serpent of the lake, who offers him untold riches in exchange for a promise he cannot keep, teaching him the cost of dishonesty.
stories.title: Inzoka the Serpent of the Lake

stories.name: Ioskeha and Tawescaron: The Twin Brothers
stories.excerpt: After Aataentsic fell to the new earth, she gave birth to twin daughters. One of these daughters, Tekawerahkwa, became the mother of twin sons — Ioskeha and Tawescaron. The twins were opposites in every way. Ioskeha, the older twin, was the benefactor of the Huron people. He created the sun from his mother's body, brou
stories.title: Ioskeha and Tawescaron: The Twin Brothers

stories.name: Iram of the Pillars (Ubar, the Atlantis of the Sands)
stories.excerpt: A legendary lost city in the Arabian desert mentioned in the Quran, built by the tyrannical King Shaddad son of Ad in an attempt to create an earthly paradise with gold and silver ramparts, pillars of chrysolite and ruby, and rivers flowing through channels of gold. God destroyed Shaddad and his entire army with a migh
stories.title: Iram of the Pillars (Ubar, the Atlantis of the Sands)

stories.name: Isis and Osiris
stories.excerpt: The Osiris myth is the most elaborate and influential story in ancient Egyptian mythology. Osiris, a wise and beloved king of Egypt, taught humanity agriculture, law, and civilization. His jealous brother Set conspired with 72 accomplices to murder him, tricking Osiris into a chest which was sealed with lead and cast i
stories.title: Isis and Osiris

stories.name: Isokelekel: The Conqueror of Pohnpei
stories.excerpt: Isokelekel, meaning shining noble or wonderful king, is a semi-mythical hero and warrior from Kosrae who overthrew the Saudeleur rulers of Pohnpei between the early 16th and early 17th centuries. According to legend, Isokelekel arrived at Pohnpei with a fleet of canoes and a band of warriors. The Saudeleur dynasty had
stories.title: Isokelekel: The Conqueror of Pohnpei

stories.name: Jab Jab: Carnival of Chains
stories.excerpt: A young masquerader discovers that the Jab Jab who dances through the streets carries the memory of slavery in every clink of its chains, and that freedom is something you must choose to carry.
stories.title: Jab Jab: Carnival of Chains

stories.name: Jack and the Bean Tree
stories.excerpt: The Appalachian African American version of the classic Jack and the Beanstalk tale. Jack, a poor mountain boy, trades his family's only cow for a handful of seemingly worthless beans. His mother, furious, throws the beans out the window. Overnight, a giant beanstalk grows all the way to the sky. Jack climbs the beanst
stories.title: Jack and the Bean Tree

stories.name: Jack and the Beanstalk
stories.excerpt: A boy climbs a magic beanstalk to a giant's castle in the sky, risking everything for his family's survival.
stories.title: Jack and the Beanstalk

stories.name: Jack and the Robbers
stories.excerpt: Jack leaves home seeking adventure and meets a group of robbers in the forest. Rather than fleeing, Jack cleverly ingratiates himself with them, pretending to be a fierce outlaw. He joins their band and joins them on a raid of a wealthy house. When the robbers send Jack in to check if the house is empty, Jack finds it
stories.title: Jack and the Robbers

stories.name: Jack and the Varmints
stories.excerpt: Jack is tasked with spending a night alone in a haunted cabin in the woods as a test of courage. The cabin is supposedly infested with 'varmints'—supernatural creatures that have driven away everyone who came before. Jack, being too lazy and stubborn to be properly scared, settles into the cabin for the night. As midni
stories.title: Jack and the Varmints

stories.name: Jack in the Giants' Newground
stories.excerpt: Jack, a lazy mountain boy, decides to seek his fortune after his mother grows tired of his idleness. He arrives at a king's house and learns that giants have overrun the king's 'newground' (newly cleared land) and will not let anyone farm it. Anyone who goes against them is eaten. Jack volunteers, armed only with his w
stories.title: Jack in the Giants' Newground

stories.name: Jacky-My-Lantern
stories.excerpt: In this African American version of the will-o'-the-wisp legend collected by Joel Chandler Harris, Jacky-My-Lantern is a wandering spirit who carries a flickering light through the swamps at night, luring travelers from the safety of the road into the treacherous marshland. According to Uncle Remus, Jacky-My-Lantern wa
stories.title: Jacky-My-Lantern

stories.name: Jaka Tarub and the Seven Heavenly Nymphs
stories.excerpt: A Javanese folktale from Central Java about a young man named Jaka Tarub who spies on seven heavenly nymphs (bidadari) bathing in a forest lake. He steals the shawl of the youngest and most beautiful, Nawang Wulan, preventing her from returning to heaven. She marries him, and they have a daughter. Nawang Wulan possesse
stories.title: Jaka Tarub and the Seven Heavenly Nymphs

stories.name: Jataka — Prince Sattva and the Starving Tigress
stories.excerpt: In this most famous Jataka tale of self-sacrifice, the Buddha in a past life was born as Prince Sattva (sometimes called Prince Mahasattva). While wandering in the forest with his brothers, he came upon a starving tigress too weak to nurse her newborn cubs, about to eat them out of desperation. Overcome with compassion
stories.title: Jataka — Prince Sattva and the Starving Tigress

stories.name: Jataka — The Banyan Deer (Nigrodhamiga Jataka)
stories.excerpt: In a past life, the Buddha was born as a golden deer named King Banyan Deer, leader of a herd of 500 deer in the forests near Benares. When the local king hunted deer excessively, the deer kings devised a lottery system where deer would sacrifice themselves in turn. One day, a pregnant doe from the Monkey Deer herd was
stories.title: Jataka — The Banyan Deer (Nigrodhamiga Jataka)

stories.name: Jesús Malverde — The Generous Bandit
stories.excerpt: Jesús Malverde (1870–1909) is a legendary Mexican bandit turned folk saint whose devotion has spread to Mexican-American communities throughout the US Southwest. Born in Sinaloa, Malverde was said to rob from the rich and give to the poor, earning him the nickname 'The Generous Bandit' or 'The Robin Hood of Sinaloa.' H
stories.title: Jesús Malverde — The Generous Bandit

stories.name: Jinn (Genie), the Djiboutian Spirit World
stories.excerpt: The jinn of Djibouti are powerful spirits of fire and air who inhabit the desert and the sea, interacting with humans through bargains and blessings.
stories.title: Jinn (Genie), the Djiboutian Spirit World

stories.name: Johan and the Trolls
stories.excerpt: A servant named Johan is sent to catch a horse but is lured by a beautiful troll maiden into a mountain. He disappears for years, forced to steal food for the trolls using a magical red hat that lets him fly through locked doors. His master eventually rescues him by throwing his clothes up the cliff, but Johan is never
stories.title: Johan and the Trolls

stories.name: John Henry
stories.excerpt: In the years after the Civil War, as America stretched its railroads across the continent, a new kind of hero emerged from the sweat and labor of the nation's working men.
stories.title: John Henry

stories.name: John Henry vs. the Steam Drill
stories.excerpt: John Henry, the legendary steel-driving man, worked as a hammer-swinging laborer blasting tunnels through mountains for the expanding railroad. When a salesman brought a steam-powered drilling machine to the worksite, claiming it could outwork any man, the captain of the crew proposed a contest: man against machine. Jo
stories.title: John Henry vs. the Steam Drill

stories.name: Jok, Lord of the Cattle Spirits
stories.excerpt: Jok, the supreme sky spirit of the Nilotic peoples, sent his cattle spirits to walk among the herds of earth, teaching the people that every ox carries a fragment of divine will within its horns.
stories.title: Jok, Lord of the Cattle Spirits

stories.name: Jong Batu (The Legend of the Stone Ship)
stories.excerpt: A beloved Bruneian legend about an unfilial son who was turned to stone, sharing the same moral motif as Malin Kundang and Si Tanggang. According to the tale, a wealthy young merchant named Awang or Si Untak returned to Brunei on his magnificent ship after making his fortune abroad. His elderly mother, who had raised h
stories.title: Jong Batu (The Legend of the Stone Ship)

stories.name: Juan Bobo: The Folk Simpleton
stories.excerpt: Juan Bobo (Simple John) is a beloved folk character in Puerto Rican and broader Caribbean folklore — a good-hearted but dim-witted boy whose adventures always go hilariously wrong. In one classic tale, Juan Bobo's mother asks him to watch the pot of rice while she goes to church. He decides to bathe the pig with the ri
stories.title: Juan Bobo: The Folk Simpleton

stories.name: Juan Machete: The Fire-Vomiting Phantom
stories.excerpt: A Colombian plainsman makes a pact with the devil but ends up cursed to guard his buried treasure for eternity.
stories.title: Juan Machete: The Fire-Vomiting Phantom

stories.name: Jumbie, the Restless Spirit
stories.excerpt: In Antiguan folklore, a Jumbie is a restless spirit of the dead that haunts the living, often appearing at crossroads or near ancient trees.
stories.title: Jumbie, the Restless Spirit

stories.name: Juoksáhkká: The Bow Woman
stories.excerpt: Juoksáhkká (Bow Woman) is a goddess depicted with a bow on Sámi drums. One of the daughters of Máttaráhkká, she could change a child's sex from female to male in the womb if given enough offerings, as sons were more valued. She helped with development and birth, protected children from shots and falls, and helped women
stories.title: Juoksáhkká: The Bow Woman

stories.name: Juracán, Lord of the Storm
stories.excerpt: Juracán is the Taino god of storms and hurricanes, the origin of the English word 'hurricane.' In Taino mythology, Juracán was once Guacar, the twin brother of Yocahú, son of the mother goddess Atabey. While Atabey and Yocahú worked together filling the world with beautiful creations, Guacar grew jealous of their bond.
stories.title: Juracán, Lord of the Storm

stories.name: Jurate and Kastytis: The Amber Legend of the Baltic Sea
stories.excerpt: A sea goddess falls in love with a mortal fisherman, and her shattered amber palace becomes the treasure of the Baltic shore.
stories.title: Jurate and Kastytis: The Amber Legend of the Baltic Sea

stories.name: Jábmiidáhkká: Ruler of the Underworld
stories.excerpt: Jábmiidáhkká is the female ruler of Jábmiidaibmu, the Sámi underworld. The dead missed their relatives, so she sometimes allowed them to cause diseases among the living. If the dead caught a living person's soul and dragged it to the underworld, that person would fall into a coma or fatal illness. She could allow the s
stories.title: Jábmiidáhkká: Ruler of the Underworld

stories.name: Kaang's Creation: The Great Tree and the First People
stories.excerpt: The San creator god Kaang (also known as /Kaggen) created a wondrous tree whose branches stretched over the entire land. At its base he dug a hole reaching down to the underworld where people and animals lived in harmony. He led them up into the world, instructing them not to build fires. When the sun set, the people g
stories.title: Kaang's Creation: The Great Tree and the First People

stories.name: Kaats' and the Bear Woman (Tlingit)
stories.excerpt: The Tlingit hunter Kaats' was hunting in the mountains near Glacier Bay when he encountered a bear who removed her skin and became a beautiful woman. He married her, and they had children who were half-human, half-bear. His bear wife provided for him and taught him about the forest, but Kaats' eventually grew homesick
stories.title: Kaats' and the Bear Woman (Tlingit)

stories.name: Kaguya-hime: The Princess of the Moon
stories.excerpt: A celestial princess found in a stalk of bamboo brings wealth and beauty to her adoptive father, but must eventually return to her lunar home.
stories.title: Kaguya-hime: The Princess of the Moon

stories.name: Kahausibware: The Creator Goddess
stories.excerpt: Kahausibware is a creator goddess in the mythology of the Mono-Alu people of the Solomon Islands. She is a supreme female deity credited with creating the world, the islands, and all living things. In the beginning, Kahausibware created the land by pulling islands up from the sea. She then fashioned humans from clay an
stories.title: Kahausibware: The Creator Goddess

stories.name: Kaji, the Fire Spirit
stories.excerpt: A spirit of fire and lightning that inhabits the hearth, protecting the home when respected and burning it when angered, because in Georgia fire is both hearth and hell.
stories.title: Kaji, the Fire Spirit

stories.name: Kalala Ilunga: The Founder of the Luba Empire
stories.excerpt: Kalala Ilunga, son of Mbidi Kiluwe and Bulanda, was born with the destiny of a conqueror. From childhood, he showed extraordinary strength, intelligence, and mystical gifts far beyond his years — he was said to praise himself for future exploits on the very day of his birth. His uncle, King Nkongolo, grew jealous and a
stories.title: Kalala Ilunga: The Founder of the Luba Empire

stories.name: Kalanoro: The Forest Spirits of Madagascar
stories.excerpt: Small, child-like spirits with backward feet haunt the remote forests of Madagascar.
stories.title: Kalanoro: The Forest Spirits of Madagascar

stories.name: Kali
stories.excerpt: In the age when the devas, the gods of heaven, were locked in an eternal struggle with the asuras, the demons of the underworld, a terror arose that threatened to unmake the balance of the cosmos.
stories.title: Kali

stories.name: Kali and the Thugs
stories.excerpt: In the frozen forests of Siberia, where the winter lasts nine months and the temperature can drop to sixty degrees below zero, there lives a creature that the Evenki reindeer herders have learned to respect.
stories.title: Kali and the Thugs

stories.name: Kalulu and the Pot of Wisdom
stories.excerpt: Kalulu the Hare, the great trickster of Malawian lore, attempted to steal a pot of wisdom from the sky-god Chiuta, only to discover that wisdom cannot be hoarded — it must be shared to multiply.
stories.title: Kalulu and the Pot of Wisdom

stories.name: Kalunga-Ngombe and the Bridge of Bones
stories.excerpt: A river monster demands a toll from those who cross the water, and only a woman with the wisdom of her ancestors learns the true price of passage.
stories.title: Kalunga-Ngombe and the Bridge of Bones

stories.name: Kamata the Culture Hero of Vanuatu
stories.excerpt: Kamata is a culture hero in Vanuatu mythology, particularly among the people of Ambrym and Malekula. He is credited with bringing fire, agriculture, and essential knowledge to humanity. Kamata journeyed across the islands performing great deeds, shaping the landscape, and teaching people how to cultivate yams, build ho
stories.title: Kamata the Culture Hero of Vanuatu

stories.name: Kanati and Selu: The Origin of Game and Corn (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: Kanati (The Lucky Hunter) and Selu (Corn) were the first Cherokee man and woman. Kanati would hunt by moving a rock at the entrance of a cave, releasing an animal and killing it. Their son befriended a Wild Boy born from the blood of slaughtered game. The boys secretly followed Kanati and discovered the cave; they open
stories.title: Kanati and Selu: The Origin of Game and Corn (Cherokee)

stories.name: Kannagi and the Burning of Madurai (Silappadikaram)
stories.excerpt: Kannagi, a virtuous merchant's daughter, married Kovalan in the Chola city of Puhar. When Kovalan fell for the courtesan Madhavi and squandered all his wealth, he eventually returned to Kannagi. The couple traveled to Madurai, where Kovalan tried to sell one of Kannagi's jeweled anklets to restart his life. The royal g
stories.title: Kannagi and the Burning of Madurai (Silappadikaram)

stories.name: Kappa: The River imp
stories.excerpt: A water spirit that lives in rivers, respects honor, and can be fooled by a simple formality.
stories.title: Kappa: The River imp

stories.name: Karakoncolos: The Winter Goblin of Anatolia
stories.excerpt: A hairy winter goblin challenges travelers with riddles during the coldest days of the year.
stories.title: Karakoncolos: The Winter Goblin of Anatolia

stories.name: Kashehotapalo (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: Kashehotapalo is a creature from Choctaw mythology that is neither man nor beast. It has the legs and hooves of a deer but the body of a man. Its head and face are small and shriveled, and it is said that anyone who looks at it will be visited by evil. Kashehotapalo delights in frightening hunters who venture near the
stories.title: Kashehotapalo (Choctaw)

stories.name: Katie Grey
stories.excerpt: The Devil himself cannot sow discord between a loving couple, so he enlists the witch Katie Grey. She tricks the wife into trying a 'charm' (cutting hairs from her sleeping husband's beard) and convinces the husband that his wife will cut his throat. The misunderstanding leads to both spouses killing each other. Even t
stories.title: Katie Grey

stories.name: Katie Woodencloak
stories.excerpt: Katie, a girl born with a wooden cloak that makes her an object of ridicule, endures hardship and loneliness. However, her resilience and the hidden magical properties of her cloak eventually lead her to a destiny of love and royalty, showing that true value lies beneath the surface.
stories.title: Katie Woodencloak

stories.name: Katrineholm Manor
stories.excerpt: An old unoccupied manor in Småland is haunted because it was built on a mountain inhabited by troll spirits. The lady of the manor helps a troll queen in childbirth and receives a box of jewels, but warns that revealing the secret will bring disaster. When her husband discovers the treasure through their sons' curiosit
stories.title: Katrineholm Manor

stories.name: Kaveh the Blacksmith and the Derafsh Kaviani
stories.excerpt: Kaveh, a humble blacksmith, loses all but one of his sons to the daily sacrifice demanded by King Zahhak's serpent-shoulders. He storms the royal court, refusing the king's bribe of signing his remaining son's death warrant. Kaveh raises his blacksmith's leather apron on a spear as a battle standard and leads the popul
stories.title: Kaveh the Blacksmith and the Derafsh Kaviani

stories.name: Kawa the Blacksmith and Newroz
stories.excerpt: The foundational Kurdish myth explaining the origins of Newroz (the Kurdish New Year on the spring equinox). The evil Assyrian king Zahhak (Zuhak) had serpents growing from his shoulders that demanded daily sacrifices of young men's brains. Kawa, a blacksmith who lost all but one of his sons to the sacrifice, rallied t
stories.title: Kawa the Blacksmith and Newroz

stories.name: Kel Essuf, the Lonely Desert
stories.excerpt: A Tuareg caravan leader learns why the Tuareg fear the Kel Essuf, the lonely spirits of the deep desert who lure travelers away from their caravans with false oases and phantom voices.
stories.title: Kel Essuf, the Lonely Desert

stories.name: Kelpie
stories.excerpt: Along the lonely shores of Scottish lochs, by the banks of dark rivers, and in the pools where the water runs deep and still, there dwells a creature both beautiful and deadly.
stories.title: Kelpie

stories.name: Kettil Runske
stories.excerpt: Two rival kings on Vising Island hire troll-men to dig a dividing ditch. Gilbertil of Östergötland begins the work, but Kettil Runske of Vestergötland defeats him with a magical staff, leaving Gilbertil bound in a deep hole that still bears his name.
stories.title: Kettil Runske

stories.name: Khan Töölö the Hero
stories.excerpt: The Tuvan epic of Khan Töölö, one of the most important figures in Tuvan oral tradition. The epic tells of a heroic warrior-prince who defends the Tuvan people against invading forces and monstrous beings from the Sayan and Altai mountains. Khan Töölö possesses supernatural strength granted by the sky spirits and rides
stories.title: Khan Töölö the Hero

stories.name: Khanyapa the Forest Spirit of the Northern Province
stories.excerpt: A Luvale boy lost in the forests of Zambia's Northern Province is guided to safety by Khanyapa, a forest spirit who tests whether travelers carry respect for the woodland in their hearts.
stories.title: Khanyapa the Forest Spirit of the Northern Province

stories.name: Khosrow and Shirin
stories.excerpt: The Persian prince Khosrow Parviz falls in love with the Armenian princess Shirin through a portrait painted by his friend Shapur. Their love is thwarted by a series of obstacles: Khosrow's forced marriage to the Byzantine princess Mariam for political alliance, his dalliance with Shekar in Isfahan, and the tragic love
stories.title: Khosrow and Shirin

stories.name: Khun Borom: The Founding Myth of the Lao People
stories.excerpt: The Khun Borom myth is the foundational creation story of the Lao and Tai peoples, detailing their origins after a great flood. According to the legend recorded in the Nithan Khun Borom chronicle, in ancient times humanity became wicked and corrupt. A powerful sky deity (Phaya Thaen) destroyed them with a great flood,
stories.title: Khun Borom: The Founding Myth of the Lao People

stories.name: Kianda and the Fisherman's Net
stories.excerpt: A water goddess of the Angolan coast tests a fisherman's humility by offering him a net that catches everything beneath the waves — except what he needs most.
stories.title: Kianda and the Fisherman's Net

stories.name: Kibo and Mawenzi: The Sister Peaks of Kilimanjaro
stories.excerpt: Two sister peaks of Mount Kilimanjaro teach a lesson about preparation and generosity.
stories.title: Kibo and Mawenzi: The Sister Peaks of Kilimanjaro

stories.name: Kibuka: The War God of Buganda
stories.excerpt: Kibuka is the fearsome war god of the Baganda people, the brother of the lake god Mukasa. According to legend, Kibuka was once a mortal man of extraordinary strength and military genius. When Buganda was threatened by invasion from the neighboring Bunyoro kingdom, Kibuka was called upon to lead the army. He fought with
stories.title: Kibuka: The War God of Buganda

stories.name: Kijuju: The Underwater People
stories.excerpt: A secret people who live beneath African lakes, coming to trade with surface dwellers—but only at night.
stories.title: Kijuju: The Underwater People

stories.name: Kikala: The First Fulani Shepherd and the Sacred Cattle
stories.excerpt: According to Fulani legend, the first Fulani shepherd was Kikala, whose hand with six fingers contains the primordial genealogy of the Fulani people. Four fingers represent the four great Fulani aristocratic families (Dyal, Ba, So, and Bari), the fifth finger represents allied tribes, and the sixth represents those in
stories.title: Kikala: The First Fulani Shepherd and the Sacred Cattle

stories.name: Kilibob and Manup: The Two Brothers of Papua New Guinea
stories.excerpt: In the mythology of northeastern Papua New Guinea, Kilibob and Manup are mythical brothers whose travels created the islands and peoples of the region. Kilibob traveled by canoe along the northern coast, creating islands and bestowing gifts like fishing nets, canoes, and knowledge of navigation. Manup followed a southe
stories.title: Kilibob and Manup: The Two Brothers of Papua New Guinea

stories.name: King Dutugemunu and Elara: The Just Rivalry
stories.excerpt: Elara (Ellalan), a Tamil Chola prince, ruled Anuradhapura with such famed justice that he earned the title Manu Needhi Cholan ('the Chola who follows justice') — he once executed his own son under a chariot wheel to give justice to a grieving cow. The young Sinhalese prince Dutugemunu, believing the island should be un
stories.title: King Dutugemunu and Elara: The Just Rivalry

stories.name: King Erik XIV's Imprisonment at Kastelholm
stories.excerpt: In the autumn of 1571, the deposed Swedish King Erik XIV was imprisoned at Kastelholm Castle by his brother Johan III. Erik had been dethroned in 1568 and was moved between various castles before being held on Åland. Local legend holds that Erik's ghost still wanders the halls of Kastelholm, his footsteps echoing throu
stories.title: King Erik XIV's Imprisonment at Kastelholm

stories.name: King Lindorm
stories.excerpt: A childless queen receives advice from an old woman: bathe in running water and eat two red onions. In her excitement, she eats one onion with the skin on, and peels the other. As a result, she gives birth first to a hideous lindorm (serpent), who is secretly thrown into the forest, and then to a beautiful prince. Year
stories.title: King Lindorm

stories.name: King Lindworm
stories.excerpt: A king is transformed into a serpent (lindworm) and can only be cured by a princess who agrees to a series of difficult tasks, eventually breaking the curse through her devotion.
stories.title: King Lindworm

stories.name: King Solomon and the Jinn
stories.excerpt: According to Islamic and Arabic folklore, Prophet Solomon (Sulayman) was granted dominion over all beings: mankind, jinn, birds, wild beasts, and the wind. He commanded armies of jinn and devils, imprisoned rebellious marids and ifrits in brass bottles sealed with molten lead and his signet ring, and cast them into the
stories.title: King Solomon and the Jinn

stories.name: Kintaro: The Golden Boy of Mountains
stories.excerpt: A supernaturally strong child raised by animals in the mountains becomes a legendary hero.
stories.title: Kintaro: The Golden Boy of Mountains

stories.name: Kintu and Nambi: The First People of Buganda
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, Kintu was the only man on earth, wandering the plains of Uganda alone with only a cow for companionship. One day, Nambi and her younger sister came down from the sky on a rainbow. Nambi saw Kintu and was curious about this strange creature she had never seen before. She fell in love with him and wante
stories.title: Kintu and Nambi: The First People of Buganda

stories.name: Kiranga, the Sacred Drum
stories.excerpt: A drum that beats on its own at midnight, its rhythm echoing across the hills — because the drum holds the heartbeat of the first king, and as long as it beats, the kingdom endures.
stories.title: Kiranga, the Sacred Drum

stories.name: Kishelamakank's Dream of Creation
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, before there was anything, there existed only an endless void of darkness. Within this emptiness dwelled Kishelamakank (He Who Creates Us By Thought), the Great Spirit. While in the void, the Creator fell into a deep sleep and dreamed of the world as it would become — mountains, forests, animals, and
stories.title: Kishelamakank's Dream of Creation

stories.name: Kitsune: The Fox Spirits
stories.excerpt: Intelligent foxes with magical powers—they can shapeshift, possess humans, and serve as messengers of the gods.
stories.title: Kitsune: The Fox Spirits

stories.name: Kitsune: The Fox Wife
stories.excerpt: A fox spirit takes human form to marry a lonely farmer, proving that love can transcend the boundary between the human and spirit worlds, even if it cannot last.
stories.title: Kitsune: The Fox Wife

stories.name: Knös
stories.excerpt: A boy born from an egg grows to giant size and becomes the strongest man at the king's court, defeating a fearsome sea troll to rescue three princesses and win the youngest's hand. This classic Swedish hero-tale draws on the Thor-like motif of the giant-slaying goblet found in the _Hymiskvida_ of the Poetic Edda.
stories.title: Knös

stories.name: Koimala: The First King of the Maldives
stories.excerpt: According to Maldivian folklore, Prince Koimala was a prince from the Indian subcontinent (or Sri Lanka, in some versions) who sailed to the Maldives with two ships. The indigenous Giraavaru people — Dravidian fishermen who cleaned tuna on a large sandbank — spotted his vessel and welcomed him, allowing him to settle o
stories.title: Koimala: The First King of the Maldives

stories.name: Kolowa: The Hairy Ogre (Creek)
stories.excerpt: Kolowa is a fearsome, hairy, man-eating ogre from Muscogee Creek mythology. Described as being covered in thick hair and possessing enormous strength, Kolowa lives in the deep forest and preys on humans who stray too far from their villages. Some modern Creek storytellers translate the name as 'gorilla.' Kolowa is part
stories.title: Kolowa: The Hairy Ogre (Creek)

stories.name: Komokwa and the Undersea Kingdom (Haida)
stories.excerpt: In Haida tradition, the undersea world is ruled by powerful supernatural beings who control the wealth of the sea. The sea chiefs live in houses made of copper and abalone shell, surrounded by supernatural beings including the killer whale people, seal people, and halibut people. Those who drown do not truly die but ar
stories.title: Komokwa and the Undersea Kingdom (Haida)

stories.name: Komokwa the Undersea Chief (Kwakwaka'wakw)
stories.excerpt: Komokwa (also known as Qomoqua or Copper-Maker) is the powerful chief of the undersea world in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology. He lives in a magnificent copper house beneath the ocean, where he controls all the wealth of the sea, including seals, sea lions, salmon, and the precious copper that gives him his name. Komokwa appe
stories.title: Komokwa the Undersea Chief (Kwakwaka'wakw)

stories.name: Kongamato of the Falls
stories.excerpt: A Lozi hunter ventures too close to a hidden cataract above Victoria Falls and encounters the Kongamato, a pterodactyl-like beast that guards the spray zones where the living are not meant to wander.
stories.title: Kongamato of the Falls

stories.name: Korkut Ata and the Search for Immortality
stories.excerpt: Korkut Ata (also Dede Korkut) is the legendary father of Kazakh music and the creator of the kobyz (horsehair string instrument). Unable to accept the inevitability of death, Korkut fled from human society into nature, seeking immortality. But every element of nature — the trees, mountains, steppes, and rivers — told h
stories.title: Korkut Ata and the Search for Immortality

stories.name: Koschei the Deathless
stories.excerpt: An immortal sorcerer hides his death inside a needle, inside an egg, inside a duck, inside a hare, inside an iron chest, buried beneath an oak tree on a distant island.
stories.title: Koschei the Deathless

stories.name: Koumen: The Fulani Initiation and the Mysteries of Pastoral Life
stories.excerpt: In Fulani esoteric tradition, Koumen is the shepherd of the primordial cattle and the depositary of pastoral initiation secrets. He was entrusted by Gueno, the eternal creator, with the care of the land and all animals. Koumen can transform wild animals into domestic ones and vice versa, appearing to humans as a child
stories.title: Koumen: The Fulani Initiation and the Mysteries of Pastoral Life

stories.name: Krakl, or Kratt, the Variant Servant
stories.excerpt: A regional variant of the kratt, told in the dialects of southern Estonia, where the servant was made from straw and bound to a different master.
stories.title: Krakl, or Kratt, the Variant Servant

stories.name: Krampus: The Christmas Devil
stories.excerpt: On December 5th, Krampus comes for naughty children—while Saint Nicholas brings gifts to the good.
stories.title: Krampus: The Christmas Devil

stories.name: Kratt, the Hay and Firewood Servant
stories.excerpt: A household servant constructed from hay and firewood, animated by dark bargains, who served his master until the price was collected.
stories.title: Kratt, the Hay and Firewood Servant

stories.name: Krishna
stories.excerpt: Krishna is the eighth avatar of Vishnu, the preserver god who sustains the universe.
stories.title: Krishna

stories.name: Krishna Tames the Serpent Kaliya
stories.excerpt: Young Krishna, during his childhood in Vrindavan, discovered that the Yamuna River had become poisoned by Kaliya, a massive multi-headed serpent who had taken residence in its waters. The river boiled with venom, killing fish, birds, and trees along the banks, and the villagers could no longer drink or approach it. Wit
stories.title: Krishna Tames the Serpent Kaliya

stories.name: Krsnik, the Slovene Daylight Hero
stories.excerpt: A heroic spirit of Slovenian folklore, the Krsnik is a being of light who fights the dark forces of the Kurent, protecting villages from evil.
stories.title: Krsnik, the Slovene Daylight Hero

stories.name: Kullervo and the Cheat-cake
stories.excerpt: Kullervo is tricked into a situation involving a 'cheat-cake', which further cements his identity as a social outcast. The experience fuels his rage and his desire for revenge against those who have wronged him.
stories.title: Kullervo and the Cheat-cake

stories.name: Kullervo As A Sheperd
stories.excerpt: Kullervo is sent to work as a shepherd, a role he finds degrading. He uses his position to express his inner turmoil and resentment, causing trouble for his masters and further isolating himself from society.
stories.title: Kullervo As A Sheperd

stories.name: Kullervo Finds His Tribe-folk
stories.excerpt: Kullervo eventually discovers his biological family, but the reunion is tragic rather than joyful. Old misunderstandings and ingrained hatreds lead to a violent confrontation, proving that blood ties cannot always heal past wounds.
stories.title: Kullervo Finds His Tribe-folk

stories.name: Kullervo's Evil Deeds
stories.excerpt: In a fit of blind rage and despair, Kullervo commits a series of terrible crimes, the most heinous of which is the abduction and murder of his own sister, whom he had not recognized. This act marks the peak of his tragic descent.
stories.title: Kullervo's Evil Deeds

stories.name: Kullerwoinen Son of Evil
stories.excerpt: Kullervo is born into a family marked by violence and hatred. Forced into slavery from a young age, he grows deeply resentful of the world and develops an intense hatred for all forms of authority, setting him on a path of destruction.
stories.title: Kullerwoinen Son of Evil

stories.name: Kullerwoinen's Victory and Death
stories.excerpt: After realizing the horror of his crimes, Kullervo finds himself unable to live with the guilt. He asks his sword if it will drink his blood, and upon the sword's agreement, he commits suicide, finally ending his cycle of suffering and violence.
stories.title: Kullerwoinen's Victory and Death

stories.name: Kulmking, the Frost King
stories.excerpt: A spirit of the Estonian winter who ruled the frozen rivers and punishing cold, feared by travelers and honored by those who survived his season.
stories.title: Kulmking, the Frost King

stories.name: Kupe Discovering Aotearoa
stories.excerpt: Kupe, a great Polynesian navigator and chief from Hawaiki, pursued the giant octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi across the Pacific Ocean after it stole his bait and caused chaos. His wife Hine-te-Aparangi sighted land and named it Aotearoa (Land of the Long White Cloud). Kupe and his crew landed at the Hokianga Harbour, wher
stories.title: Kupe Discovering Aotearoa

stories.name: Kurupira, the Forest Guardian
stories.excerpt: A small, green-skinned forest spirit with backwards feet who protects the trees and wildlife of Uruguay from those who take too much.
stories.title: Kurupira, the Forest Guardian

stories.name: Kusillo, the Hairy Trickster
stories.excerpt: A small, hairy creature with reversed feet leads travelers in circles through the highland puna, mimicking their laughter to lure them deeper into the fog.
stories.title: Kusillo, the Hairy Trickster

stories.name: Kuutkh (Raven) Creates the World
stories.excerpt: The central creation myth of the Chukchi, Koryak, and Itelmen peoples of northeastern Siberia. Kuutkh, the Great Raven, is both creator and trickster who shaped the cosmos from primordial chaos. In the beginning, there was nothing but darkness and water. Kuutkh flew over the endless sea and, through his actions — purpo
stories.title: Kuutkh (Raven) Creates the World

stories.name: Kuveni: The Yakshini Queen
stories.excerpt: Kuveni (also known as Sesapati or Kuvanna) was a Yakshini queen ruling in Lanka when Prince Vijaya arrived. Described as a shape-shifting demoness who could assume the form of a beautiful sixteen-year-old maiden, she initially imprisoned Vijaya's men in a chasm. After Vijaya overpowered her, she swore loyalty and helpe
stories.title: Kuveni: The Yakshini Queen

stories.name: Kwanokasha: The Spirit Who Grants Powers (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: Kwanokasha is a powerful Choctaw spirit associated with caves and rock shelters, who appears to young children during vision quests. According to legend, Kwanokasha takes children who wander into certain caves into the spirit world, where they are tested. The spirit offers them three choices: a knife (representing the
stories.title: Kwanokasha: The Spirit Who Grants Powers (Choctaw)

stories.name: Kwatyat and Tihtipihin Rescue Their Mother (Nuu-chah-nulth)
stories.excerpt: Two Nuu-chah-nulth brothers, Tihtipihin and Kwatyat, witnessed a great monster swallow their mother whole. Without hesitation, they willingly allowed themselves to be swallowed by the same monster so they could rescue her. Inside the monster's stomach, they found their mother alive along with other swallowed victims. U
stories.title: Kwatyat and Tihtipihin Rescue Their Mother (Nuu-chah-nulth)

stories.name: Kwatyat the Transformer (Nuu-chah-nulth)
stories.excerpt: Kwatyat is one of the most important transformer figures in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology. After his adventures with his brother Tihtipihin rescuing their mother from the monster, Kwatyat traveled the land transforming the world and making it ready for human beings. He changed dangerous beings into harmless animals, taught
stories.title: Kwatyat the Transformer (Nuu-chah-nulth)

stories.name: Kyllikki's Broken Vow
stories.excerpt: Lemminkainen woos the beautiful Kyllikki, eventually winning her heart and promising her marriage. However, he betrays her vows to pursue other interests, leading a heartbroken Kyllikki to place a powerful curse upon him. This betrayal drives Lemminkainen into a life of further wandering and instability.
stories.title: Kyllikki's Broken Vow

stories.name: Kyys Debiliye (The Warrior Maiden)
stories.excerpt: A rare Yakut Olonkho epic featuring a female warrior as its main protagonist. Kyys Debiliye is a powerful heroine who fights alongside and against male heroes, demonstrating the full range of martial prowess and determination. She defends her people against the evil Abaasy spirits and enemies that threaten the Middle W
stories.title: Kyys Debiliye (The Warrior Maiden)

stories.name: Kääk, the Luxembourgish Forest Spirit
stories.excerpt: A small, mischievous forest spirit of Luxembourg, Kääk dwells in the deep forests and delights in leading travelers astray.
stories.title: Kääk, the Luxembourgish Forest Spirit

stories.name: Kópakonan (The Seal Woman of Mikladalur)
stories.excerpt: A fisherman named Torkil from Mikladalur on Kalsoy Island watches a group of seal-people dancing on the shore after shedding their sealskins. He falls in love with the most beautiful seal-woman, steals her sealskin, and locks it in a chest. Unable to return to the sea, she marries him and bears his children. Years late
stories.title: Kópakonan (The Seal Woman of Mikladalur)

stories.name: Kópakonan's Curse (The Seal Woman's Revenge)
stories.excerpt: The darker sequel to the Kópakonan legend. After the seal woman returned to the sea, her human husband Torkil began sealing (hunting seals). Kópakonan appeared to him in a dream, begging him not to kill her seal husband and children. Torkil ignored her warning. When he killed her seal family, Kópakonan rose from the se
stories.title: Kópakonan's Curse (The Seal Woman's Revenge)

stories.name: L'Ankou, the Dark Coachman of the Low Countries
stories.excerpt: A death omen spirit who drives a ghostly coach across the Belgian countryside, collecting the souls of those about to die.
stories.title: L'Ankou, the Dark Coachman of the Low Countries

stories.name: La Cegua: The Shrouded Specter
stories.excerpt: A young man encounters a beautiful woman on a dark road, only to discover she is La Cegua — a veiled spirit whose terrifying face beneath her shawl punishes the unfaithful and the arrogant.
stories.title: La Cegua: The Shrouded Specter

stories.name: La Ciguapa of the Dominican Mountains
stories.excerpt: La Ciguapa is a legendary creature from Dominican folklore — a beautiful woman with long, flowing hair and dark skin who has her feet on backwards. She inhabits the remote mountainous regions of the Dominican Republic, particularly the Cordillera Central and Bahoruco Mountains. According to legend, La Ciguapa lures men
stories.title: La Ciguapa of the Dominican Mountains

stories.name: La Ciguapa: The Backward-Footed Woman of the Dominican Mountains
stories.excerpt: A wild woman with backward-facing feet lures men into the mountains with an irresistible call.
stories.title: La Ciguapa: The Backward-Footed Woman of the Dominican Mountains

stories.name: La Culebra Mayor, the Great Serpent
stories.excerpt: A monstrous serpent of Costa Rican legend, La Culebra Mayor is a winged snake that guards hidden treasures and devours anyone who seeks them.
stories.title: La Culebra Mayor, the Great Serpent

stories.name: La Curandera of the Llano — The Healing Woman of the Plains
stories.excerpt: Across the Hispanic villages of New Mexico and Colorado, the figure of La Curandera — the wise healing woman — is both a historical reality and a legendary archetype. These women were the primary healthcare providers in isolated communities, using knowledge of medicinal herbs passed down through generations, prayer, an
stories.title: La Curandera of the Llano — The Healing Woman of the Plains

stories.name: La Diablera of the Crossroads
stories.excerpt: A seductive spirit of the crossroads offers travelers impossible bargains — wealth, knowledge, love — but always demands a price that cannot be paid until it is too late.
stories.title: La Diablera of the Crossroads

stories.name: La Diablesse at the Crossroads
stories.excerpt: A beautiful stranger appears at a rural crossroads to lure a young farmer to his doom, but his mother's warnings and an old obeah charm may yet save him.
stories.title: La Diablesse at the Crossroads

stories.name: La Diablesse of the Crossroads
stories.excerpt: A charming stranger lures a proud young man down a moonlit road, but La Diablesse reveals her true nature only when he is far too late to turn back.
stories.title: La Diablesse of the Crossroads

stories.name: La Diablesse, the Devil Woman
stories.excerpt: La Diablesse is a seductive she-devil from Trinidadian folklore who appears as a breathtakingly beautiful woman in an old-fashioned embroidered dress and wide-brimmed hat, smelling of expensive perfume. By moonlight, the perceptive may glimpse her true nature — one cloven hoof hidden beneath the hem. She lures unfaithf
stories.title: La Diablesse, the Devil Woman

stories.name: La Garita: The Goat Children
stories.excerpt: La Garita (also known as the Goat Children or the Legend of the Garita) is a Puerto Rican folktale about two children who were transformed into goats as punishment or protection. The story is traditionally told to explain the presence of wild goats in the Puerto Rican countryside and to warn children against disobedien
stories.title: La Garita: The Goat Children

stories.name: La Lechuza — The Witch-Owl of the Border
stories.excerpt: La Lechuza is a terrifying figure in Mexican-American folklore, particularly along the Texas-Mexico border. She is described as a witch who transforms into a giant owl — specifically a great horned owl or barn owl — with a wingspan of up to ten feet and the face of an old woman. According to legend, a woman who makes a
stories.title: La Lechuza — The Witch-Owl of the Border

stories.name: La Llorona
stories.excerpt: In Mexico, the rivers and canals hold a sorrow that never dies—that of La Llorona, the Weeping Woman.
stories.title: La Llorona

stories.name: La Llorona as La Malinche's Curse
stories.excerpt: One of the most powerful variants of the La Llorona legend connects her directly to La Malinche, the Nahua woman who served as Hernán Cortés's interpreter, advisor, and mother of his son. In this telling, Malinche—cursed by her people for betraying the Aztec Empire—became La Llorona, condemned to wander forever weeping
stories.title: La Llorona as La Malinche's Curse

stories.name: La Llorona de los Ríos de Tejas — The Weeping Woman of the Texas Rivers
stories.excerpt: In the South Texas borderlands along the Rio Grande, Mexican-American communities tell of La Llorona appearing near irrigation canals and arroyos where children have drowned. Unlike the classic Mexican version, the Texas variant often emphasizes her role as a protector of children rather than a predator — some say she
stories.title: La Llorona de los Ríos de Tejas — The Weeping Woman of the Texas Rivers

stories.name: La Llorona — The Weeping Woman
stories.excerpt: La Llorona is the vengeful ghost of a woman who drowned her children in a river after discovering her husband's infidelity, then drowned herself in grief. She now wanders along rivers and lakes across Mexico and the US Southwest, dressed in white with long black hair, weeping and wailing '¡Ay, mis hijos!' Those who hea
stories.title: La Llorona — The Weeping Woman

stories.name: La Llorona: The Weeping Woman
stories.excerpt: A woman who drowned her children now wanders near water, searching—and anyone who hears her cry is marked for death.
stories.title: La Llorona: The Weeping Woman

stories.name: La Loba — The Wolf Woman of the Desert
stories.excerpt: La Loba (The Wolf Woman) is a figure from New Mexican and Chicano folklore who protects the wild places and animals of the Southwestern desert. Older than any human, she is the guardian of wolf and coyote spirits, and it is said that when a wolf dies, La Loba collects its bones and sings over them until the animal is r
stories.title: La Loba — The Wolf Woman of the Desert

stories.name: La Mano Pachona — The Disembodied Hand of the Border
stories.excerpt: La Mano Pachona is a chilling legend from northern Mexico and the US Southwest about a disembodied, hairy hand that attacks travelers at night. The hand is described as large, dark, and covered in thick hair, with long fingernails. It is said to wander along lonely roads, scratching at windows and car doors, or reachin
stories.title: La Mano Pachona — The Disembodied Hand of the Border

stories.name: La Masa, the Honduran Monster
stories.excerpt: A monstrous creature of Honduran folklore, La Masa is a shapeless, crushing entity that stalks the forests and crushes anyone who trespasses on sacred ground.
stories.title: La Masa, the Honduran Monster

stories.name: La Planchada — The Ghost Nurse in White
stories.excerpt: La Planchada (The Ironed One, referring to her perfectly pressed uniform) is a ghost legend from Mexico City hospitals that has spread through Mexican-American communities in the US Southwest. According to the story, a beautiful nurse named Eulalia was deeply in love with a doctor who rejected her. Heartbroken, she too
stories.title: La Planchada — The Ghost Nurse in White

stories.name: La Siguanaba — The Horse-Faced Woman
stories.excerpt: La Siguanaba (or Sihuanaba) is a beautiful woman spirit from Mesoamerican folklore, particularly prevalent in El Salvador, Guatemala, and southern Mexico, with variants told in Mexican-American communities. She appears as a stunningly beautiful woman with long, flowing hair, seen bathing in rivers or washing clothes. S
stories.title: La Siguanaba — The Horse-Faced Woman

stories.name: La Silampa, the Forest Fire
stories.excerpt: A ball of fire that rolls through the forest at night, burning everything in its path, because in Panama the forest holds grudges.
stories.title: La Silampa, the Forest Fire

stories.name: La Trola: The Deceiver
stories.excerpt: La Trola is a cunning shapeshifting spirit who lures travelers into the wilderness with false promises, teaching a timeless lesson about the dangers of greed and trusting strangers.
stories.title: La Trola: The Deceiver

stories.name: La Tulivieja, the Drowned Woman
stories.excerpt: A woman who drowned herself and her child in a river, now wanders the waterways searching for her baby, luring men to their deaths with her beauty.
stories.title: La Tulivieja, the Drowned Woman

stories.name: Lady Barbro of Brokind
stories.excerpt: The cruel Lady Barbro would bind her servants and place food before them they could not reach laughing at their suffering. After death her ghost haunted Linkoping cathedral until her body was impaled in a swamp. Yet even this did not quiet her spirit and strange lights still appear at Brokind.
stories.title: Lady Barbro of Brokind

stories.name: Lady Guinevere
stories.excerpt: She was said to be the loveliest woman in all the island.. Her name was Guinevere, daughter of King Leodegrance of Cameliard, and when Arthur first heard of her beauty, he knew he must have her as his queen.
stories.title: Lady Guinevere

stories.name: Lafaek Diak (The Good Crocodile)
stories.excerpt: The foundational creation myth of Timor-Leste, explaining why the island is shaped like a crocodile. A young boy discovered a baby crocodile struggling to reach the sea and compassionately carried it to the water. The grateful crocodile promised to repay the boy and invited him to ride on its back for many journeys. De
stories.title: Lafaek Diak (The Good Crocodile)

stories.name: Lagahoo: Midnight on the Estuary
stories.excerpt: A plantation-era overseer who abused his workers is cursed to become the Lagahoo, doomed to shapeshift each night and haunt the very roads he once patrolled.
stories.title: Lagahoo: Midnight on the Estuary

stories.name: Lakota Star Husband Story
stories.excerpt: Two Lakota girls lay outside their tipi one night, and one pointed at the brightest star saying she wished to marry it. The next day the girls found themselves in the sky world, where the first girl became the wife of a star. She was told not to dig around a certain turnip-like root, but curiosity overcame her. When sh
stories.title: Lakota Star Husband Story

stories.name: Lalibela: The Rock-Hewn Churches
stories.excerpt: In the 12th century, King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty was visited by a vision from God. In the vision, he was taken to heaven and shown magnificent churches built by angels. When he returned to earth, God commanded him to build a New Jerusalem in the rocky mountains of Ethiopia. King Lalibela gathered thousands of wo
stories.title: Lalibela: The Rock-Hewn Churches

stories.name: Lamia of the Dark Valleys
stories.excerpt: A vengeful spirit with the body of a serpent and the face of a woman haunts the mountain passes of Cyprus, luring travelers with her weeping before revealing her true form.
stories.title: Lamia of the Dark Valleys

stories.name: Lamia, the Child Eater
stories.excerpt: A beautiful woman who was once a queen, now a monster who steals children in the night — because in Lebanon, grief can turn love into hunger.
stories.title: Lamia, the Child Eater
