stories.name: Language on a Mountain
stories.excerpt: After a great flood swept through the land, Na'pi (Old Man) gathered all the people on top of a large mountain. He gave them water of different colors—black, red, yellow, and white—and told them to drink and then speak. Each group that drank the colored water spoke a different language. Only those who received the blac
stories.title: Language on a Mountain

stories.name: Lars, My Lad!
stories.excerpt: A spendthrift duke, reduced to poverty, discovers a scrap of paper in a hidden chest that summons a magical servant named Lars who grants every wish. He builds a palace, marries a princess, but foolishly gives the paper back to Lars and loses everything, ending up naked in a ruined hut and nearly hanged before tricking
stories.title: Lars, My Lad!

stories.name: Las Gorras Blancas — The Night Riders of the San Luis Valley
stories.excerpt: Las Gorras Blancas (The White Caps) were a secret society of Mexican-American vigilantes who rode at night in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado between 1889 and 1891, terrorizing Anglo landowners and railroad companies who were stealing Hispanic land grants. Clad in white caps and masks, they cut down fences, b
stories.title: Las Gorras Blancas — The Night Riders of the San Luis Valley

stories.name: Lasse, My Thrall!
stories.excerpt: A ruined nobleman discovers a magic scrap of paper that summons a tireless servant named Lasse, who builds him a castle and wins him a princess — but losing the paper costs him everything until he learns wisdom. This popular Swedish tale is a distinctive Nordic variant of the Aladdin cycle, set down in the dialect of N
stories.title: Lasse, My Thrall!

stories.name: Lauma, the Spinning Fairy of Latvia
stories.excerpt: Lauma, a luminous fairy of Latvian lore, haunts the spinning rooms and riverbanks, rewarding industrious maidens and punishing the idle with tangled thread and cold water.
stories.title: Lauma, the Spinning Fairy of Latvia

stories.name: Laumas, the Plural Spirits of the Meadow
stories.excerpt: The Laumas are a chorus of meadow spirits who sing in the twilight, weaving fate into the flax and luring wanderers into the mist with their otherworldly voices.
stories.title: Laumas, the Plural Spirits of the Meadow

stories.name: Laxdæla Saga - The Curse of the Leg-Biter
stories.excerpt: The sword 'Leg-Biter' (Fótbítur) is a legendary weapon that brings misfortune to those who wield it. It is stolen and recovered several times, eventually being used by Bolli to kill his foster-brother Kjartan, sealing a tragic fate for both and illustrating the theme of an inevitable, cursed destiny.
stories.title: Laxdæla Saga - The Curse of the Leg-Biter

stories.name: Laxdæla Saga - The Ghost of the Third Husband
stories.excerpt: Guðrún Ósvífursdóttir, a woman of great beauty and ambition, suffers the loss of three husbands. Following the death of her second husband, she is haunted by his spirit, which serves as a reminder of the tragic consequences of her own pride and the cycle of vengeance that consumes her family and friends.
stories.title: Laxdæla Saga - The Ghost of the Third Husband

stories.name: Layla and Majnun
stories.excerpt: Based on the true 7th-century story of Qays ibn al-Mulawwah, a Bedouin poet of the Banu Amir tribe in Najd, who fell deeply in love with his cousin Layla. When her father refused the match due to Qays's obsessive behavior (seen as madness or jinn-possession, earning him the epithet 'Majnun' meaning 'crazy'), and forced
stories.title: Layla and Majnun

stories.name: Leap the Elk and Little Princess Cottongrass
stories.excerpt: Princess Cottongrass (Tuvstarr) has lived her entire life in the Dream Castle, a sheltered world of safety and beauty. One day, a magnificent elk named Long-Leap (Skutt) appears. Enchanted by his stately bearing and crown-like antlers, she begs him to carry her out into the world. The elk warns her: 'The world is big a
stories.title: Leap the Elk and Little Princess Cottongrass

stories.name: Legba and the Divine Gate (Fon/Dahomey)
stories.excerpt: Legba is the youngest son of Mawu-Lisa, the trickster god who serves as the gatekeeper between the human world and the spirit world. Unlike the other gods who dwell in distant heavens, Legba walks among humans. He is the master of languages, the interpreter of the gods, and the lord of crossroads. In one tale, Mawu gav
stories.title: Legba and the Divine Gate (Fon/Dahomey)

stories.name: Lemminikainen's Second Wooing
stories.excerpt: Determined to find a new bride, Lemminkainen travels to Pohjola to woo the Daughter of Louhi. Louhi sets a series of nearly impossible tasks for him, including the requirement to kill the magical swans of Tuonela, which eventually leads to his downfall and death.
stories.title: Lemminikainen's Second Wooing

stories.name: Lemminkainen's Lament
stories.excerpt: The reckless and handsome warrior Lemminkainen enters a singing match with Wainamoinen, believing his charm and skill are sufficient. He is decisively defeated and humiliated by Wainamoinen's superior magic, leading him to lament his misfortune and seek a way to regain his lost honor.
stories.title: Lemminkainen's Lament

stories.name: Lemminkainen's Restoration
stories.excerpt: Driven by maternal love, Lemminkainen's mother travels to the depths of Tuonela. She painstakingly retrieves every fragment of her son's body from the river and uses powerful magic to piece him back together. He is restored to life, though the experience leaves him forever changed.
stories.title: Lemminkainen's Restoration

stories.name: Leuk the Hare and the Chief's Daughter (Wolof)
stories.excerpt: A powerful chief announced that whoever could make him laugh would win his daughter's hand in marriage. Many tried and failed. Leuk the Hare presented himself and performed a series of absurd tricks, piling animals on top of each other in increasingly ridiculous ways. The chief finally burst out laughing, but then said
stories.title: Leuk the Hare and the Chief's Daughter (Wolof)

stories.name: Libahunt, the Werewolf of the Baltic
stories.excerpt: The Estonian werewolf, a man cursed to become a beast under the full moon, caught between human guilt and animal hunger.
stories.title: Libahunt, the Werewolf of the Baltic

stories.name: Ligaroo: Silver Teeth of the Mountains
stories.excerpt: A boy in the high villages above St. George's encounters the Ligaroo, a vampiric shapeshifter who takes the form of someone you trust, and learns that silver and faith are the only weapons.
stories.title: Ligaroo: Silver Teeth of the Mountains

stories.name: Ligobubfanu the Creator Goddess
stories.excerpt: Ligobubfanu is the creator goddess in the mythology of Chuuk, Micronesia, and the wife of the god Anulap. She is one of the supreme deities responsible for creating the world and all life within it. As a female creator, Ligobubfanu represents the fertile, nurturing aspect of the cosmos. She created the islands of Micro
stories.title: Ligobubfanu the Creator Goddess

stories.name: Lilith, the Night Demoness
stories.excerpt: A powerful female demon from Jewish folklore, Lilith is Adam's first wife who refused to submit and became a night demon preying on infants and solitary men.
stories.title: Lilith, the Night Demoness

stories.name: Linda-Gold and the Old King
stories.excerpt: Long ago there lived an eccentric old king who had suffered great sorrow: his queen and children had died, and someone had torn his heart to pieces — someone 'with claws,' he said. Ever since, the king imagines that everyone has claws on their hands. No one is allowed to come within two arm's lengths of him. Servants m
stories.title: Linda-Gold and the Old King

stories.name: Liongo Fumo: The Birth of a Hero
stories.excerpt: Liongo Fumo's birth was marked by supernatural signs. His mother, a secondary wife of the king of Pate, was childless for many years. Desperate, she prayed at the shrine of the sea spirits, offering her finest cloth and sweetest dates. That night, a spirit appeared in her dreams and told her she would bear a son of ext
stories.title: Liongo Fumo: The Birth of a Hero

stories.name: Little Annie the Goose-Girl
stories.excerpt: A young woman is betrayed by her companions and forced to work as a goose-girl, hiding her royal identity. Through patience and the help of her animal friends, she eventually regains her status and finds true love.
stories.title: Little Annie the Goose-Girl

stories.name: Little Claus and Big Claus
stories.excerpt: Little Claus outsmarts Big Claus through a series of tricks, including pretending to have a wizard in a sack and tricking him into paying for the skin of a dead horse. He eventually tricks Big Claus into being drowned in a river after convincing him he can get cattle from a mermaid.
stories.title: Little Claus and Big Claus

stories.name: Little Giver: The Corn Spirit (Seminole)
stories.excerpt: Little Giver is the Seminole corn spirit who brought agriculture to the people. According to tradition, Little Giver appeared as a small, generous being who taught the Seminole how to plant, cultivate, and harvest corn. The spirit showed them the proper way to prepare the fields, the right time to plant, and the ritual
stories.title: Little Giver: The Corn Spirit (Seminole)

stories.name: Little John
stories.excerpt: When Robin Hood was about twenty years old and still gathering the men who would become his Merry Men, he grew restless after fourteen days without sport.
stories.title: Little John

stories.name: Little Red Riding Hood
stories.excerpt: In Jamaica, when the sun goes down and the shadows grow long, grandmothers gather the children on their porches and tell them about Rolling Calf.
stories.title: Little Red Riding Hood

stories.name: Ljungby Horn and Pipe
stories.excerpt: At Trolle-Ljungby Castle in Scania, southern Sweden, a large glacial boulder called Maglestenen stands in the fields. Legend says that trolls live beneath this stone, and every Christmas Eve, the stone rises on golden pillars while the trolls feast and make merry beneath it. In the mid-16th century, the widowed Lady Si
stories.title: Ljungby Horn and Pipe

stories.name: Lodge-Boy and Thrown-Away (Creek)
stories.excerpt: Lodge-Boy (or By-The-Door) and Thrown-Away are mythical twin heroes in Muscogee Creek (and Natchez) tradition. The twins were born after their pregnant mother was killed by a monster. One twin was found inside the lodge and the other was thrown away, giving them their names. They grew up with extraordinary strength and
stories.title: Lodge-Boy and Thrown-Away (Creek)

stories.name: Lodge-Boy and Thrown-Away (Natchez)
stories.excerpt: Lodge-Boy and Thrown-Away are twin culture heroes in Natchez mythology. The twins were born when their pregnant mother was killed by a monster — one was found inside the lodge (Lodge-Boy) and the other was found where he had been thrown away (Thrown-Away). They grew up in a single day, blessed with supernatural strengt
stories.title: Lodge-Boy and Thrown-Away (Natchez)

stories.name: Lofa: The Stinking Ogre (Chickasaw)
stories.excerpt: Lofa is a hideous, foul-smelling ogre from Chickasaw mythology, similar to the Choctaw Shampe. Lofa is a bigfoot-like creature that dwells in the remote swamps and forests of Chickasaw territory. It is covered in shaggy hair and emits an unbearable stench that can be smelled from a great distance. The creature's odor i
stories.title: Lofa: The Stinking Ogre (Chickasaw)

stories.name: Long-Ears: The Wolf Monster (Seminole)
stories.excerpt: Long-Ears is a wolf-like monster from Seminole folklore. This enormous, predatory creature is distinguished by its unusually long ears and its insatiable hunger for human flesh. Long-Ears dwells in the remote swamps and hammocks of Florida, emerging to hunt when food is scarce. The monster is said to be incredibly fast
stories.title: Long-Ears: The Wolf Monster (Seminole)

stories.name: Lord Peter
stories.excerpt: A story of a young man who overcomes the challenges set by a vengeful father-in-law to prove his worth. Through his courage and a series of magical quests, including defeating a dragon, he secures his marriage and attains great wealth and honor.
stories.title: Lord Peter

stories.name: Los Aluxes — The Maya Trickster Spirits
stories.excerpt: Los Aluxes (singular: Alux) are small, elf-like trickster spirits from Yucatec Maya tradition that survived into the Hispanic folklore of Yucatán and spread through Mexican-American communities. These mischievous beings, standing only knee-high, are said to inhabit ancient Maya ruins, cenotes, and forests. They are kno
stories.title: Los Aluxes — The Maya Trickster Spirits

stories.name: Lotan, the Seven-Headed Serpent
stories.excerpt: A seven-headed sea serpent that served Yamm in the war against Baal, and whose heads were cut off by the storm god — but each head grew back, and the serpent still thrashes in the deep.
stories.title: Lotan, the Seven-Headed Serpent

stories.name: Lougawou: The Werewolf of Haiti
stories.excerpt: A sorcerer removes their skin at night to transform into a beast that preys on children.
stories.title: Lougawou: The Werewolf of Haiti

stories.name: Louhi Steals Sun, Moon, and Fire
stories.excerpt: As revenge for the theft of the Sampo, Louhi uses her dark magic to steal the sun, moon, and fire from the world, plunging the land of Kalevala into a terrifying and eternal darkness and freezing cold.
stories.title: Louhi Steals Sun, Moon, and Fire

stories.name: Loulou and the Stolen Moonlight
stories.excerpt: A mischievous forest spirit called Loulou steals the moonlight from a fishing village, plunging the lagoon into darkness so the fish cannot find their way home.
stories.title: Loulou and the Stolen Moonlight

stories.name: Loundja the Sultan's Daughter
stories.excerpt: An Algerian folktale in which a sultan's baby daughter, Loundja, is kidnapped from her crib by a female ghoul (ghoula) who raises her as her own daughter. Loundja grows up in the ghoul's cave home, unaware that her mother is a monster. When Loundja reaches maturity, she meets a handsome young man in the forest and fall
stories.title: Loundja the Sultan's Daughter

stories.name: Lumiuk the Blind Boy
stories.excerpt: Lumiuk is a blind boy who suffers extreme abuse from his family. He finds refuge in the sea, where the spirits of the ocean grant him sight and a new purpose. He returns as a powerful figure, proving that those cast out by society can find strength and redemption in the natural world.
stories.title: Lumiuk the Blind Boy

stories.name: Luna, the Flame Spirit of Flemish Hearths
stories.excerpt: A gentle household spirit who protects Flemish hearths but punishes those who let the fire die out of laziness.
stories.title: Luna, the Flame Spirit of Flemish Hearths

stories.name: Luz de Yara: The Spirit Light of Hatuey
stories.excerpt: The soul of a Taíno chief burned by Spanish colonizers wanders the Cuban coast as a mysterious light.
stories.title: Luz de Yara: The Spirit Light of Hatuey

stories.name: Lávrukaš and the Russian Chudes
stories.excerpt: A legend about a Sámi woman named Lávrukaš who outwits Russian Chude attackers through bravery and cunning. This story from the coastal Sámi tradition features a female protagonist who saves her community from raiders. It reflects the strong women in Sámi storytelling tradition, particularly in Emilie Demant Hatt's col
stories.title: Lávrukaš and the Russian Chudes

stories.name: Lạc Long Quân and Âu Cơ
stories.excerpt: In the mountains of Papua New Guinea, where the jungle is so dense that villages can be separated by a day's walk and never know each other, the Kalam people tell stories of the Krim.
stories.title: Lạc Long Quân and Âu Cơ

stories.name: Mae Nak Phra Khanong
stories.excerpt: The most famous ghost legend in Thai folklore tells the tragic love story of Mae Nak, a young woman who died in childbirth while her husband Mak was away at war. Upon returning home, Mak found his wife and newborn baby seemingly alive and well, unaware they were both ghosts. When Mak discovered the truth after witnessi
stories.title: Mae Nak Phra Khanong

stories.name: Mae Phosop: The Rice Goddess of Laos and Thailand
stories.excerpt: Mae Phosop (Mother of the Rice Kernel) is the ancient rice goddess revered in Lao and Thai agricultural traditions. According to legend, Mae Phosop was a beautiful celestial maiden who descended to earth to become the spirit of rice — the essence that gives life to all who consume it. She is believed to possess a spiri
stories.title: Mae Phosop: The Rice Goddess of Laos and Thailand

stories.name: Maha Sona: The Great Graveyard Demon of Sri Lanka
stories.excerpt: A decapitated warrior giant becomes the most feared demon in Sinhalese folklore, haunting graveyards and crossroads.
stories.title: Maha Sona: The Great Graveyard Demon of Sri Lanka

stories.name: Mahogany Tree, the Sacred Sentinel
stories.excerpt: The sacred mahogany tree of Antigua is believed to be inhabited by a powerful guardian spirit who protects the island's forests and punishes those who harm them.
stories.title: Mahogany Tree, the Sacred Sentinel

stories.name: Mahsuri of Langkawi
stories.excerpt: The tragic legend of Mahsuri, a beautiful and virtuous woman from Kedah who lived on the island of Langkawi in the early 19th century. Falsely accused of adultery by a jealous rival, Mahsuri was found guilty by the village chief and sentenced to death by keris (ceremonial dagger). When executed, white blood flowed from
stories.title: Mahsuri of Langkawi

stories.name: Mahsuri: The Cursed Maiden of Langkawi
stories.excerpt: A falsely accused woman curses the island of Langkawi for seven generations with her dying breath.
stories.title: Mahsuri: The Cursed Maiden of Langkawi

stories.name: Maid Lena
stories.excerpt: A story about a humble maid whose innate kindness, purity of heart, and resilience lead her to overcome adversity and find a happy ending.
stories.title: Maid Lena

stories.name: Maid Marian
stories.excerpt: Maid Marian was the heart of Sherwood Forest.. While Robin Hood was its soul and Little John its strength, Marian was the pulse that kept the Merry Men alive.
stories.title: Maid Marian

stories.name: Maiden Bright-eye
stories.excerpt: A tale of a maiden with extraordinary beauty and spiritual insight who positively influences the people around her, acting as a beacon of hope and purity.
stories.title: Maiden Bright-eye

stories.name: Maiden of the Rainbow
stories.excerpt: Wainamoinen encounters the elusive Maiden of the Rainbow, whose beauty is matched only by her distance. Their interaction involves a complex process of courtship and magical tests, further exploring the themes of longing, desire, and the inherent difficulty of finding a peer in love and magic.
stories.title: Maiden of the Rainbow

stories.name: Makemake and the Birdman Cult
stories.excerpt: Makemake, the supreme creator god of Rapa Nui, shaped the world and gave life to the island. He created the birds, the fish, and the people, then withdrew to watch over them from the heavens. As Rapa Nui's society evolved, Makemake became associated with the Tangata Manu (Birdman) cult centered at the ceremonial villag
stories.title: Makemake and the Birdman Cult

stories.name: Malakas at Maganda (The First Man and Woman)
stories.excerpt: According to ancient Tagalog creation myth, the world began as a vast emptiness with only the sea and sky. A huge bird grew tired of flying and stirred up the sea, causing an island to emerge. From a bamboo stalk split by the bird, the first man Malakas (Strong) and the first woman Maganda (Beautiful) sprang forth, bec
stories.title: Malakas at Maganda (The First Man and Woman)

stories.name: Malin Kundang
stories.excerpt: A tragic folktale from West Sumatra about a poor boy named Malin Kundang who leaves his mother to seek fortune overseas. After years of hardship, he becomes a wealthy merchant, marries a princess, and returns to his home village in a grand ship. His aging mother, overjoyed to see him, rushes to embrace him, but Malin K
stories.title: Malin Kundang

stories.name: Mam and Zin (Mem û Zîn)
stories.excerpt: The Kurdish national epic, written down in 1692 by poet Ahmad Khani. Mem, a chivalrous youth of the Alan clan and heir to the City of the West, falls in love with Zin, the beautiful daughter of the governor of Botan (Cizre). They meet during a Newroz celebration. Their union is blocked by the jealous Bakr, who conspire
stories.title: Mam and Zin (Mem û Zîn)

stories.name: Mama Cocha, Water Mother
stories.excerpt: Mama Cocha, mother of all waters, commands the lakes and rivers, and the fishermen who forget her name find their boats overturned and their nets empty.
stories.title: Mama Cocha, Water Mother

stories.name: Mama D'Leau and the Lost Children
stories.excerpt: Two children wandering near the mangroves encounter Mama D'Leau, the mysterious water woman, who tests their hearts before revealing the hidden path home.
stories.title: Mama D'Leau and the Lost Children

stories.name: Mama D'Leau of the River
stories.excerpt: A water spirit of terrifying beauty guards the rivers of Dominica, punishing those who disrespect the water while rewarding those who approach with reverence.
stories.title: Mama D'Leau of the River

stories.name: Mama Dlo and the River Guardian
stories.excerpt: A greedy fisherman ignores the warnings of the river spirits and takes more than his share from the waters, drawing the wrath of Mama Dlo.
stories.title: Mama Dlo and the River Guardian

stories.name: Mama Dlo, Mother of the Waters
stories.excerpt: Mama Dlo (also known as Mama D'Leau or Mama Glo) is a water spirit from Trinidadian folklore, the wife of Papa Bois. She is the mother of the waters, a beautiful woman from the waist up but a serpent or fish from the waist down — similar to a mermaid. Mama Dlo guards rivers, ponds, and wetlands, and is known to grant r
stories.title: Mama Dlo, Mother of the Waters

stories.name: Mama Glo: Lights of the Lagoon
stories.excerpt: A fisherman ignores his grandmother's warnings about the lagoon lights and is drawn beneath the water by Mama Glo, learning too late that some waters keep what they claim.
stories.title: Mama Glo: Lights of the Lagoon

stories.name: Mamba Muntu, the Dragon of the Kuilu
stories.excerpt: A great dragon dwells in the Kuilu River, guarding the boundary between the living and the dead, and only those who carry no fear may pass its domain unharmed.
stories.title: Mamba Muntu, the Dragon of the Kuilu

stories.name: Mame Coumba Bang: The River Goddess of Saint-Louis
stories.excerpt: A powerful river goddess controls the waters of the Senegal River and demands offerings from fishermen.
stories.title: Mame Coumba Bang: The River Goddess of Saint-Louis

stories.name: Mami Wata, the Liberian Water Spirit
stories.excerpt: Mami Wata is a beautiful and powerful water spirit of West African tradition who lures men with her beauty and grants wealth to those who please her.
stories.title: Mami Wata, the Liberian Water Spirit

stories.name: Mami Wata: The Water Spirit
stories.excerpt: A beautiful water spirit of rivers and oceans brings wealth and beauty to those who honor her.
stories.title: Mami Wata: The Water Spirit

stories.name: Mamlambo: The River Goddess Who Brings Wealth and Death
stories.excerpt: Mamlambo is a shapeshifting water deity of the Zulu and Xhosa peoples, often depicted as a giant serpent with a horse's head or a beautiful woman who lures men to their doom. She controls the waters, causing floods when angered and droughts when she withdraws. Those who seek her out for wealth must make terrible sacrif
stories.title: Mamlambo: The River Goddess Who Brings Wealth and Death

stories.name: Manananggal: The Vampire Woman
stories.excerpt: A beautiful woman who splits in half at night, flying to drink the blood of pregnant women—her upper torso flies while her lower body remains.
stories.title: Manananggal: The Vampire Woman

stories.name: Manas: The Great Campaign and Death of the Hero
stories.excerpt: The second major cycle of the Manas epic describes how Manas united the forty Kyrgyz tribes under the Tengrist sky-banner and led them to reclaim the Ala-Too mountains from Chinese and Kalmyk invaders. His magical white stallion Ak-Kula carried him through epic battles, advising him with human speech and prophetic warn
stories.title: Manas: The Great Campaign and Death of the Hero

stories.name: Mandukhai the Wise Queen
stories.excerpt: Mandukhai Khatun (also known as Mandukhai Sechen Khongorjin) was a 15th-century Mongol queen who reunified the fractured Mongol nation after the fall of the Yuan dynasty. According to legend, she raised the orphaned Dayan Khan from childhood, then married him when he came of age. At age thirty-two, she led the Mongol a
stories.title: Mandukhai the Wise Queen

stories.name: Mangadhai: The Multi-Headed Dragons of Mongolia
stories.excerpt: Terrible multi-headed serpent-dragons threaten the world in Mongolian epic folklore.
stories.title: Mangadhai: The Multi-Headed Dragons of Mongolia

stories.name: Mannegishi (Little People)
stories.excerpt: The Mannegishi are small, bald humanoid beings in Crow mythology, described as having large, bulging eyes and tiny, tan bodies. They are tricksters who live in rocky areas and along riverbanks. These little people are known for playing pranks on humans, leading travelers astray, and causing mischief. Despite their trou
stories.title: Mannegishi (Little People)

stories.name: Mariatta--Wainamoinen's Departure
stories.excerpt: A virgin girl named Marjatta becomes pregnant after stepping on a rye grain. Her son is born and baptized as a Christian king. Realizing that the era of pagan magic is ending, Wainamoinen sails away into the sunset, leaving the world to the new order.
stories.title: Mariatta--Wainamoinen's Departure

stories.name: Marmennilin (The Merman of Elduvík)
stories.excerpt: A farmer named Arnfinn from Elduvík encountered a Marmennil—a merman who lives at the bottom of the sea, smaller than a human with long fingers, who delights in teasing fishermen by stealing bait and snagging hooks. One day, the merman tried to stick Arnfinn's hook to the seabed but accidentally hooked his own hand and
stories.title: Marmennilin (The Merman of Elduvík)

stories.name: María Sabina — The Mushroom Shaman of Oaxaca
stories.excerpt: María Sabina (1894–1985) was a Mazatec curandera and shaman from Huautla de Jiménez, Oaxaca, whose use of sacred psilocybin mushrooms in healing ceremonies gained worldwide fame. Her legend — part historical, part mythic — tells of a poor indigenous woman who discovered the sacred mushrooms as a child and was called by
stories.title: María Sabina — The Mushroom Shaman of Oaxaca

stories.name: Masalai: The Spirits of the Papua New Guinea Forest
stories.excerpt: Shape-shifting place spirits guard sacred sites and punish those who break taboos in the jungle.
stories.title: Masalai: The Spirits of the Papua New Guinea Forest

stories.name: Master and Pupil
stories.excerpt: A story exploring the complex relationship between a mentor and a student, focusing on themes of artistic growth, ambition, and the eventual surpassing of the master.
stories.title: Master and Pupil

stories.name: Master of Breath (Hesaketvmesē) (Creek)
stories.excerpt: Hesaketvmesē, also called Epohfvnkv, is the supreme being in Muscogee Creek religion. Known as the 'Maker of Breath' or 'the One Above who holds life's breath,' Hesaketvmesē is a solar deity who spoke to and guided the Muscogee people on their journey from the west. The name emphasizes the belief that breath and life a
stories.title: Master of Breath (Hesaketvmesē) (Creek)

stories.name: Matlose the Hobgoblin (Nuu-chah-nulth)
stories.excerpt: Matlose is the most feared hobgoblin spirit of the Nuu-chah-nulth people, described as a monstrous Caliban-like creature. His head resembles something that might have been human but is not, and his uncouth bulk is horrid with black bristles. His monstrous teeth and curved claws are like those of a bear, capable of rend
stories.title: Matlose the Hobgoblin (Nuu-chah-nulth)

stories.name: Matsieng's Footprints: The Tswana Creation
stories.excerpt: According to Tswana tradition, Matsieng, a powerful one-legged giant considered the first ancestor of the Batswana people, emerged from a waterhole in southeastern Botswana. As he climbed out, he was followed by his people, domestic animals, and wildlife, all sinking their feet into the soft, unformed early earth. Thei
stories.title: Matsieng's Footprints: The Tswana Creation

stories.name: Matsya
stories.excerpt: In the dawn of the current cosmic age, before the world as we know it took shape, there lived a king named Manu.
stories.title: Matsya

stories.name: Maui and Hine-nui-te-po: The Quest for Immortality
stories.excerpt: Maui sought to conquer death itself by destroying Hine-nui-te-po, the goddess of death. He knew that if he could pass through her body unharmed, humanity would gain immortality. He took the smallest forest birds as his companions and found the goddess sleeping. Maui instructed the birds to remain silent while he crawle
stories.title: Maui and Hine-nui-te-po: The Quest for Immortality

stories.name: Maui and the Sun
stories.excerpt: Long ago, when the world was young and the rhythms of nature were far more erratic than they are today, the sun, Tama-nui-te-rā, was a capricious and hurried deity.
stories.title: Maui and the Sun

stories.name: Maui Fishing Up the North Island
stories.excerpt: Maui's brothers refused to take him fishing, so he hid in their canoe and revealed himself at sea. Using a magical fishhook made from the jawbone of his ancestor Murirangawhenua, and chanting powerful incantations, Maui caught a gigantic fish. He instructed his brothers to wait until he had appeased Tangaroa before car
stories.title: Maui Fishing Up the North Island

stories.name: Maui Pulling Up the Tongan Islands
stories.excerpt: Maui Kisikisi (Little Maui) sat in his canoe fishing but catching nothing. Growing frustrated, he reached down through the ocean with his powerful arms and grasped the sea floor. With tremendous effort, he pulled upward, bringing the Tongan islands to the surface. As he hauled, the coral, sand, and rock emerged from th
stories.title: Maui Pulling Up the Tongan Islands

stories.name: Maui Slowing the Sun
stories.excerpt: Maui observed that the sun, Tamanuitera, moved across the sky too quickly, leaving insufficient daylight for working, cooking, and fishing. He convinced his brothers to help capture the sun and force it to slow down. They traveled east to the pit where the sun rose, built a wall of clay to hide behind, and wove strong
stories.title: Maui Slowing the Sun

stories.name: Maui Stealing Fire from Mahuika
stories.excerpt: After all fires in Hawaiki had been extinguished, Maui volunteered to visit his ancestress Mahuika, the goddess of fire, to obtain new flames. She pulled out one of her burning fingernails and gave it to him. However, Maui's trickster nature took over and he extinguished it, then returned for another. He repeated this
stories.title: Maui Stealing Fire from Mahuika

stories.name: Mavka: The Forest Spirit of the Carpathians
stories.excerpt: The spirit of an unbaptized child lures young men to their doom in the Carpathian forests.
stories.title: Mavka: The Forest Spirit of the Carpathians

stories.name: Mawu, the Supreme Creator (Ewe/Fon)
stories.excerpt: Mawu is the supreme creator god of the Ewe and Fon people, a lunar goddess who created the cosmos and all living beings. She is often paired with Lisa, the sun god, forming a dual-sexed creator deity (Mawu-Lisa). Mawu is considered distant from everyday human affairs, having delegated the running of the world to her ch
stories.title: Mawu, the Supreme Creator (Ewe/Fon)

stories.name: Mbatian the Great Laibon
stories.excerpt: Mbatian was the most powerful laibon (spiritual leader) in Maasai history, a descendant of the Inkindongi clan. His prophetic powers were legendary — he could predict droughts, locate lost cattle, and communicate directly with Enkai. As he grew old, Mbatian had to choose which of his many sons would inherit his powers.
stories.title: Mbatian the Great Laibon

stories.name: Mbidi Kiluwe: The Culture Hero of the Luba
stories.excerpt: Mbidi Kiluwe was a mysterious prince who came from the east, distinguished by his light skin and his refined, dignified manners. He arrived at the court of King Nkongolo Mwamba, the red-skinned ruler of the Luba. Where Nkongolo was crude and violent, Mbidi Kiluwe was gentle and wise. He introduced new customs: eating i
stories.title: Mbidi Kiluwe: The Culture Hero of the Luba

stories.name: Mbona, the Rain Prophet
stories.excerpt: Mbona was a powerful spirit of rain and water who could summon storms with a word and end droughts with a gesture. The people of the Shire River valley revered him as a living bridge between earth and sky.
stories.title: Mbona, the Rain Prophet

stories.name: Mbwiri, the Gabonese Initiate
stories.excerpt: The Mbwiri ceremony of Gabon is a sacred initiation where a possessed individual is purified through ritual dance and community support.
stories.title: Mbwiri, the Gabonese Initiate

stories.name: Meandash: The Celestial Reindeer Hunt
stories.excerpt: In Kola Sámi tradition, Meandash also exists as a celestial reindeer hunted by the thunder god in the sky. The cosmic hunt is reflected in the constellations—Orion, the Pleiades, and Arcturus belong to the cosmic elk-reindeer hunt tradition. When the thunder god strikes Meandash down, everything falls apart: fire envel
stories.title: Meandash: The Celestial Reindeer Hunt

stories.name: Meandash: The Mythic Wild Reindeer
stories.excerpt: The central creation myth of the wild reindeer from eastern Sámi (Kola Peninsula) tradition. Meandash is a shapeshifter—human inside his hut, wild reindeer outside. He is the son of a female noaidi. An earthly girl crosses a river of blood, lungs, and livers to reach him and becomes his wife. She bears his children, wh
stories.title: Meandash: The Mythic Wild Reindeer

stories.name: Medea's Vengeance
stories.excerpt: A sorceress who sacrificed everything for love takes a terrifying and absolute revenge on her faithless husband.
stories.title: Medea's Vengeance

stories.name: Medusa
stories.excerpt: In the ancient world, before the age of heroes faded into memory, there lived three sisters whose names struck terror into the hearts of all who heard them.
stories.title: Medusa

stories.name: Melqart, the Tyrian Hercules
stories.excerpt: The god of Tyre who died and rose again each year, his resurrection bringing the return of spring — because in Lebanon, even gods must die before they can be reborn.
stories.title: Melqart, the Tyrian Hercules

stories.name: Melusine: The Serpent Woman
stories.excerpt: A woman who hides her serpent tail on Saturdays—until her husband discovers the truth.
stories.title: Melusine: The Serpent Woman

stories.name: Menes-Antti's Adventures in France
stories.excerpt: An Inari Sámi humorous folktale collected by Koskimies and Itkonen about Menes-Antti traveling to France. He arrived in Paris in shabby clothing and went to a grand party building where he was almost thrown out. He overheard a king's daughter arranging a liaison, and pretending to be the suitor, he got into her bed. Wh
stories.title: Menes-Antti's Adventures in France

stories.name: Merger the Hero (Nanai Epic)
stories.excerpt: The central Nanai epic hero Merger, whose adventures form the core of Nanai oral tradition. The epic follows Merger as he journeys along the Amur River, battling evil spirits, demons, and rival clans to protect the Nanai people. He is aided by his shamanic powers, his supernatural strength, and the spirits of the Amur
stories.title: Merger the Hero (Nanai Epic)

stories.name: Merlin
stories.excerpt: Long before Arthur drew the sword from the stone, before Camelot rose from the plains of Logres, there was Merlin.
stories.title: Merlin

stories.name: Merlin's Madness in the Forest
stories.excerpt: After foreseeing the destruction of Camelot, Merlin wanders the forest of Brocéliande in a madness born of knowledge he can never unlearn.
stories.title: Merlin's Madness in the Forest

stories.name: Metsavana, the Old Man of the Woods
stories.excerpt: A forest keeper who punishes those who take too much from his woodland and rewards those who respect the sacred groves of hiis.
stories.title: Metsavana, the Old Man of the Woods

stories.name: Mimi Spirits: The First Rock Artists
stories.excerpt: In the Aboriginal Australian mythology of Arnhem Land in northern Australia, Mimi spirits (also called Mimih) are fairy-like beings with extremely thin and elongated bodies. They are so thin that they risk breaking in strong winds, which is why they spend most of their time living in rock crevices. According to traditi
stories.title: Mimi Spirits: The First Rock Artists

stories.name: Mirza Sahiba — Elopement and Betrayal
stories.excerpt: Mirza and Sahiba were cousins from the Jatt tribe of Punjab who fell in love. When Sahiba's parents arranged her marriage to another man, Mirza arrived at her wedding on horseback and eloped with her. As they fled across the countryside, Sahiba's brothers and their armed men pursued them. Mirza, a skilled archer, shot
stories.title: Mirza Sahiba — Elopement and Betrayal

stories.name: Mishipeshu, the Underwater Panther
stories.excerpt: Mishipeshu, the Great Lynx, is one of the most powerful water beings in Ojibwe mythology, ruling the depths of Lake Superior from his home on Michipicoten Island. He has the head and paws of a giant cat but is covered in scales with dagger-like spikes along his back and tail. He is the master of all water creatures, in
stories.title: Mishipeshu, the Underwater Panther

stories.name: Miss Cow Falls a Victim to Mr. Rabbit
stories.excerpt: Brer Rabbit, hungry and with nothing to eat, approaches Miss Cow and asks her for some milk, claiming his children are starving. Miss Cow refuses, saying the milk is for her calf. Brer Rabbit then asks her to come to Miss Meadows's house where there is plenty of grass, but Miss Cow refuses again. Later, Brer Rabbit hid
stories.title: Miss Cow Falls a Victim to Mr. Rabbit

stories.name: Mlouka and the Strand of Hair
stories.excerpt: An Algerian folktale from the west of the country, famous among Berber communities. Mlouka was a young peasant girl renowned for her extraordinarily long, strong, and beautiful hair—so long she could not wash it alone, and all the women of her family had to walk to the river to help her. A jealous cousin plucked a stra
stories.title: Mlouka and the Strand of Hair

stories.name: Mockingbird Gives Out the Calls
stories.excerpt: In this Hopi story, Mockingbird was responsible for distributing the languages and calls among all the peoples of the world. During the migrations after the emergence into the Fourth World, the people were all speaking the same language. Mockingbird called the people together and assigned different languages and dialec
stories.title: Mockingbird Gives Out the Calls

stories.name: Moddey Dhoo
stories.excerpt: The phantom Moddey Dhoo, a spectral black dog, haunts the lanes of Peel, serving as a grim reminder of the boundaries between the living and the dead.
stories.title: Moddey Dhoo

stories.name: Modimo: The Supreme God of the Sotho-Tswana
stories.excerpt: Modimo is the supreme deity in the traditional religion of the Sotho-Tswana people, recognized as the creator of all things, the source of life, and the controller of destiny. Intangible and all-pervasive, Modimo is addressed by praise names including Mme (Mother) and Lesedi (Light), but also Selo (Monster) for his dan
stories.title: Modimo: The Supreme God of the Sotho-Tswana

stories.name: Moko Jumbie: The Tall Guardian
stories.excerpt: On the night before a village festival, a young stilt-walker named Corwin learns why the Moko Jumbie towers above the rooftops — not for spectacle, but to see the spirits that creep toward the sleeping village.
stories.title: Moko Jumbie: The Tall Guardian

stories.name: Mokélé-Mbembé, the Gabonese River Dragon
stories.excerpt: The Mokélé-Mbembé is a legendary river creature said to inhabit the swamps and rivers of Gabon, resembling a long-necked reptile with a single tusk.
stories.title: Mokélé-Mbembé, the Gabonese River Dragon

stories.name: Momotaro: The Boy Born from a Peach
stories.excerpt: In the province of Suruga, by a great mountain, an old woodcutter and his wife lived alone.
stories.title: Momotaro: The Boy Born from a Peach

stories.name: Momoy and the Firefly Dance
stories.excerpt: A tiny fairy of the Venezuelan forests leads lost children through the trees with a trail of fireflies, guiding them home only when they promise never to return alone.
stories.title: Momoy and the Firefly Dance

stories.name: Mooin, the Bear's Child
stories.excerpt: A young Mi'kmaq boy wandered into the forest and became lost. A great she-bear found him and, instead of harming him, adopted him as her own cub. The boy grew up among the bear people, learning their ways and understanding the language of animals. He became strong and brave, but he always remembered that he was human.
stories.title: Mooin, the Bear's Child

stories.name: Moremi Ajasoro and the Liberation of Ife (Yoruba)
stories.excerpt: Moremi Ajasoro was a legendary queen of Ile-Ife who sacrificed her own happiness to save her people from repeated raids by the neighboring Ugbo people. The Ife warriors were unable to defend against the Ugbo, who were disguised as forest spirits. Moremi allowed herself to be captured and taken to Ugbo as a slave. There
stories.title: Moremi Ajasoro and the Liberation of Ife (Yoruba)

stories.name: Morgan le Fay
stories.excerpt: Morgan le Fay was Arthur's half-sister and one of the most powerful enchantresses in all of British legend.
stories.title: Morgan le Fay

stories.name: Morgan's Exile to Avalon
stories.excerpt: After the fall of Camelot, Morgan le Fay departs Britain for the mystical isle of Avalon, carrying with her the last fragments of Arthur's broken crown.
stories.title: Morgan's Exile to Avalon

stories.name: Moso's Footprint
stories.excerpt: The giant Moso was one of the first humans created by Tagaloa on the island of Savai'i. His enormous footprint can still be seen pressed deep into solid lava rock at the village of Salelologa. According to legend, Moso stood so tall that he could step from one island to another. His footprint was left when he stood on
stories.title: Moso's Footprint

stories.name: Mothman: The Prophet of Death
stories.excerpt: A winged man with red eyes appeared before the Silver Bridge collapse in 1966—prophecy or coincidence?
stories.title: Mothman: The Prophet of Death

stories.name: Mount Cudi and Noah's Ark (Kurdish Tradition)
stories.excerpt: According to Kurdish creation myths, Noah's Ark landed on Mount Cudi (Cudi Dagh) in southeastern Turkey, not Mount Ararat as in the biblical tradition. The Kurdish tradition holds that after the flood, Melik Kurdim, a member of Noah's tribe, established rule over Mount Cudi and built the first post-diluvian civilizatio
stories.title: Mount Cudi and Noah's Ark (Kurdish Tradition)

stories.name: Mountain God Nyenchen Thanglha
stories.excerpt: The Tibetan legend of Nyenchen Thanglha, one of the most powerful mountain gods in Tibetan mythology. He is the spirit of the Nyenchen Thanglha mountain range in central Tibet, revered as a protector deity who commands armies of elemental spirits. In pre-Buddhist Bon tradition, he was a wrathful, dangerous spirit who d
stories.title: Mountain God Nyenchen Thanglha

stories.name: Mr. Bear Catches Old Mr. Bull-Frog
stories.excerpt: Brer Bear, hungry and irritable, decides he will catch the enormous bullfrog that keeps him awake at night with its croaking. He finds the frog at the pond's edge and makes a grab, but the frog leaps into the water. Brer Bear decides to drink the entire pond dry. He drinks until his belly is swollen, but the pond level
stories.title: Mr. Bear Catches Old Mr. Bull-Frog

stories.name: Mr. Fox and the Deceitful Frogs
stories.excerpt: Brer Fox, having not eaten for days, spots a large bullfrog at the edge of the pond and makes a grab for him. The frog dives deep, and Brer Fox, desperate, decides to drink the pond dry. He drinks until his belly swells enormously, but the pond level barely drops. Meanwhile, the frogs mock him from the safety of the wa
stories.title: Mr. Fox and the Deceitful Frogs

stories.name: Mukasa: The God of Lake Victoria
stories.excerpt: Mukasa is the powerful god of Lake Victoria (Nalubaale) and the most important of the Lubaale (national deities) in Buganda tradition. According to legend, Mukasa was a human prince who was transformed into a lake deity because of his extraordinary wisdom and compassion. He lives in a magnificent palace beneath the wat
stories.title: Mukasa: The God of Lake Victoria

stories.name: Mulan
stories.excerpt: The ballad of Mulan was first sung in the northern dynasties of China, during a time when the Toba people ruled the north and the Rouran tribes pressed against the borders like a relentless tide.
stories.title: Mulan

stories.name: Muldjewangk the Murray River Monster
stories.excerpt: Muldjewangk is a malevolent water spirit from the Aboriginal Australian mythology of the Murray River region in South Australia. This powerful and dangerous creature dwells in the deep waters of the Murray River, particularly around Lake Alexandrina and the river's lower reaches. Muldjewangk is described as a large, da
stories.title: Muldjewangk the Murray River Monster

stories.name: Munda Creation — The Egg That Became the World
stories.excerpt: The Munda people of Jharkhand believe that before creation there was nothing but water. The supreme god Singbonga floated above this water and set a cosmic egg afloat on its surface. From this egg hatched the first beings: Horo, the tortoise, and Karakom, the crab. The tortoise dove into the waters and brought earth to
stories.title: Munda Creation — The Egg That Became the World

stories.name: Murdered Children: The Returning Spirits
stories.excerpt: A dark Sámi legend from Emilie Demant Hatt's By the Fire collection about murdered babies who come back to haunt their parents. This reflects the Sámi belief that improperly buried souls become restless spirits (eahpáraš). They can cause illness, misfortune, or wail in the wilderness. The only remedy is to perform prop
stories.title: Murdered Children: The Returning Spirits

stories.name: Muscogee Creation: Emergence from the Lower World (Creek)
stories.excerpt: In Muscogee Creek belief, the cosmos is divided into three worlds: the Upper World (home of Hesaketvmesē, the Maker of Breath, along with the Sun, Moon, and Thunder), the Middle World (where humans live), and the Lower World (inhabited by the Tie Snake and the Horned Serpent). Human beings first emerged from beneath th
stories.title: Muscogee Creation: Emergence from the Lower World (Creek)

stories.name: Mvelincanti and the First Cattle
stories.excerpt: The sky deity Mvelincanti sends the first cattle down to earth on a spider's silk thread, entrusting them to a humble woman who understands their sacred worth.
stories.title: Mvelincanti and the First Cattle

stories.name: My Chau and Trong Thuy: The Tragedy of Co Loa Citadel
stories.excerpt: One of Vietnam's most tragic love legends tells the story of Princess My Chau and Prince Trong Thuy against the backdrop of the fall of the Au Lac kingdom. King An Duong Vuong built the spiral-shaped Co Loa Citadel with the help of the Golden Turtle God (Kim Qui), who gave him a magic crossbow that could fire hundreds
stories.title: My Chau and Trong Thuy: The Tragedy of Co Loa Citadel

stories.name: Myrkr
stories.excerpt: The enchanted mist of Norse lore that causes travelers to become hopelessly lost.
stories.title: Myrkr

stories.name: Myrmidons: The Ant Soldiers
stories.excerpt: On the sun-drenched shores of Aegina, where the Aegean Sea laps against white cliffs and the air smells of wild thyme and salt, there once ruled a king named Aeacus.
stories.title: Myrmidons: The Ant Soldiers

stories.name: Mô-sîn-á, the Grass Spirit
stories.excerpt: A mischievous grass spirit from Taiwanese Hokkien folklore who tangles the feet of travelers and leads them astray.
stories.title: Mô-sîn-á, the Grass Spirit

stories.name: Na'pi Creates the Buffalo
stories.excerpt: After Na'pi (Old Man) created the world and the first people, he saw that they were hungry. He went to a cave deep in the mountains where the buffalo were kept. Na'pi opened the cave and the buffalo poured out across the plains, providing food, clothing, and shelter for the people. He taught the Blackfoot how to conduc
stories.title: Na'pi Creates the Buffalo

stories.name: Nafanua: The Warrior Goddess
stories.excerpt: Nafanua, daughter of Saveasi'uleo (god of Pulotu) and Tilafaiga, was born a female but hidden in the forest by her mother out of shame. She emerged as a fierce warrior when Samoa was oppressed by tyrannical rulers. Disguising her chest so enemies would not know she was a woman, Nafanua led rebellions that freed the peo
stories.title: Nafanua: The Warrior Goddess

stories.name: Nag-drang and the River of Names
stories.excerpt: A monster called Nag-drang haunts a river that carries the names of the dead, and a woman who has lost her son must trade her own name to retrieve his before it washes into forgetting.
stories.title: Nag-drang and the River of Names

stories.name: Naga: The Serpent Kings
stories.excerpt: Semi-divine serpents who guard treasures, live in underground palaces, and bless those who honor them.
stories.title: Naga: The Serpent Kings

stories.name: Nakk, the Water Spirit of Estonia
stories.excerpt: A shape-shifting water spirit who haunted Estonia's rivers and lakes, luring the unwary with beauty and song before dragging them beneath the surface.
stories.title: Nakk, the Water Spirit of Estonia

stories.name: Nalusa Chito: The Soul Eater (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: Nalusa Chito, also known as Impa Shilup ('Soul Eater'), is a great black shadow being of Choctaw legend. If individuals allow evil thoughts, depression, or negativity to enter their minds, Nalusa Chito will creep inside them and devour their souls. Many Choctaw people will not speak its name aloud, for fear of summonin
stories.title: Nalusa Chito: The Soul Eater (Choctaw)

stories.name: Nalusa Falaya: The Shadow Being (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: Nalusa Falaya, meaning 'Long Black Being,' is a terrifying shadow creature from Choctaw mythology. It resembles a man but with a shriveled face, very small eyes, long pointed ears, and an elongated nose. Nalusa Falaya is known to frighten hunters and can transfer its power to do harm. It prefers to approach people by s
stories.title: Nalusa Falaya: The Shadow Being (Choctaw)

stories.name: Nanabozho and the Creation of the World (Ojibwe)
stories.excerpt: The Ojibwe creation story tells how Nanabozho, the son of Epingishmook (the West Wind) and a human mother, was born with great spiritual powers. After his mother died, he was raised by his grandmother Nokomis. When the underwater panthers and horned serpents killed his beloved wolf-brother, Nanabozho pursued them and i
stories.title: Nanabozho and the Creation of the World (Ojibwe)

stories.name: Nanabozho and the Great Serpent
stories.excerpt: The Great Horned Serpent Mishiginebig, ruler of the underwater world, had been devouring the people who lived near the Great Lakes. Nanabozho, the culture hero, vowed to destroy the monster. He transformed into a tree stump on the shore and waited. When the serpent surfaced, its antlered head rising like an island from
stories.title: Nanabozho and the Great Serpent

stories.name: Nanabozho and the Theft of Fire
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, fire belonged only to the spirits and the people shivered in the cold. Nanabozho, the culture hero, decided to steal fire for humanity. He traveled to the lodge of the Old Man who guarded the only flame, guarded by a fierce serpent. Nanabozho transformed himself into a rabbit to sneak past the serpent
stories.title: Nanabozho and the Theft of Fire

stories.name: Nanapush and the Sacred Pipe
stories.excerpt: After Kishelamakank created the world, the human tribes fell into conflict over a magical bear tooth, leading to wars and divisions between families. The Creator saw that the people had lost their way and sent the spirit Nanapush to restore harmony. Nanapush gathered the warring peoples together at a council fire. He i
stories.title: Nanapush and the Sacred Pipe

stories.name: Nandi
stories.excerpt: In every temple dedicated to Lord Shiva across the vast expanse of India, from the snowy peaks of the Himalayas to the sun-baked shores of Kanyakumari, there sits a stone figure of a great white bull.
stories.title: Nandi

stories.name: Nang Kwak: The Cat-Calling Goddess of Prosperity
stories.excerpt: Nang Kwak is a benevolent female deity in Thai folklore who is believed to bring good fortune, prosperity, and customers to businesses. She is depicted as a beautiful woman in traditional Thai dress, seated with her right hand raised in a beckoning gesture (the 'cat-calling' wave). According to legend, Nang Kwak was a
stories.title: Nang Kwak: The Cat-Calling Goddess of Prosperity

stories.name: Napi and the Rolling Skull
stories.excerpt: Na'pi was walking across the prairie when he kicked a buffalo skull and told it to get out of his way. The skull began to roll after him, chasing him across the plains. Na'pi ran to a tree and climbed it, but the skull called to the tree, asking it to bend down. The tree bent, and the skull rolled up to Na'pi's hiding
stories.title: Napi and the Rolling Skull

stories.name: Narcissus
stories.excerpt: In the frozen lands of the far north, where the aurora borealis paints the sky in ribbons of green and purple, the Inuit people tell stories of the Qallupilluq.
stories.title: Narcissus

stories.name: Natchez Creation: The People of the Sun (Natchez)
stories.excerpt: The Natchez creation tradition centers on the Great Sun, the divine ruler who descended from the sun itself. According to legend, the first Great Sun was born of a woman who was impregnated by a ray of sunlight. This established the Sun lineage, which was matrilineal — the Great Sun was always the son of the Female Sun
stories.title: Natchez Creation: The People of the Sun (Natchez)

stories.name: Ndundiro and the Mountain of Gold
stories.excerpt: The giant Ndundiro guards a hidden mountain of gold deep in the Rwandan wilderness, and a clever shepherd girl must use wit rather than force to pass him and save her starving village.
stories.title: Ndundiro and the Mountain of Gold

stories.name: Neang Kakey: The Unfaithful Wife of Khmer Literature
stories.excerpt: A beautiful but unfaithful wife meets a tragic end in this classic Khmer cautionary tale.
stories.title: Neang Kakey: The Unfaithful Wife of Khmer Literature

stories.name: Ngabia Bate, the Marsh Monster
stories.excerpt: A monstrous creature said to inhabit the marshlands of southern Chad, the Ngabia Bate is a serpentine beast that drags livestock and people into the water.
stories.title: Ngabia Bate, the Marsh Monster

stories.name: Ngai on Mount Kenya
stories.excerpt: Ngai, also known as Mwene Nyaga (the Possessor of Brightness), made his home upon the snow-capped peak of Kirinyaga, Mount Kenya. He is the creator and giver of all things, the union of masculine and feminine principles, the divider of the universe who has no mother, no father, and no companion. From his mountain thron
stories.title: Ngai on Mount Kenya

stories.name: Ngake and Whataitai: The Taniwha of Wellington Harbour
stories.excerpt: The great taniwha Ngake and Whataitai lived in Lake Rotoroa (now Wellington Harbour) when it was still an enclosed lake. Ngake heard tales of the vast ocean beyond the hills and grew restless. He threw his body against the land at the southern end, eventually breaking through at what is now the harbor entrance, creatin
stories.title: Ngake and Whataitai: The Taniwha of Wellington Harbour

stories.name: Niels and the Giants
stories.excerpt: A story about a small boy named Niels who uses his ingenuity and quick thinking to outsmart towering giants and save his village from their threats.
stories.title: Niels and the Giants

stories.name: Nihancan and the Dwarf's Arrow
stories.excerpt: Nihancan the trickster was wandering when he encountered a small dwarf armed with a bow and arrow. Nihancan laughed at the dwarf, mocking his small size and tiny weapon. The dwarf challenged Nihancan to shoot the arrow at a target. Nihancan agreed, but when he tried to pull the bow, he found it impossibly heavy. The dw
stories.title: Nihancan and the Dwarf's Arrow

stories.name: Nihancan the Spider Trickster
stories.excerpt: Nihancan is the Arapaho trickster figure, a spider-like being similar to Iktomi of the Lakota and Wihio of the Cheyenne. He is both clever and foolish, often causing trouble through his greed and selfishness. In one tale, Nihancan tricked a bear family and killed the children, only to be outwitted himself. Another stor
stories.title: Nihancan the Spider Trickster

stories.name: Nimba, the Guinean Protector
stories.excerpt: A protective spirit of the Baga people of Guinea, the Nimba is a sacred guardian of fertility and motherhood, represented by a ritual mask.
stories.title: Nimba, the Guinean Protector

stories.name: Ninki Nanka: The Dragon of Rivers
stories.excerpt: In the hushed whispers of the Mandinka people, passed down through countless generations beside the winding Gambia River, there lives a terror that no man dares speak of aloud after dark.
stories.title: Ninki Nanka: The Dragon of Rivers

stories.name: Nis Puk
stories.excerpt: A legendary nisse (household spirit) who is mischievous but helpful. He interacts with humans in a trickster-like manner, often protecting the home while playing pranks on those who do not treat him with respect.
stories.title: Nis Puk

stories.name: Nisse
stories.excerpt: The general tradition of the household nisse, a small creature with a red cap who protects the farm and its animals. They are helpful if treated properly, particularly with a bowl of porridge and butter at Christmas, but cause chaos if offended.
stories.title: Nisse

stories.name: Njáls Saga - The Burning of Bergþórshvoll
stories.excerpt: A protracted blood feud culminates in the attack on the home of the wise Njáll. Despite Njáll's prophetic warnings and attempts to mediate, his enemies set fire to the building. Njáll, his wife Bergþóra, and their sons choose to perish in the flames rather than surrender, creating one of the most tragic and iconic scen
stories.title: Njáls Saga - The Burning of Bergþórshvoll

stories.name: Noion the Keeper of Hearths
stories.excerpt: A household spirit called Noion watches over a family that has forgotten the old offerings, and when the youngest child falls ill, the grandmother must remember the ancient formula of barley, butter, and breath to restore the compact.
stories.title: Noion the Keeper of Hearths

stories.name: Nonoma the Spirit of Thunder
stories.excerpt: Nonoma is the Cheyenne spirit of thunder, a powerful being who controls storms and brings rain to the plains. When Nonoma flaps his wings, thunder rolls across the sky. He is both feared and respected, as his storms can bring life-giving rain or destructive hail. The Cheyenne perform ceremonies to honor Nonoma and ask
stories.title: Nonoma the Spirit of Thunder

stories.name: Norna-Gestr's Journey
stories.excerpt: Norna-Gestr is a legendary traveler who possesses the gift of prophecy. His tales describe journeys to the edges of the known world and encounters with supernatural beings. He uses his foresight to navigate the dangers of the north, acting as a bridge between the human world and the realm of fate.
stories.title: Norna-Gestr's Journey

stories.name: Not a Pin to Choose Between Them
stories.excerpt: A humorous story about two brothers who are so identical in appearance and temperament that no one can tell them apart. This symmetry leads to a series of comical misunderstandings, eventually forcing them to find their own unique identities.
stories.title: Not a Pin to Choose Between Them

stories.name: Nuckelavee
stories.excerpt: If the Kelpie is a danger to individual travelers, the Nuckelavee is a terror to entire communities.
stories.title: Nuckelavee

stories.name: Nuckelavee: The Horse Demon
stories.excerpt: A demon horse of the sea—its breath kills crops, its touch brings disease, and it appears during summer storms.
stories.title: Nuckelavee: The Horse Demon

stories.name: Num and Nga: The Duel of Creation
stories.excerpt: The central Nenets dualistic creation myth about the sky god Num and his evil counterpart Nga. According to the legend, Num created the world out of chaos, shaping the land and sky, populating the earth with reindeer and people who lived in happiness. But Nga, the deity of destruction and death, constantly tried to und
stories.title: Num and Nga: The Duel of Creation

stories.name: Nyabingi and the Last Rain
stories.excerpt: Nyabingi, the ancient rain deity of the highlands, withdraws her blessing from the land after the people abandon their sacred rituals, and only a blind shepherd's faith restores the cycle of rain.
stories.title: Nyabingi and the Last Rain

stories.name: Nyamgondho Wuod Ombare
stories.excerpt: Nyamgondho was a poor fisherman who lived on the shores of Lake Victoria. He owned nothing — no cattle, no goats, not even proper clothes. One morning, starving and desperate, he cast his net into the lake and pulled out a hideously ugly woman. Terrified, he tried to throw her back, but the woman spoke. She promised to
stories.title: Nyamgondho Wuod Ombare

stories.name: Nyaminyami and the Breaking of the Dam
stories.excerpt: When engineers came to dam the Zambezi, the Tonga people warned that Nyaminyami, the river god, would not tolerate the severing of his body, and the floods that followed proved them right.
stories.title: Nyaminyami and the Breaking of the Dam

stories.name: Nyikang and the Bridge of Spirits
stories.excerpt: The legendary Shilluk hero-king Nyikang built a bridge between the world of the living and the world of the spirits, ensuring that the ancestors would never abandon their descendants in times of need.
stories.title: Nyikang and the Bridge of Spirits

stories.name: Nykur (The Nix of Sørvágsvatn)
stories.excerpt: Nykur is a shapeshifting water spirit that inhabits lakes, most famously Sørvágsvatn on Vágar Island. It appears most often as a beautiful white horse that lures people onto its back, then gallops into the lake to drown them. A popular tale tells of two brothers playing at the lakeshore. The older brother climbed onto
stories.title: Nykur (The Nix of Sørvágsvatn)

stories.name: Nykur and the Brothers (Lake Vatnsdalsvatn Variant)
stories.excerpt: A variant of the Nykur legend told around Lake Vatnsdalsvatn. Two children were playing by the lakeshore when they saw a beautiful white horse grazing nearby. The older brother, being tall enough, climbed onto the horse's back. Immediately the horse began galloping toward the deep water. The younger brother, who only w
stories.title: Nykur and the Brothers (Lake Vatnsdalsvatn Variant)

stories.name: Nyurgun Bootur the Swift
stories.excerpt: The most well-known Olonkho epic of the Yakut (Sakha) people, consisting of over 36,000 verses. It tells the story of the hero Nyurgun Bootur, a warrior of the Aiyy (good) tribe who protects the Middle World (human realm) from the evil Abaasy spirits of the Lower World. The epic explores the balance between three cosmi
stories.title: Nyurgun Bootur the Swift

stories.name: Nzambi Mpungu and the Creation of the World
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, there was only Nzambi Mpungu, the supreme creator, and the dark, formless waters. Nzambi Mpungu spoke the world into existence, separating the waters above from the waters below to create the sky and the earth. He created the sun, moon, and stars, then the plants, animals, and finally the first man an
stories.title: Nzambi Mpungu and the Creation of the World

stories.name: Nzazi: The Thunder Spirit of the Kongo
stories.excerpt: Nzazi is the powerful spirit of thunder and lightning in Kongo mythology, a fearsome being who lives in the sky and hurls bolts of fire at those who break the sacred laws. According to tradition, Nzazi was once a man who climbed too high in his ambitions and was transformed into a sky spirit as punishment. Now he patro
stories.title: Nzazi: The Thunder Spirit of the Kongo

stories.name: Obatala and the Creation of Humanity (Yoruba)
stories.excerpt: Obatala, the king of white cloth and the creator of human bodies, was given the task of molding the first humans from clay by Olodumare. However, Obatala grew thirsty during his work and drank palm wine, becoming intoxicated. In his drunken state, he molded some bodies imperfectly, creating people with physical disabil
stories.title: Obatala and the Creation of Humanity (Yoruba)

stories.name: Ochi-Bala and Kan-Altyn
stories.excerpt: Ochi-Bala and Kan-Altyn are two of the most important Altai heroic tales, recorded from the legendary kaichy (epic singer) Aleksei Kalkin in the 20th century. Ochi-Bala tells of a warrior woman of extraordinary skill who defends her people with a bow made of birch and arrows tipped with the teeth of defeated demons. Ka
stories.title: Ochi-Bala and Kan-Altyn

stories.name: Odin and the Runes
stories.excerpt: The Banshee is Ireland's most famous supernatural figure. Centers on Odin, from Norway mythology. Known for astral projection and aquatic speed and energy manipulation..
stories.title: Odin and the Runes

stories.name: Oduduwa and the Founding of the Yoruba Kingdoms (Yoruba)
stories.excerpt: Oduduwa was the legendary progenitor of the Yoruba people and the first ruler of Ile-Ife. According to tradition, Oduduwa descended from heaven on a chain with a rooster, some soil, and a palm nut, completing the creation Obatala had begun. He became the first king and his sixteen sons became the founders of the sixtee
stories.title: Oduduwa and the Founding of the Yoruba Kingdoms (Yoruba)

stories.name: Ogun Releases the Gods (Yoruba)
stories.excerpt: After the creation of the world, the Orishas found themselves trapped between heaven and earth, unable to descend to the newly formed land. Ogun, the god of iron and war, used his machete to clear a path through the dense forest, creating the first road and allowing the other gods to reach the earth. He also taught hum
stories.title: Ogun Releases the Gods (Yoruba)

stories.name: Okwa Naholo: White Water People (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: Okwa Naholo (or Oka Nahullo), meaning 'White people of the water,' are supernatural beings from Choctaw mythology who dwell in deep pools, rivers, and springs. They have light-colored skin like the underside of trout, which makes them almost invisible in the water. These powerful water spirits sometimes capture human b
stories.title: Okwa Naholo: White Water People (Choctaw)

stories.name: Ol' Hige the Vampiric Witch
stories.excerpt: Ol' Hige is a witch from Jamaican folklore who sheds her skin at night and flies through the air in the form of an owl or a ball of fire. She harms people — especially babies — by sucking their breath while they sleep. Her habit of shedding her skin makes her vulnerable: if someone discovers her empty skin and fills it
stories.title: Ol' Hige the Vampiric Witch

stories.name: Old Age, Cold, Poverty, and Hunger
stories.excerpt: After the Hero Twins killed the major monsters, four lesser monsters remained: Old Age (Są́), Cold (Dǫǫh), Poverty (Téʼéʼį́), and Hunger (Báhí). When the twins confronted these beings, they pleaded for their lives. Old Age argued that without him, the world would become overcrowded and people would not appreciate youth
stories.title: Old Age, Cold, Poverty, and Hunger

stories.name: Old Hopgiant
stories.excerpt: A poor peasant shares his meager food with a strange old giant who rewards him with a magic mill that grinds anything — but the greedy neighbor learns that kindness cannot be stolen. Old Hopgiant is a genuine folk-tale figure who aids the poor against oppression.
stories.title: Old Hopgiant

stories.name: Old Man Coyote Creates the World
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, Old Man Coyote (Isáahkawuattee) was alone upon a great ocean. He saw two male ducks floating on the water and asked them what lay beneath. One duck dove deep and returned with a root in its beak; a second more dangerous dive brought up mud. Using this mud, Old Man Coyote built an island that grew into
stories.title: Old Man Coyote Creates the World

stories.name: Old Mr. Rabbit, He's a Good Fisherman
stories.excerpt: Brer Rabbit, tired and hungry, finds his way to a creek where he sees Brer Fox and Brer Wolf fishing. Rather than asking for food, Brer Rabbit pretends to be a great fisherman himself. He cuts a willow branch, ties a string to it, and sits downstream, pretending to fish while actually eating the berries he finds nearby
stories.title: Old Mr. Rabbit, He's a Good Fisherman

stories.name: Old Nick and the Girl
stories.excerpt: A poor girl mad for dancing makes a deal with Old Nick (the Devil) for leather dancing shoes. After a year, she tricks him into a race around Lake Fryken by using her identical twin sister at both ends of the lake, wearing out Old Nick's shoes while proving her bark shoes superior.
stories.title: Old Nick and the Girl

stories.name: Old Nick and the Pedlar
stories.excerpt: A struggling pedlar makes a bargain with Old Nick: he will sell all he buys, but if his bags ever become empty he belongs to the Devil. Business booms until a buyer (Old Nick in disguise) purchases the entire lot. The pedlar escapes by claiming Katie Grey is in one of the bags, and Old Nick—terrified of her—flees.
stories.title: Old Nick and the Pedlar

stories.name: Old Woman's Water and the Buffalo Cap
stories.excerpt: An old woman who lived by a sacred spring found that her water had healing powers. She shared it with a young warrior who was wounded, and he was miraculously healed. The woman then revealed herself as a manifestation of the earth's power. She gave the warrior a buffalo cap made from the scalp of a sacred buffalo, whic
stories.title: Old Woman's Water and the Buffalo Cap

stories.name: Ole Higue, the Guyanese Vampire
stories.excerpt: A vampire-like spirit of Guyanese folklore, the Ole Higue is an old woman who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of light to drink blood.
stories.title: Ole Higue, the Guyanese Vampire

stories.name: Ole Lukøje
stories.excerpt: The sandman who visits children at night, telling them beautiful stories through their eyelids to ensure they have sweet dreams, while those who are unkind receive empty stories.
stories.title: Ole Lukøje

stories.name: Olifat the Trickster God
stories.excerpt: Olifat is a trickster god in Micronesian mythology, particularly among the islands of Chuuk. He was the grandson of the great god Anulap, born to the god Lugeleng and the mortal woman Tarisso, daughter of the octopus goddess Hit. When Lugeleng's wife tried to prevent the union, Hit danced so lewdly that the wife fainte
stories.title: Olifat the Trickster God

stories.name: Olobit (Ukteni): The Great Serpent (Natchez)
stories.excerpt: Olobit (also called Olobis or Intsiyacdoo'cgu, 'sharp-breasted snake') is a monstrous serpent from Natchez folklore. Similar to the Cherokee Uktena, Olobit is a giant serpent with supernatural powers and a deadly gaze. It also has a sharp, breast-like protrusion on its chest that can impale victims. Olobit dwells in de
stories.title: Olobit (Ukteni): The Great Serpent (Natchez)

stories.name: Onditichiae: The Thunder Beings
stories.excerpt: The Onditichiae are the Thunder beings of the Wyandot and related Tobacco Indians. They are a race of giant sky beings who control the storms. According to tradition, they were created to serve as the eternal enemies of all water monsters. Whenever a great serpent or underwater panther becomes too dangerous, the Onditi
stories.title: Onditichiae: The Thunder Beings

stories.name: One Who Walks All Over the Sky (Tsimshian)
stories.excerpt: This Tsimshian myth explains the origin of the sun, moon, and night sky. After Weeget (Giant/Raven) brought light from heaven, there was still the question of who would carry the sun across the sky each day and what the patterns of stars meant. The One Who Walks All Over the Sky is a supernatural being assigned to carr
stories.title: One Who Walks All Over the Sky (Tsimshian)

stories.name: One's Own Children Are Always Prettiest
stories.excerpt: A satirical look at parental bias through the eyes of several families who insist their children are the most beautiful in the world. A neutral judge is brought in to settle the dispute, leading to a lesson about the nature of love and perception.
stories.title: One's Own Children Are Always Prettiest

stories.name: Oochigeas and the Invisible Boy (The Mi'kmaq Cinderella)
stories.excerpt: A great chief had a son who was invisible. Only a woman who spoke the truth could see him. Many vain young women tried and failed, always lying that they could see the Invisible Boy. In a nearby village lived Oochigeas, the youngest daughter, whose face and hands were scarred from tending fires because her cruel elder
stories.title: Oochigeas and the Invisible Boy (The Mi'kmaq Cinderella)

stories.name: Origin of Iron
stories.excerpt: Wainamoinen and the smith Ilmarinen seek to uncover the origin of iron, a material essential for tools and weapons. They discover that iron is a divine gift forged in the heavens. This story establishes Ilmarinen as the preeminent master smith, capable of working with the most challenging materials in existence.
stories.title: Origin of Iron

stories.name: Origin of Poison (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: Long ago, a poison vine grew in a pool where Choctaw people bathed. Everything that touched the vine would die. The vine loved the Choctaw people and did not want to hurt them, but it could not warn them when its poison would infect the water. It decided to rid itself of the poison and called the chiefs of the snakes,
stories.title: Origin of Poison (Choctaw)

stories.name: Origin of the Chinook People (Chinook)
stories.excerpt: When Old Man South Wind was traveling north, he met an Old Woman who was a giant. Hungry and tired, he asked for food. She gave him a net and told him to catch fish. South Wind caught a little whale and was about to cut it crossways when the old giantress warned him to slit it down the back instead. He ignored her and
stories.title: Origin of the Chinook People (Chinook)

stories.name: Origin of the Pleiades (The Dancing Children)
stories.excerpt: Long ago, seven young Iroquois children loved to dance in the woods. Every evening they would gather in a clearing, singing and dancing even as others told them to stop. They refused to go to sleep or do their chores, so absorbed were they in their joyous dancing. The Creator, watching from the sky, decided to preserve
stories.title: Origin of the Pleiades (The Dancing Children)

stories.name: Origin of the Seminole Clans (Seminole)
stories.excerpt: According to Seminole tradition, the clans were established at the time of creation. The Seminole have several matrilineal clans, including the Panther, Bear, Deer, Bird, Wind, and Otter clans. The legend tells that Breathmaker created the animals and asked them to protect the human people. Each animal agreed, and in r
stories.title: Origin of the Seminole Clans (Seminole)

stories.name: Origin of the Serpent
stories.excerpt: A myth explaining the creation of the first serpent. The story describes how a divine accident led to the emergence of the snake, introducing the concepts of danger, poison, and cunning into the natural world and human experience.
stories.title: Origin of the Serpent

stories.name: Origin of the Wind
stories.excerpt: Na'pi discovered two bags containing summer and winter. Determined to make the seasons equal, he tried to steal them but failed. He sent a prairie chicken who successfully grabbed the summer bag. The guardians chased the bird, slicing at the grass and cutting the bag open. Strong wind burst forth. Later, Napi burned hi
stories.title: Origin of the Wind

stories.name: Ormur (The Feared Farmer of Skála)
stories.excerpt: Ormur ('Worm') was a notoriously savage farmer in Skála, a giant of a man who stole sheep from neighboring farms. When farmer Pætur of Funningur caught him, Ormur forced him to swear silence under threat of his axe. Later, Pætur visited Ormur's home and was served sheep heads—but Ormur had forgotten to remove the ears,
stories.title: Ormur (The Feared Farmer of Skála)

stories.name: Oro: God of War and the Arioi Society
stories.excerpt: Oro, son of Ta'aroa, was the Tahitian god of war and peace. He descended to earth on a rainbow and took a mortal woman as his wife, establishing the Arioi—a secret society of warriors, artists, and priests who spread his cult throughout the Society Islands. The Arioi traveled between islands performing sacred dances, c
stories.title: Oro: God of War and the Arioi Society

stories.name: Orochi the Eight-Headed Serpent
stories.excerpt: The storm god Susanoo-no-Mikoto had been banished from Takamagahara, the Plain of High Heaven, after a furious quarrel with his sister Amaterasu, the sun goddess.
stories.title: Orochi the Eight-Headed Serpent

stories.name: Orpheus and Eurydice
stories.excerpt: Orpheus was the greatest musician who ever lived—the son of Apollo, god of music.
stories.title: Orpheus and Eurydice

stories.name: Oshún, Goddess of the River
stories.excerpt: Oshún (Ochún) is the orisha of fresh water, love, fertility, beauty, and sensuality in Cuban Santería, syncretized with the Virgen de la Caridad del Cobre, Cuba's patron saint. According to the Ifá literary corpus, Oshún was the only female irunmole (primordial spirit) sent to assist in creating the world. The male spi
stories.title: Oshún, Goddess of the River

stories.name: Osiris
stories.excerpt: Osiris was the first king of Egypt — a god who walked among mortals and taught them civilization.
stories.title: Osiris

stories.name: Osmotar the Bride-adviser
stories.excerpt: Osmotar, a wise advisor, provides guidance to the new bride, offering essential wisdom on the expectations of marriage and how to navigate the social and emotional complexities of life in the land of heroes.
stories.title: Osmotar the Bride-adviser

stories.name: Ossobó, the Sacred Bird
stories.excerpt: A sacred bird of São Tomé and Príncipe, the Ossobó is a forest spirit that protects travelers and punishes those who harm the rainforest.
stories.title: Ossobó, the Sacred Bird

stories.name: Otso the Honey-eater
stories.excerpt: The story of Otso, the Bear, the most sacred and feared animal in Finnish tradition. The heroes must use precise and respectful magical songs to appease the bear and safely obtain the precious honey from his lair.
stories.title: Otso the Honey-eater

stories.name: Ounamir and the Sky Maiden
stories.excerpt: The Ounamir myth is a cornerstone of Amazigh oral tradition from southern Morocco, particularly around Tata and Tagoujgalt. Hemmou Ounamir is a gifted student whose beauty attracts Tanirt, a celestial being (often rendered as an angel, fairy, or djinn princess). She secretly marks his hand with henna. After being expos
