stories.title: Ounamir and the Sky Maiden

stories.name: Pabuji Ki Phad — The Epic of the Rajasthani Deity
stories.excerpt: Pabuji is a legendary folk deity from Rajasthan worshipped by the Rabari (shepherd) community. The epic poem Pabuji Ki Phad, performed with a painted scroll, tells of Pabuji's life as a 14th-century Rathore prince who became a folk hero. After marrying the princess of Umarkot, Pabuji's camel was stolen by demons. In tr
stories.title: Pabuji Ki Phad — The Epic of the Rajasthani Deity

stories.name: Pahuk and the Sacred Sites
stories.excerpt: Pahuk (hill island) is a sacred bluff on the south side of the Platte River near Cedar Bluffs, Nebraska. It is the foremost of the five nahurac lodges, where the animal spirit messengers of Tirawa gather. According to Pawnee legend, a young man once visited Pahuk seeking a vision. After four days of fasting, the animal
stories.title: Pahuk and the Sacred Sites

stories.name: Pamola, the Snow Bird Spirit of Mount Katahdin
stories.excerpt: Pamola (also called Bemola or Pomola) is a powerful snow bird spirit who dwells on the summit of Mount Katahdin, the highest mountain in Maine and the most sacred peak of the Penobscot and Abenaki people. Pamola has the body of a man and the head and wings of a giant eagle and makes the cold weather by beating his enor
stories.title: Pamola, the Snow Bird Spirit of Mount Katahdin

stories.name: Panchatantra — The Brahmin and the Mongoose
stories.excerpt: A Brahmin couple adopts a pet mongoose, raising it as their own child alongside their newborn son. One day, the wife goes to fetch water, leaving the baby with the husband, who also leaves to beg for alms. While they are away, a deadly snake slithers toward the cradle. The loyal mongoose attacks and kills the snake, sa
stories.title: Panchatantra — The Brahmin and the Mongoose

stories.name: Panchatantra — The Lion and the Bull
stories.excerpt: The first book of Panchatantra, 'Mitra Bheda' (The Loss of Friends), tells of a lion king named Pingalaka who befriends a bull named Sanjivaka. A jealous jackal named Damanaka, who serves the lion, sows discord between them by feeding lies to both parties. He convinces the lion that the bull plans to usurp the throne,
stories.title: Panchatantra — The Lion and the Bull

stories.name: Panchatantra — The Monkey and the Crocodile
stories.excerpt: A clever monkey living in a rose-apple tree by a river befriends a crocodile, sharing sweet fruits with him daily. The crocodile's wife grows jealous and demands to eat the monkey's heart. The crocodile tricks the monkey into climbing onto his back for a ride, then reveals his plan. Quick-witted, the monkey claims he l
stories.title: Panchatantra — The Monkey and the Crocodile

stories.name: Papa Bois and the Last Hunter
stories.excerpt: A hunter who takes too much from the forest encounters Papa Bois, the lord of the woods, and learns that the forest remembers every creature it has lost.
stories.title: Papa Bois and the Last Hunter

stories.name: Papa Bois, the Guardian of the Trinidadian Forest
stories.excerpt: Papa Bois (Father of the Woods) is the ancient protector spirit of Trinidad's forests, a figure of Afro-Trinidadian Creole folklore with roots in West African forest guardians. He appears as an impossibly old man with bark-like skin, a mossy beard tangled with vines, and deer-like legs ending in cloven hooves, with sta
stories.title: Papa Bois, the Guardian of the Trinidadian Forest

stories.name: Papa Bois: Keeper of the Green
stories.excerpt: When a logging crew begins clearing the old forest above Grand Etang, each man falls mysteriously ill until they meet Papa Bois, the ancient guardian of the bush.
stories.title: Papa Bois: Keeper of the Green

stories.name: Papa Bois: The Old Man of the Forest
stories.excerpt: A hairy old man with cloven hooves protects the forests and punishes hunters who kill for sport.
stories.title: Papa Bois: The Old Man of the Forest

stories.name: Papa Legba and the Gate of the Spirit World
stories.excerpt: Papa Legba is the most important lwa (spirit) in Haitian Vodou, serving as the gatekeeper between the human and spirit worlds. No human can communicate with any other spirit without Papa Legba's permission. He stands at the spiritual crossroads, deciding whether a person is allowed to speak with other lwa. Believed to
stories.title: Papa Legba and the Gate of the Spirit World

stories.name: Pate Island Chronicles: The Founding of the Sultanate
stories.excerpt: According to the Pate Chronicle, the island of Pate was first settled by refugees from the crumbling Persian port of Shiraz in the 13th century. Led by Sultan Suleiman, they found the island inhabited by African Bantu-speaking fishermen. Rather than conquering them, Suleiman married the local chief's daughter and creat
stories.title: Pate Island Chronicles: The Founding of the Sultanate

stories.name: Paul Bunyan
stories.excerpt: In the early days of America, when the continent was covered with vast, untamed forests stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific, there lived a lumberjack so enormous, so strong, and so skilled that he became the greatest hero the North Woods have ever known.
stories.title: Paul Bunyan

stories.name: Pele and Kamapua'a
stories.excerpt: The volcano goddess Pele and Kamapua'a, the pig demigod, had a tumultuous relationship oscillating between love and war. Kamapua'a could transform between human and giant pig forms and commanded the rains and forests. When he pursued Pele, she refused him, and a great battle erupted across the Big Island. Pele sent riv
stories.title: Pele and Kamapua'a

stories.name: Pele and the Lava
stories.excerpt: Across the vast, sapphire expanse of the Pacific, where the horizon dissolves into a haze of gold and blue, lies the archipelago of Hawaiʻi—a chain of emerald peaks born from the violent passion of a single deity.
stories.title: Pele and the Lava

stories.name: Pele's Journey from Kahiki to Hawaii
stories.excerpt: Pele, the volcano goddess, was born in Tahiti (Kahiki) to Haumea and Kane Milohai. Banished by her father because of her fierce temper, Pele sailed with her brothers in a great canoe across the Pacific. She dug fire pits at each island she visited, creating Diamond Head on Oahu and Haleakala on Maui. On Maui, her siste
stories.title: Pele's Journey from Kahiki to Hawaii

stories.name: Pele's Tears
stories.excerpt: In the heart of the Pacific, where the earth breathes fire and the ocean churns against volcanic shores, the goddess Pele reigns as both creator and destroyer.
stories.title: Pele's Tears

stories.name: Pemba and Faro: The Bambara Twin Creation
stories.excerpt: In Bambara (Bamana) mythology, the creator god Bemba (Maa Ngala) created the universe in three stages. In the first stage, Pemba, a grain that fell to earth and became an acacia tree, created Mousso Koroni Koundye from rotten wood and his saliva. She became the first woman, but her creations were disordered and chaotic
stories.title: Pemba and Faro: The Bambara Twin Creation

stories.name: Pepo: The Sea Spirits of Zanzibar
stories.excerpt: The Pepo are powerful sea spirits that inhabit the waters around Zanzibar and the Swahili coast. They are invisible beings who can influence human destiny — bringing good fortune, madness, or illness as they choose. According to tradition, the Pepo were the original inhabitants of the coast before humans arrived. When
stories.title: Pepo: The Sea Spirits of Zanzibar

stories.name: Peri, the Winged Spirit of Afghanistan
stories.excerpt: Beautiful winged spirits who dwell between heaven and earth, the Peri are benevolent beings who guide lost souls and protect sacred springs.
stories.title: Peri, the Winged Spirit of Afghanistan

stories.name: Phoenix
stories.excerpt: In the burning sands of Arabia, where the sun beats down like a hammer on an anvil and the heat shimmers in waves across the desert, there lives a bird unlike any other in creation.
stories.title: Phoenix

stories.name: Phra Lak Phra Ram: The Lao Ramayana
stories.excerpt: Phra Lak Phra Ram is the national epic of the Lao people, a distinctive adaptation of the Indian Ramayana that thoroughly Lao-izes the story. Unlike the Indian version, the Lao epic explicitly frames the tale as a Jataka — a previous life story of the Buddha — making it entirely compatible with Theravada Buddhism. The
stories.title: Phra Lak Phra Ram: The Lao Ramayana

stories.name: Pichal Peri: The Backward-Footed Spirit of Pakistan
stories.excerpt: A vengeful female spirit with backward-facing feet lures men to their doom in the Punjab countryside.
stories.title: Pichal Peri: The Backward-Footed Spirit of Pakistan

stories.name: Plague Spirits, the Riders of Pestilence
stories.excerpt: Dark spirits of European folklore that rode through the continent during the Black Death, spreading plague and despair wherever they appeared.
stories.title: Plague Spirits, the Riders of Pestilence

stories.name: Poliahu and Pele: The Snow Goddess Rivalry
stories.excerpt: Poliahu, the lovely snow goddess who drapes Mauna Kea in white, and Pele, the volcano goddess of Kilauea, were rivals for the affections of a handsome chief. Poliahu was renowned for her beauty and cool temperament, while Pele was passionate and jealous. During a gathering of goddesses, Pele challenged Poliahu and ridi
stories.title: Poliahu and Pele: The Snow Goddess Rivalry

stories.name: Pombero, the Night Whistler
stories.excerpt: A mischievous forest spirit who whistles in the night, the Pombero is both feared and respected by rural Uruguayans for his tricks and his punishments.
stories.title: Pombero, the Night Whistler

stories.name: Pontianak: The Vampire Ghost of Malaysia
stories.excerpt: The vengeful spirit of a woman who died in childbirth hunts men and babies in the darkness.
stories.title: Pontianak: The Vampire Ghost of Malaysia

stories.name: Popa Medaw and the Mahagiri Nat
stories.excerpt: The most important nat (spirit) legend in Burmese folklore tells the tragic story of the Mahagiri Nat and his sister Popa Medaw. The tale begins with a powerful blacksmith named Nga Tin De, who forged weapons of unparalleled quality in the village of Taungbyon. King Thinligyawng of Tagaung, fearing the blacksmith's gro
stories.title: Popa Medaw and the Mahagiri Nat

stories.name: Pope Sylvester and the Dragon
stories.excerpt: Pope Sylvester I confronts a terrible dragon beneath the Lateran Palace, whose poisonous breath has killed thousands, and chains it through the power of faith alone.
stories.title: Pope Sylvester and the Dragon

stories.name: Popobawa: The Bat-Wing Terror of Zanzibar
stories.excerpt: A shape-shifting evil spirit with bat wings terrorizes the island of Zanzibar, attacking victims in their sleep.
stories.title: Popobawa: The Bat-Wing Terror of Zanzibar

stories.name: Porgupõrgu, the Estonian Hell
stories.excerpt: The Estonian concept of the underworld, a place beneath the earth where the dead journeyed and where ancient spirits guarded the boundary between worlds.
stories.title: Porgupõrgu, the Estonian Hell

stories.name: Potto-Podnie and Stállo
stories.excerpt: From the Solsönernas Saga. Potto-Podnie ('the useful old man') of the Sirkas tribe was a skilled noaidi with a magic drum. Stállo, an evil wandering giant sent by Adtjis-ene, dwelt in a mountain across the marsh from Potto-Podnie's camp. When Stállo coveted Potto-Podnie's beautiful daughter Waimokatta, a battle ensued.
stories.title: Potto-Podnie and Stállo

stories.name: Preah Ko Preah Keo: The Sacred Ox and Sacred Gem
stories.excerpt: Preah Ko Preah Keo is a famous Cambodian legend about two orphaned brothers from humble origins who discover extraordinary destinies. The elder brother, Preah Ko, was born under a sacred ox and grew to be strong and virtuous, while the younger, Preah Keo, was born under a shining gem and possessed magical powers. The b
stories.title: Preah Ko Preah Keo: The Sacred Ox and Sacred Gem

stories.name: Preah Thong and Neang Neak: The Founding of the Khmer Nation
stories.excerpt: The foundational creation myth of the Khmer people tells the story of Preah Thong (Kaundinya), an Indian Brahmin prince, and Neang Neak (Queen Soma), a Naga serpent princess. According to the legend recorded by Chinese envoys Kang Tai and Zhu Ying in the 3rd century CE, Kaundinya received a divine instruction in a drea
stories.title: Preah Thong and Neang Neak: The Founding of the Khmer Nation

stories.name: Prince Siddhartha's Great Renunciation
stories.excerpt: Siddhartha Gautama was born c. 563 BCE in Lumbini (present-day Nepal) to King Suddhodana and Queen Maya Devi. Legend recounts that Queen Maya dreamed of a white elephant entering her womb, and the newborn Siddhartha immediately took seven steps, declaring this his last birth. Protected from suffering by his father, Sid
stories.title: Prince Siddhartha's Great Renunciation

stories.name: Prince Vijaya and the Founding of Sri Lanka
stories.excerpt: Prince Vijaya, grandson of a lion and son of King Sinhabahu, was banished from Sinhapura in India for his violent deeds. He and his 700 followers sailed to Lanka, landing at Tambapanni on the very day of the Buddha's parinibbana. There they encountered the Yakkhini queen Kuveni, who through magical threads and bravery
stories.title: Prince Vijaya and the Founding of Sri Lanka

stories.name: Prince Whitebear
stories.excerpt: A prince is cursed to live as a white bear. He is eventually saved and restored to human form through the unwavering love and devotion of a princess.
stories.title: Prince Whitebear

stories.name: Prince Wolf
stories.excerpt: A story about a prince transformed into a wolf, exploring themes of identity, animal nature, and the path to redemption and human restoration.
stories.title: Prince Wolf

stories.name: Puss in Boots
stories.excerpt: A clever cat in boots uses trickery and deceit to win his poor master wealth, a castle, and a princess. The cat's cunning elevates his master from poverty to royalty.
stories.title: Puss in Boots

stories.name: Pygmalion
stories.excerpt: On the island of Cyprus, where the foam of the sea first gave birth to Aphrodite, there lived a young sculptor named Pygmalion.
stories.title: Pygmalion

stories.name: Pygmalion and the Ivory Bride
stories.excerpt: A sculptor of Cyprus carves his ideal woman from ivory and worships her so faithfully that the gods breathe life into his creation, teaching that devotion can move heaven itself.
stories.title: Pygmalion and the Ivory Bride

stories.name: Púca
stories.excerpt: On the night of Samhain, when the veil between worlds is thinnest and the dead walk among the living, there are tricks to be wary of.
stories.title: Púca

stories.name: Pūķis, the Household Dragon of Latvia
stories.excerpt: Pūķis, a dragon-like household spirit of Latvia, guards the home from above the hearth, demanding respect and offerings in exchange for prosperity and protection.
stories.title: Pūķis, the Household Dragon of Latvia

stories.name: Qals (Mink) and the Transformations (Coast Salish)
stories.excerpt: Qals (Mink) is a major trickster figure in Coast Salish mythology, particularly in the Fraser River region. In the longest and most important story told by George StsE'lis to Franz Boas, Qals shapes the world through his encounters with various flawed ancestors. Mink tricked a chief's daughter into sleeping with him, p
stories.title: Qals (Mink) and the Transformations (Coast Salish)

stories.name: Qamar al-Zaman and the Princess of the Jinn
stories.excerpt: A tale from the Arabian Nights about Prince Qamar al-Zaman (Moon of the Age), son of King Shahriman, who refuses marriage and is imprisoned. The princess of the jinn, in a parallel story, also refuses marriage and is imprisoned by her father the jinn king. Through the machinations of a devious jinn and a fairy, they ar
stories.title: Qamar al-Zaman and the Princess of the Jinn

stories.name: Qamata and the Creation of the Xhosa World
stories.excerpt: Qamata (also known as uThixo) is the supreme creator god of the Xhosa people who existed before all things. From a primordial void of darkness and silence, Qamata created the world using Uhlanga, a bed of sacred reeds that became the material for all life. He divided existence into three realms: the sky for himself, th
stories.title: Qamata and the Creation of the Xhosa World

stories.name: Qat and the Sky Maidens
stories.excerpt: One day Qat discovered a group of sky maidens who had removed their wings to bathe. He quickly buried one pair of wings so that one maiden, Vinmara, had to remain behind. She became his wife and was called Ro-Lei. They lived happily until Qat's mother reproached her daughter-in-law and made her cry. Ro-Lei's tears wash
stories.title: Qat and the Sky Maidens

stories.name: Qat the Creator and the Birth of Night
stories.excerpt: In the Banks Islands of Vanuatu, the principal god Qat emerged from a stone that exploded as his mother. He had eleven brothers called Tagaro and a companion named Marawa the spider. Qat carved the first three pairs of humans from dracaena wood and brought them to life by playing drums, making them dance. When his brot
stories.title: Qat the Creator and the Birth of Night

stories.name: Qozy Körpesh and Bayan Sulu
stories.excerpt: The oldest Kazakh love dastan, dating back over 1,500 years to the era of the Türgesh Khaganate. Qozy and Bayan are promised to each other from birth, but Qozy's father dies before the marriage can take place. Bayan's ambitious father, Karabai, breaks the promise and betroths her to a wealthy rival. Qozy searches for h
stories.title: Qozy Körpesh and Bayan Sulu

stories.name: Queen Abla Pokou: The Mother of the Baoule People
stories.excerpt: In the 18th century, a great crisis divided the Ashanti Kingdom in what is now Ghana.
stories.title: Queen Abla Pokou: The Mother of the Baoule People

stories.name: Queen Arawelo: The Warrior Queen of Somalia
stories.excerpt: Queen Arawelo (Carraweelo) was a legendary proto-Somali queen who established a matriarchal society in the Sanaag region around the 1st century CE. According to tradition, Arawelo was born to Haramaanyo and raised during a time of brutal clan warfare and devastating drought. After her husband and children died in the v
stories.title: Queen Arawelo: The Warrior Queen of Somalia

stories.name: Queen Crane
stories.excerpt: A poor shepherd boy named Proud is befriended by a crane who is actually an enchanted queen, and through a series of magical transformations, he wins her hand and a kingdom. This very popular Northern tale features a seemingly witless hero with an unusual transformation motive.
stories.title: Queen Crane

stories.name: Queen Makeda and King Solomon
stories.excerpt: In the 10th century BCE, Queen Makeda of Ethiopia (known as the Queen of Sheba) heard of King Solomon's unparalleled wisdom and journeyed to Jerusalem with a magnificent caravan laden with gold, spices, and precious stones. Solomon was captivated by her beauty and intelligence. Through clever trickery, he persuaded her
stories.title: Queen Makeda and King Solomon

stories.name: Quetzalcoatl
stories.excerpt: Quetzalcoatl, whose name means Feathered Serpent, was one of the most important deities in the Mesoamerican pantheon.
stories.title: Quetzalcoatl

stories.name: Quetzalcóatl — The Feathered Serpent
stories.excerpt: Quetzalcóatl, the Feathered Serpent, is the most important syncretic deity in Mexican and Mexican-American spiritual folklore. In Aztec tradition, he was the god of wind, knowledge, learning, and the priesthood — credited with creating humanity by descending to Mictlan (the underworld) and mixing his blood with the bon
stories.title: Quetzalcóatl — The Feathered Serpent

stories.name: Ra and the Hidden Name
stories.excerpt: Isis, the great enchantress, desired power equal to Ra himself. As Ra aged, saliva dripped from his mouth and fell upon the ground. Isis gathered the saliva, mixed it with earth, and shaped it into a venomous serpent which she placed on Ra's path. When Ra was bitten by the invisible serpent, he suffered agonizing pain.
stories.title: Ra and the Hidden Name

stories.name: Ra and the Secret Name
stories.excerpt: Ra, the sun god, was the most powerful being in the Egyptian pantheon.. He created the world from the primordial waters of Nun.
stories.title: Ra and the Secret Name

stories.name: Ra and the Snake
stories.excerpt: In the golden age of the world, when the gods walked among men and the boundaries between heaven and earth were thin, Ra the sun god ruled over all creation.
stories.title: Ra and the Snake

stories.name: Ragnarök: The End and Rebirth
stories.excerpt: The seeress sat in the shadows, her eyes white as milk, her voice rising from a place deeper than mortal memory.
stories.title: Ragnarök: The End and Rebirth

stories.name: Rainbow Crow (Mànàka'has)
stories.excerpt: In the time before fire, the world was cold and dark. The animals suffered, unable to keep warm or cook their food. Kishelamakank, the Creator, took pity on them and placed a great fire at the top of a high mountain, but only the birds could reach it. The crow, who in those days had a beautiful rainbow-colored song and
stories.title: Rainbow Crow (Mànàka'has)

stories.name: Rakshasa: The Shape-Shifting Demon
stories.excerpt: Ancient demons from Hindu mythology who can change form, drink blood, and cause chaos—until smarter beings outwit them.
stories.title: Rakshasa: The Shape-Shifting Demon

stories.name: Rana Niejta: Daughter of the Green Earth
stories.excerpt: Rana Niejta is the Sámi spring goddess, daughter of Radien-attje and Raedieahkka. Her name means 'the green' or 'the fertile fields.' She makes the southern slopes of mountains green so hungry reindeer have food after winter. She is one of three divine sisters: Sala Niejta (Sun's daughter) ends winter's cold, Rana Niej
stories.title: Rana Niejta: Daughter of the Green Earth

stories.name: Rangi and Papa: The Separation of Sky and Earth
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, Ranginui (Sky Father) and Papatuanuku (Earth Mother) lay locked in a tight embrace, leaving their children trapped in darkness between them. The children grew weary of the cramped darkness and debated how to gain freedom. Tane Mahuta, god of forests, proposed separating their parents. While Tawhirimat
stories.title: Rangi and Papa: The Separation of Sky and Earth

stories.name: Rannamaari: The Sea Demon That Demanded Sacrifice
stories.excerpt: In pre-Islamic Maldives, a terrible sea demon called Rannamaari rose from the ocean each month to demand a sacrificed virgin. The girls were dressed in fine clothes and left alone in a Buddhist temple on the eastern seafront of Malé; by dawn, they were found violated and dead. This terror continued until a Maghrebi Mus
stories.title: Rannamaari: The Sea Demon That Demanded Sacrifice

stories.name: Rapunzel
stories.excerpt: Once upon a time, a married couple lived next to an old witch's garden.. The wife became pregnant and craved the rapunzel plants growing there.
stories.title: Rapunzel

stories.name: Ravana
stories.excerpt: Ravana, whose name means "He of the Terrifying Roar," was the most powerful demon king ever to rule the three worlds.
stories.title: Ravana

stories.name: Raven and the Beaver (Tlingit)
stories.excerpt: Near a bay near Kôts!ê'L! there was a seawater pond where a beaver lived. Raven very much wanted to catch and kill this beaver, so he dug two trenches to drain the lake at low tide. After the water ran out and the beaver was visible at the bottom, Raven lowered a hook and pulled the beaver up. After killing the beaver,
stories.title: Raven and the Beaver (Tlingit)

stories.name: Raven and the First Men
stories.excerpt: Raven, the trickster-creator, finds the first humans hiding in a clamshell on the beach and coaxes them out into the world.
stories.title: Raven and the First Men

stories.name: Raven and the First Woman
stories.excerpt: In this creation myth, the trickster god Raven wanders the shores of the world and finds a beautiful woman made of clay or shell. With a touch of his magic, he brings her to life, creating the first human woman. This story establishes Raven as the architect of human life and the source of the spark of consciousness in
stories.title: Raven and the First Woman

stories.name: Raven and the Fog Woman (Tlingit)
stories.excerpt: Raven wanted to marry and went to the chief called Fog-Over-The-Salmon, who had a young daughter. The chief agreed but made Raven promise to treat her with respect. They married and lived contentedly through summer and fall, but winter brought famine. Raven's wife began making a basket, and despite Raven's testy commen
stories.title: Raven and the Fog Woman (Tlingit)

stories.name: Raven and the Moon Woman (Haida)
stories.excerpt: Raven became the son of Moon Woman and cried incessantly, saying 'Boo-hoo, moon!' His mother, exhausted by his noise, stopped up all the holes in the house and untied the strings of a box containing the moon, letting Raven play with it. When she left, Raven turned into a raven and flew about the house with the moon in
stories.title: Raven and the Moon Woman (Haida)

stories.name: Raven Annoys Octopus (Nuu-chah-nulth)
stories.excerpt: One morning as the tide went out, the old people came to sit and watch the ocean. They saw a woman walking along the beach with her hair long and strung into eight braids — she was Octopus, carrying a digging stick to look for clams. She sat down on a rock and began to dig. Soon another person came along the beach, tal
stories.title: Raven Annoys Octopus (Nuu-chah-nulth)

stories.name: Raven Becomes Voracious (Tsimshian)
stories.excerpt: This Tsimshian myth explains how Raven acquired his insatiable appetite and voracious nature. Before this story, Raven was not known for his hunger. Through a series of events involving trickery, greed, and supernatural encounters, Raven's appetite grew beyond all bounds. He began devouring everything in sight, from sa
stories.title: Raven Becomes Voracious (Tsimshian)

stories.name: Raven Brings Light (Nuxalk - Qwaxw)
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, when the world was covered in darkness, the people were in constant sadness and prayed to the Creator Alhkw'ntam for light. Alhkw'ntam held the sun in a box in his longhouse in Nusmata (the land above) and let no one see it. The Four Carpenters who made the world were sitting around a fire when the el
stories.title: Raven Brings Light (Nuxalk - Qwaxw)

stories.name: Raven Mocker (Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï) (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï, the Raven Mocker, is a malevolent Cherokee spirit that preys on the dying. These witches are said to be ordinary-looking people during the day who transform at night into raven-like spirits. They gather around the home of a dying person and torment them, stealing their remaining years of life for t
stories.title: Raven Mocker (Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï) (Cherokee)

stories.name: Raven Pulls the Salmon (Tlingit)
stories.excerpt: After Raven brought light to the world and created rivers and lakes, there were still no salmon in the coastal waters. The salmon, herrings, and ooligans were kept in a magical house in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, where they spawned without ever coming to shore. Only rich chiefs could paddle out to catch them, lea
stories.title: Raven Pulls the Salmon (Tlingit)

stories.name: Raven Steals the Light (Tlingit - Yeil)
stories.excerpt: In the Tlingit version of this foundational myth, Yeil (Raven) was born as the son of Kit-ka'ositiyi-qâ and was instructed and trained in every way to make a world. At that time there was no light in the world, but Raven knew that far up the Nass River was a large house where a chief kept light just for himself. Raven
stories.title: Raven Steals the Light (Tlingit - Yeil)

stories.name: Raven Steals the Sun (Nuu-chah-nulth)
stories.excerpt: In the Nuu-chah-nulth version of this foundational myth, there was a time before sunlight when light was kept securely in a box guarded by a great chief sometimes called the Old Fisherman. Raven wanted this light and attempted various methods to release it. He transformed himself into a floating leaf that ended up in t
stories.title: Raven Steals the Sun (Nuu-chah-nulth)

stories.name: Raven Steals the Sun, Moon, and Stars (Haida)
stories.excerpt: In the time before light, Raven (Nang Kilslas) was tired of living in darkness. He discovered an old chief who kept all the light of the universe hidden in a nested set of five boxes. Raven transformed himself into a hemlock needle and dropped into the river where the chief's daughter came to drink. She swallowed the n
stories.title: Raven Steals the Sun, Moon, and Stars (Haida)

stories.name: Raven the Creator (Nivkh Tradition)
stories.excerpt: The Nivkh creation myth centered on the Raven, a central figure shared with neighboring Chukchi and Koryak traditions. In Nivkh mythology, the Raven (known as Kurka or similar names) created the world by diving into the primordial sea and bringing up earth on his beak. He shaped the land of Sakhalin Island and the Amur
stories.title: Raven the Creator (Nivkh Tradition)

stories.name: Raven Turns Himself into a Woman (Tlingit)
stories.excerpt: Having lost his wife Fog Woman, Raven decided to marry again so people would look after him. Rather than finding a good wife, he turned himself into a woman and married a man from the Killerwhale people. As a wife, Raven was lazy and deceitful — she stole from the Killerwhale people. Eventually she decided to kill her
stories.title: Raven Turns Himself into a Woman (Tlingit)

stories.name: Restoration of the Sun and Moon
stories.excerpt: Through a combination of trickery, persistence, and magical songs, Wainamoinen and his companions manage to deceive Louhi into releasing the sun and moon, returning light and life to the world.
stories.title: Restoration of the Sun and Moon

stories.name: Rich Peter the Pedlar
stories.excerpt: Peter, a humble pedlar, discovers a way to acquire wealth through honest trade and a touch of serendipity. The story follows his ascent from poverty to riches and the lessons he learns about the true value of money and friendship.
stories.title: Rich Peter the Pedlar

stories.name: Rinkusteinar (The Rocking Stones of Oyndarfjørður)
stories.excerpt: Two large boulders rest at the shore near Oyndarfjørður, constantly rocking back and forth with the rhythm of the waves. Legend says that a local sorceress (witch) saw pirate ships approaching her village after they had already attacked Fuglafjørður, robbing and killing. She rushed to the shore and cast a spell, transf
stories.title: Rinkusteinar (The Rocking Stones of Oyndarfjørður)

stories.name: Risin og Kellingin (The Giant and the Witch)
stories.excerpt: Two giant sea stacks off the northern coast of Eysturoy, near Eiði. Legend says that giants in Iceland grew envious of the Faroe Islands and sent a giant and his wife (a witch) to drag the islands back to Iceland. The giant stood in the sea while the witch climbed the mountain Eiðiskollur with a heavy rope to tie the i
stories.title: Risin og Kellingin (The Giant and the Witch)

stories.name: River Mumma and the Golden Table
stories.excerpt: River Mumma is a female water spirit who guards the sources of Jamaica's rivers. She is sometimes seen sitting by the river, combing her long hair with a golden comb, leaving the comb on rocks to entice victims whom she then draws into the water. Associated with her is the Legend of the Golden Table: a table of pure go
stories.title: River Mumma and the Golden Table

stories.name: Robin and Blue-Jay (Chinook)
stories.excerpt: Blue Jay and Robin, two brothers, were hungry. Blue Jay called a large fish (the sleeper) to come ashore through trickery and speared it. When they returned home, Robin asked for the tail, breast, and head, making Blue Jay angry. He said that the Q!têê'nse (a supernatural monster) would eat the fish instead. Robin crie
stories.title: Robin and Blue-Jay (Chinook)

stories.name: Robin Hood
stories.excerpt: In the days when King Richard the Lionheart was away fighting in the Crusades and his brother Prince John ruled England with greed and cruelty, a young man from Locksley in Nottinghamshire was forced into the greenwood.
stories.title: Robin Hood

stories.name: Roro Jonggrang and the Legend of Prambanan Temple
stories.excerpt: A Javanese legend explaining the origin of Prambanan Temple. Bandung Bondowoso, a powerful prince with supernatural abilities and an army of invisible genies, fell in love with Princess Roro Jonggrang. When she rejected his proposal, he attacked her father's kingdom and conquered it. Forced to consider marriage, Roro J
stories.title: Roro Jonggrang and the Legend of Prambanan Temple

stories.name: Rostam and Sohrab
stories.excerpt: The most famous tragedy of the Persian Shahnameh. Rostam, Iran's greatest hero, travels to Samangan where he marries Princess Tahmineh. He returns to Iran, leaving her pregnant with Sohrab. Years later, Sohrab, now Turan's mightiest warrior, leads an army against Iran, hoping to find his father. Unaware of each other's
stories.title: Rostam and Sohrab

stories.name: Rostam's Seven Trials (Haft Khan-e Rostam)
stories.excerpt: To rescue King Kay Kavus, captured by the White Demon (Div-e Sepid) in Mazandaran, Rostam undertakes seven impossible labors: (1) Killing Rakhsh's attacker, a ferocious lion; (2) Surviving a waterless desert with his horse Rakhsh; (3) Slaying a monstrous dragon; (4) Killing a powerful witch through divine discernment;
stories.title: Rostam's Seven Trials (Haft Khan-e Rostam)

stories.name: Rounce: The Forest Keeper
stories.excerpt: A timber cutter who defies the old prohibition against felling trees in the deep forest encounters the Rounce, a nature spirit that punishes those who take more than they need and rewards those who leave offerings of respect.
stories.title: Rounce: The Forest Keeper

stories.name: Rounces: The Night Riders
stories.excerpt: A fisherman who mocks his grandmother's warnings about the Rounces discovers that the spirit-animals which ride the sleeping have their own terrible logic, and that the paralysis they bring is not cruelty but a test of the soul.
stories.title: Rounces: The Night Riders

stories.name: Ruwa and the Sacred Mountain Kilimanjaro
stories.excerpt: Ruwa, the supreme god of the Chaga people, dwells upon the snow-capped peak of Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa. According to Chaga cosmology, Ruwa is associated with the sun and resides in the sky alongside his consort, the moon. From his celestial throne on Kibo peak, Ruwa watches over the Chaga people and
stories.title: Ruwa and the Sacred Mountain Kilimanjaro

stories.name: Ryangombe and the Fire of the Hills
stories.excerpt: Ryangombe, the great hero of the Rwandan hills, descends into the caverns beneath Mount Muhabura to reclaim the stolen fire that a jealous spirit has hidden from the people.
stories.title: Ryangombe and the Fire of the Hills

stories.name: Rávga: The Undead Sea Creature
stories.excerpt: Rávga is an undead sea creature in Sámi folklore, the soul of a drowned person whose body was never found and properly buried. It appears as a long-haired, large-mouthed creature in human form. It harasses sailors and people on shore by calling out and imitating the speech of the living. It can be driven away by readin
stories.title: Rávga: The Undead Sea Creature

stories.name: Sadko and the Sea King
stories.excerpt: A gusli player from Novgorod is pulled beneath Lake Ilmen by the Sea King, who demands a song in exchange for safe return and a fortune in sea-stone.
stories.title: Sadko and the Sea King

stories.name: Saint George and the Dragon
stories.excerpt: A Roman soldier of unwavering faith slays a terrifying dragon to save a princess and leads a city toward a new spiritual awakening.
stories.title: Saint George and the Dragon

stories.name: Samodiva: The Wood Nymphs of the Bulgarian Mountains
stories.excerpt: Eternal beautiful forest spirits lure men to dance until they die in the mountains of Bulgaria.
stories.title: Samodiva: The Wood Nymphs of the Bulgarian Mountains

stories.name: Samudra Manthan — The Churning of the Ocean
stories.excerpt: After sage Durvasa cursed Indra and the gods to lose all their strength, the demons (asuras) took over the universe. Lord Vishnu advised the gods to churn the Ocean of Milk with the demons to obtain amrita, the nectar of immortality. They used Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope. Howeve
stories.title: Samudra Manthan — The Churning of the Ocean

stories.name: Sang Kancil and the Crocodile
stories.excerpt: The most famous fable from the Malay Archipelago features Sang Kancil, the clever mouse-deer, outsmarting a river full of hungry crocodiles. Wanting to cross the river to reach the fruit trees on the other side, Kancil tells the crocodiles that the king has ordered a headcount of all crocodiles, instructing them to lin
stories.title: Sang Kancil and the Crocodile

stories.name: Sang-ngag of the Hidden Temple
stories.excerpt: A dragon named Sang-ngag guards a temple that appears only between breaths, and a young monk who has failed three times learns that the temple's real treasure is not what is inside it, but what it costs to reach it.
stories.title: Sang-ngag of the Hidden Temple

stories.name: Sangkuriang and Mount Tangkuban Perahu
stories.excerpt: A Sundanese legend from West Java telling of Sangkuriang, a young man who unknowingly falls in love with his mother Dayang Sumbi, a goddess-blessed princess who remains eternally young. When Dayang Sumbi recognizes her son by a scar, she sets impossible tasks to prevent their marriage: he must dam the Citarum River and
stories.title: Sangkuriang and Mount Tangkuban Perahu

stories.name: Santa Muerte — Holy Death
stories.excerpt: Santa Muerte (Holy Death or Saint Death) is a female folk saint and personification of death venerated primarily in Mexico and the US Southwest, with an estimated 12 million followers worldwide. She is depicted as a female skeleton wearing a long robe and carrying a scythe and a globe. Her origins blend pre-Columbian d
stories.title: Santa Muerte — Holy Death

stories.name: Santhal Creation Myth — The World Born from Water
stories.excerpt: The Santhal tribe, one of India's largest Adivasi communities, tells that in the beginning, the world was covered entirely with water. The supreme being Thakur Jiu (or Singbonga) sent the divine crow Marangbonga to find earth. The crow tried but found only water. Next, a tortoise and a crab attempted but failed. Finall
stories.title: Santhal Creation Myth — The World Born from Water

stories.name: Saraswati
stories.excerpt: In the deep waters of Scotland's lochs, where the surface is black as ink and the bottom has never been touched by human hands, there lives a creature more terrifying than any sea monster.
stories.title: Saraswati

stories.name: Sassi Punnun — Searching Across the Desert
stories.excerpt: Sassi, a princess born to the king of Bhambore but abandoned at birth due to an astrological prophecy, was raised by a washerman. She grew into a woman of extraordinary beauty. Hearing of her, Punnun, a Baloch prince, traveled to Bhambore and fell in love with her at first sight. They married in secret, but Punnun's je
stories.title: Sassi Punnun — Searching Across the Desert

stories.name: Savitri and Satyavan — Love That Conquered Death
stories.excerpt: Princess Savitri chose to marry Satyavan despite the sage Narada's warning that he was destined to die within a year. On the fated day, Yama, the god of death, came to claim Satyavan's soul. As Yama carried the soul away, Savitri followed him through the wilderness. Impressed by her devotion, Yama granted her three boo
stories.title: Savitri and Satyavan — Love That Conquered Death

stories.name: Scheherazade
stories.excerpt: The chronicles of the Sassanian kings tell of a monarch named Shahryar, who ruled an empire stretching from India to China.
stories.title: Scheherazade

stories.name: Sea Maid, the Monacan Siren
stories.excerpt: A beautiful siren of the French Riviera, the Sea Maid of Monaco lures sailors with her enchanting song beneath the waves.
stories.title: Sea Maid, the Monacan Siren

stories.name: Selkie
stories.excerpt: On the rocky coasts of the Orkney and Shetland Islands, where the sea is never far and the storms come fierce in winter, there are tales of the Selkies—the seal folk, who can shed their skin and walk on land as humans.
stories.title: Selkie

stories.name: Semetey: The Son of Manas
stories.excerpt: After Manas's death, his treacherous younger brothers Abyke and Bobosh seized power and tried to kill Manas's son Semetey. Kanykey, Manas's widow, escaped with the infant Semetey to Bukhara, where her father ruled as khan. Semetey grew up unaware of his heritage until his mother revealed his identity. He returned to th
stories.title: Semetey: The Son of Manas

stories.name: Seminole Creation: Breathmaker and the Earth (Seminole)
stories.excerpt: The Seminole creation story begins with Breathmaker, the great Creator god, who existed before anything else. Breathmaker created the earth and all living things. In the Seminole version of the Muskogean creation tradition, the earth was formed from mud brought up from the primordial waters, similar to the Cherokee sto
stories.title: Seminole Creation: Breathmaker and the Earth (Seminole)

stories.name: Serpan of the Deep Channel
stories.excerpt: A serpent-like creature haunts the deep channel between two islands, dragging boats beneath the waves when sailors fail to toss a handful of salt into the sea.
stories.title: Serpan of the Deep Channel

stories.name: Shahmaran, Queen of Serpents
stories.excerpt: A young man discovers Shahmaran, the serpent queen who rules a hidden kingdom beneath the earth, and must choose between the world above and the world below.
stories.title: Shahmaran, Queen of Serpents

stories.name: Shahmaran: The Serpent Queen of Turkey
stories.excerpt: A half-woman half-serpent queen rules an underground kingdom of snakes in Anatolian legend.
stories.title: Shahmaran: The Serpent Queen of Turkey

stories.name: Shakuru and Pah: The Sun and Moon
stories.excerpt: Shakuru (the Sun) and Pah (the Moon) were the last of all gods placed in the heavens by Tirawa. They are of relatively minor standing in Skidi Pawnee mythology compared to the star gods. The Sun and Moon produced a son, a boy who was placed on Earth to be the ancestor of the Pawnee people. The Sun is associated with wa
stories.title: Shakuru and Pah: The Sun and Moon

stories.name: Shango and the Dual Death (Yoruba)
stories.excerpt: Shango was the fourth king of Oyo who deified himself as the god of thunder and lightning. According to legend, Shango was a powerful but tyrannical ruler who accidentally destroyed his own palace with lightning when his enemies provoked him. Overcome with grief and shame, he fled Oyo and hanged himself from an ayan tr
stories.title: Shango and the Dual Death (Yoruba)

stories.name: Shir the Holy Ram
stories.excerpt: In the ages before the Ark came to rest on Ararat, a sacred ram carried the seeds of all living things through the floodwaters, guided by the light between its horns.
stories.title: Shir the Holy Ram

stories.name: Shiva
stories.excerpt: In the vast pantheon of Hindu deities, no figure is more complex, more paradoxical, or more awe-inspiring than Shiva.
stories.title: Shiva

stories.name: Shortshanks
stories.excerpt: A small boy named Shortshanks is underestimated by everyone due to his size. He embarks on a journey where he uses his exceptional cunning to outwit several ogres and trolls, eventually winning the hand of a princess and proving that size is no measure of capability.
stories.title: Shortshanks

stories.name: Shteli Kherkher, the Mountain Guardian
stories.excerpt: A nature spirit of the Hindu Kush mountains who protects the wild animals and punishes hunters who kill for sport.
stories.title: Shteli Kherkher, the Mountain Guardian

stories.name: Shurale the Forest Spirit
stories.excerpt: Shurale is the most famous mythological creature in Tatar folklore — a forest spirit depicted as a hairy man with a horn on his forehead, one eye, and extremely long fingers. Shurale lures travelers into the forest, rides their horses at night, and tickles his victims to death. The most famous story, immortalized by Ta
stories.title: Shurale the Forest Spirit

stories.name: Shuten-Doji
stories.excerpt: The sake-stealing demon who terrorized Kyoto until defeated by the hero Minamoto no Yorimitsu.
stories.title: Shuten-Doji

stories.name: Si Bungsu and the Seven Brothers
stories.excerpt: A traditional Bruneian folktale about the youngest of seven brothers who was underestimated and mistreated by his six elder siblings. While the elder brothers were strong, skilled, and proud, Si Bungsu (meaning 'the youngest') was gentle, humble, and assigned the most menial tasks. When the Sultan announced a challenge
stories.title: Si Bungsu and the Seven Brothers

stories.name: Si Tanggang (The Unfilial Son)
stories.excerpt: A Malaysian folktale from Negeri Sembilan closely related to the Indonesian Malin Kundang. Tanggang, the son of a poor fisherman, leaves his mother to seek fortune overseas. After becoming a wealthy captain with a fine ship, he returns to his village. His elderly mother, overjoyed, wades into the water to greet him, bu
stories.title: Si Tanggang (The Unfilial Son)

stories.name: Si'lat of the Old City
stories.excerpt: A variant of the Si'lat said to haunt the ancient streets of Jerusalem, preying on those who stray from the path of righteousness.
stories.title: Si'lat of the Old City

stories.name: Si'lat, the Femme Fatale of the Levant
stories.excerpt: A beautiful female jinn who seduces men and leads them to their doom, a cautionary figure in Palestinian folklore.
stories.title: Si'lat, the Femme Fatale of the Levant

stories.name: Sickness Spirits and the Noaidi's Healing
stories.excerpt: A collection of legends about sickness spirits that cause disease. Illness was understood spiritually—either as soul-loss, as punishment for broken taboos, or as an attack by a hostile noaidi. The noaidi would use his drum to diagnose the cause, then journey in trance to retrieve the lost soul or confront the malevolen
stories.title: Sickness Spirits and the Noaidi's Healing

stories.name: Sikakokuh and the Hunting Dog
stories.excerpt: A Hopi story about a boy named Sikakokuh who had a remarkable hunting dog. The dog was no ordinary animal but possessed spiritual power, able to track game without fail and communicate with its master. Sikakokuh's success as a hunter made others jealous. Through the dog's guidance, Sikakokuh learned the proper rituals
stories.title: Sikakokuh and the Hunting Dog

stories.name: Silamaka and Pullori: The Fulani Epic Heroes
stories.excerpt: The Fulani epic of Silamaka and Pullori recounts the adventures of two bound-by-friendship heroes from the Macina region of Mali. Silamaka, the saber-wielding warrior, is challenged to prove his temerity against the mighty Bambara king Da Monzon Diarra. He consults a geomancer who tells him that to become invulnerable,
stories.title: Silamaka and Pullori: The Fulani Epic Heroes

stories.name: Silverwhite and Lillwacker
stories.excerpt: Two faithful brothers journey to rescue their sister from a sea troll who killed their father, overcoming enchanted forests, talking animals, and magical trials through unbreakable brotherly loyalty. The tale draws on an ancient Indo-Germanic cycle of faithful brothers.
stories.title: Silverwhite and Lillwacker

stories.name: Simbi: The River Spirits of the Kongo
stories.excerpt: The Simbi are powerful water spirits who inhabit the rivers, streams, and sacred pools of the Kongo region. They are ancient beings who existed before humanity and witnessed the creation of the world. Simbi can appear as beautiful human figures, snakes, or shimmering reflections on the water's surface. They are guardia
stories.title: Simbi: The River Spirits of the Kongo

stories.name: Simurgh and Zal
stories.excerpt: Sam of Zabulistan abandons his albino infant son Zal on Mount Alborz, ashamed of his white hair. The mythical bird Simurgh, a wise, benevolent creature resembling a giant dog-bird, finds the baby and raises him as her own. Zal grows into a handsome, powerful youth. Sam has a dream of reproach and seeks forgiveness. Zal
stories.title: Simurgh and Zal

stories.name: Sina and the Eel (Origin of the Coconut)
stories.excerpt: The beautiful maiden Sina drew water from a pool where she discovered a young eel. She took it home as a pet and named it Tuna. The eel grew rapidly, outgrowing bowls, then pools, and becoming unnaturally large. Wherever Sina bathed, the eel appeared and encircled her. Frightened, she fled across multiple islands, but
stories.title: Sina and the Eel (Origin of the Coconut)

stories.name: Sinbad the Sailor (Seven Voyages)
stories.excerpt: A wealthy Baghdad merchant known as Sinbad the Sailor recounts his seven extraordinary voyages to a poor porter named Sinbad the Landsman. Each voyage brings shipwreck, monstrous creatures (the giant bird Roc, gigantic serpents, whale-islands, cyclopean giants), and fantastic lands. Sinbad outwits cannibals, escapes th
stories.title: Sinbad the Sailor (Seven Voyages)

stories.name: Sint-Holo: The Horned Serpent (Chickasaw)
stories.excerpt: Sint-Holo is a dragon-like horned serpent from Chickasaw mythology. This powerful water monster dwells in deep rivers, lakes, and underground springs. Sint-Holo has a serpentine body covered with scales, a horned or antlered head, and possesses supernatural powers. Unlike some malevolent serpents in neighboring tribes'
stories.title: Sint-Holo: The Horned Serpent (Chickasaw)

stories.name: Sinti Lapitta: The Horned Serpent (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: Sinti Lapitta is a great horned serpent from Choctaw mythology, a water monster with immense power. Described as a giant snake with a head like a panther or with two horns on its head, it dwells in deep rivers, lakes, and water holes. Unlike the malevolent horned serpents of some tribes, Sinti Lapitta was sometimes kno
stories.title: Sinti Lapitta: The Horned Serpent (Choctaw)

stories.name: Sir Birre and the Trolls
stories.excerpt: Sir Birre lives on a farm below the mountain where two trolls, Jock and Turing, dwell. When his sweetheart Tinka is kidnapped by the troll Domp-Domp-Dubbeldomp, Birre must ask Jock and Turing for help. In exchange, he teaches them to build a house and smelt iron. The trolls rescue Tinka, who traveled in Turing's furry
stories.title: Sir Birre and the Trolls

stories.name: Sir Olof and the Elves
stories.excerpt: A young knight riding to his wedding encounters the elf queen in the forest. She offers him her love, but he refuses — and her curse leads to tragedy on his wedding day.
stories.title: Sir Olof and the Elves

stories.name: Sisimito of the Blue Hole
stories.excerpt: A Garifuna fisherman glimpses the Sisimito near the Great Blue Hole and learns that some creatures prefer the shadows between what is real and what is remembered.
stories.title: Sisimito of the Blue Hole

stories.name: Sisiutl the Double-Headed Serpent (Kwakwaka'wakw)
stories.excerpt: The Sisiutl is a fearsome three-headed sea serpent whose glance can turn an adversary into stone. Typically depicted as a double-headed serpent with a central humanoid face representing Baxbaxwalanuksiwe' or Komokwa, it has horned heads, protruding tongues, and spiral noses that indicate supernatural power. The Sisiutl
stories.title: Sisiutl the Double-Headed Serpent (Kwakwaka'wakw)

stories.name: Sita: The Abducted Queen
stories.excerpt: In the ancient city of Ayodhya, Prince Rama was the beloved heir to the throne—brave, virtuous, and beloved by all.
stories.title: Sita: The Abducted Queen

stories.name: Siyavash and Sudabeh
stories.excerpt: Prince Siyavash, son of Kay Kavus, rejects the seductive advances of his stepmother Sudabeh. To prove his innocence, he rides through a mountain of fire and emerges unscathed. Despite this vindication, he cannot remain in Iran and voluntarily exiles himself to Turan, where King Afrasiab initially welcomes him and gives
stories.title: Siyavash and Sudabeh

stories.name: Skunk Outwits Coyote
stories.excerpt: Coyote came upon a prairie dog village and decided to catch himself a meal. He blocked all the holes except one and waited with his mouth open at the entrance. But Skunk saw what Coyote was doing and decided to teach him a lesson. Skunk approached Coyote and asked what he was doing. Coyote explained his plan, and Skunk
stories.title: Skunk Outwits Coyote

stories.name: Sleeping Beauty
stories.excerpt: The Erl-King is the darkest fairy tale that the Brothers Grimm collected, a poem of terror that has haunted German children for centuries.
stories.title: Sleeping Beauty

stories.name: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
stories.excerpt: A beautiful princess escapes her jealous stepmother-queen and finds refuge with seven dwarfs. The queen tricks her with a poisoned apple, but a prince's kiss awakens her.
stories.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs

stories.name: Snæbjørn (Snow Bear of Suðuroy)
stories.excerpt: Snæbjørn was a powerful, brave, and proud servant working for a wealthy farmer in Hvalba on Suðuroy. He was secretly in love with a milkmaid. When a Dutch ship illegally traded luxury goods, Snæbjørn bought four silk scarves for her. The judge sentenced him to four years imprisonment on Bremerholm in Denmark for this c
stories.title: Snæbjørn (Snow Bear of Suðuroy)

stories.name: Sodani the Great Shaman
stories.excerpt: The Evenki epic tale of Sodani, the most powerful shaman who ever lived, who could journey between the Upper, Middle, and Lower Worlds. The story follows Sodani's initiation by spirits, his epic journey to the Lower World to retrieve a lost soul, and his battle against hostile spirits that threaten the Evenki people. H
stories.title: Sodani the Great Shaman

stories.name: Sohni Mahiwal — Love Across the River
stories.excerpt: Sohni, a beautiful pottery-maker's daughter, fell in love with Izzat Baig (later called Mahiwal), a wealthy merchant from another land who had come to trade. When her family married her to another man, Sohni still swam each night across the Chenab River using an earthenware pot as a float to reach her beloved Mahiwal o
stories.title: Sohni Mahiwal — Love Across the River

stories.name: Sohni Mahiwal: The Tragic Lovers of Sindh
stories.excerpt: A potter's daughter drowns crossing a river to meet her lover in one of South Asia's greatest love stories.
stories.title: Sohni Mahiwal: The Tragic Lovers of Sindh

stories.name: Son Tinh and Thuy Tinh
stories.excerpt: In the mountains of Japan, where the bamboo forests rustle with secrets and the old Shinto shrines stand weathered by centuries of rain, there lives a yokai who is neither malevolent nor kind.
stories.title: Son Tinh and Thuy Tinh

stories.name: Songa Raudhat and the Lost Children
stories.excerpt: When children vanish into the highland mist above Moroni, it is Songa Raudhat who leads them astray, and only the call to prayer can guide them home again.
stories.title: Songa Raudhat and the Lost Children

stories.name: Songtsen Gampo and the Founding of Tibet
stories.excerpt: The semi-legendary account of King Songtsen Gampo (7th century CE), the founder of the Tibetan Empire and the first Dharma King. According to Tibetan tradition, he was an emanation of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, sent to bring civilization and Buddhism to the Tibetan people. He built the Jokhang Temple in Lhasa, su
stories.title: Songtsen Gampo and the Founding of Tibet

stories.name: Soria Moria Castle
stories.excerpt: Halvor, a boy known for his laziness, leaves home to see the world. He travels to the legendary Soria Moria Castle, where he defeats three trolls and rescues three princesses, returning home with immense wealth and the love of the youngest princess.
stories.title: Soria Moria Castle

stories.name: Soucouyant, the Antiguan Fireball
stories.excerpt: A fearsome vampire of the Caribbean, the Soucouyant sheds her skin by night and flies as a fireball to suck the blood of her victims.
stories.title: Soucouyant, the Antiguan Fireball

stories.name: Soucouyant: The Fire in the Dark
stories.excerpt: A young woman who dismisses the old protective rituals of salt and garlic discovers the Soucouyant is real when she sees a ball of fire cross the yard and finds her baby's cribside stained with ash.
stories.title: Soucouyant: The Fire in the Dark

stories.name: Soucouyant: The Fireball Hag of the Caribbean
stories.excerpt: An old woman sheds her skin at night to become a ball of fire that hunts the blood of the living.
stories.title: Soucouyant: The Fireball Hag of the Caribbean

stories.name: Spearfinger (U'tlun'ta): The Stone Witch (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: Spearfinger, also known as Nûñ'yunu'ï or 'Stone-dress,' is a fearsome Cherokee monster and witch who lives along the eastern side of Tennessee and western North Carolina. She has a long, sharp forefinger on her right hand like a spear or obsidian knife, which she uses to cut open her victims. She wears a dress made of
stories.title: Spearfinger (U'tlun'ta): The Stone Witch (Cherokee)

stories.name: Sphinx
stories.excerpt: The Sphinx is ancient—so ancient that she predates the pyramids themselves. Centers on Sphinx, of royal power and wisdom in Egypt; symbol of dangerous knowledge in Greece..
stories.title: Sphinx

stories.name: Spider Woman and the Origin of Weaving
stories.excerpt: In the Third World of Navajo tradition, Spider Woman and Spider Man, who lived near the Crossing of the Waters, taught the people the art of weaving. Spider Man showed them how to shape a spindle wheel and spin cotton thread from planted cotton seeds. First Woman declared that spinning must be done toward the body to a
stories.title: Spider Woman and the Origin of Weaving

stories.name: Splinter Foot Girl
stories.excerpt: A childless Arapaho woman found a splinter embedded in her foot. To her amazement, the splinter grew and transformed into a baby girl. The girl grew rapidly and possessed supernatural abilities. She could communicate with animals and had the power to heal. She brought good fortune to her family and community, helping t
stories.title: Splinter Foot Girl

stories.name: Sri Thanonchai: The Royal Trickster
stories.excerpt: Sri Thanonchai is the legendary trickster figure in Thai folklore, a clever and witty commoner who used his sharp intellect to outsmart kings, nobles, and corrupt officials. Born with extraordinary cleverness, Sri Thanonchai could talk his way out of any situation and often turned the tables on those in power who sough
stories.title: Sri Thanonchai: The Royal Trickster

stories.name: St. Christopher and the Dog-Headed Men
stories.excerpt: St. Christopher, depicted with the head of a dog in ancient Vatican iconography, encounters the Cynocephali and discovers they possess a faith purer than that of many Christians.
stories.title: St. Christopher and the Dog-Headed Men

stories.name: St. Joseph in the Forest
stories.excerpt: An Austrian folk tale where St. Joseph tests three sisters by appearing as a beggar. Two sisters are cruel and are punished; the kind youngest is rewarded with a blessed life.
stories.title: St. Joseph in the Forest

stories.name: St. Peter and the Two Women
stories.excerpt: St. Peter, disguised as a poor traveler, is turned away by a rich farmer's wife but welcomed by a poor widow. He blesses the widow so that whatever she starts doing she continues all day—she measures cloth that grows endlessly and becomes wealthy. The greedy rich woman demands the same blessing but begins pumping water
stories.title: St. Peter and the Two Women

stories.name: Stagolee in Hell (Stagolee vs. the Devil)
stories.excerpt: After Stagolee was hanged for murder, he arrived at the gates of Hell, still wearing his Stetson hat and carrying his .44 pistol. When the Devil tried to send him to his eternal punishment, Stagolee refused to submit. He pulled his pistol and challenged the Devil himself. The Devil, for all his power, found he could no
stories.title: Stagolee in Hell (Stagolee vs. the Devil)

stories.name: Stagolee Shoots Billy Lyons
stories.excerpt: On Christmas night, 1895, in a St. Louis saloon, the notorious bad-man Stagolee (based on historical figure Lee Shelton) shot William 'Billy' Lyons after a dispute. In the folk tradition, the argument began when Billy Lyons snatched Stagolee's prized Stetson hat from his head and refused to return it. Stagolee warned h
stories.title: Stagolee Shoots Billy Lyons

stories.name: Stagolee's Funeral
stories.excerpt: The folk ballad describes Stagolee's funeral as an event unlike any before seen. Thousands of people came from miles around to see the baddest man who ever lived laid to rest. A procession of mourners stretched for blocks—the women weeping, the men silent and respectful. His coffin was reportedly so fine it cost more t
stories.title: Stagolee's Funeral

stories.name: Stalo and Kauras
stories.excerpt: This tale originates from the Sami people of northern Sweden (Lapland) and features a Stalo — a giant, man-eating troll-like creature from Sami folklore. Stalo is described as a large, evil being who wears impenetrable black iron clothing, hunts and devours people and reindeer, and terrorizes the region. He is rich, po
stories.title: Stalo and Kauras

stories.name: Starkad and Bale
stories.excerpt: The legendary hero Starkad — raised by Odin himself and the greatest warrior of the North — teams up with the sly trickster Bale to exact revenge through feats of impossible strength and clever deception against a treacherous king.
stories.title: Starkad and Bale

stories.name: Stikini: The Owl Witches (Seminole)
stories.excerpt: Stikini are dreaded owl-witches from Seminole folklore. During the day, Stikini appear as ordinary humans, but at night they transform into monstrous owls with supernatural powers. They are known to prey on humans, particularly those who are alone in the forest at night. A Stikini can be identified by its bloodshot eye
stories.title: Stikini: The Owl Witches (Seminole)

stories.name: Stompe Pilt
stories.excerpt: A giant named Stompe Pilt terrorizes a parish until a brave little shepherd boy challenges him with a sling and a bag of tricks, proving that size is no match for wit. The tale is an entertaining parody of David and Goliath.
stories.title: Stompe Pilt

stories.name: Stone Coat (Nûñ'yunu'ï): The Rock Giants (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: Stone Coat, also called Nûñ'yunu'ï, is a race of giant beings covered in stone-like skin that makes them nearly invulnerable. They dwell in the remote mountains and caves of Cherokee territory. These rock giants are cannibalistic and prey upon humans who venture too far into their domain. They are incredibly strong, ca
stories.title: Stone Coat (Nûñ'yunu'ï): The Rock Giants (Cherokee)

stories.name: Storsjöodjuret
stories.excerpt: A mysterious serpentine creature haunts the depths of Lake Storsjön in Sweden, appearing as a spectral guardian of the water.
stories.title: Storsjöodjuret

stories.name: Strigoi, the Undead of the Carpathians
stories.excerpt: Restless spirits of the dead who rise from their graves to plague the living, the Strigoi are among the most feared creatures in Moldovan folklore.
stories.title: Strigoi, the Undead of the Carpathians

stories.name: Strigoi: The Undead Spirits of Romania
stories.excerpt: Restless spirits rise from their graves to prey on the living in the land of Dracula.
stories.title: Strigoi: The Undead Spirits of Romania

stories.name: Stuorra-Jouni and the Stállu on Áiligas Fell
stories.excerpt: A legend from Talvadas on the Teno River. Stuorra-Jouni ('Big Jouni') is a legendary Sámi proto-hero, a wild deer hunter and storyteller. A noaidi from Varanger sent a Stállu to attack Jouni. Jouni met the Stállu on Áiligas fell and they fought according to the ritual pattern. The Stállu escaped on skis, leaving only i
stories.title: Stuorra-Jouni and the Stállu on Áiligas Fell

stories.name: Stállo and Kauras
stories.excerpt: The classic Sámi Stállo tale. The evil giant Stállo lived in Storfjellet and demanded reindeer sacrifices from the Sámi. He controlled all predators and would kill reindeer if not appeased. The brave Sámi boy Kauras decides to defeat him. After a head-butting contest where Kauras tricks Stállo by hiding his head in a h
stories.title: Stállo and Kauras

stories.name: Su Anasi: The Water Mother
stories.excerpt: Su Anasi ('Mother of Water') is the Tatar water spirit, analogous to the Russian rusalka but with distinct Tatar characteristics. Long-haired and beautiful, she lives in rivers and lakes, with a golden comb that she uses to brush her hair while sitting on riverbanks. The most famous version, retold by poet Gabdulla Tuk
stories.title: Su Anasi: The Water Mother

stories.name: Sufax and the Founding of Tangier
stories.excerpt: In the syncretic mythology that blends Berber, Greek, and Phoenician traditions, Sufax was the son of the Greek hero Heracles (Hercules) and Tinge, the Berber earth goddess. According to the legend, Heracles performed one of his labors in North Africa, where he met and married Tinge. Their son Sufax founded the city of
stories.title: Sufax and the Founding of Tangier

stories.name: Sumpurnis, the Shapeshifter of the Birch Forest
stories.excerpt: Sumpurnis, a terrifying shapeshifter wrapped in shaggy fur, roams the birch forests of Latvia, shifting form to lure or terrify those who stray from the path.
stories.title: Sumpurnis, the Shapeshifter of the Birch Forest

stories.name: Sun Goat, the Chadian Steppe Sprite
stories.excerpt: A legendary goat-like creature of Chadian folklore, the Sun Goat is a spirit of the Sahel that appears during droughts and leads herds to water.
stories.title: Sun Goat, the Chadian Steppe Sprite

stories.name: Sundew and the Ghosts
stories.excerpt: In the village of Skruväng, deep in the forests of Småland, there lived a girl named Sundew—called sårfot in the old tongue because her grandmother said she was as delicate and as keen as the tiny carnivorous plant that grew in the boggy meadows.
stories.title: Sundew and the Ghosts

stories.name: Sundiata: The Lion King of Mali
stories.excerpt: A disabled prince who was exiled, returns to found the greatest empire in African history—the Mali Empire.
stories.title: Sundiata: The Lion King of Mali

stories.name: Supay, Lord of the Ujku
stories.excerpt: Supay rules the underworld beneath the mountains, and the miners who descend into his domain must leave offerings at the entrance or face his wrath.
stories.title: Supay, Lord of the Ujku

stories.name: Supay, Lord of Uku Pacha
stories.excerpt: The Aymara lord of the underworld Uku Pacha demands tribute from miners who dig too deep, and those who forget his offerings vanish into tunnels that have no end.
stories.title: Supay, Lord of Uku Pacha

stories.name: Swan Maiden
stories.excerpt: A hunter captures a celestial swan maiden by stealing her feather cloak, leading to a marriage built on a secret that eventually reveals the cost of forced love.
stories.title: Swan Maiden

stories.name: Sweet Medicine and the Four Sacred Arrows
stories.excerpt: Sweet Medicine (Motsé'eóeve) was the great prophet and law-giver of the Cheyenne people. He journeyed to Nóávóse (Bear Butte) in the Black Hills where Ma'heo'o (the Wise One Above) gave him the four sacred arrows—the Maahótse. Two arrows were for hunting, to ensure success in finding buffalo, and two were for warfare,
stories.title: Sweet Medicine and the Four Sacred Arrows

stories.name: Sáráhkká: The Childbirth Goddess
stories.excerpt: Sáráhkká is the most important birth goddess in Sámi mythology, daughter of Máttaráhkká. She lives under the hearth of the goahti. She places the fetus in the woman's womb. She protects both human women and reindeer during birth. Before birth, women drank 'Sáráhkká's booze' and after, ate 'Sáráhkká's porridge.' Wood wa
stories.title: Sáráhkká: The Childbirth Goddess

stories.name: Símun of Kirkjubøur (Hulda-Símun and the Hidden Woman)
stories.excerpt: Símun Símunarson, nicknamed Hulda-Símun or Troll-Símun, was a massive farmer at Kirkjubøur on Streymoy. A hulduman (hidden woman) lived on Kirkjubøur Felltop. The legend tells how Símun was kidnapped by the Huldufólk and taken to the cliffs near Kirkjubøur. After his encounter with the Hidden People, the Huldufólk were
stories.title: Símun of Kirkjubøur (Hulda-Símun and the Hidden Woman)

stories.name: Ta'aroa Creates the World from His Shell
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, Ta'aroa, the supreme creator god of Tahiti, existed alone inside a great shell called Rumia, spinning through the endless void. Bored with his solitude, he shook himself and cracked the shell open. He threw pieces of shell outward to form the rocks, sand, and foundation of the world. From his backbone
stories.title: Ta'aroa Creates the World from His Shell

stories.name: Tabaldak Creates Glooscap and Malsumis
stories.excerpt: In Abenaki tradition, the Great Spirit Tabaldak first created the world and all the people. When he finished making humans, he wiped the dust from his hands, and from this divine dust were born twin brothers — Glooscap and Malsumis. Glooscap was given the power to create a good world, full of kind animals, sweet fruits
stories.title: Tabaldak Creates Glooscap and Malsumis

stories.name: Taema and Tilafaiga: The Origin of Tattooing
stories.excerpt: The twin sisters Taema and Tilafaiga, divine daughters of the god Tagaloa, journeyed from Fiji to Samoa carrying the sacred art of tattooing. They swam across the ocean holding a basket containing the tools and patterns for tatau. As they approached the Samoan shore, they began singing 'Fafafofoga o le tama' ('The tatt
stories.title: Taema and Tilafaiga: The Origin of Tattooing

stories.name: Tagaloa Creates the Samoan Islands
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, only Tagaloa existed in the heavens above the endless waters. He looked down and decided to create a place to rest. He formed a great rock called Manu'atele, then divided it into pieces that became the stepping stones of the Pacific. The largest pieces became the islands of Savai'i and Upolu, while sm
stories.title: Tagaloa Creates the Samoan Islands

stories.name: Tagaro and Suqe-Matua: The Creation of Good and Evil
stories.excerpt: On Ambae Island in Vanuatu, the culture hero Tagaro is a creator figure pitted against his twelfth brother Suqe-matua. Tagaro and Suqe-matua shared the work of creation, but whatever Suqe-matua did was wrong. They always disagreed, but the word of Tagaro always prevailed. Tagaro created useful plants, gentle animals, a
stories.title: Tagaro and Suqe-Matua: The Creation of Good and Evil

stories.name: Taktshang Palphug: The Tiger's Nest Monastery
stories.excerpt: Paro Taktshang (Tiger's Nest) is Bhutan's most sacred monastery, clinging to a cliff-face 900 meters above the Paro Valley. In the 8th century, Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava) flew from Tibet to this location riding on the back of Yeshe Tshogyel, his consort, who had transformed herself into a tigress. At the cave known
stories.title: Taktshang Palphug: The Tiger's Nest Monastery

stories.name: Taleju and the Origin of Kumari Worship
stories.excerpt: Goddess Taleju Bhawani, a fearsome tantric form of Durga, served as the royal tutelary deity of the Malla kings of the Kathmandu Valley. Legend recounts that King Mahendra Malla dreamed of the goddess and built her the Taleju Temple in Kathmandu Durbar Square. The goddess would visit King Jayaprakash Malla nightly to p
stories.title: Taleju and the Origin of Kumari Worship

stories.name: Tales of the Trolls
stories.excerpt: Three short tales of troll encounters: a peasant meets a troll at a spring, a girl is lured into a mountain by a handsome troll, and a farmer outwits a troll who steals his harvest. These tales reflect the Scandinavian belief in _bergtagning_ — being taken into the mountain by trolls.
stories.title: Tales of the Trolls

stories.name: Tam and Cam: The Vietnamese Cinderella
stories.excerpt: Tam and Cam is a classic Vietnamese fairy tale with similarities to Cinderella, though with a distinctly Vietnamese character and a notably darker second half. The story follows Tam, a kind and hardworking girl whose mother dies, leaving her with a cruel stepmother and a lazy, jealous stepsister named Cam. After comple
stories.title: Tam and Cam: The Vietnamese Cinderella

stories.name: Taming the Shrew
stories.excerpt: A comedic and satirical story about a headstrong woman who believes she is superior to all suitors. A clever youth uses unconventional psychological tactics and persistence to win her respect and affection, eventually leading to a harmonious marriage.
stories.title: Taming the Shrew

stories.name: Tangaroa and Tane: The War of Forest and Sea
stories.excerpt: After the separation of Rangi and Papa, furious Tawhirimatea drove his brother Tangaroa, god of the sea, into the ocean depths. Tangaroa's descendants included Ikatere (fish) and Tu-te-wehiwehi (reptiles). When Tane Mahuta, god of the forest, offered shelter to Tu-te-wehiwehi and his reptile children, they abandoned th
stories.title: Tangaroa and Tane: The War of Forest and Sea

stories.name: Tangaroa Creation Myth (Cook Islands)
stories.excerpt: In the Cook Islands version of creation, Vari-ma-te-takere (the primordial mother) lived confined in a narrow space within Avaiki. She plucked pieces from her right side and left side to create six children. The first was Avatea (Vatea), a moon god with the right half of a man and left half of a fish. Avatea married Pa
stories.title: Tangaroa Creation Myth (Cook Islands)

stories.name: Tangiia and Karika Divide Rarotonga
stories.excerpt: Two great warrior chiefs, Tangiia and Karika, both arrived at Rarotonga claiming ownership of the island. They fought fiercely, neither able to defeat the other. Realizing their conflict would destroy the land they sought to rule, they agreed to negotiate. Tangiia and Karika divided Rarotonga between them, establishing
stories.title: Tangiia and Karika Divide Rarotonga

stories.name: Tantal, the Shapeshifter of the Gulf
stories.excerpt: A shape-shifting spirit from Kuwaiti coastal folklore who appears as a beautiful woman to lure sailors to their doom.
stories.title: Tantal, the Shapeshifter of the Gulf

stories.name: Tao and the Mountain
stories.excerpt: In ancient times, during the Warring States period, two great mountains stood between the southern part of Jizhou and the northern bank of the Yellow River.
stories.title: Tao and the Mountain

stories.name: Taotaomo'na, the Guamanian Ancestor Spirit
stories.excerpt: The Taotaomo'na are the spirits of the ancient Chamorro people of Guam who inhabit the jungle and punish those who disrespect the old ways.
stories.title: Taotaomo'na, the Guamanian Ancestor Spirit

stories.name: Tata Duende and the Lost Hunter
stories.excerpt: A hunter who disrespects the deep forest is turned around by Tata Duende, the ancient guardian spirit who protects the wild places of Belize from those who take without giving thanks.
stories.title: Tata Duende and the Lost Hunter

stories.name: Tatar and the Little People
stories.excerpt: In the mountains above the village of Szováta, in the匈牙利 (Hungarian) highlands, there lived a poor orphan boy called Tatar.
stories.title: Tatar and the Little People

stories.name: Tatterhood
stories.excerpt: A girl dressed in rags and underestimated by society possesses profound wisdom and courage. Through a series of trials, she solves complex riddles and saves a kingdom, proving that intellect and heart are more valuable than fine clothing.
stories.title: Tatterhood

stories.name: Tawa Creates the Worlds
stories.excerpt: In the Hopi creation story, in the beginning only Tawa, the Sun Spirit, existed in endless space (Tokpella). Tawa formed the First World but its insect-like creatures lived unhappily in caves. To improve things, Tawa created Sotuknang, his nephew, who in turn created Spider Woman (Spider Grandmother) as a messenger and
stories.title: Tawa Creates the Worlds

stories.name: Tek-ko-kui, the Bamboo Giant
stories.excerpt: A giant nature spirit made of bamboo who protects the forests of Taiwan from those who would harm them.
stories.title: Tek-ko-kui, the Bamboo Giant

stories.name: Teke Teke: The Railway Ghost
stories.excerpt: A woman who died on the railway returns as a vengeful spirit, her body sliced in half, hunting the living.
stories.title: Teke Teke: The Railway Ghost

stories.name: Tenali Raman — The Biggest Fool in the Kingdom
stories.excerpt: Tenali Ramakrishna was the witty court jester and advisor in the court of King Krishnadevaraya of the Vijayanagara Empire. In this famous tale, a horse trader cheats the king by taking 5,000 gold coins as advance for three Arabian horses and never returns. When the king laments being tricked, Tenali presents him with a
stories.title: Tenali Raman — The Biggest Fool in the Kingdom

stories.name: Tengu: The Long-Nosed Goblin
stories.excerpt: A proud monk is abducted by mountain spirits and taught that true wisdom begins with humility.
stories.title: Tengu: The Long-Nosed Goblin

stories.name: Thagyamin: The King of the Nats of Myanmar
stories.excerpt: The highest spirit in Burmese folk religion rules over 37 nats from his heavenly throne.
stories.title: Thagyamin: The King of the Nats of Myanmar

stories.name: Thanh Gióng the Giant Saint
stories.excerpt: In the folklore of the Philippines, there is a creature that every child learns about before they can walk.
stories.title: Thanh Gióng the Giant Saint

stories.name: The Aasik of the Dog Pens
stories.excerpt: The Aasik is a giant worm that dwells near dog pens where it feeds on puppies. While feared, it can be tamed by a strong-willed human and used as a mount or food source. Some legends describe Aasiks marrying humans, creating hybrid descendants.
stories.title: The Aasik of the Dog Pens

stories.name: The Abada of the Ubangi Forest
stories.excerpt: A young BaAka hunter follows a trail of shimmering footprints deep into the equatorial forest, seeking the legendary Abada whose single horn holds the power to purify poisoned water.
stories.title: The Abada of the Ubangi Forest

stories.name: The Abchanchu, Shapeshifter of the Road
stories.excerpt: A shapeshifting vampire that appears as a beautiful stranger on the road, inviting travelers to share food and wine before revealing its true form — a skeletal figure that drinks the fat from human bodies.
stories.title: The Abchanchu, Shapeshifter of the Road

stories.name: the Acalica Water Spirits
stories.excerpt: Tiny silver-skinned spirits that live in Lake Titicaca emerge at dawn to tend the reeds, and fishermen who see them must look away — or be drawn beneath the water to live among them forever.
stories.title: the Acalica Water Spirits

stories.name: The Afriq Demon: The Origin of Africa's Name
stories.excerpt: According to Berber tradition, the name 'Africa' (Ifriqiya) derives from Afriq, a legendary demon or tribal deity worshiped by ancient North African peoples. The Afriq was a powerful spirit associated with the cave-dwelling peoples of Libya and Tunisia. Some accounts describe Afriq as a serpentine demon who demanded hu
stories.title: The Afriq Demon: The Origin of Africa's Name

stories.name: The Ahö'li and the Kachinas of Walpi
