stories.excerpt: In Walpi lived an old Ahö'li Kachina with his sister, the Kachin-mana, leading her because of his age and frailty. They planted in their field south of Walpi, depositing prayer offerings at a báho shrine. Meanwhile, the Ââ'ototo, Big-Horn Kachina, and others gathered and descended the mesa, marking shrines between vill
stories.title: The Ahö'li and the Kachinas of Walpi

stories.name: The Aku-Aku Spirits of Rapa Nui
stories.excerpt: The Aku-Aku are the powerful ancestral spirits of Rapa Nui, believed to inhabit the island's caves, cliffs, and sacred sites. These spirits could be both protectors and tricksters, guiding the living toward prosperity or leading them astray. The Aku-Aku were deeply connected to the moai statues—each moai embodied an an
stories.title: The Aku-Aku Spirits of Rapa Nui

stories.name: The Akvan Div (The Demon of Madness)
stories.excerpt: In the Shahnameh, the Akvan Div is a fearsome demon of madness who terrorizes Iran. King Kay Khosrow sends Rostam to destroy him. The demon finds Rostam sleeping and, instead of killing him outright, tosses him into the sea (a trick of his mad nature). Rostam swims ashore and, using cleverness, tricks the Akvan Div int
stories.title: The Akvan Div (The Demon of Madness)

stories.name: The Al (Childbirth Demoness)
stories.excerpt: In Persian folklore, the Al is a demonic being personifying puerperal fever, targeting women during and after childbirth. The name derives from Iranian 'al' meaning red, and she is described as a red-haired, stunted female creature with a rudimentary black humanoid form. She attacks mothers within the first six days af
stories.title: The Al (Childbirth Demoness)

stories.name: The Al and the Shepherd's Fire
stories.excerpt: A band of shepherds on the high pastures of Ararat discover that the darkness between their campfires is not empty, and that the Al watches from the space between flames.
stories.title: The Al and the Shepherd's Fire

stories.name: the Al-Mi'raj, the Desert Unicorn
stories.excerpt: A yellow, rabbit-like creature with a single spiraling horn that can kill any beast — because in the deserts of Lebanon, the most dangerous thing is not the lion or the scorpion, but the thing you do not see coming.
stories.title: the Al-Mi'raj, the Desert Unicorn

stories.name: The Altai Creation Myth
stories.excerpt: The Altai creation myth is the foundational cosmology of the Altai Turks. In the beginning, there was only water — a primordial ocean covering everything. The supreme god Kayra Han (also Bai-Ulgen) sent a loon (or in some versions, a golden bird called galbingaa) to dive to the bottom of the ocean to bring up mud. From
stories.title: The Altai Creation Myth

stories.name: the Amaru, Sacred Serpent of the Andes
stories.excerpt: A massive winged serpent that lives in the deepest lakes of the Andes, carrying the bones of the dead between worlds — and when it surfaces, earthquakes split the mountains.
stories.title: the Amaru, Sacred Serpent of the Andes

stories.name: The Amur River Spirit
stories.excerpt: A Nanai legend about the powerful spirit of the Amur River, known as the 'Dragon River' or Amur Father. According to tradition, the Amur is a living entity with its own will and consciousness. The river spirit can be generous or wrathful, providing abundant fish to those who respect it and drowning those who offend it.
stories.title: The Amur River Spirit

stories.name: the Anata, Spirit of the Carnival
stories.excerpt: An ancient spirit of joy and chaos that wakes each February to ride through the streets on the backs of devils, scattering flowers and coins and madness — because the Aymara believe that grief must be drowned in celebration.
stories.title: the Anata, Spirit of the Carnival

stories.name: The Ancestor Who Guarded the Forest
stories.excerpt: Ema, the ancestor-spirit, protects the mountain forests of Timor and punishes those who take more than they need from the land.
stories.title: The Ancestor Who Guarded the Forest

stories.name: The Angara River's Escape
stories.excerpt: A famous Buryat legend about the Angara River, the only river that flows out of Lake Baikal. According to the tale, Baikal had many sons (the rivers that flow into the lake) and one beautiful daughter named Angara. Baikal, a stern and possessive father, kept Angara imprisoned beneath a great rock to prevent her from le
stories.title: The Angara River's Escape

stories.name: The Angel
stories.excerpt: A literary fairy tale about a celestial being's interaction with humans, emphasizing themes of redemption, divine intervention, and the contrast between the earthly and the spiritual realms.
stories.title: The Angel

stories.name: The Animal Dance
stories.excerpt: The Animal Dance was a hunting ceremony received by Sweet Medicine at the Sacred Mountain (Bear Butte) to bring success to Cheyenne hunters. In this elaborate ceremony, men dressed as various animals—buffalo, deer, elk, antelope—while members of the Bowstring Society pretended to hunt them. Everything was done backward
stories.title: The Animal Dance

stories.name: The Anqa (Mythical Bird of Arabia)
stories.excerpt: The Anqa (or Anqa Mughrib) is a golden, fabulous female bird in pre-Islamic Arab mythology, described as very beautiful and colorful with a long neck, human face, four pairs of wings, and a whiteness in its neck. She lives alone on Mount Qaf, flies far away, and only appears once in ages. Created by God with all perfec
stories.title: The Anqa (Mythical Bird of Arabia)

stories.name: The Ants That Pushed on the Pine Tree
stories.excerpt: A Pueblo story from Isleta about Kahp-too-óo-yoo (Corn-stalk Young Man), a famous hunter, warrior, and wizard who controlled the clouds and brought rain. After being bewitched by a false friend, he was imprisoned in the top of a giant pine tree that reached the sky. His family and village suffered from drought without
stories.title: The Ants That Pushed on the Pine Tree

stories.name: The Apache Origin of the Animals
stories.excerpt: After the Apaches emerged from the underworld, they traveled south for four days with only seeds to eat. A Raven brought a quiver with meat to a teepee, and when children ate the meat they became instantly fat. The Raven's meat was stolen, and he flew to his eastern mountain home. An Apache boy was transformed into a p
stories.title: The Apache Origin of the Animals

stories.name: The Ark of the Covenant at Axum
stories.excerpt: After Menelik I was anointed king of Ethiopia in Jerusalem, the elders of Israel's tribes — jealous of Solomon's favor toward his Ethiopian son — decided that the firstborn sons of Israel's nobles should accompany Menelik back to Ethiopia. Before departing, Azariah, son of the high priest Zadok, stole the Ark of the Co
stories.title: The Ark of the Covenant at Axum

stories.name: The Artful Lad
stories.excerpt: A clever servant lad helps a poor farmer by exposing his unfaithful wife who feeds the neighbor instead of her husband. The lad tricks the neighbor into giving him grain, repeatedly exhumes a spying old woman (the neighbor's mother-in-law) who dies in a chest, and manages three funerals before finally burying her for g
stories.title: The Artful Lad

stories.name: The Aurora Spirits' Dance
stories.excerpt: The Northern Lights are the spirits of the dead playing ball in the sky — and if you whistle to them, they will send you a gift.
stories.title: The Aurora Spirits' Dance

stories.name: The Awful Fate of Mr. Wolf
stories.excerpt: Brer Wolf, determined to catch and eat Brer Rabbit, devises a plan to trap him in his own home. Brer Wolf hides in Brer Rabbit's house, planning to spring out when Brer Rabbit returns. But Brer Rabbit, always cautious, notices fresh tracks around the door and realizes something is wrong. He calls out, pretending to tal
stories.title: The Awful Fate of Mr. Wolf

stories.name: The Awonawilona Creation (Zuni)
stories.excerpt: In the Zuni creation myth recorded by Frank Cushing, only Áwonawílona, the All-Father, Maker and Container of All, existed in the beginning. He made himself into the Sun Father (Yatoka). The mist clouds formed into the Great Waters, from which Earth Mother (Áwitelin Tsíta) and Sky Father (Ápoyan Ta'chu) emerged. Togeth
stories.title: The Awonawilona Creation (Zuni)

stories.name: The Baccoo and the Provisions
stories.excerpt: A small, hairy, one-eyed trickster spirit sneaks into kitchens at night to steal food and tangle household work, punishing the lazy and rewarding the generous.
stories.title: The Baccoo and the Provisions

stories.name: The Bakwa of the Morning
stories.excerpt: The Bakwa, a great serpent of Kalinago legend, brings mist and rain to the island, and its appearance is both a blessing and a warning.
stories.title: The Bakwa of the Morning

stories.name: The Ball Game of the Hero Twins
stories.excerpt: The Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque descend to Xibalba and challenge the Lords of Death to a ball game — with their own lives as stakes.
stories.title: The Ball Game of the Hero Twins

stories.name: The Ballad of Mahua — Forbidden Love in Bengal
stories.excerpt: One of the most famous ballads of the Maimansingha Gitika, Mahua tells the story of a young Brahmin man named Naderchand who falls in love with Mahua, a beautiful girl from the much lower Kaibarta (fisherman) caste. Despite the rigid social hierarchies of 18th-century Bengal, the two lovers pursue their forbidden roman
stories.title: The Ballad of Mahua — Forbidden Love in Bengal

stories.name: The Bamboo of a Hundred Sections
stories.excerpt: A classic Vietnamese folk tale about a poor, hardworking orphan named Anh (or Khoai) who was taken in by a wealthy but cruel landlord. The landlord promised his beautiful daughter in marriage to Anh if he worked for three years without complaint. Anh faithfully completed his service, but the landlord refused to honor h
stories.title: The Bamboo of a Hundred Sections

stories.name: The Banshee
stories.excerpt: A spectral guardian whose mournful wail heralds the passing of those from the ancient bloodlines of Ireland.
stories.title: The Banshee

stories.name: The Banshee: Weeping Woman of Ireland
stories.excerpt: A spirit who wails before death, foretelling the end of a family line—the O'Brien clan is marked.
stories.title: The Banshee: Weeping Woman of Ireland

stories.name: The Baobab Tree's Origin (Mande/Senegal)
stories.excerpt: According to the Mande people, the baobab tree once grew in the heavens, and its fruits were reserved for the gods. A trickster spirit stole a baobab seedling and planted it on Earth so humans could enjoy its fruit and medicine. The gods were furious and pulled the tree upside down, leaving its roots exposed in the air
stories.title: The Baobab Tree's Origin (Mande/Senegal)

stories.name: The Barrel Bung
stories.excerpt: Famine has struck the parish of Bolinge. All the cows have gone dry except for those belonging to the rich, elderly Lady Skinflint and her ugly daughter, who somehow have hundreds of cheeses and tubs of butter from only four cows. When Jerker, the eldest son of the poor farmer Jonson, discovers that his family's cow St
stories.title: The Barrel Bung

stories.name: The Basilisk in the Cistern
stories.excerpt: When a basilisk takes up residence in the Vatican's ancient cistern, a young seminarian must descend into the dark to face the creature whose gaze alone can kill.
stories.title: The Basilisk in the Cistern

stories.name: The Battle of the Mountains
stories.excerpt: The mountains of the central North Island were once living warriors who fought for the love of the beautiful mountain Pihanga. Tongariro, the greatest volcano, won her heart. In jealousy, Taranaki (then located in the center) challenged Tongariro. During their terrible battle, Tongariro erupted in fury and Taranaki was
stories.title: The Battle of the Mountains

stories.name: The Battle of the Noaidis
stories.excerpt: A story about two powerful noaidi who engage in a spiritual battle using their drums and helping spirits. The noaidi could send their free souls into animals and control them to spy on enemies. The most powerful could create a Stállu from earth, wood, or turf, giving it part of their own life force, and send it to figh
stories.title: The Battle of the Noaidis

stories.name: The Battle of the Twins
stories.excerpt: Sapling and Flint's conflict over the world they had created came to a head when they agreed to settle their rivalry through combat. Sapling chose the branches of the giant crab apple tree as his weapon, while Flint preferred poisonous roots, monster's teeth, and serpent fangs. They fought for many days across the land
stories.title: The Battle of the Twins

stories.name: The Bear Ceremony
stories.excerpt: A 48-part antiphonal bear song recorded in 1775 that reenacts the Sámi bear ceremony. The bear was considered sacred, 'the only animal related to man.' The ceremonial hunt aimed to remove a fierce competitor while winning the bear's power and ensuring its reincarnation. The bear's death was celebrated with the bear par
stories.title: The Bear Ceremony

stories.name: The Bear Ceremony (Chakhlynd)
stories.excerpt: The central Nivkh myth explaining the origin of the bear ceremony (chakhlynd), the most important ritual in Nivkh culture. The legend tells of a woman who married a bear in human form. She returned to her village with her bear-children, and the bear was killed by her relatives. Before dying, the bear promised that if p
stories.title: The Bear Ceremony (Chakhlynd)

stories.name: The Bear Mother (Haida)
stories.excerpt: In this classic Haida narrative, a woman who mocked the bears was taken by a bear who made her his wife. She was led into the bear's den deep in the forest, where she lived among the bear people and bore children who were half-human, half-bear. Her human brothers eventually tracked her down and killed the bears in a gr
stories.title: The Bear Mother (Haida)

stories.name: The Bear Who Married a Woman (Tsimshian)
stories.excerpt: A Tsimshian woman gathering berries in the forest encountered a bear who removed his bearskin and revealed himself as a handsome man. He took her to his village, where the bear people lived just like humans inside their lodges but appeared as bears to outsiders. The woman married him, learned the ways of the bear peopl
stories.title: The Bear Who Married a Woman (Tsimshian)

stories.name: The Beaver Bundle Ceremony
stories.excerpt: The Beaver Bundle is the most sacred medicine bundle of the Blackfoot people, said to have been given by the underwater spirits. According to legend, a Blackfoot man encountered beavers who taught him sacred songs, rituals, and the use of medicinal plants. The bundle contains various sacred objects including animal ski
stories.title: The Beaver Bundle Ceremony

stories.name: The Bell of the Morning
stories.excerpt: The Sphinx of ancient Greece is one of the most famous monsters in all of mythology.
stories.title: The Bell of the Morning

stories.name: The Bell Witch
stories.excerpt: Although the Bell Witch of Tennessee is one of America's most famous supernatural legends, its African American dimensions are often overlooked. Enslaved people on the Bell plantation near Adams, Tennessee, had their own interpretations of the entity that tormented the Bell family from 1817 to 1821. While white account
stories.title: The Bell Witch

stories.name: The Bennu Bird and the Primordial Mound
stories.excerpt: The Bennu bird—the inspiration for the Greek phoenix—was a self-created being associated with the sun god Ra and the city of Heliopolis. According to the Heliopolitan creation myth, before the world existed there was only the dark, watery abyss of Nun. From these primordial waters arose a mound of earth—the Benben—the
stories.title: The Bennu Bird and the Primordial Mound

stories.name: The Berber Creation Myth
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, the universe was vast empty darkness. Within this void existed a supreme being known as Amun or Anzar, the embodiment of perfection with the power to create and destroy. First, the sky and earth were formed in perfect harmony—the sky personified as a male deity, the earth as a female. From their union
stories.title: The Berber Creation Myth

stories.name: The Best Wish
stories.excerpt: Three brothers each receive one wish. The elders wish for money, but the youngest wishes that every woman he sees falls in love with him, leading to a life of luxury and affection.
stories.title: The Best Wish

stories.name: The Betrayal of Friends
stories.excerpt: Two lifelong friends living in different parts of Greenland maintain a deep bond by exchanging gifts of seal and reindeer meat. However, jealousy grows in one friend, who decides to curse the other by rubbing seal fat with a piece of a corpse onto the food he shares. The betrayed friend, warned by his tornak (protectiv
stories.title: The Betrayal of Friends

stories.name: The Bewitching of Sultan in the Desert
stories.excerpt: A young Bedouin merchant traveling alone through the Empty Quarter encounters Umm Al Duwais, whose deadly beauty nearly claims his life before the adhan saves him.
stories.title: The Bewitching of Sultan in the Desert

stories.name: The Bewitchment of Angutisugsuk
stories.excerpt: A family is plagued by sudden, unexplained hatred and violence. It is revealed that they have been bewitched by a malevolent spirit, forcing family members to fight one another. The story serves as a cautionary tale about the power of external spiritual influence and the importance of shamanic intervention to restore h
stories.title: The Bewitchment of Angutisugsuk

stories.name: The Big Bird Dan
stories.excerpt: A tale involving a giant bird named Dan who becomes an unlikely ally to a courageous protagonist. The story explores the relationship between humans and the mythical creatures of the wild, focusing on trust and the breaking of ancient curses.
stories.title: The Big Bird Dan

stories.name: The Big House Ceremony (Xinkwikaon)
stories.excerpt: The Big House Ceremony is the paramount spiritual tradition of the Lenape people. According to oral tradition, the ceremony was given to the ancestors long ago when the people lived in the East. It is held in a special longhouse built to face the east, with carved faces on the center posts representing the Creator and
stories.title: The Big House Ceremony (Xinkwikaon)

stories.name: The Big White Dog and the Sacred Pole (Chickasaw)
stories.excerpt: In this Chickasaw origin story, a great white dog led the people on their migration and guided them with the sacred pole. The white dog was sent by Ababinili to protect the Chickasaw people during their long journey from the west. Each day, the dog would lead the way, and at night, the sacred pole was planted in the gr
stories.title: The Big White Dog and the Sacred Pole (Chickasaw)

stories.name: The Bird Grip
stories.excerpt: A king goes blind, and an old woman tells him that only the song of the magical bird Grip — kept in a cage by a king in another land — can restore his sight. His eldest son sets out to fetch the bird but stops at a merry inn and forgets his mission, drinking and gambling. The second son does the same. The youngest son,
stories.title: The Bird Grip

stories.name: The Birth of Changing Woman
stories.excerpt: In the Navajo tradition, Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé) was the first human born in the Fourth World. She was originally born as Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ (White Shell Girl) and matured into Changing Woman, a central deity who represents the cycles of life, the seasons, and the earth itself. She later gives birth to the He
stories.title: The Birth of Changing Woman

stories.name: The Birth of the Twin Brothers: Sapling and Flint
stories.excerpt: After Sky Woman's daughter Tekawerahkwa (Breath of the Wind) gave birth, the twin boys emerged in different ways. The right-handed twin, Sapling (Hahgwehdi-yu or Kanehtó:ton), was born naturally and became the creator of all that is good and beautiful in the world. The left-handed twin, Flint (Hahgwehdaetgah or Okaraht
stories.title: The Birth of the Twin Brothers: Sapling and Flint

stories.name: The Biton Who Dwelt in the River
stories.excerpt: A Biton spirit claimed a stretch of the White Nile as its own, flooding the banks each night in retribution for a fisherman's greed, until an elder brokered a fragile peace between the human and spirit worlds.
stories.title: The Biton Who Dwelt in the River

stories.name: The Black Bull of Norroway
stories.excerpt: A princess defies her family's wishes to follow a magical bull to a kingdom of wonder.
stories.title: The Black Bull of Norroway

stories.name: The Black-Necked Crane of Bhutan
stories.excerpt: In Bhutan, the black-necked crane (Thrung Thrung Karmo) is revered as a sacred bird and believed to be the soul of virtuous monks returned to earth in elegant form. Legend says the cranes circle the Gangteng Monastery three times in a clockwise direction upon their arrival in the Phobjikha Valley each October — a tradi
stories.title: The Black-Necked Crane of Bhutan

stories.name: The Blackfoot Creation: Apistotoke, Na'pi, and the World
stories.excerpt: Apistotoke (Ihtsipatapiyohpa), the Great Spirit, created first the Sky Beings: Naato'si the Sun, Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, and the stars including Aapisowaahs the Morning Star. He then created Ksahkomitapi (Earth) as mother to all creation. Apistotoke created Na'pi (Old Man), the first man and demigod who shaped the wor
stories.title: The Blackfoot Creation: Apistotoke, Na'pi, and the World

stories.name: The Blind Men and the Elephant
stories.excerpt: In a bustling city of ancient India, six blind men heard that a strange animal called an elephant had been brought to the town.
stories.title: The Blind Men and the Elephant

stories.name: The Blue Belt
stories.excerpt: A protagonist obtains a magical blue belt that grants superhuman strength and the ability to overcome impossible trials. Using the belt, they defeat monsters and solve the puzzles of a distant king to win a great reward.
stories.title: The Blue Belt

stories.name: The Blue Cap of Dalkeith
stories.excerpt: A coal miner in the Dalkeith colliery befriends a Blue Cap spirit who shows him rich seams of coal, but warns that the gift comes with a price when greed overrides gratitude.
stories.title: The Blue Cap of Dalkeith

stories.name: The Blue Caps
stories.excerpt: In the coal mines of Scotland, deep beneath the earth where the daylight never reaches, there are helpers that the miners call the Blue Caps.
stories.title: The Blue Caps

stories.name: The Blue Lantern
stories.excerpt: A ghost lantern leads travelers to ghostly villages in the Vietnamese mountains.
stories.title: The Blue Lantern

stories.name: The Blue Wolf and the Fallow Doe: Ancestors of the Mongols
stories.excerpt: According to the Secret History of the Mongols, the Mongol people descend from a blue wolf (Börte Chino) and a fallow doe (Göo Maral) sent by Tengri (Heaven). The wolf and doe crossed the Tengis Sea and settled near the source of the Onon River at Mount Burkhan Khaldun, where they gave birth to the first Mongol, named
stories.title: The Blue Wolf and the Fallow Doe: Ancestors of the Mongols

stories.name: The Bluejay Cycle (Coast Salish)
stories.excerpt: Bluejay is a prominent trickster figure in Coast Salish mythology, particularly among the Chemainus, Cowichan, and other Salish communities. He is generally a benevolent being who helps people, but he is also extremely foolish and careless, and stories about him are often humorous or slapstick. In one classic story, Bl
stories.title: The Bluejay Cycle (Coast Salish)

stories.name: The Boiadeira of the Pantanal
stories.excerpt: A phantom cattlewoman leads her ghostly herd through the mist of the Pantanal, and the cowboy who follows her into the swamp never returns.
stories.title: The Boiadeira of the Pantanal

stories.name: The Boitatá Who Gave Sight
stories.excerpt: A massive fire serpent guards the night fields, blinding the wicked with its gaze but lighting the way for those who walk with respect.
stories.title: The Boitatá Who Gave Sight

stories.name: The Boo Hag
stories.excerpt: In Gullah Geechee folklore, a young man named Emmet Fisher falls in love with a beautiful but mysterious woman who lives deep in the marsh. Against all warnings, he marries her. One night, Emmet pretends to be asleep and witnesses his bride remove her skin, hang it on a hook, and transform into a skinless red creature
stories.title: The Boo Hag

stories.name: The Book of the Dead: The Weighing of the Heart
stories.excerpt: Central to ancient Egyptian funerary mythology is the judgment scene where the deceased's heart is weighed against the feather of Maat (truth and cosmic order) in the Hall of Two Truths. After death, the soul (the ba) journeys through the underworld (Duat), facing dangerous demons, fiery lakes, and gatekeepers. The cli
stories.title: The Book of the Dead: The Weighing of the Heart

stories.name: The Bori Dance of Iskoki
stories.excerpt: A Hausa healer undergoes the bori trance ritual to negotiate with the Iskoki spirits, discovering that the boundary between madness and divine knowledge is thinner than a drumbeat.
stories.title: The Bori Dance of Iskoki

stories.name: The Boto Who Wore a Hat
stories.excerpt: A pink river dolphin transforms into a handsome man to attend a village party, but a white hat cannot fully hide his true form.
stories.title: The Boto Who Wore a Hat

stories.name: The Bouda: Were-Hyenas of Ethiopia
stories.excerpt: Certain clans are believed to possess the power to transform into hyenas at night.
stories.title: The Bouda: Were-Hyenas of Ethiopia

stories.name: The Boy and the Tomte Cap
stories.excerpt: A burlesque story about a boy who borrows the tomte's invisibility cap and embarks on hair-raising adventures. With the cap's magic, he rescues an enchanted girl from a troll's power and wins both her hand and great riches. The tale follows the classic trickster-hero pattern common in Swedish folklore where a clever hu
stories.title: The Boy and the Tomte Cap

stories.name: The Boy and the Trolls, or The Adventure
stories.excerpt: An unnamed young lad packs his lunch, leaves the city, and heads into the woods in search of adventure. Meanwhile, in the kingdom, the young princess has gone missing, and her father the king has surrendered control of the realm to his second wife — a conniving woman suspected of orchestrating her stepdaughter's disapp
stories.title: The Boy and the Trolls, or The Adventure

stories.name: The Boy Hunter Who Never Sacrificed to the Deer
stories.excerpt: A Zuni story about a boy who was an excellent hunter but never performed the proper sacrifices or prayers to the spirits of the deer he killed. As a result, the deer spirits became angry. The boy's disrespectful hunting caused supernatural consequences — his kills became tainted, and he began to have bad luck. The spir
stories.title: The Boy Hunter Who Never Sacrificed to the Deer

stories.name: The Boy Who Ate with the Giant
stories.excerpt: A clever little boy uses a series of tricks — a bag of porridge, a handful of bird feathers, and a stone — to convince a giant that he is stronger and hungrier than the giant himself.
stories.title: The Boy Who Ate with the Giant

stories.name: The Boy Who Crossed the Great Water and Returned
stories.excerpt: A Hopi tale of a boy who journeyed across the great waters and returned with knowledge and power. The boy's curiosity led him to leave his village and travel east toward the rising sun. He encountered various supernatural beings and overcame trials, including crossing a body of water that no Hopi had crossed before. Gu
stories.title: The Boy Who Crossed the Great Water and Returned

stories.name: The Boy Who Had an Eating Match with a Troll
stories.excerpt: A small but hungry boy is challenged to an eating contest by a massive troll. Using a clever trick involving a hidden bag of food and a misunderstanding of proportions, the boy manages to out-eat the troll and win a great prize.
stories.title: The Boy Who Had an Eating Match with a Troll

stories.name: The Boy Who Never Feared
stories.excerpt: A boy devoid of fear is sent on perilous tasks by his father to teach him caution, only to outsmart a mountain troll through sheer audacity and wit.
stories.title: The Boy Who Never Feared

stories.name: The Boy Who Strapped the Troll to the Sled
stories.excerpt: A boy wanders deep into the forest and comes to the trolls' cave. Because he is not receptive to their temptations, the trolls have no power to hold him and are forced to bring him home. The tale illustrates the folk belief that trolls can only hold power over those who yield to their enticements.
stories.title: The Boy Who Strapped the Troll to the Sled

stories.name: The Boy Who Went to the Wind's Cave
stories.excerpt: Little Mats sets out on a perilous journey to the end of the world to find his kidnapped sister. To reach the Wind's Cave and the magical realm where she is held, he must make terrible sacrifices along the way, giving up one ear, one eye, and one hand, each loss enabling him to pass through a different barrier. When he
stories.title: The Boy Who Went to the Wind's Cave

stories.name: The Boy With Enormous Nostrils
stories.excerpt: An abused boy is mocked for his enormous nostrils. However, he discovers that his condition allows him to hear secrets and distant conversations that others cannot. He uses this hidden power to outsmart his tormentors, demonstrating that what others see as a flaw can be a great strength.
stories.title: The Boy With Enormous Nostrils

stories.name: The Breath of Mze Moya
stories.excerpt: When the great storm deity Mze Moya turned away from the island, the coconut palms withered and the sea went still, teaching the Comorian people that even the mightiest powers must be entreated with reverence.
stories.title: The Breath of Mze Moya

stories.name: The Brewing of Beer
stories.excerpt: A high-stakes contest of beer-brewing takes place, where the quality of the brew is used as a measure of a person's magical skill and social status. The winners gain immense prestige, while those whose brews fail are subjected to public shame and ridicule.
stories.title: The Brewing of Beer

stories.name: The Bride's Farewell
stories.excerpt: The bride reflects on her transition from the familiar lands of Pohjola to the strange shores of Kalevala. She expresses the profound sadness of leaving her family and the anxiety and uncertainty associated with her new life in a foreign land.
stories.title: The Bride's Farewell

stories.name: The Bride's Farewell (Variant)
stories.excerpt: A further reflection on the bride's journey and the emotional weight of the union between the two rival lands. It emphasizes the role of women in bridging the gap between opposing cultures through marriage.
stories.title: The Bride's Farewell (Variant)

stories.name: The Brooms' Broom, King of All Brooms
stories.excerpt: Jon, a poor broom-maker living in the forest, decides to bind a magical broom: Kvastarnas kvast, alla kvastars kung. He visits three forest hags for help — Vingmor (flight), Tassmor (bouncing), and Labbmor (striking power). At the Great Mountain, he confronts the troll king, commands his broom to steal his scepter, and
stories.title: The Brooms' Broom, King of All Brooms

stories.name: The Brothers: A Tale of Two Brothers
stories.excerpt: Two brothers inherit a farm and discover that true fortune is found in the kindness of one's heart, not the wealth in one's purse.
stories.title: The Brothers: A Tale of Two Brothers

stories.name: The Brown Bull of Cooley
stories.excerpt: One night in the royal bedchamber of Cruachan, the capital of Connacht, a conversation began that would lead to one of the bloodiest wars in Irish mythology.
stories.title: The Brown Bull of Cooley

stories.name: The Brownie
stories.excerpt: In the misty glens and rolling hills of Scotland, there lived a creature that was neither fairy nor ghost, but something in between.
stories.title: The Brownie

stories.name: The Brownies (Tomtar)
stories.excerpt: In Swedish folklore, tomtar (also called brownies or nisses) are small, elderly-looking men about the size of a three- or four-year-old child, dressed in gray clothes with red caps. They live on farms, usually in barns or pantries, and work tirelessly to maintain the household. They wake servants for threshing, help in
stories.title: The Brownies (Tomtar)

stories.name: The Buda of the Lowlands
stories.excerpt: A Tigre herdsman encounters a Buda, a shapeshifter who can take the form of any animal or person, and learns that the most dangerous monsters look exactly like you.
stories.title: The Buda of the Lowlands

stories.name: The Buda Woman of Asmara
stories.excerpt: A Nara woman in Asmara is suspected of being a Buda when her neighbors notice her shadow does not match her body, forcing a community to confront the line between suspicion and justice.
stories.title: The Buda Woman of Asmara

stories.name: The Buffalo Woman of the Mande (Mande)
stories.excerpt: In the land of Dô, a buffalo terrorized the countryside, destroying crops and killing hunters. Two brothers, Oulamba and Oulani, discovered that the buffalo was actually a woman named Sogolon who transformed into the beast each night after being cursed by a rival. Following the advice of a wise hunter, one brother marr
stories.title: The Buffalo Woman of the Mande (Mande)

stories.name: the Bukit Timah Monkey Man
stories.excerpt: A half-man half-monkey creature that lurks in the dense forest of Bukit Timah, stealing fruit and scaring hikers, because even in a city of five million the jungle remembers.
stories.title: the Bukit Timah Monkey Man

stories.name: The Bulgasari Who Ate the Iron
stories.excerpt: A metal-eating beast born from the famine of the 1990s, devouring the iron fences and copper wires of a nation that locked its gates from the inside — because hunger makes beasts of everything.
stories.title: The Bulgasari Who Ate the Iron

stories.name: The Bura of the Deep Waters
stories.excerpt: Fishermen on the Kura River encounter a Bura, a water demon who demands a price for every fish pulled from the deep pools, and learn that some bargains are best left unmade.
stories.title: The Bura of the Deep Waters

stories.name: The Buryat Earth-Diver Creation
stories.excerpt: The classic Buryat creation myth — an earth-diver story similar to those found across Central Asia. In the beginning, the sky god Sombov looked down upon the primordial waters and saw the water bird Anghir. He commanded the bird to dive to the depths and retrieve material for making the earth. Anghir brought up black e
stories.title: The Buryat Earth-Diver Creation

stories.name: The Butterfly Lovers
stories.excerpt: A young woman disguises herself as a man to study, falling in love with a fellow student, only to face a tragic end that transforms them into eternal companions.
stories.title: The Butterfly Lovers

stories.name: The Bäckahästen – The Brook Horse of Åland's Waters
stories.excerpt: The bäckahästen (brook horse) is a shapeshifting water spirit that appears as a beautiful, seemingly tame horse near streams, lakes, or the sea. When someone climbs onto its back, the horse gallops into the water and drowns its rider. The legend was particularly used to warn children away from dangerous waters. In some
stories.title: The Bäckahästen – The Brook Horse of Åland's Waters

stories.name: The Böögg: The Swiss Bogeyman
stories.excerpt: A mythical monster used to frighten children now burns every spring as a snowman effigy that predicts the summer weather.
stories.title: The Böögg: The Swiss Bogeyman

stories.name: The Cadejo at the Crossroads
stories.excerpt: Two supernatural dogs — one white, one black — guard the roads of El Salvador at night, one protecting the faithful and the other preying upon the wicked.
stories.title: The Cadejo at the Crossroads

stories.name: The Cadejo Chico and the Children
stories.excerpt: A small, mischievous variant of the Cadejo spirit haunts children who misbehave, appearing as a tiny dog that grows larger with each act of disobedience.
stories.title: The Cadejo Chico and the Children

stories.name: The Cadejo Grande of the Coffee Roads
stories.excerpt: The largest of the Cadejo spirits — a towering, spectral dog that guards the remote mountain roads where coffee pickers walk alone before dawn.
stories.title: The Cadejo Grande of the Coffee Roads

stories.name: The Cadejo of the Dangriga Road
stories.excerpt: A Garifuna woman walking home at dusk encounters both the white and black Cadejo on the road to Dangriga, and learns that good and evil travel the same path, differing only in intention.
stories.title: The Cadejo of the Dangriga Road

stories.name: The Cadejo of the Road
stories.excerpt: Two spectral dogs — one white, one black — guard the roads of Central America, one protecting the righteous and the other preying on the wicked.
stories.title: The Cadejo of the Road

stories.name: The Caipora and the Logger
stories.excerpt: A hairy forest guardian rides a wild pig through the Atlantic rainforest, punishing loggers who take more than the jungle can bear.
stories.title: The Caipora and the Logger

stories.name: The Calèche de Lallmatie
stories.excerpt: Along the road to Lallmatie, a phantom horse-drawn carriage appears on moonless nights, its wheels soundless on the pavement, its passenger a figure no one dares look at twice.
stories.title: The Calèche de Lallmatie

stories.name: The Cannibal Woman Society (Kwakwaka'wakw)
stories.excerpt: Long ago when totemic beings walked the earth, there was Dzunukwa (Cannibal Woman), a gigantic female being with great wealth and powerful magic who ate people. The other beings became alarmed and decided only Raven could stop her. Raven flew to the North End of the World and recruited a flock of fearsome Cannibal Bird
stories.title: The Cannibal Woman Society (Kwakwaka'wakw)

stories.name: The Capelobo of the Interior
stories.excerpt: A headless, ape-like creature with a gaping chest wound prowls the Brazilian backlands, and the traveler who encounters it must run or be devoured.
stories.title: The Capelobo of the Interior

stories.name: The Carver Who Gave Shetani Form
stories.excerpt: A gifted Makonde carver discovers that the figures emerging from his ebony are not inventions of his imagination but true portraits of the shetani that haunt the forests, and that giving them form gives them power over the waking world.
stories.title: The Carver Who Gave Shetani Form

stories.name: The Cat of Norrhult
stories.excerpt: The people of Norrhult are driven from their homes by trolls. A bear keeper arrives and his bear scatters the trolls then directs villagers to raise a cross on the mountain. A troll later asks if that vicious cat is still alive and upon hearing she has seven fierce kittens flees forever.
stories.title: The Cat of Norrhult

stories.name: The Cat on the Dovrefjell
stories.excerpt: A youth journeys to the Dovrefjell mountains where he encounters a magical cat. The cat, acting as a guide, leads the youth through perilous landscapes to a hidden treasure and helps him win the heart of a princess.
stories.title: The Cat on the Dovrefjell

stories.name: The Cat Ra
stories.excerpt: In the land of ancient Egypt, where the Nile flows through golden sands and the pyramids pierce the sky, there lived a belief more powerful than any pharaoh's decree.
stories.title: The Cat Ra

stories.name: The Cave of Caguana: Taino Creation
stories.excerpt: According to Taino mythology, all human life began in a sacred cave called Cacibajagua (Cave of the Jagua) on the island of Haiti (Hispaniola). The first humans emerged from this cave, while the gods dwelt in the Cave of the Serpent and the Cave of Coaybay. The deity Iguanaboína was among the first beings from the rive
stories.title: The Cave of Caguana: Taino Creation

stories.name: The Celestial Star Gods
stories.excerpt: The Skidi Pawnee organized their entire society around the stars. Six major stars represented gods controlled by Tirawa: the North Star (watched over the people), Northeast Star (Big Black Meteoric Star, controlled animals and bison), Southeast Star (Red Star, regulated day and animals), South Star (ruled the land of t
stories.title: The Celestial Star Gods

stories.name: The Chains of Abu Al-Salasil
stories.excerpt: A wealthy merchant who cheated his workers is visited by Abu Al-Salasil, the spirit of chains, who forces him to confront the weight of his injustices before dawn.
stories.title: The Chains of Abu Al-Salasil

stories.name: The Chameleon Who Carried God's Message
stories.excerpt: When Chiuta needed a messenger to carry the word of immortality to humanity, he chose the Chameleon — slow, patient, and deliberate — but the Hare, sent second with the message of death, arrived first.
stories.title: The Chameleon Who Carried God's Message

stories.name: The Chamos of the Underground
stories.excerpt: Mischievous goblin-like creatures live in tunnels beneath Venezuelan cities, stealing small objects and playing tricks on anyone who wanders too close to their underground dwellings.
stories.title: The Chamos of the Underground

stories.name: The Changeling
stories.excerpt: A mother suspects her child has been replaced by a troll changeling and uses clever tricks — including brewing beer in an eggshell — to force the troll mother to return her real baby.
stories.title: The Changeling

stories.name: The Chickcharney of Andros Island
stories.excerpt: The Chickcharney is a legendary creature from Bahamian folklore, specifically from Andros Island. It resembles a small, elf-like being with owl-like feathers, glowing red eyes, three fingers on each hand, and three toes on each foot. It walks upright and is said to whistle softly as it moves. According to tradition, ho
stories.title: The Chickcharney of Andros Island

stories.name: The Child and the Cannibal (Nuxalk)
stories.excerpt: This Nuxalk legend tells of a magical boy who defeats a man-eating monster that terrorized the people. A cannibal giant (Boqs) had been stealing children from a Nuxalk village, carrying them off to his remote mountain lair to devour. The people were helpless against the monster's supernatural strength and ferocity. A y
stories.title: The Child and the Cannibal (Nuxalk)

stories.name: The Child-Snatcher of the Shore
stories.excerpt: A cautionary tale about the Qalupalik, a scaly creature that lives beneath the ice and uses a pouch to kidnap children who wander too close to the water's edge. The story blends practical safety advice with supernatural fear to keep children safe from drowning.
stories.title: The Child-Snatcher of the Shore

stories.name: The Children of La Llorona — The Weeping Children
stories.excerpt: A poignant variant of the La Llorona legend tells that the spirits of the children she drowned did not pass on but remain as eternal, weeping children along the same waterways. Known sometimes as Los Hijos de la Llorona, these child spirits are said to appear as small, translucent figures playing near rivers and canals
stories.title: The Children of La Llorona — The Weeping Children

stories.name: The Children of Lir
stories.excerpt: Long ago, in the mist-shrouded dawn of Ireland, when the Tuatha Dé Danann still walked among the hills and the land was alive with magic, there ruled a great king named Lir.
stories.title: The Children of Lir

stories.name: The Chiruwi of the Deep Forest
stories.excerpt: Deep in the forests of southern Malawi, the Chiruwi — a shape-shifting forest spirit — tested the courage of hunters by leading them astray, teaching them that the forest gives only to those who respect its mysteries.
stories.title: The Chiruwi of the Deep Forest

stories.name: The Chudes Are Defeated by a Loon's Beak
stories.excerpt: A humorous Sámi legend where Sámi outwit Chude raiders using minimal means—in this case, a loon's beak. The story illustrates the theme that superior force can be overcome by cleverness and that even small, humble tools can defeat powerful enemies.
stories.title: The Chudes Are Defeated by a Loon's Beak

stories.name: The Chudes Are Tricked by a Boy Pathfinder
stories.excerpt: A recurring Sámi legend type (Christiansen ML 8000). A band of Chude raiders attacks a Sámi settlement and captures a young boy, forcing him to guide them to other Sámi groups. The boy leads the raiders along a dangerous mountain path. He ties a rope around himself connected to the raiders, then at a critical moment on
stories.title: The Chudes Are Tricked by a Boy Pathfinder

stories.name: The Chudes in Notozero
stories.excerpt: A Skolt Sámi legend about Chude attackers in the Notozero region. The Sámi use their knowledge of the Arctic landscape and weather to evade and defeat the raiders. The story is part of the extensive cycle of Chude legends reflecting historical conflicts between Sámi and East Slavic raiders. The Chudes are always portra
stories.title: The Chudes in Notozero

stories.name: The Chullachaqui and the Hunter
stories.excerpt: A forest guardian with one human foot and one wooden foot punishes hunters who take more than they need from the jungle.
stories.title: The Chullachaqui and the Hunter

stories.name: The Chureca, the Virgin Islands Beast
stories.excerpt: A fearsome beast of the Virgin Islands, the Chureca is a monstrous creature that emerges from the forest to devour livestock and threaten villagers.
stories.title: The Chureca, the Virgin Islands Beast

stories.name: The Cipitío of the Volcanic Fields
stories.excerpt: A small, mischievous trickster spirit born from the union of earth and fire, the Cipitío steals food and causes mischief among the villages near the volcanic highlands.
stories.title: The Cipitío of the Volcanic Fields

stories.name: The Circle Kachina and His Wife Become Stars
stories.excerpt: In Hopi tradition, a maiden grinding corn was approached by the Póngo (Circle) Kachina, who danced at various kivas around the village. She agreed to marry him and went to the Kachina kiva where many different Kachinas gathered. She prepared their food while they prepared her bridal costume. They had two children, also
stories.title: The Circle Kachina and His Wife Become Stars

stories.name: The City of Brass
stories.excerpt: Caliph Abd al-Malik sends Emir Musa and his party across the Sahara to find the legendary City of Brass, built by King Solomon to imprison rebellious jinn. They encounter a brass horseman statue that points the way, a chained Ifrit imprisoned in a pillar, and an ancient city with walls eighty cubits high and twenty-fiv
stories.title: The City of Brass

stories.name: The Clever Girl of Kairouan
stories.excerpt: A Tunisian folktale from the ancient city of Kairouan about a poor man and his brilliant daughter. When famine strikes, the man seeks help from a corrupt judge who sets an impossible condition: 'You must come to me neither dressed nor undressed, neither walking nor riding, neither by day nor by night.' The man's daught
stories.title: The Clever Girl of Kairouan

stories.name: The Cock and Hen a-Nutting
stories.excerpt: A cock and a hen venture out to gather nuts in the forest, where they encounter a dangerous troll. Using their wit and coordination, they manage to trick the troll and escape his clutches, illustrating that intelligence and teamwork can overcome brute strength and predatory threats.
stories.title: The Cock and Hen a-Nutting

stories.name: The Cock and the Crested Hen
stories.excerpt: A vain little crested hen thinks herself too good for the other farmyard hens and goes off alone against the cock's warnings. A hawk swoops down and nearly catches her; she escapes but loses her finest feathers, learning humility.
stories.title: The Cock and the Crested Hen

stories.name: The Cock and the Mouse (Zuni)
stories.excerpt: A Zuni folktale of the hybrid type, combining Native and European story elements. The Cock (rooster) and the Mouse were friends living together. Mouse was industrious, gathering food and maintaining their home, while Cock was boastful and lazy. When danger came in the form of a cat or predator, Cock's crowing alerted e
stories.title: The Cock and the Mouse (Zuni)

stories.name: The Cockatrice of the Garden
stories.excerpt: In the Vatican Gardens, a basilisk born from a rooster's egg hatches under a serpent's care, and only the simplest act of faith — refusing to look — saves the gardener who must destroy it.
stories.title: The Cockatrice of the Garden

stories.name: The Coming of Death
stories.excerpt: In Navajo mythology, death came into being when one of the hermaphrodite twins (Nádleeh) stopped breathing after the first day of the Sun's journey. The people abandoned the body in fear, and the next day it was gone — a man looked down through the reed to the Third World and saw the twin sitting by the river. Coyote F
stories.title: The Coming of Death

stories.name: The Comorian Dragon of Karthala
stories.excerpt: Deep beneath Mount Karthala sleeps a dragon born from volcanic fire and ocean brine, and the Comorians know that the mountain's occasional tremors are merely the dragon turning in its restless sleep.
stories.title: The Comorian Dragon of Karthala

stories.name: The Comorian Jinn of the Clove Grove
stories.excerpt: The Mashetani, Comoros' restless jinn, are said to inhabit the ancient clove groves, and a young bride learns that negotiating with spirits requires more courage than fleeing from them.
stories.title: The Comorian Jinn of the Clove Grove

stories.name: The Conjure Doctor Who Outwitted the Master
stories.excerpt: On a Virginia plantation, the master hired a notorious slave driver to break the spirit of the enslaved people. Whippings and punishments only increased, and the people grew desperate. An old conjure doctor named Uncle Monday was called from a neighboring plantation. Uncle Monday walked through the quarters, speaking t
stories.title: The Conjure Doctor Who Outwitted the Master

stories.name: The Contendings of Horus and Set
stories.excerpt: The epic struggle between Horus, the son of Osiris, and Set, the murderer of Osiris, for the throne of Egypt is one of the most dramatic myths from ancient Egypt. After Osiris descended to the underworld, his son Horus came of age and demanded the kingship that was rightfully his. Set, Osiris's brother, refused to yiel
stories.title: The Contendings of Horus and Set

stories.name: The Corn Maidens (Zuni)
stories.excerpt: In Zuni tradition, the Corn Maidens are sacred beings who embody the spirit of corn. They are associated with Paiyatuma, the god of the dawn and of music, and with the Kachina society. According to the myth, Paiyatuma courted the Corn Maidens, who were beautiful but shy. He played his flute for them, and they danced. T
stories.title: The Corn Maidens (Zuni)

stories.name: The Corn Mother
stories.excerpt: The Sluagh are the most feared of all Irish fairy creatures, and for good reason.
stories.title: The Corn Mother

stories.name: The Cosmic Egg Creation (Bon Tradition)
stories.excerpt: The pre-Buddhist Tibetan Bon creation myth describing the origin of the universe from a cosmic egg. According to this tradition, in the beginning there was only emptiness. From the void emerged five pure lights, which condensed into a luminous egg. From this cosmic egg hatched the primordial being, who then created the
stories.title: The Cosmic Egg Creation (Bon Tradition)

stories.name: The Cougar Guardian's Two Heads
stories.excerpt: A two-headed cougar spirit guards the boundary between the living world and the spirit world, and the traveler who passes without permission is dragged into the forest forever.
stories.title: The Cougar Guardian's Two Heads

stories.name: The Countess of Höjentorp
stories.excerpt: When King Charles XI confiscates her property the Countess of Hojentorp greets him with a box on the ear. She feeds him only a herring's tail and oat cake. When the king asks for her gold she gives him a second slap, and the king retreats ordering she be left in peace.
stories.title: The Countess of Höjentorp

stories.name: The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl
stories.excerpt: Star lovers separated by the Milky Way, reunited once a year on a bridge formed by thousands of magpies.
stories.title: The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl

stories.name: The Coyote and the Locust
stories.excerpt: A Zuni trickster story about Coyote who heard Locust singing and playing his flute on a piñon branch. Coveting the song, Coyote demanded Locust teach it to him. Locust, wary of Coyote's intentions, tricked him by shedding his skin and placing a stone inside the empty shell on the branch. When Coyote returned and Locust
stories.title: The Coyote and the Locust

stories.name: The Crane Guardian's Warning
stories.excerpt: A sacred crane spirit warns the village of an approaching enemy, and the warrior who listens survives the battle while the others fall.
stories.title: The Crane Guardian's Warning

stories.name: The Crane Wife
stories.excerpt: In a small village in Korea, during the days of the Joseon dynasty, a poor woodcutter lived alone in a cottage at the edge of the forest.
stories.title: The Crane Wife

stories.name: The Crane's Repayment
stories.excerpt: A wounded crane is rescued and repays the kindness with magic, only for the gift to be lost through a breach of trust.
stories.title: The Crane's Repayment

stories.name: The Creation of Earth and the Great Buzzard (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, all was water, and animals lived in the sky world above the stone vault. The water beetle Dâyuni'sï volunteered to explore below and brought up soft mud from the ocean floor, which grew into the earth. The earth was initially soft and flat. The Great Buzzard flew down to survey the land, and his wings
stories.title: The Creation of Earth and the Great Buzzard (Cherokee)

stories.name: The Creation of Haida Gwaii
stories.excerpt: Before the days of the grandfathers, there was nothing but water except a single reef where the supernatural beings lived crowded together. Raven flew about looking for a place to land but could alight nowhere. He flew up to the Sky Land, where he tricked a chief's family by taking the form of a baby. He caused mischie
stories.title: The Creation of Haida Gwaii

stories.name: The Creation of Lake Baikal
stories.excerpt: A Buryat legend explaining the origin of Lake Baikal, the world's deepest and oldest lake. According to the myth, there was once a great earthquake — the mightiest ever seen — which created a massive crack in the earth's surface. Fire and lava erupted from the crack, threatening to destroy everything. The Buryat people
stories.title: The Creation of Lake Baikal

stories.name: The Creation of Lake Issyk-Kul
stories.excerpt: An alternate legend describes the origin of Issyk-Kul ('Warm Lake') as the tears of the heavens. An old man and his beautiful daughter lived on the shores of a small river. When invaders came, the daughter prayed to Tengri for salvation. The sky god answered by sending a flood that drowned the invaders but also the old
stories.title: The Creation of Lake Issyk-Kul

stories.name: The Creation of the Faroe Islands
stories.excerpt: Two folk explanations exist for the archipelago's creation. The first says the islands were formed from dirt that gathered under God's fingernails while He created the world and flicked away. The second, more dramatic myth connects to Norse mythology: after the World Serpent Jörmungandr (child of Loki) was defeated, a
stories.title: The Creation of the Faroe Islands

stories.name: The Creation of the Karakum Desert
stories.excerpt: According to Turkmen legend, the Karakum ('Black Sands') Desert was created by a battle between good and evil forces. The devil challenged the creator god to a contest — who could cover more land in one night. The creator god began covering the land with fertile soil, but the devil raised giant sandstorms. The creator
stories.title: The Creation of the Karakum Desert

stories.name: The Creation of the Kathmandu Valley by Manjushri
stories.excerpt: According to the Swayambhu Purana, the Kathmandu Valley was once a great lake called Nagavasahrada, inhabited by serpent beings (Nagas). On the lake floated a miraculous self-arisen flame (Swayambhu Jyotirupa) emanating from a thousand-petalled lotus. The Bodhisattva Manjushri, meditating on the Five-Peaked Mountain in
stories.title: The Creation of the Kathmandu Valley by Manjushri

stories.name: The Creation of the Niger River (Mande)
stories.excerpt: Long ago, the Niger River flowed only underground. A heroic hunter named Fara Makan tracked a wounded antelope for seven days without water. When he was dying of thirst, he shot an arrow into the ground, and water burst forth, creating the Niger River. The river then wound its way across the Sahel, bringing life to the
stories.title: The Creation of the Niger River (Mande)

stories.name: The Creation of the World (Fon/Dahomey)
stories.excerpt: Before the world existed, there was only water, darkness, and the supreme deity Nana Buluku. Nana Buluku gave birth to twins: Mawu, the goddess of the moon and night, and Lisa, the god of the sun and day. Together, Mawu-Lisa created the world. They then gave birth to children who became the heads of the great vodun pan
stories.title: The Creation of the World (Fon/Dahomey)

stories.name: The Creation of the World (Yoruba)
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, there was only water and chaos. Olodumare, the Supreme Being, sent Obatala down from the heavens with a calabash filled with soil, a rooster, and a palm nut. Obatala poured the soil onto the waters, and the rooster spread it to create dry land at Ile-Ife, the cradle of existence. He planted the palm n
stories.title: The Creation of the World (Yoruba)

stories.name: The Creek Flood Myth and the Dog's Sacrifice (Creek)
stories.excerpt: The Muscogee Creek tell a flood story in which the Great Flood covered the entire earth. As the waters rose, the people prayed to the Creator for deliverance. A great dog appeared and offered to sacrifice himself by lying across a creek to dam the water. The dog's noble self-sacrifice allowed the people to cross to hig
stories.title: The Creek Flood Myth and the Dog's Sacrifice (Creek)

stories.name: The Crocodile Who Formed the Island
stories.excerpt: The great crocodile spirit Lafaek sacrificed himself to create the island of Timor, and his body became the land upon which the people live.
stories.title: The Crocodile Who Formed the Island

stories.name: The Crossroads Spirit
stories.excerpt: In African American conjure tradition, the crossroads is the most spiritually charged place—the intersection where the physical world meets the spirit world. The story tells of a young man who went to a crossroads at midnight seeking power. He was instructed by a rootworker to bring a black chicken, a bottle of whiskey
stories.title: The Crossroads Spirit

stories.name: The Crowing Cobra of Zambezia
stories.excerpt: A boy who mocks the old warnings about the Crowing Crested Cobra learns too late that the wilderness holds creatures whose very names are meant to keep the unwary alive.
stories.title: The Crowing Cobra of Zambezia

stories.name: The Crystal Ball
stories.excerpt: In a small German village at the edge of a dark forest, a poor boy was given a crystal ball by an old woman he met on the road.
stories.title: The Crystal Ball

stories.name: The Curse of the Dolls — La Isla de las Muñecas
stories.excerpt: The legend of the Island of the Dolls (La Isla de las Muñecas) in the Xochimilco canals near Mexico City is a modern legend that has spread widely through Mexican-American communities. According to the story, a man named Don Julián Santana found the body of a drowned girl in the canals and, haunted by her spirit, began
stories.title: The Curse of the Dolls — La Isla de las Muñecas

stories.name: The Curse of the Raven's Eye
stories.excerpt: A man steals a gemstone from the eye of a carved raven statue in an ancient temple. The gem gives him the ability to see the future, but it also attracts the attention of the raven's spirit, which slowly consumes his sanity until he returns the stone to its rightful place.
stories.title: The Curse of the Raven's Eye

stories.name: The Cursed Ring of the Highlands
stories.excerpt: A traveler finds a gold ring in a mountain stream, only to discover it is cursed. The ring brings immense wealth but also attracts the attention of the Draugrs who previously owned it. The wearer is haunted by whispers and nightmares until they return the ring to the stream from which it came.
stories.title: The Cursed Ring of the Highlands

stories.name: The Curupira and the City Boy
stories.excerpt: A city boy visits the Amazon and ignores the warnings about the Curupira, whose backward feet lead him in circles until he learns to respect the forest.
stories.title: The Curupira and the City Boy

stories.name: The D'Sonoqua Who Became Wealth (Kwakwaka'wakw)
stories.excerpt: In one Kwakwaka'wakw narrative, a clever boy was captured by D'Sonoqua and carried in her basket to her forest house. While she prepared to cook him, the boy noticed that D'Sonoqua was dim-witted with poor eyesight. He tricked her into showing him her treasures and then pushed her into her own cooking fire. As she burn
stories.title: The D'Sonoqua Who Became Wealth (Kwakwaka'wakw)

stories.name: The Dahomey Amazons (Fon/Dahomey)
stories.excerpt: The Dahomey Amazons (Mino, meaning 'our mothers') were an all-female military regiment of the Kingdom of Dahomey. According to legend, Queen Hangbe, who ruled briefly in the early 1700s, established the first female bodyguards. But the legend says that the Amazons were blessed by the vodun spirits, who gave them supern
stories.title: The Dahomey Amazons (Fon/Dahomey)

stories.name: The Dakhanavars of the Mountain Pass
stories.excerpt: Two vampires haunt a remote mountain pass in Armenia, draining travelers of their blood through their feet, until a clever monk devises a trap of iron and prayer.
stories.title: The Dakhanavars of the Mountain Pass

stories.name: the Dangun, Founding of the First Kingdom
stories.excerpt: A bear and a god's son, transformed by patience and garlic and mugwort into the first humans — and from their line, a kingdom was born.
stories.title: the Dangun, Founding of the First Kingdom

stories.name: The Daughter of the Moon and the Son of the Sun
stories.excerpt: A romantic Sámi folk tale. Niekia, the Moon's daughter raised by an elderly Sámi couple, had a face like cloudberries and hair of silver. When Peivalke (the Sun's son) fell in love with her, she refused him and fled. She found an empty house by the sea, cleaned it, and hid as a spindle. Northern Light warriors led by N
stories.title: The Daughter of the Moon and the Son of the Sun

stories.name: The Day-Labourer and the Hidden People
stories.excerpt: A poor youth is helped by magical hidden people after showing kindness to their dog.
stories.title: The Day-Labourer and the Hidden People

stories.name: The Death of Hun Hunahpu
stories.excerpt: The father of the Hero Twins is summoned to Xibalba for playing ball too loudly, and the Lords of Death sacrifice him — but his blood gives rise to new life.
stories.title: The Death of Hun Hunahpu

stories.name: The Death of John Henry
stories.excerpt: After defeating the steam drill, John Henry's heart, strained beyond its limit, gave out. With his hammer still in his hand, the mighty steel-driving man collapsed and died. His fellow workers gathered around as the man who had beaten the machine lay still. The ballad recounts that John Henry had a woman—Polly Ann, Mar
stories.title: The Death of John Henry

stories.name: The Death of Osiris
stories.excerpt: Osiris was the ideal king of Egypt—good, fair, beloved by all who knew him. Centers on Osiris, from Egypt mythology. Known for aquatic speed and soul sight and immortality..
stories.title: The Death of Osiris

stories.name: The Death of the Sun's Daughter
stories.excerpt: The Sun's daughter Njávisheatne lived a long and good life. When she felt death approaching, she ordered that she be buried atop the highest peak so she could watch over the people forever. She was wrapped in a shroud of njavvi (reindeer neck hair) and laid to rest on a mountain now called Sun Daughter's Mountain. Ston
stories.title: The Death of the Sun's Daughter

stories.name: The Deathless Horseman
stories.excerpt: A headless rider known as the Dullahan wanders the night, heralding death with a single call of a name.
stories.title: The Deathless Horseman

stories.name: The Deer Stone Legends
stories.excerpt: Across the Mongolian steppe stand ancient megalithic Deer Stones — carved monoliths dating back 3,000 years to the Bronze Age. Mongol legend says these stones are warriors turned to stone by the sky god Tengri for their arrogance. The deer depicted leaping across the stones represent the souls of fallen warriors ascend
stories.title: The Deer Stone Legends

stories.name: The Deer Who Became the River
stories.excerpt: A sacred deer sacrifices itself to create the river that feeds the village, and its antlers become the trees that line its banks.
stories.title: The Deer Who Became the River

stories.name: The Dekki H'd'rtna, Shadow Walkers of the Highlands
stories.excerpt: In the Eritrean highlands, shadow spirits walk between the living and the dead, and a grieving widow who tries to speak with her dead husband learns that some doors should stay closed.
stories.title: The Dekki H'd'rtna, Shadow Walkers of the Highlands

stories.name: The Descent of the Tzitzimimeh
stories.excerpt: When the gods grow weak and the cosmic order falters, skeletal star-demons descend from the sky to devour humanity — and only a solar eclipse can stop them.
stories.title: The Descent of the Tzitzimimeh

stories.name: The Destroyer, Guaraní Chieftain
stories.excerpt: A fierce Guaraní war spirit who leads the souls of fallen warriors through the forest, and the hunter who hears his war cry must lie face-down or be driven mad.
stories.title: The Destroyer, Guaraní Chieftain

stories.name: The Destruction of Humanity by Sekhmet
stories.excerpt: When the sun god Ra grew old, humanity rebelled against his rule. Ra assembled the gods and proposed to destroy mankind. Following their counsel, he sent his Eye—the goddess Hathor—in the form of the fierce lioness Sekhmet to punish humanity. Sekhmet descended upon the earth and slaughtered people with relish, wading i
stories.title: The Destruction of Humanity by Sekhmet

stories.name: The Dev of the Iron Cave
stories.excerpt: A giant Dev imprisoned in a cave beneath the Armenian highlands offers a miner riches beyond measure in exchange for his freedom, testing the limits of mortal greed.
stories.title: The Dev of the Iron Cave

stories.name: The Devil's Dance at Bomarsund (Djävulsdansen)
stories.excerpt: One of Åland's most famous legends, the Devil's Dance tells of a masked ball at the Russian military settlement of Skarpans near Bomarsund in the 1830s–1840s. A mysterious, elegantly dressed stranger arrived at the dance and asked which woman was the finest dancer. A priest's wife stepped forward. The stranger danced w
stories.title: The Devil's Dance at Bomarsund (Djävulsdansen)

stories.name: The Devil's Golden Sword
stories.excerpt: In medieval Germany, during the reign of the Saxon emperors, there lived a knight named Sir Hartmann von Aue.
stories.title: The Devil's Golden Sword

stories.name: The Diablada of Oruro
stories.excerpt: Every year during Carnival, the devils of the mine emerge to dance through the streets of Oruro, wearing masks of hammered silver and carrying pitchforks of twisted ore — a reminder that the mountain never forgets.
stories.title: The Diablada of Oruro

stories.name: The Div and the Fortress of Fire
stories.excerpt: A Div, a powerful demon of ancient Zoroastrian and Turkic tradition, builds a fortress of black stone to block the sun, and only a fearless blacksmith can challenge it.
stories.title: The Div and the Fortress of Fire

stories.name: The Diving Duck Creation Myth
stories.excerpt: The Yakut creation myth about a diving duck that brought the first earth from the bottom of the primordial sea. In the beginning, there was only water. The supreme deity sent a diving duck (or loon) down into the depths to retrieve mud from the ocean floor. The bird succeeded in bringing up a small piece of earth, whic
stories.title: The Diving Duck Creation Myth

stories.name: The Djinn of the Aures Mountains
stories.excerpt: Powerful spirits inhabit the mountains of eastern Algeria, testing the faith of those who cross their territory.
stories.title: The Djinn of the Aures Mountains

stories.name: The Djinn of the Hollow Baobab
stories.excerpt: A young Hausa herdsman discovers that an ancient baobab tree near the village well shelters a Toula djinn who tests the character of those who seek his aid.
stories.title: The Djinn of the Hollow Baobab

stories.name: The Djinn of the Sahara Well
stories.excerpt: A Tunisian desert folktale about a lone traveler crossing the Sahara who discovers a hidden well. As he drinks from its cool water, a voice emerges from the darkness—a djinn, keeper of the well, bound to the place since ancient times. The traveler, driven by greed, demands riches. The djinn three tests: first, carry wa
stories.title: The Djinn of the Sahara Well

stories.name: The Dodo and the Hunter's Fire
stories.excerpt: Three Hausa hunters track a Dodo into the deep bush, only to discover that the monstrous shapeshifter feeds not on flesh but on fear, and the only weapon that defeats it is courage unmasked.
stories.title: The Dodo and the Hunter's Fire

stories.name: The Dog-Turks and the Sámi Women
stories.excerpt: A story from Emilie Demant Hatt's collection featuring mysterious 'Dog-Turks' as attackers. Sámi women are the protagonists who outfox their attackers and save their people. The tale reflects the historical vulnerability of Sámi communities to various outside groups and highlights the agency and cleverness of Sámi wome
stories.title: The Dog-Turks and the Sámi Women

stories.name: the Dokkaebi and the Magic Club
stories.excerpt: A mischievous goblin who can grant wishes with his magic club — but only to those who can answer his riddles — and if you steal his club, you become a goblin yourself.
stories.title: the Dokkaebi and the Magic Club

stories.name: The Dokkaebi Between the Fences
stories.excerpt: A goblin who carries whispered messages across the DMZ for families separated by the war, slipping between barbed wire and landmines because even goblins know that some messages cannot wait.
stories.title: The Dokkaebi Between the Fences

stories.name: the Dokkaebi Gam, the Medicine Goblin
stories.excerpt: A goblin who lives in the market, stealing spices from greedy merchants and healing the sick with stolen herbs — because in Korea, even goblins have a sense of justice.
stories.title: the Dokkaebi Gam, the Medicine Goblin

stories.name: The Dokkaebi of the Erased Village
stories.excerpt: A goblin who continues to play his games in a village that was demolished by the state, its houses torn down and its name removed from every map — because the Dokkaebi remembers what the state wants forgotten.
stories.title: The Dokkaebi of the Erased Village

stories.name: The Domovoi of Izba 17
stories.excerpt: A house spirit who protects a peasant family tests their gratitude by disappearing for a week, and the chaos that follows teaches them never to forget his name.
stories.title: The Domovoi of Izba 17

stories.name: The Donkey
stories.excerpt: Once upon a time, in a small German village, there lived a young prince who found himself transformed into a donkey.
stories.title: The Donkey

stories.name: The Donkey Skin
stories.excerpt: A princess flees an unwanted marriage to her father by wearing a donkey skin disguise. She works as a servant until a prince falls in love with her true identity.
stories.title: The Donkey Skin

stories.name: The Doomed Prince
stories.excerpt: In this ancient Egyptian tale, a king and queen are finally granted a son after long prayers. The Hathor goddesses arrive at the birth and prophesy that the child will die by either a crocodile, a serpent, or a dog. Desperate to protect his son, the king builds an isolated fortress in the desert where the prince is con
stories.title: The Doomed Prince

stories.name: The Douen: Lost Children of Trinidad
stories.excerpt: Douen are the spirits of unbaptized children who died before receiving Christian names in Trinidadian folklore. They appear as small children wearing large straw hats that hide their faces, and they walk with their feet pointing backwards — making their footprints appear to go in the opposite direction. Douen are known
stories.title: The Douen: Lost Children of Trinidad

stories.name: The dragon and daughter
stories.excerpt: A traditional tale involving a dragon and a princess, typically focusing on a hero's quest to rescue the maiden or a bargain made to save the kingdom from the dragon's wrath.
stories.title: The dragon and daughter

stories.name: The Dragon Gate
stories.excerpt: A story explaining how carp transform into dragons by leaping the Dragon Gate waterfall.
stories.title: The Dragon Gate

stories.name: The Dragon of Babylon
stories.excerpt: A simple shepherd saves a city from a terrifying dragon, proving that faith and wit are more powerful than the sharpest sword.
stories.title: The Dragon of Babylon

stories.name: The Dragon of Belgrade
stories.excerpt: Long ago, a fearsome dragon made its lair beneath what would become Belgrade Fortress, at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers.
stories.title: The Dragon of Belgrade

stories.name: The Dragon of Lopburi
stories.excerpt: In the ancient city of Lopburi, there lived a powerful dragon beneath the great temple.
stories.title: The Dragon of Lopburi

stories.name: The Dragon of Mount Pilatus
stories.excerpt: A dragon crash-landed on a Swiss mountain, and the healing stone from its blood is preserved in a museum to this day.
stories.title: The Dragon of Mount Pilatus

stories.name: The Dragon of Wawel Castle
stories.excerpt: A humble shoemaker saves the city of Kraków by defeating a terrible dragon through cunning rather than strength.
stories.title: The Dragon of Wawel Castle

stories.name: The Draugr's Treasure Guard
stories.excerpt: Across the highlands, many burial mounds are said to be guarded by draugrs—corporeal undead who possess immense strength and magical abilities. These spirits protect their gold and jewelry, attacking any looter who dares disturb their slumber with a crushing grip and a frozen gaze.
stories.title: The Draugr's Treasure Guard

stories.name: The Dream Fast: The Boy Who Became a Robin
stories.excerpt: An Ojibwe boy underwent his vision fast alone in the wilderness, seeking a guardian spirit as was traditional for young people. He prayed and fasted for many days without eating, asking the Creator for guidance. On the final day of his fast, a spirit appeared to him in a vision and promised that he would become a messe
stories.title: The Dream Fast: The Boy Who Became a Robin

stories.name: The Dreamtime
stories.excerpt: The time before time when ancestral spirits created the world and all living things.
stories.title: The Dreamtime

stories.name: The Drekavac in the Cemetery
stories.excerpt: A wailing spirit that rises from the graves of unbaptized children cries through the villages of Bosnia at night, and those who listen too closely hear the names of the children no one spoke aloud.
stories.title: The Drekavac in the Cemetery

stories.name: The Drowned Church
stories.excerpt: In the Czech Republic, the golem is the most famous creature of Jewish folklore — a being made of clay and brought to life by the power of God's name.
stories.title: The Drowned Church

stories.name: The Drum of Thunder Calls Rain
stories.excerpt: A humble drum maker is asked to make a sacred drum for the Thunder God—but pride leads to disaster.
stories.title: The Drum of Thunder Calls Rain

stories.name: The Duende of Machu Picchu
stories.excerpt: A small forest spirit guards the hidden ruins of Machu Picchu, testing the worthiness of those who climb to the sacred city.
stories.title: The Duende of Machu Picchu

stories.name: The Duppy of Brimstone Hill
stories.excerpt: A young soldier stationed at Brimstone Hill Fort ignores the old guard's warning about duppies and is visited by a restless spirit in the dead of night.
stories.title: The Duppy of Brimstone Hill

stories.name: The Dzin of the Bazaar
stories.excerpt: A spirit bound to the old marketplaces of Bosnia, the Dzin grants fortunes to those it favors and misfortune to those who deal dishonestly, serving as an unseen guardian of fair trade.
stories.title: The Dzin of the Bazaar

stories.name: The Dödning of Skåne
stories.excerpt: In the rich farmlands of Skåne, the southernmost province of Sweden, there was a farmer named Nils who was known for one thing: he never paid his debts.
stories.title: The Dödning of Skåne

stories.name: The Eagle and Whale Husbands
stories.excerpt: A legendary tale of Inuit women who find themselves married to powerful animal spirits — an eagle and a whale. These unions are fraught with difficulty as the women struggle to balance their human needs with the demands of their supernatural spouses. The story highlights the complexities of kinship and the influence of
stories.title: The Eagle and Whale Husbands

stories.name: The Eland Creation: /Kaggen's Favorite Animal
stories.excerpt: /Kaggen's wife /Hunntu!att!atten gave birth to the eland, and /Kaggen hid it near a secluded cliff to let it grow. His sons Cogaz and Gewi, not knowing their father's love for the animal, went hunting and killed it. Enraged, /Kaggen told Gewi to churn the eland's blood in a pot. Blood spattered onto the ground and turn
stories.title: The Eland Creation: /Kaggen's Favorite Animal

stories.name: The Elephant and the Sparrow
stories.excerpt: In a lush forest of ancient India, there lived a great elephant named Channa.. He was massive and powerful, with tusks white as pearls and ears like great fans.
stories.title: The Elephant and the Sparrow

stories.name: The Elk and the Lucky Reindeer
stories.excerpt: A hunting legend from Emilie Demant Hatt's collection about an elk with supernatural qualities and the concept of 'reindeer luck.' stories.title: The Elk and the Lucky Reindeer

stories.name: The Eloko of the BaAka Forest
stories.excerpt: A BaAka family traveling through the forest at dusk hears the laughter of an Eloko, a cannibal dwarf spirit, and must use their knowledge of ancient songs and forest lore to evade the creature.
stories.title: The Eloko of the BaAka Forest

stories.name: The Eloko Who Wanted a Name
stories.excerpt: A lonely Eloko spirit approaches a Gbaya village not to hunt but to ask for a human name, believing it will grant passage into the world of people, and learns a painful lesson about the boundaries between worlds.
stories.title: The Eloko Who Wanted a Name

stories.name: The Elusive White Reindeer
stories.excerpt: A Sámi nature myth about the white reindeer, considered a sacred and powerful creature. Seeing a white reindeer was considered an omen, and its appearance in dreams signaled major life changes.
