stories.title: The Elusive White Reindeer

stories.name: The Elves and the Shoemaker
stories.excerpt: On the misty moors of Devon and Cornwall, where the fog rolls in from the sea and covers the land like a blanket, there is a light that leads travelers to their doom.
stories.title: The Elves and the Shoemaker

stories.name: The Emadloti of King Sobhuza
stories.excerpt: When a Swazi king is buried with his cattle, the spirit-emadloti rise as guardians of the royal lineage, protecting the bloodline from those who would seize the throne.
stories.title: The Emadloti of King Sobhuza

stories.name: The Emergence (Jicarilla Apache)
stories.excerpt: In the Jicarilla Apache emergence story, White God of the East made a mountain that grew toward the sky and caused reeds to stand in the center. stories.title: The Emergence (Jicarilla Apache)

stories.name: The Emperor's New Clothes
stories.excerpt: There was an emperor in Denmark who was so vain—so obsessed with new clothes—that he spent all his money on the finest garments.
stories.title: The Emperor's New Clothes

stories.name: The Enchanted Deer
stories.excerpt: In the sun-drenched hills of Italy, there once lived a poor hunter who spent his days tracking game through the dense forests that covered the mountainsides.
stories.title: The Enchanted Deer

stories.name: The Enchanted Duck
stories.excerpt: A humble princess endures years of absolute silence to save her sisters from a magical curse.
stories.title: The Enchanted Duck

stories.name: The Enchanted Forest
stories.excerpt: Two siblings lost in the enchanted forest of Tiveden must use their wisdom and purity of heart to solve riddles posed by mystical spirits to find their way home.
stories.title: The Enchanted Forest

stories.name: The Enchanted Mule
stories.excerpt: In the hills of Andalusia, where Spain meets the Mediterranean sun, there lies a path that appears only at night—a road that leads to a place beyond human understanding.
stories.title: The Enchanted Mule

stories.name: The Epic of Ak-Kaan
stories.excerpt: Ak-Kaan ('White Khan') is an Altai heroic epic telling of a shining white khan who brought justice to the Altai mountains. Born with a divine radiance, Ak-Kaan could see through deception and hear lies hidden in words. His quest was to defeat the dark shamans serving Erlik and restore balance between the upper and lowe
stories.title: The Epic of Ak-Kaan

stories.name: The Epic of Alpamysh (Uzbek Version)
stories.excerpt: The Uzbek version of Alpamysh (Alpomish) is the national heroic epic of Uzbekistan, with the largest recorded version by bard Fazil Yuldashogli containing 14,000 verses. stories.title: The Epic of Alpamysh (Uzbek Version)

stories.name: The Epic of Amir Timur's Rise
stories.excerpt: According to Uzbek legend, the great conqueror Amir Timur (Tamerlane) was born with a clot of dried blood in his fist — a sign of his destiny as a warrior. As a young man, he was a sheep thief and a bandit until a vision from the spirit of his ancestor showed him his true path. After being wounded in battle, he limped
stories.title: The Epic of Amir Timur's Rise

stories.name: The Epic of Dimdim (Kela Dimdimê)
stories.excerpt: A Kurdish heroic epic based on the historical siege of Dimdim Castle (1609-1610) in the Bradost region near Lake Urmia. The Kurdish leader Emir Khan Lepzerin (Xanê Lepzêrîn, 'Gold-Arm Khan') rebuilt the ancient fortress of Dimdim on a 2,000-meter mountain. The Persian Safavid Shah Abbas the Great, seeing the growing Ku
stories.title: The Epic of Dimdim (Kela Dimdimê)

stories.name: The Epic of Geser Khan
stories.excerpt: Geser Khan is the central hero of one of the great Mongolian epics. Born as a runny-nosed, despised child on the Mongolian steppe, he is actually the son of the sky-deity Khürmasta Tengri, sent to earth to defeat the demons (mangus) that are devouring the world. Despite being mocked and rejected, Geser grows to defeat
stories.title: The Epic of Geser Khan

stories.excerpt: Jangar is a heroic epic of the Oirat Mongols (Kalmyks), comprising hundreds of thousands of lines. stories.title: The Epic of Jangar

stories.excerpt: Maadai-Kara is one of the greatest Altai heroic epics, narrating a thousand-year struggle compressed into two generations. stories.title: The Epic of Maadai-Kara

stories.excerpt: The Epic of Manas is the longest epic poem in the world (500,000+ lines), central to Kyrgyz national identity. Manas was born to the elderly and childless Jakyp in exile on the Altai. His birth was marked by supernatural signs — a mysterious light filled the tent, the earth trembled, and the sky thundered. Even as an i
stories.title: The Epic of Manas: The Birth of the Hero

stories.name: The Epic of Sundiata (Mande)
stories.excerpt: Sundiata Keita was the crippled son of King Naré Maghann Konaté and the ugly, hunchbacked woman Sogolon. A prophecy foretold that Sogolon's son would become a great king. After his father's death, Sundiata and his mother were persecuted by the king's first wife and forced into exile. During his exile in the Mema kingdo
stories.title: The Epic of Sundiata (Mande)

stories.name: The Erlking
stories.excerpt: A father rode through the dark forest late at night, his feverish child pressed close against his chest.
stories.title: The Erlking

stories.name: The Eternal Chase of the Sun and Moon
stories.excerpt: Aningaut (the Moon) and his sister Malina (the Sun) are locked in a perpetual race across the sky. The conflict began when Aningaut marked Malina's face with soot. stories.title: The Eternal Chase of the Sun and Moon

stories.name: The Eternal Fool
stories.excerpt: Once upon a time, in a quiet corner of Sweden, there lived a boy who was known to everyone as the Fool.
stories.title: The Eternal Fool

stories.excerpt: Before the world as we know it existed, before the sun rose and set, before the first humans walked the earth, there were two brothers whose eternal struggle shaped the cosmos itself.
stories.title: The Eternal Struggle: Quetzalcoatl

stories.name: The Eternal Wisdom of Ifa Divination (Yoruba)
stories.excerpt: Orunmila, the Orisha of wisdom and divination, received the sacred Odu Ifa from Olodumare at the beginning of time. The Ifa system consists of 256 sacred verses (Odu) that encode the entire knowledge of the universe—history, medicine, philosophy, and prophecy. Orunmila taught the Ifa to humanity through Babalawos (fath
stories.title: The Eternal Wisdom of Ifa Divination (Yoruba)

stories.name: The Evil One and Kitta Grau
stories.excerpt: The Devil meets Kitta Grau, a sharp-tongued old woman, and she out-argues, out-cheats, and out-schemes him at every turn — proving that a clever woman can best even the Prince of Darkness. This tale from Halland shows that a wicked woman outdoes the Devil himself.

stories.name: The Exodus from Notsie (Ewe)
stories.excerpt: The Ewe people once lived under the tyrannical rule of King Agokoli (Togbe Agorkoli) in the walled city of Notsie (in present-day Togo). stories.title: The Exodus from Notsie (Ewe)

stories.name: The Eyes of Horus
stories.excerpt: The battle between Horus and Set raged across the sky and earth for eighty years.
stories.title: The Eyes of Horus

stories.name: The Fairy of the Well
stories.excerpt: In a small Polish village, there lived a girl called Złota—the golden one—not because she was wealthy, but because her hair shone like wheat in the summer sun.
stories.title: The Fairy of the Well

stories.name: The Fairy Ointment
stories.excerpt: A young woman's curiosity leads her to use a forbidden fairy ointment, revealing a hidden world of both wonder and unsettling truth.
stories.title: The Fairy Ointment

stories.name: The Faithful Animals
stories.excerpt: A poor woodcutter lived with his wife and children in a cottage at the edge of a great forest.
stories.title: The Faithful Animals

stories.name: The Fanditha Sorcerer and the Demon of Fuvahmulah
stories.excerpt: On the atoll of Fuvahmulah in the Maldives, legend tells of a kan'du fureytha (ocean demon) that emerged from the water as a 'pale, large flame looming over the rocks,' terrifying the islanders. The demon dragged people into the sea, and in despair, the inhabitants of one island sought help from Edhurutakkaange Mohamed
stories.title: The Fanditha Sorcerer and the Demon of Fuvahmulah

stories.name: The Farsakh Walker
stories.excerpt: A giant who measured distances with his stride is said to have carved the great passes through the Pamir, leaving behind valleys that mortals still travel.
stories.title: The Farsakh Walker

stories.name: The Fate of Aino
stories.excerpt: Wainamoinen falls in love with the young Aino, but she is horrified by his advanced age and lacks any affection for him. Despite her desperate pleas, her parents force her to marry the old enchanter. In a final act of desperation to escape her fate, Aino leaps into the sea, where she is transformed into a mermaid-like
stories.title: The Fate of Aino

stories.name: The Ferocity of the Adlet
stories.excerpt: The Adlet are a race of half-dog, half-human hybrids, possessing the lower body of a canine and the upper body of a human. stories.title: The Ferocity of the Adlet

stories.name: The Fiddler Who Got the Madonna's Golden Shoe
stories.excerpt: A wandering fiddler (spelman) in medieval Sweden finds himself blessed by a miraculous encounter with the Madonna, who gives him one of her golden shoes as a reward for his devoted music. The tale draws on Catholic and folk motifs, blending Christian iconography with Scandinavian folk music tradition.
stories.title: The Fiddler Who Got the Madonna's Golden Shoe

stories.name: The Fig Tree Covenant
stories.excerpt: When Ngai created Gikuyu and showed him the land, he made a sacred covenant beneath the wild fig tree (Mukuyu). Ngai said to Gikuyu: 'Descend from my home and establish your homestead among these fig trees. Whenever you are in need of me, make a sacrifice upon this tree and raise your hands to Kirinyaga, and I, the Pos
stories.title: The Fig Tree Covenant

stories.name: The Fire Keeper of the Gaucho Camps
stories.excerpt: A spirit of the campfire who appears to gauchos in the wilderness, testing their hospitality and generosity.
stories.title: The Fire Keeper of the Gaucho Camps

stories.name: The Firebird
stories.excerpt: A humble prince embarks on a perilous quest for a magical bird, learning that kindness and integrity are the true keys to success.
stories.title: The Firebird

stories.name: The First Areíto Drum
stories.excerpt: A Taíno legend explaining the origin of the sacred areíto drum. One night, a cacique (chief) prayed to the zemís asking h
stories.title: The First Areíto Drum

stories.name: The First Banana: A Baganda Legend
stories.excerpt: According to Baganda tradition, the banana (matooke) was a gift from the gods to sustain humanity. In the time after Kintu, the people had grain but no fruit trees. One day, a woman named Nalongo was mourning the death of her twin children. She buried them in her courtyard and watered their graves with her tears. From
stories.title: The First Banana: A Baganda Legend

stories.name: The First Corn
stories.excerpt: The gods sacrifice themselves to feed humanity. Centers on Spirit, human attempt to understand the soul, afterlife, and the unseen forces that govern existence..
stories.title: The First Corn

stories.name: The First Fire Stolen from the Sky
stories.excerpt: An Evenki myth explaining how humans first obtained fire. In the beginning, the ancestors of the Evenki lived in eternal cold without fire. A brave shaman or culture hero transformed into a bird and flew up to the sky, where he stole a burning ember from the celestial realm. He brought the fire down to the frozen taiga
stories.title: The First Fire Stolen from the Sky

stories.name: The First Hmong Shaman: How the Shaman Got His Power
stories.excerpt: One of the most sacred Hmong myths explains the origins of shamanic power and the relationship between the human and spirit worlds. stories.title: The First Hmong Shaman: How the Shaman Got His Power

stories.name: The First Navigator
stories.excerpt: An ancient navigator discovers the secrets of the stars and the ocean's swells, guiding his people to new lands and establishing the art of wayfinding.
stories.title: The First Navigator

stories.name: The First Prayer Flag
stories.excerpt: A Tibetan legend explaining the origin of the iconic Tibetan prayer flags (Lungta or Wind Horse flags). According to the tradition, when the Buddha's teachings were first spreading in Tibet, harmful spirits and negative energies threatened the people. The great master Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche) used prayer flags as
stories.title: The First Prayer Flag

stories.name: The First Reindeer
stories.excerpt: A Chukchi legend explaining the origin of the domesticated reindeer, essential to Chukchi survival in the Arctic tundra. According to the myth, Kuutkh created the reindeer from the scattered hairs of his own body or from the remnants of a celestial hunt. The reindeer was given to humanity as a gift from the sky spirits
stories.title: The First Reindeer

stories.name: The First Strawberries (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: The first man and the first woman quarreled, and the woman left their home in anger. The man, sad and remorseful, tried to bring her back. The Sun, taking pity on the man, created huckleberries along the path to tempt the woman to stop, but she paid them no mind. Next the Sun created blackberries, but she ignored them
stories.title: The First Strawberries (Cherokee)

stories.name: The First Sweat Lodge (Lakota)
stories.excerpt: According to Lakota tradition, the sweat lodge was given to the people by the spirits as a means of purification and healing. A warrior who had been wounded in battle was near death when a spirit appeared and instructed him to build a framework of willow branches and cover it with buffalo hides. He was to heat stones i
stories.title: The First Sweat Lodge (Lakota)

stories.name: The Fisherman and His Wife
stories.excerpt: There was once a poor fisherman who lived with his wife, Ilsebill, in a miserable hovel by the sea — a place so small and filthy it was scarcely better than a pigsty.
stories.title: The Fisherman and His Wife

stories.excerpt: A poor fisherman casts his net four times daily. On the fourth cast, he hauls up a copper jar sealed with Solomon's seal. stories.title: The Fisherman and the Jinni

stories.name: The Fisherman Sikur and the Troll Net
stories.excerpt: Sikur the fisherman acquires a magical fishing net. When a troll steals the net, Sikur's three sons — one the fastest in the world, one the strongest, and one the wisest — team up to trick the troll and retrieve the net. stories.excerpt: Deep in the Swedish forest, on the sun-drenched peak of Sunnymount Crest (Solberga klint), grows a magical flower that grants happiness to whoever finds it. Two young girls set out on a perilous journey through the deep woods where trolls, fairies, and witches keep their secrets. Their only hope of true happiness lies
stories.title: The Flower of Happiness on Sunnymount Crest

stories.name: The Flying Canoe (Passamaquoddy)
stories.excerpt: Three Passamaquoddy brothers, all skilled canoe-builders, competed to see who could build the finest canoe. The eldest two built large, sturdy vessels decorated with porcupine quills and painted designs. But the youngest brother, instead of building an ordinary canoe, consulted the spirits and built a magical canoe tha
stories.title: The Flying Canoe (Passamaquoddy)

stories.name: The Flying Dutchman
stories.excerpt: The Flying Dutchman is the most famous ghost ship in maritime history — a vessel condemned to sail the oceans forever, never making port, never finding rest.
stories.title: The Flying Dutchman

stories.name: The Flying Dutchman of the Cape
stories.excerpt: A ghost ship doomed to sail forever around the Cape of Good Hope, appearing to doomed sailors as a warning.
stories.title: The Flying Dutchman of the Cape

stories.name: The Flying Head (Kanontsistóntie)
stories.excerpt: The Flying Head is a terrifying monster in the form of a giant disembodied head as tall as a man, covered in thick black hair with bat-like wings and long sharp claws. It comes to the homes of widows and orphans at night, beating its wings on the walls and issuing terrible cries, presaging death within days. According
stories.title: The Flying Head (Kanontsistóntie)

stories.name: The Flying Trunk
stories.excerpt: A man acquires a magic trunk that allows him to fly. He uses this power to travel the world and eventually wins the hand of a princess by demonstrating his supernatural abilities.
stories.title: The Flying Trunk

stories.name: The Forest Keeper of Mount Manengouba
stories.excerpt: Deep in the forests of Mount Manengouba, the Boumba forest spirit protects the ancient trees and punishes those who would destroy what took centuries to grow.
stories.title: The Forest Keeper of Mount Manengouba

stories.name: The Forty Robbers of the Steppe (Kirk Kazak)
stories.excerpt: The legend of the 'Forty Kazakhs' (Kirk Kazak) tells of forty exiled warriors who formed a brotherhood on the Kazakh steppe. According to tradition, the sons of a khan's younger wife, offended by their older brothers, fled to the steppe with thirty-three other exiles. They banded together as forty warriors, defending t
stories.title: The Forty Robbers of the Steppe (Kirk Kazak)

stories.name: The Foster-Child of the Deer
stories.excerpt: A Zuni story about a child abandoned in the wilderness who was adopted and raised by deer. The deer taught the child to live in harmony with nature, to understand the language of animals, and to know the sacred plants of the forest. When the child grew up and encountered human hunters, a conflict arose between the huma
stories.title: The Foster-Child of the Deer

stories.name: The Four Big Trolls and Little Peter Pastureman
stories.excerpt: When the old Troll King dies, four enormous trolls — each as large as a mountain — vie for the throne. Their vicious rivalry threatens all magical folk in the kingdom, as their power struggles cause chaos throughout the land. Little Peter, a brave and lighthearted shepherd boy (called Vill-Vallareman in Swedish) who wo
stories.title: The Four Big Trolls and Little Peter Pastureman

stories.name: The Four Carpenters and the Creation of the World (Nuxalk)
stories.excerpt: When the world was first created, the Creator Alhkw'ntam had help from Four Carpenters called the Masmasalanicw, who were like human beings with wings — angels. They carved the first ancestors from the cosmic tree Tcncniyaaq (the Milky Way). There were 45 original families, each with their own room in the House of Smay
stories.title: The Four Carpenters and the Creation of the World (Nuxalk)

stories.name: The Four White Umbrellas: The Burmese Creation of Kingship
stories.excerpt: According to Burmese mythology, the institution of kingship began in the earliest age of the world when human society descended into chaos and conflict after losing its primordial harmony. The people, suffering from theft, violence, and disorder, gathered together and elected the most virtuous and handsome man among th
stories.title: The Four White Umbrellas: The Burmese Creation of Kingship

stories.name: The Fox as Herdsman
stories.excerpt: A farmer hires a fox to be a herdsman for his sheep, believing the fox's promises of efficiency. However, the fox uses his cunning to deceive the farmer, stealing the sheep one by one while making the farmer believe the sheep are disappearing due to supernatural causes.
stories.title: The Fox as Herdsman

stories.name: The Fox Spirit
stories.excerpt: In the mountains and forests of Japan, where the bamboo sways in the wind and the shrines disappear into mist, there live foxes—yoko, the animal foxes.
stories.title: The Fox Spirit

stories.name: The Fox Tricks the Bear
stories.excerpt: A Sámi animal fable where the cunning fox outsmarts the bear. The fox uses clever words and deception to avoid being eaten. These tales parallel international trickster traditions but with distinct Sámi elements—the animals are those of the Arctic. The tales teach that intelligence is more valuable than brute strength.
stories.title: The Fox Tricks the Bear

stories.name: The Frog Prince
stories.excerpt: In the days when wishes still worked and magic was as common as morning dew, there lived a king whose youngest daughter was so beautiful that the sun itself stopped to stare when she stepped into the garden.
stories.title: The Frog Prince

stories.name: The Frog Princess
stories.excerpt: A tsar commands his three sons to marry, and the youngest chooses a frog from the river who is really a princess under a spell.
stories.title: The Frog Princess

stories.name: The Frost Giant's Breath
stories.excerpt: A village is plagued by a sudden, unnatural winter that kills all the crops. It is discovered that a Frost Giant has awakened from his sleep beneath the glacier. The villagers must travel to the heart of the ice and perform a ritual of fire and song to lull the giant back into a deep slumber.
stories.title: The Frost Giant's Breath

stories.name: The Frost-fiend
stories.excerpt: The heroes face an encounter with the personification of winter, the Frost-fiend. They must rely on their wit, resilience, and magical songs to survive the killing cold and the oppressive environment of the extreme north.
stories.title: The Frost-fiend

stories.name: The Fur Coat
stories.excerpt: In a cold German winter, in a village nestled deep in the Black Forest, a poor girl was walking home through a forest when she found a fur coat lying in the snow.
stories.title: The Fur Coat

stories.name: The Gahe: Apache Mountain Spirit Dancers
stories.excerpt: The Gahe (called Gaan by Western Apache) are the Mountain Spirits, powerful supernatural beings who live inside sacred mountains. The first Mountain Spirit ceremony originated when children of the Sun taught the Apache how to call and honor these spirits. The Mountain Spirits appear as masked dancers wearing distinctiv
stories.title: The Gahe: Apache Mountain Spirit Dancers

stories.name: the Gangsi, the Hungry Ghost
stories.excerpt: A reanimated corpse that hops through the night with outstretched arms, draining the life force from the living — because in Korea, the dead do not always stay dead.
stories.title: the Gangsi, the Hungry Ghost

stories.name: The Garamantes: Lost People of the Fezzan
stories.excerpt: The Garamantes were an ancient civilization that flourished in the Fezzan region of southwestern Libya from approximately 1000 BCE to 700 CE. According to Herodotus, who first wrote of them in the 5th century BCE, the Garamantes were a 'very great nation' who cultivated date palms, bred cattle, and hunted cave-dwelling
stories.title: The Garamantes: Lost People of the Fezzan

stories.name: The Garden of Paradise
stories.excerpt: A contemplative story exploring themes of beauty, the unattainable nature of a perfect world, and the human desire for a paradise that exists only in dreams or the afterlife.
stories.title: The Garden of Paradise

stories.name: The Ghost Bride of the Sea Islands
stories.excerpt: A young Gullah man named Joshua fell in love with a woman named Eloise, the most beautiful woman on the Sea Islands. They were to be married, but on the night before the wedding, Eloise fell ill and died of a sudden fever. Joshua was heartbroken. On the night of what would have been their wedding, Joshua sat alone on t
stories.title: The Ghost Bride of the Sea Islands

stories.name: The Ghost Monk of Eynhallow
stories.excerpt: The ghost of a medieval monk haunts the abandoned island of Eynhallow in Orkney, appearing each night to ring a bell that no living ear can hear.
stories.title: The Ghost Monk of Eynhallow

stories.name: The Ghost of the Lhamo (Tibetan Wrathful Deities)
stories.excerpt: Tibetan legends of the Lhamo — powerful female wrathful deities who serve as protectors of the Buddhist teachings. The most famous is Palden Lhamo (Glorious Goddess), the principal female protector deity of Tibetan Buddhism. According to legend, she was a wild, blood-drinking demoness who was converted to Buddhism by t
stories.title: The Ghost of the Lhamo (Tibetan Wrathful Deities)

stories.name: The Ghost Torch
stories.excerpt: In the islands of Fiji, where the jungle meets the coral reefs and the nights are thick with the songs of insects, the villagers tell a story about a flickering light that appears on the mountain paths after dark.
stories.title: The Ghost Torch

stories.name: The Ghost Who Walked Between Worlds
stories.excerpt: A family discovers their deceased grandfather still lingers at the edge of the village, walking the moonlit path between the living and the dead.
stories.title: The Ghost Who Walked Between Worlds

stories.name: The Ghostly Monks of Trondheimsfjorden
stories.excerpt: Three monasteries in the Trondheimsfjord left behind more than ruins — their ghostly monks still walk the shores.
stories.title: The Ghostly Monks of Trondheimsfjorden

stories.name: The Ghostly Wedding of the Highlands
stories.excerpt: Two lovers, separated by death, are said to meet every century in a hidden valley in the highlands. They hold a ghostly wedding feast attended by other spirits of the land. Those who stumble upon the feast are often entranced for days, waking up to find that a hundred years have passed in the human world.
stories.title: The Ghostly Wedding of the Highlands

stories.name: The Ghoul of Kerak Castle
stories.excerpt: A Crusader-era garrison at Kerak Castle discovers that the dungeons beneath the fortress house a ghoul older than the castle itself, and that it has been feeding on the fears of every army that has claimed these walls.
stories.title: The Ghoul of Kerak Castle

stories.name: The Ghoul of Oualata
stories.excerpt: A young widower in the ancient city of Oualata is stalked by a female ghoul who takes the form of his late wife, and must use the wisdom of a blind marabout to survive her embrace.
stories.title: The Ghoul of Oualata

stories.name: The Ghoul of the Desert
stories.excerpt: In pre-Islamic Arabic folklore, the ghul (ghoul) is a demonic, shape-shifting creature inhabiting deserts and graveyards. Usually appearing female to lure unwary travelers, the ghul has donkey-like hooves, a feline head, forked tongue, and hairy skin. It calls victims by name in the voice of a loved one, then devours t
stories.title: The Ghoul of the Desert

stories.name: The Ghoul of the Roman Road
stories.excerpt: A merchant travelling the ancient Roman road near Jerash is lured from his path by a ghoul disguised as a woman selling bread, and learns too late that the desert's most dangerous predators take human form.
stories.title: The Ghoul of the Roman Road

stories.name: The Ghoula of the Date Palm Grove
stories.excerpt: A young pearl diver encounters a shape-shifting Al Ghoula in the date palm groves near Riffa, and must outwit her to survive the night.
stories.title: The Ghoula of the Date Palm Grove

stories.name: The Giant Cloud-Swallower
stories.excerpt: A Zuni story about a giant being who swallowed clouds, causing drought and suffering among the people. With the clouds gone, no rain fell, and the crops withered. The people performed ceremonies and made prayer offerings, but nothing worked. The twin war gods took action, pursuing the Giant Cloud-swallower across the s
stories.title: The Giant Cloud-Swallower

stories.name: The Giant Maiden in Boråseröd Mountain
stories.excerpt: A young peasant captures a beautiful giant's daughter by throwing his knife between her and the mountain. At the wedding feast the giant eats until half full, ensuring only half the couple's descendants become great. After years of abuse the wife reveals her supernatural strength, teaching her husband true humility.
stories.title: The Giant Maiden in Boråseröd Mountain

stories.name: The Giant of Dovrefjell
stories.excerpt: Deep in the mountains of the north lives a giant king who rules over a court of trolls and mountain spirits. He is known for his immense size and his ability to manipulate the weather. In legends, he challenges brave heroes to riddles and tests of strength, often rewarding them with gold or cursing them with madness.
stories.title: The Giant of Dovrefjell

stories.name: The Giant Puke
stories.excerpt: The giant Puke lives in a mountain near Lofta church, tormented by church bells and holy water. His daughter throws a stone at the church but misses. She later finds human children at play and brings them to her father, who declares that the age of giants is past. Puke leaves for Götland and gives a ship captain a magi
stories.title: The Giant Puke

stories.name: The Giant Vrål of Bohuslän
stories.excerpt: The giant Vrål of Bohuslän forces a farmer to give up his daughter in marriage, and she serves him a bowl of porridge laced with 24 horseshoe nails — which he eats without noticing until the last one.
stories.title: The Giant Vrål of Bohuslän

stories.name: The Giant Without a Heart
stories.excerpt: The youngest prince, known as Boots, embarks on a perilous quest to save his six brothers who were turned to stone by a heartless giant with a hidden weakness.
stories.title: The Giant Without a Heart

stories.name: The Gift of Fire (Comanche)
stories.excerpt: Long ago, the Comanche people had no fire and ate their food raw. Coyote, always clever, decided to steal fire from the fire people who guarded it jealously. Coyote crept into their camp and, when they weren't looking, grabbed a burning branch and ran. The fire people chased him across the plains. Coyote threw the fire
stories.title: The Gift of Fire (Comanche)

stories.name: The Gifts From the Underworld
stories.excerpt: An envious old bachelor seeks a way to surpass a younger, more successful hunter. Guided by his mother, he discovers a hidden path to the underworld. He is instructed to ignore the first boat he sees and take a piece of matak (whale-skin) from the second. The matak grants him incredible hunting luck, but when he tries
stories.title: The Gifts From the Underworld

stories.name: The Girl and the Snake
stories.excerpt: A girl lost in the forest meets a talking snake who offers to guide her home in exchange for a promise — a promise that leads to an enchanted romance beneath the earth. This tale from Södermanland shows distinctive Scandinavian features.
stories.title: The Girl and the Snake

stories.name: The Girl and the Spirit Drum
stories.excerpt: In the heart of Sudan, where the sun beats down with a relentless intensity and the dust of the desert chokes the breath of the living, a terrible famine had descended upon the land.
stories.title: The Girl and the Spirit Drum

stories.name: The Girl Chenoo
stories.excerpt: A beautiful Mi'kmaq woman was lost in the frozen north and suffered terrible hunger. To survive, she ate human flesh and was transformed into a Chenoo — a cannibalistic ice monster with a heart of ice and an insatiable hunger for human beings. Her family searched for her but when they found her, she had become a monstr
stories.title: The Girl Chenoo

stories.name: The Girl Who Climbed to the Sky
stories.excerpt: An Arapaho girl was picking berries when she saw a porcupine in a tree. She climbed after it, but the tree grew taller and taller, carrying her into the sky world. In the sky, she found a beautiful land populated by spirits. She married a sky spirit and was happy, but she missed her earthly family. The spirits taught h
stories.title: The Girl Who Climbed to the Sky

stories.name: The Girl Who Had No Eyes
stories.excerpt: In the wild and windswept Highlands of Scotland, where the mist rolls down from the mountains like a grey river and the heather stretches purple to the horizon, there lived a girl named Mhairi.
stories.title: The Girl Who Had No Eyes

stories.name: The Girl Who Married a Star
stories.excerpt: A Crow girl gazed at the sky and wished to marry the Morning Star. Her wish was granted, and she was taken to the sky world where she became the wife of a star. She was happy but was told never to dig up a certain root. Lonely for her family, she eventually disobeyed and pulled the root, revealing a hole through which
stories.title: The Girl Who Married a Star

stories.name: The Girl Who Stood in the Door
stories.excerpt: There was a little girl—her name was Lis, and she was the happiest, most content child in the village.
stories.title: The Girl Who Stood in the Door

stories.name: The Girl Who Understood Birds
stories.excerpt: A quiet girl who can communicate with birds uses her unique gift to save a dying child and teach her village the value of listening to nature.
stories.title: The Girl Who Understood Birds

stories.name: The Girl Who Was Not Satisfied
stories.excerpt: This moral tale from the Iroquois tradition tells of a young girl who was never content with what she had, always wanting more and better things. She rejected the simple life of her village and the young men who courted her. One day she met a handsome stranger who was actually a great serpent in disguise. She went away
stories.title: The Girl Who Was Not Satisfied

stories.name: The Girls Who Wished to Marry Stars
stories.excerpt: Two Ojibwe girls slept outside one summer night, gazing at the stars. They began to wish out loud — one wished to marry the brightest star, the other wished to marry the Morning Star. To their astonishment, the stars descended and took them to the sky world. At first, everything was wonderful beyond imagination, but th
stories.title: The Girls Who Wished to Marry Stars

stories.name: The Glass Mountain
stories.excerpt: A brave youth overcomes an impossible ascent to rescue a princess from a crystal peak.
stories.title: The Glass Mountain

stories.name: The Goblin and the Grocer
stories.excerpt: A comedic tale about a goblin who attempts to trade his magic for human goods, resulting in a series of misunderstandings and mishaps between the supernatural creature and the practical grocer.
stories.title: The Goblin and the Grocer

stories.name: The Goddess Oshun and the Dried Riverbeds (Yoruba)
stories.excerpt: When the Orishas were creating the world, they neglected to consult Oshun, the goddess of love, fertility, and rivers. Enraged by this disrespect, Oshun withheld her waters, causing the rivers to dry up and the land to become barren. The other Orishas grew desperate as crops failed and life became impossible. Obatala a
stories.title: The Goddess Oshun and the Dried Riverbeds (Yoruba)

stories.name: The Goddess Pattini and the Burning of Madurai
stories.excerpt: Pattini, revered by both Sinhalese Buddhists and Tamil Hindus, originates from Kannaki, the chaste heroine of the Tamil epic Cilappatikaram. Kannaki's husband Kovalan was unjustly executed in Madurai for allegedly stealing the queen's anklet. To prove his innocence, Kannaki revealed her ruby-filled anklet (the queen's
stories.title: The Goddess Pattini and the Burning of Madurai

stories.name: The Golden Cradle
stories.excerpt: A ship carrying a golden cradle for Queen Elenor is wrecked off Tjorn and the islanders murder the crew and plunder the cargo. The cradle is buried in Stordal Heath where it remains hidden to this day. The dying peasant who concealed it tried to reveal its location but his final words were unintelligible.
stories.title: The Golden Cradle

stories.name: The Golden Fish
stories.excerpt: A humble fisherman releases a magical golden fish and discovers that true wealth lies in contentment.
stories.title: The Golden Fish

stories.name: The Golden Frog Creation Myth
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, the earth was submerged in a boundless ocean. When the lord of the universe, Buddha Sakyamuni, flew over the ocean seeking to create land, he saw a golden-bodied frog swimming from north to south. Using his bow and arrows, he shot the frog's east side, turning it northward. Fire gushed from its mouth
stories.title: The Golden Frog Creation Myth

stories.name: The Golden Keys
stories.excerpt: Lena, a humble meadow-maid, encounters three fairies who present her with a golden key that leads to a magical dream garden. This gift comes with a strict condition: the secret must never be revealed to anyone. Lena accepts and experiences the joy of the dream garden, but her loyalty is soon tested when the young king
stories.title: The Golden Keys

stories.name: The Golden Stool Descends from Heaven (Ashanti/Akan)
stories.excerpt: During the reign of the Ashanti King Osei Tutu I, the great priest Okomfo Anokye summoned a golden stool from the sky in a cloud of dust and thunder. The stool, made of pure gold, descended onto the lap of the king, signifying that the Ashanti nation was united under his rule. The Golden Stool is believed to house the
stories.title: The Golden Stool Descends from Heaven (Ashanti/Akan)

stories.name: The Golden Time and How It Ended
stories.excerpt: A southern Sámi creation myth. Jupmele (God) created a perfect world where mountains were clad in gold and silver, flowers bloomed everywhere, and there was no cold, night, or sorrow. Biejjie (the Sun) guarded this world. Two brothers lived: good Naevie and greedy Adtjis. Adtjis' wife came from the underworld with a sa
stories.title: The Golden Time and How It Ended

stories.name: The Golden-Antlered Deer and the Thunder God
stories.excerpt: A Sámi myth about a golden-antlered deer that tries to escape the thunder god Horagalles. The thunder god hunts the celestial deer across the sky—this is the Sámi interpretation of the constellation Orion pursuing the Pleiades. The Milky Way is the tracks of the skis of the mythic elk-hunter.
stories.title: The Golden-Antlered Deer and the Thunder God

stories.name: The Goose Girl
stories.excerpt: There once lived an old queen whose husband had died years before.. She had one beautiful daughter, who was promised in marriage to a prince in a distant kingdom.
stories.title: The Goose Girl

stories.name: The Graveyard Dust Spell
stories.excerpt: In Hoodoo tradition, graveyard dust is among the most potent and dangerous conjure materials. The tale tells of a woman whose husband was stolen away by a rival through love magic. Desperate, she went to a rootworker who instructed her to go to a graveyard at midnight, find the grave of someone who had been a faithful
stories.title: The Graveyard Dust Spell

stories.name: The Great Flood and the Origin of the Tides (Tlingit)
stories.excerpt: Raven made a woman under the earth to have charge of the rise and fall of the tides. One time he wanted to explore everything beneath the ocean and commanded the tide woman to raise the water. She made the tide rise very slowly so the people had time to load their canoes and climb to the mountaintops. As the water lift
stories.title: The Great Flood and the Origin of the Tides (Tlingit)

stories.name: The Great Flood and the Voyage to the Fourth World
stories.excerpt: In the alternative Hopi emergence story, mainly told at Oraibi, Tawa destroyed the Third World in a great flood because of the people's wickedness. Before the destruction, Spider Grandmother sealed the more righteous people inside hollow reeds, which floated as boats. After the waters receded, the survivors found thems
stories.title: The Great Flood and the Voyage to the Fourth World

stories.name: The Great Head and the Old Woman
stories.excerpt: Cusick's story of the dispersion of the Great Heads recounts how an old Onondaga woman was sitting alone in her wigwam one evening, parching acorns over the fire, when a monstrous Flying Head appeared at her door. The head was enormous, with blazing eyes and long hair draping like wings. The old woman, showing no fear,
stories.title: The Great Head and the Old Woman

stories.name: The Great Horned Serpent (Oniare)
stories.excerpt: Oniare is a dragon-like horned serpent of the Great Lakes region, deeply feared by the Iroquois and neighboring tribes for its habit of capsizing canoes and devouring people. It lives in the deepest parts of lakes and rivers, controlling the waters and causing storms. The serpent has a single horn or a crest of antlers
stories.title: The Great Horned Serpent (Oniare)

stories.name: The Great Medicine Road
stories.excerpt: The Pawnee believe that after death, the soul travels along the Milky Way, which they call the Great Medicine Road or the Path of the Dead. This celestial road leads the deceased to the land of the dead in the south, ruled by the South Star. Spirits must walk this path, and the journey is long. The stars in the Milky W
stories.title: The Great Medicine Road

stories.name: The Great Peacemaker (Deganawida / Skennenrahawi)
stories.excerpt: The Great Peacemaker, known as Deganawida in the sacred language and Skennenrahawi in Mohawk, was a legendary leader who founded the Iroquois Confederacy, the oldest living democracy in North America. Born among the Huron, he crossed Lake Ontario in a stone canoe to bring peace to the warring Iroquois nations. With the
stories.title: The Great Peacemaker (Deganawida / Skennenrahawi)

stories.name: The Great Race (Arapaho)
stories.excerpt: Long ago, the animals decided to hold a great race to determine which would be the fastest and most powerful. All creatures gathered from across the plains. The two-leggeds and four-leggeds each chose their champion. The race was long and grueling, crossing rivers and mountains. The buffalo was winning for the four-leg
stories.title: The Great Race (Arapaho)

stories.name: The Great Race of the Animals
stories.excerpt: The Great Race is a Lakota legend about a competition between the four-legged animals and the two-legged birds to determine who would eat whom. The race was proposed by Ksapela the Wise One to settle conflicts among the creatures. Representing the four-leggeds was the buffalo, while the magpie represented the two-legge
stories.title: The Great Race of the Animals

stories.name: The Great Turtle of the Pacific
stories.excerpt: A cosmic turtle carries the islands of Tuvalu on its back, balancing the world against the rising tides through an ancient pact with the sea gods.
stories.title: The Great Turtle of the Pacific

stories.name: The Green Children of Woolpit
stories.excerpt: Two green-skinned children appear from an underground world, leaving behind a land of perpetual twilight for a life in medieval England.
stories.title: The Green Children of Woolpit

stories.name: The Green Knight
stories.excerpt: A tale featuring a mysterious Green Knight who challenges others to a contest of courage, honor, and strength, testing the character of the protagonists through a series of trials.
stories.title: The Green Knight

stories.name: The Green Knight's Challenge
stories.excerpt: On New Year's Eve at Camelot, an enormous green knight rides into the hall and issues a deadly challenge to any who would dare strike him, setting Sir Gawain upon a path of honor and terror.
stories.title: The Green Knight's Challenge

stories.name: The Green Lady and the Fisherman's Heart
stories.excerpt: A grief-stricken fisherman climbs Mount Liamuiga at sunset and witnesses the Green Lady's flash, receiving a sign that love endures beyond loss.
stories.title: The Green Lady and the Fisherman's Heart

stories.name: The Green Traveller of Wadi Rum
stories.excerpt: A Bedouin lost in Wadi Rum encounters Al-Khidr, the enigmatic green traveller, and discovers that the desert holds wisdom for those who surrender their pride.
stories.title: The Green Traveller of Wadi Rum

stories.name: the Gu, Guardian of the Crossing
stories.excerpt: A sacred crocodile that guards the river crossing, granting safe passage to those who show respect — and dragging beneath the water those who do not.
stories.title: the Gu, Guardian of the Crossing

stories.name: The Guardian of the Basilica
stories.excerpt: A humble Swiss Guard discovers that his guardian angel has walked beside him through every night watch, defending the Holy See from threats unseen.
stories.title: The Guardian of the Basilica

stories.name: The Guardian of the Hidden Valley
stories.excerpt: Deep in the highlands lies a valley that remains green and warm even in the dead of winter. It is guarded by a massive white wolf who allows only those with a selfless heart to enter. Those who enter find a paradise where time stands still and all wounds are healed.
stories.title: The Guardian of the Hidden Valley

stories.name: The Gumiho of the Demilitarized Zone
stories.excerpt: A nine-tailed fox spirit trapped in the no-man's land between two Koreas, feeding on the grief of families who can never reunite — because some borders cut deeper than flesh.
stories.title: The Gumiho of the Demilitarized Zone

stories.name: The Gumiho Who Drank Belief
stories.excerpt: A nine-tailed fox who abandoned feeding on souls and learned to feed on the belief of the faithful — and found the people of the hermit kingdom were the most nourishing meal she had ever tasted.
stories.title: The Gumiho Who Drank Belief

stories.name: The Gumiho: Nine-Tailed Fox of Korea
stories.excerpt: A fox spirit with nine tails seeks to gain immortality by stealing human hearts.
stories.title: The Gumiho: Nine-Tailed Fox of Korea

stories.name: the Gyeong, the Vengeful Spirit
stories.excerpt: A ghost born from the agony of a death by fire, its body twisted and burned, seeking justice in a world that has forgotten its name — because in Korea, some wrongs are never forgotten.
stories.title: the Gyeong, the Vengeful Spirit

stories.name: The Haetae of the Eternal Flame
stories.excerpt: A fire-eating guardian that was commanded to protect not a palace but an ideology, feeding on the flames of propaganda — but the fire it swallows tastes different than the fire it remembers.
stories.title: The Haetae of the Eternal Flame

stories.name: The Haetae That Guarded the Border Fire
stories.excerpt: A fire-eating guardian that patrols the northern edge of the DMZ, swallowing the campfires of refugees who try to cross in the dark — because even the guardian has its orders.
stories.title: The Haetae That Guarded the Border Fire

stories.name: the Haetae, the Fire-Eating Guardian
stories.excerpt: A lion-like creature covered in scales that devours fire itself, protecting villages from conflagrations — and when the great fire came, only the Haetae stood between the palace and the flames.
stories.title: the Haetae, the Fire-Eating Guardian

stories.name: The Hako (Calumet) Ceremony
stories.excerpt: The Hako ceremony, also known as the Calumet ceremony, was a complex Pawnee ritual centered on the sacred pipe. It was a peace-making and adoption ceremony that created bonds between individuals, families, and even tribes. The ceremony lasted several days and involved singing, dancing, smoking the sacred pipe, and the
stories.title: The Hako (Calumet) Ceremony

stories.name: The Hamatsa Cannibal Spirit (Kwakwaka'wakw)
stories.excerpt: Baxbaxwalanuksiwe' (Man-Eater at the North End of the World) is the most important supernatural being in Kwakwaka'wakw winter ceremonies. This cannibal spirit has mouths all over his body and can transform into various man-eating birds. His attendants include the Hamatsa bird-masks: Gwaxwgwakwalanuksiwe' (a man-eating
stories.title: The Hamatsa Cannibal Spirit (Kwakwaka'wakw)

stories.name: The Happy Hunting Ground
stories.excerpt: The Lakota believe the soul journeys after death to the happy hunting ground, a realm resembling the living world with better weather and more plentiful animals that are easier to hunt. Some traditions say the soul travels along the Sky-Road (Milky Way) to reach this destination. At the entrance, the deceased must pres
stories.title: The Happy Hunting Ground

stories.name: The Hare Trickster of the Tswana
stories.excerpt: In Tswana folklore, the hare (mmutla) is a classic trickster figure who uses intelligence to overcome physically stronger opponents. In the well-known tale of 'The Lion and the Hare,' the hare repeatedly outwits the lion through clever schemes and quick thinking, teaching that wit and strategy can defeat brute strength
stories.title: The Hare Trickster of the Tswana

stories.name: The Heartman of Bridgetown
stories.excerpt: A spectral figure walks the night streets of Bridgetown, searching for those whose hearts carry the heaviest burdens of guilt, and either absolves or claims them.
stories.title: The Heartman of Bridgetown

stories.name: The Heavenly Camel: A Somali Creation Myth
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, the sky was low enough to touch, and the Somali people lived in close communion with the stars. The creator god Waaq formed the first camel from the morning mist and gave it to the people as the most valuable of all animals — able to travel for days without water, carry heavy loads, and provide milk,
stories.title: The Heavenly Camel: A Somali Creation Myth

stories.name: The Hermit Mitsina
stories.excerpt: A Zuni story about Mitsina, a hermit who lived in seclusion with spiritual power. Mitsina had withdrawn from human society to live in a remote cave, where he communed with the spirits and gained deep knowledge of the sacred world. When the people faced a crisis, they sought him out for his wisdom and power. Mitsina, de
stories.title: The Hermit Mitsina

stories.name: The Hero Twins: Monster Slayer and Child of the Water
stories.excerpt: In Navajo mythology, Changing Woman gave birth to the Hero Twins, Monster Slayer (Naayééʼ Neizghání) and Child of the Water (Tóbájíshchíní), fathered by the Sun. The twins were born to rid the world of monsters (anaye) that terrorized the people. They journeyed to their father the Sun, passing tests of strength and cou
stories.title: The Hero Twins: Monster Slayer and Child of the Water

stories.name: The Hidden Paths of the Vittra
stories.excerpt: The Vittra are invisible underground beings who live in parallel cities. They have their own cattle and roads that cross human lands. If a farmer builds a house over a Vittra-path, the invisible residents will cause accidents, make the cows sick, or drive the family out of the home through relentless noise.
stories.title: The Hidden Paths of the Vittra

stories.name: The Hintha Bird Legend
stories.excerpt: The Hintha bird — a mythical golden goose or Brahminy duck — is the sacred emblem of the Mon people and the symbol of Bago (Pegu) Region in Myanmar. According to Mon Buddhist legend, the Hintha bird was the Bodhisatta (a previous incarnation of the Buddha) in the form of a wise golden goose. In the Jataka tale of the H
stories.title: The Hintha Bird Legend

stories.name: The Hmong Creation Myth: The Flood and the Siblings
stories.excerpt: The Hmong creation myth centers on a great flood that destroyed the world and the surviving sibling pair who repopulated it. According to the oral tradition passed down through generations, a great argument between the Sky Father (Saub) and the Earth led to a devastating flood that covered the entire world. Only two si
stories.title: The Hmong Creation Myth: The Flood and the Siblings

stories.name: The Holy Grail
stories.excerpt: At the height of Camelot's glory, on the eve of Pentecost, the knights of the Round Table sat in the great hall at a celebration unlike any other.
stories.title: The Holy Grail

stories.name: The Honest Penny
stories.excerpt: A poor boy finds a money box but throws it away, believing it contains stolen wealth, keeping only one silver penny that floats on water, which he deems 'honest.' This act of integrity leads him to a series of adventures and eventual immense wealth.
stories.title: The Honest Penny

stories.name: The Hopi Clan Migrations
stories.excerpt: Upon arriving in the Fourth World, the Hopi divided and began great migrations across the land. Led by various signs and helped by Spider Woman, clans traveled to every direction, sometimes stopping to build towns, then abandoning them to continue their migrations. They left symbols on rocks to show that Hopi had been
stories.title: The Hopi Clan Migrations

stories.name: The Horned Women
stories.excerpt: The night lay heavy over the Irish countryside, a winter's night so cold that the thatch on the cottage roofs crackled with frost and the breath of sleeping cattle rose in white clouds from the byres.
stories.title: The Horned Women

stories.name: The How the Twins of War and Chance Fared with the Unborn-Made Men
stories.excerpt: In this complex Zuni myth, Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, the Twins of War and Chance (or Morning Star and Evening Star), journeyed to the underworld to confront the Unborn-made Men. These were unfinished beings who had not yet been given their final form — they existed in a state of potential. The twins had to navigate the
stories.title: The How the Twins of War and Chance Fared with the Unborn-Made Men

stories.name: The Huanca, Stone Guardian
stories.excerpt: A petrified warrior stands watch over the mountain passes, and the traveler who passes without offering a stone to the ground will lose their way forever.
stories.title: The Huanca, Stone Guardian

stories.name: The Huldra's Seduction
stories.excerpt: The Huldra is a beautiful forest woman who lures lonely men into the woods with her singing and charm. While she appears human from the front, she possesses a long cow's tail which she carefully hides. If a man discovers the tail and treats her with kindness, she may become a loyal wife, but otherwise, she leads men to
stories.title: The Huldra's Seduction

stories.name: The Huldufólk Nursery Rhyme: Hulda, Mulda, Tulda
stories.excerpt: A traditional Faroese skjaldur (short nursery rhyme or tale) that invokes the Huldufólk. The rhyme 'Hulda, mulda, tulda' is a charm asking the Hidden People not to hide lost objects. It reflects the common belief that Huldufólk, being mischievous tricksters, enjoy hiding household items from humans. The rhyme tradition
stories.title: The Huldufólk Nursery Rhyme: Hulda, Mulda, Tulda

stories.name: The Hunger of the Amarok
stories.excerpt: In this darker version of the wolf legend, the Amarok is a sinister force that hunts those who disturb the balance of nature. A man, consumed by grief, seeks out the Amarok to distract himself. After killing the wolf's young to lure the adult, the man is swiftly judged. The Amarok returns and takes the man's soul as pu
stories.title: The Hunger of the Amarok

stories.name: The Hunter of the Sun (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: None of the Choctaw prophets or chief leaders could answer what happened to the Sun when it disappeared each night. A young man embarked on a mission to discover this mystery. He left his family, community, and country to dedicate his life to tracking the Sun's path. Many years passed — the young men became old, and th
stories.title: The Hunter of the Sun (Choctaw)

stories.name: The Huntress and the Great Serpent
stories.excerpt: A brave huntress must defeat a great serpent that has been terrorizing her village—and discovers a unexpected truth.
stories.title: The Huntress and the Great Serpent

stories.name: The Huron Creation: Aataentsic and the Earth Diver
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, the Wyandot people lived in the Sky Land. The shaman told the people to dig around the roots of the wild apple tree by the chief's lodge. As they dug, they broke through the floor of the Sky Land, and the tree and the chief's daughter Aataentsic fell through. Below was only water. Swans swimming on th
stories.title: The Huron Creation: Aataentsic and the Earth Diver

stories.name: The Hyena Who Wanted to Be King
stories.excerpt: In the golden, shimmering plains of the Sahel, where the acacia trees cast long, skeletal shadows across the scorched earth, the animals of the wild once gathered for a great council.
stories.title: The Hyena Who Wanted to Be King

stories.name: The Iatiku and Nautsiti Creation (Acoma Pueblo)
stories.excerpt: In the Acoma Pueblo creation myth, two sisters named Iatiku (Life Bringer) and Nautsiti (Full Basket) emerged from the underworld through a sacred place called Shipapu, guided by Tsichtinako (Thought Woman). They were given two baskets containing seeds, animal figurines, and sacred objects. Tsichtinako instructed them
stories.title: The Iatiku and Nautsiti Creation (Acoma Pueblo)

stories.name: The Ice Maiden
stories.excerpt: There was once a boy named Rudy who lived in the Swiss Alps, near the foot of a great glacier.
stories.title: The Ice Maiden

stories.name: The Ice-Maiden
stories.excerpt: A youth becomes enchanted by a cold, ethereal Ice-Maiden. The story explores themes of love, frozen emotions, and the danger of being lured away from the warmth of human society.
stories.title: The Ice-Maiden

stories.name: the Imandwa, Spirits of the Hill
stories.excerpt: Spirits that live in the tallest hills, appearing as balls of light at dusk — because in Burundi, every hill has a guardian, and the guardian demands respect.
stories.title: the Imandwa, Spirits of the Hill

stories.name: the Imizimu, the Ancestors Who Walk
stories.excerpt: The spirits of the dead who walk among the living, visible only in the flicker of a candle flame — because in Burundi, death does not end the conversation.
stories.title: the Imizimu, the Ancestors Who Walk

stories.name: The Imugi Who Lost the Waterfall
stories.excerpt: A giant serpent dreaming of dragonhood waits beneath a waterfall that was dammed by the state, coiling in the dark reservoir, waiting for a heaven that may never come.
stories.title: The Imugi Who Lost the Waterfall

stories.name: The Inkanyamba of the Deep Pool
stories.excerpt: A colossal serpent dwelling in a mountain pool summons devastating storms when angered, and only an old healer learns the secret of calming its wrath.
stories.title: The Inkanyamba of the Deep Pool

stories.name: The Iron Pig
stories.excerpt: A kind boy treats a mysterious iron pig with tenderness and discovers a hidden treasure.
stories.title: The Iron Pig

stories.name: The Isle of Refuge
stories.excerpt: A poignant tale of seeking sanctuary during a time of war or political persecution. It explores the psychological toll of exile and the universal human search for a place of peace and safety away from conflict.
stories.title: The Isle of Refuge

stories.name: The Jack Ball: A Conjure Tale
stories.excerpt: In Hoodoo tradition, a Jack Ball (sometimes called a 'follow-me-boy' or 'trick ball') is one of the most powerful conjure objects. The tale tells of a rootworker who created a Jack Ball from wax, graveyard dust, personal concerns of the target, and the rootworker's own blood, empowered by nine days of prayer and fastin
stories.title: The Jack Ball: A Conjure Tale

stories.name: The Jade Emperor
stories.excerpt: Long before the dynasties of China rose from the yellow earth, before emperors ruled from golden palaces, there was only the Jade Emperor—the ruler of heaven, the most powerful of all the celestial beings.
stories.title: The Jade Emperor

stories.name: The Jengu Who Married a Fisherman
stories.excerpt: A Sawa fisherman rescues a beautiful Jengu from a hunter's net, and she grants him a season of extraordinary catches in return, until the price of her love demands he choose between the river and the shore.
stories.title: The Jengu Who Married a Fisherman

stories.name: The Jenun of Chinguetti
stories.excerpt: In the ancient library city of Chinguetti, a fqih discovers that the jenun who haunt the desert roads are not demons to be exorcised but forgotten scholars, bound to guard the books that no one reads anymore.
stories.title: The Jenun of Chinguetti

stories.name: The Jicarilla Apache Creation
stories.excerpt: In the beginning there was nothing — no earth, no living beings, only darkness, water, and Cyclone the wind. Only the Hactcin (supernatural beings) existed. They made the earth as a woman facing upward and the sky as a man facing downward. Black Hactcin, the most powerful, created the first four-legged animal from clay
stories.title: The Jicarilla Apache Creation

stories.name: The Jinn of Jerusalem
stories.excerpt: A powerful jinn said to guard the holy places of Jerusalem, testing the worthiness of those who seek to enter.
stories.title: The Jinn of Jerusalem

stories.name: The Jinn of the Asmara Market
stories.excerpt: A Tigrinya merchant ignores the warnings about a jinn dwelling beneath the old market square in Asmara, and pays a price that no amount of coffee can undo.
stories.title: The Jinn of the Asmara Market

stories.name: The Jinn of the Dead Sea
stories.excerpt: A fisherman on the Dead Sea encounters a jinn imprisoned in the salt flats since the time of the prophet Lut, and discovers that even a trapped spirit can bargain for freedom.
stories.title: The Jinn of the Dead Sea

stories.name: The Jinn of the Empty Quarter
stories.excerpt: A Bedouin traveler encounters a powerful Jinn in the Rub' al Khali, engaging in a battle of riddles to secure safe passage across the shifting sands.
stories.title: The Jinn of the Empty Quarter

stories.name: The Jinn Who Tended the Well
stories.excerpt: Um Hmaar, a jinn bound to an ancient well in the Bahraini desert, tests the character of those who draw water from her domain.
stories.title: The Jinn Who Tended the Well

stories.name: The Jomala Runestone – Odin's Mark on Åland
stories.excerpt: The Jomala runestone, located at Jomala Church — the oldest stone church in Finland — is one of the most significant Viking-age artifacts on Åland. The runestone bears inscriptions invoking Odin's guidance and names voyagers who once crossed the Baltic. Its serpent forms curl around the old Younger Futhark alphabet in
stories.title: The Jomala Runestone – Odin's Mark on Åland

stories.name: The Journey to the Land of the Dead
stories.excerpt: In Hopi tradition, the journey to the land of the dead begins at the sipapu in the Grand Canyon. The spirit travels westward, following the path of the setting sun, to the land of the ancestors. Along the way, the spirit encounters various challenges and must have the proper knowledge, gained through ceremonial instruc
stories.title: The Journey to the Land of the Dead

stories.name: The Journey to the West
stories.excerpt: Long ago in China, there lived a powerful monkey king named Sun Wukong. Centers on Sun Wukong, to the West protagonist.
stories.title: The Journey to the West

stories.name: The Kabouter of the Belgian Forests
stories.excerpt: A tiny forest spirit who helps those who respect nature and plays tricks on those who do not, found in the woods of Flanders.
stories.title: The Kabouter of the Belgian Forests

stories.name: The Kachina Spirits of the Pueblo
stories.excerpt: Across Pueblo cultures, the Kachinas (Katsinam) are supernatural beings who are the spirits of ancestors, natural forces, and all things in the universe — rocks, stars, animals, and plants. They reside in the San Francisco Peaks (north of Flagstaff, Arizona) and come to the pueblos for six months each year during the w
stories.title: The Kachina Spirits of the Pueblo

stories.name: The Kachina Tradition (Zuni)
stories.excerpt: In Zuni tradition, the Kachinas (Kâkâ) originated from the search for itiwana, the Middle Place. The priest Ka'wimosa sent his sons in different directions to find the center of the world. Kiaklo went north, the Ánahoho áchi went south, and Síweluhsiwa and Síwiluhsitsa went east, where they had ten children from an inc
stories.title: The Kachina Tradition (Zuni)

stories.name: The Kachinas Bring Agriculture
stories.excerpt: In Hopi tradition, during a great drought when the people were starving, they heard singing and dancing coming from the San Francisco Peaks (Nuvatukya'ovi). Investigating, they met the Kachinas — ancestral spirits and supernatural beings who inhabit the peaks. The Kachinas returned with the Hopi to their villages and t
stories.title: The Kachinas Bring Agriculture

stories.name: The Kakamora: Elves of the Solomon Islands
stories.excerpt: The Kakamora are mythical elf-like creatures in the folklore of Makira and Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands. They are described as small, hairy beings with great strength, living in the deep forests and remote mountains. The Kakamora are known to be shy but mischievous, sometimes stealing food from villages or playin
stories.title: The Kakamora: Elves of the Solomon Islands

stories.name: The Kana-a Kachinas of Sunset Crater
stories.excerpt: At old Mishongnovi lived a young maiden who refused all suitors. A Kachina youth from the San Francisco Peaks courted her through magical means — traveling by rainbow — and brought her across the desert to Palotsmo (Sunset Crater), home of the Kana-a Kachinas. There she underwent tests in the kiva, surviving four night
stories.title: The Kana-a Kachinas of Sunset Crater

stories.name: The Kano Chronicle and the Founding of the Seven Hausa States
stories.excerpt: The Kano Chronicle records the oral traditions of the Hausa people, tracing the founding of the seven legitimate Hausa states (Hausa Bakwai) to the sons of Bayajidda. After Bayajidda married Queen Daurama of Daura, their son Bawo fathered six sons who founded Kano, Katsina, Zaria, Gobir, Rano, and Daura itself, while B
stories.title: The Kano Chronicle and the Founding of the Seven Hausa States

stories.name: The Kapre
stories.excerpt: A giant tree spirit of Philippine folklore that waits and watches from the branches.
stories.title: The Kapre

stories.name: the Karakondzola's Midnight Rite
stories.excerpt: On Christmas Eve, the Karakondzola descends from the rooftops and enters the homes of the dead — because on this night, it does not call names, it remembers them.
stories.title: the Karakondzola's Midnight Rite

stories.name: the Karakondzola, the Night Walker
stories.excerpt: A hunched creature with burning eyes that walks the rooftops at midnight, stopping at every house and calling residents by name — and whoever answers will never sleep again.
stories.title: the Karakondzola, the Night Walker

stories.name: the Karanga, the Diviner's Secret
stories.excerpt: A sorcerer who reads the future in the patterns of millet flour scattered on water — but the future he reads is not the one you want to hear.
stories.title: the Karanga, the Diviner's Secret

stories.name: The Kastelholm Witch Trials (1665–1668)
stories.excerpt: The Kastelholm witch trials were the largest witch trials in Finnish history, held at Kastelholm Castle in Åland between 1665 and 1668. Governor Nils Psilander, educated at the University of Dorpat (Tartu) where witchcraft demonology was a major subject, conducted the trials. Unlike typical Finnish witch trials which i
stories.title: The Kastelholm Witch Trials (1665–1668)

stories.name: The Kazan Creation Myth
stories.excerpt: The founding myth of Kazan explains how the city got its name. According to legend, a Bulgar prince was hunting on the banks of the Volga when his party stopped to prepare a meal. They put a copper cauldron (kazan in Tatar) on the fire to boil water. A serpent emerged from the water, warning the prince that a great cit
stories.title: The Kazan Creation Myth

stories.name: the Keemse, Spirit of the River
stories.excerpt: A water spirit that lives in the deep pools of the Volta River, granting fish to those who respect it — and drowning those who do not.
stories.title: the Keemse, Spirit of the River

stories.name: The Keepers of the Sacred Law
stories.excerpt: The Lulik Spirits, guardians of Timorese sacred law, punish those who break taboos and reward those who uphold the ancient protocols.
stories.title: The Keepers of the Sacred Law

stories.name: The Kelpie
stories.excerpt: The Rainbow Serpent is one of the most important and widespread figures in Aboriginal Australian mythology.
stories.title: The Kelpie

stories.name: The Kidnapping of Angangujuk
stories.excerpt: A traditional tale of a child, Angangujuk, who is kidnapped by supernatural beings and taken to a hidden realm. The story follows the desperate efforts of the parents to locate the child and the moral lessons learned about the dangers of wandering too far from the community and the strength of familial bonds in the fac
stories.title: The Kidnapping of Angangujuk

stories.name: The Kikimora in the Walls
stories.excerpt: A farmer's wife discovers that the mischievous spirit nesting in her home is not malicious but deeply offended, and must be appeased with respect rather than chased away with force.
stories.title: The Kikimora in the Walls

stories.name: The Kikimora Who Kept House
stories.excerpt: A household spirit who appears to a widow as a tiny old woman, spinning flax by moonlight and keeping the house in order while the widow sleeps.
stories.title: The Kikimora Who Kept House

stories.name: The King's Choice
stories.excerpt: King Gustav must leave his country on a long journey and needs to choose one of his six councilors to govern in his absence — but each has a flaw: one is too bossy, another too young, one drinks too much, one is obsessed with money, another with his appearance, and the last is simply uninspiring. Riding through the for
stories.title: The King's Choice

stories.name: the Kinkirsi, the Human Animal
stories.excerpt: A being that is half-human, half-animal, born when a mother's craving during pregnancy crosses the boundary between species — and lives forever in the forest, caught between two worlds.
stories.title: the Kinkirsi, the Human Animal

stories.name: the Kintogou, the Fire Serpent
stories.excerpt: A serpent made of fire that coils beneath the village, its heat warming the earth in winter and its rage burning the village in summer — because fire is a gift, but it is never free.
stories.title: the Kintogou, the Fire Serpent

stories.name: The Kishi at the Crossroads
stories.excerpt: A seductive forest demon with two faces lures travelers from the path, offering them their heart's desire in exchange for a single step into the bush.
stories.title: The Kishi at the Crossroads

stories.name: The Knight of Ellenholm
stories.excerpt: A knight on his way to Christmas matins stops to rest by a mountainside, where a giantess forces him into the mountain to meet her husband. He refuses their food, and the giantess breaks his little finger as a warning against sleeping on the way to church.
stories.title: The Knight of Ellenholm

stories.name: The Knights of Ållaberg
stories.excerpt: A peasant discovers a grand mansion in Allaberg where twelve golden-helmeted knights sleep in glittering armor. When he touches a bridle a voice asks "Is it time now?" and another answers "No, not yet!" He has glimpsed the warriors who will defend Sweden in its hour of greatest need.
stories.title: The Knights of Ållaberg

stories.name: the Koreisha, the Bear Woman
stories.excerpt: A bear that was once a woman, or a woman that was once a bear — the boundary between them blurred by hunger, by faith, by the slow transformation of flesh into something that is neither and both.
stories.title: the Koreisha, the Bear Woman

stories.name: The Kumiho and the Scholar
stories.excerpt: A nine-tailed fox spirit who has lived a thousand years must collect one thousand human souls to become human herself — but the scholar she targets teaches her that some desires are worth more than transformation.
stories.title: The Kumiho and the Scholar

stories.name: The Kumulipo: Hawaiian Creation Chant
stories.excerpt: The Kumulipo is the sacred Hawaiian creation chant, a genealogical epic tracing the universe from its primordial origins. It begins in total darkness (Po) with the birth of coral, seaweed, and the first sea creatures. The chant follows the emergence of life from ocean to land, from the humblest plants to animals and fi
stories.title: The Kumulipo: Hawaiian Creation Chant

stories.name: The Kurupí of the Forest
stories.excerpt: A wild-haired forest spirit with impossibly long genitalia that he wraps around his waist ties women to trees in the deepest jungle, and only the smell of tobacco can drive him away.
stories.title: The Kurupí of the Forest

stories.name: The Lad and the Devil
stories.excerpt: A clever lad tricks the Devil into shrinking himself and entering a nut, which the lad then seals with a pin. He later uses a blacksmith's hammer to destroy the nut, effectively defeating the Devil with wit.
stories.title: The Lad and the Devil

stories.name: The Lad and the Fox
stories.excerpt: A lad on his way to church sees a fox sleeping on a stone and begins daydreaming about killing it, selling the skin, buying rye, and shouting at passersby to stay off his field—but he screams so loudly in his fantasy that he wakes the fox, which escapes.
stories.title: The Lad and the Fox

stories.name: The Lad Who Went to the North Wind
stories.excerpt: A poor boy asks the North Wind to return flour it blew away. The North Wind sends him on a journey with magical objects that help him outwit a greedy innkeeper and the king.
stories.title: The Lad Who Went to the North Wind

stories.name: The Lady of Pintorp
stories.excerpt: A cruel noblewoman makes a pact with the Devil, and after a life of wickedness, her ghost returns to haunt Pintorp Castle in a spectral carriage on stormy nights. The lady may have been a historical figure — the wife of the royal counselor Erik Gyllenstjerna.
stories.title: The Lady of Pintorp

stories.name: The Lady of the Lake
stories.excerpt: The ethereal guardian of a mystical lake who provides King Arthur with his most powerful weapon and shapes the fate of Camelot.
stories.title: The Lady of the Lake

stories.name: The Lady Who Fell from the Sky
stories.excerpt: Before the world was a world, before there were mountains or rivers or forests, there was only water.
stories.title: The Lady Who Fell from the Sky

stories.name: The Lakhey: The Demon Guardian of Kathmandu
stories.excerpt: A fearsome demon tamed by a goddess now protects the children of the Kathmandu Valley.
stories.title: The Lakhey: The Demon Guardian of Kathmandu

stories.name: The Lakota Creation: Inyan, Maka, and the First Dawn
stories.excerpt: In the beginning there was only Inyan (Rock) and the omnipresent spirit Wakan Tanka, the Great Mystery, and the darkness Han. Inyan wished to exercise his powers of compassion, so he created Maka (Earth) from himself, sacrificing much of his blood which became water. Inyan shriveled and lost his powers. The water gave
stories.title: The Lakota Creation: Inyan, Maka, and the First Dawn

stories.name: The Lame Dog
stories.excerpt: A royal couple longing for a child trust a mysterious old woman who gives them a son with a terrible prohibition — if he ever sees the face of the one who loves him most, he will vanish like morning mist.
stories.title: The Lame Dog

stories.name: The Lame Warrior and the Skeleton
stories.excerpt: A lame Arapaho warrior, unable to fight alongside his people, was left behind when the village moved. As he sat alone, a skeleton approached him. The skeleton offered to carry the warrior to battle if the warrior would promise to give the skeleton a proper burial afterward. They formed a pact. The skeleton carried the
stories.title: The Lame Warrior and the Skeleton

stories.name: The Lamia in the Archives
stories.excerpt: A Vatican librarian discovers that the ancient Lamia has been feeding on the memories of scholars who venture too deep into the restricted archives beneath the basilica.
stories.title: The Lamia in the Archives

stories.name: The Lamia of the Nursery
stories.excerpt: A Lamia infiltrates the Vatican's ancient orphanage, luring children with the voice of their dead mothers, until a quick-witted nun discovers the creature's true nature.
stories.title: The Lamia of the Nursery

stories.name: The Land Otter Son (Kushtaka) (Tlingit)
stories.excerpt: After their son was lost at sea, a grieving Tlingit couple living in poverty heard whistling outside their home at night. The wife called out, begging her son to come in. Without being seen entering, a figure appeared seated opposite them with his hands over his face. He only whistled by drawing in his breath. Toward m
stories.title: The Land Otter Son (Kushtaka) (Tlingit)

stories.title: The Lizard Who Brought Sunrise

stories.name: The Loogaroo and the Obeah Man
stories.excerpt: When a loogaroo terrorizes a village through a series of unexplained attacks, only the village obeah man has the knowledge and courage to confront it.
stories.title: The Loogaroo and the Obeah Man

stories.name: The Lord of the Bears
stories.excerpt: In a remote Austrian valley, where snow-capped peaks scraped the sky and forests of pine stretched for miles, there lived a young girl named Liesl.
stories.title: The Lord of the Bears

stories.name: The Lorelei
stories.excerpt: Near the ancient town of Sankt Goarshausen, where the Rhine River narrows between towering cliffs of slate, there stands a rock that has haunted the imaginations of sailors and poets for centuries.
stories.title: The Lorelei

stories.name: The Lost Bell
stories.excerpt: In the old port city of Kołobrzeg on the Baltic coast, there is a legend that has been whispered for centuries.
stories.title: The Lost Bell

stories.name: The Lost City of Sijilmasa
stories.excerpt: Sijilmasa was a legendary medieval city in southeastern Morocco, founded in 757 CE on the Ziz River near the Sahara. stories.title: The Lost City of Sijilmasa

stories.name: The Lost Hunters of Orion
stories.excerpt: The stars forming Orion's Belt are known as the Siagtut, representing a group of hunters who became permanently lost on the vast arctic ice. stories.title: The Lost Hunters of Orion

stories.name: The Lost Treasure
stories.excerpt: When enemies invaded Sweden, the people of Stenbrohult hid their treasure in a copper kettle sunk in Lake Möckeln, where it remains unreachable. stories.title: The Lost Treasure

stories.name: The Lost Treasure of Montezuma — Aztec Gold in the Southwest
stories.excerpt: The legend of Montezuma's hidden treasure is one of the most persistent treasure myths in the US Southwest, blending Aztec history with Spanish colonial folklore and Mexican-American oral tradition. stories.title: The Lost Treasure of Montezuma — Aztec Gold in the Southwest

stories.name: The Lougarou Who Wore the Moon
stories.excerpt: On the sugar estates of Mauritius, a shapeshifting lougarou stalks the cane fields under a full moon, seeking the one person who knows how to send it back to the form it once held.
stories.title: The Lougarou Who Wore the Moon

stories.name: The Luison of the Uruguayan Pampas
stories.excerpt: A cursed seventh son who becomes a werewolf-like creature roaming the pampas of Uruguay, feared by gauchos and villagers alike.
stories.title: The Luison of the Uruguayan Pampas

stories.name: The Lukasa: The Luba Memory Board
stories.excerpt: The Lukasa (memory board) is a sacred object in Luba tradition, a wooden board covered with beads and shells arranged in patterns that encode the entire history of the Luba people. stories.title: The Lukasa: The Luba Memory Board

stories.excerpt: A Bemba fisherman who overfishes a sacred river encounters the Lungu, a colossal serpent guardian who demands he restore what he has taken before the waters turn against the village.
stories.title: The Lungu of the Deep River

stories.excerpt: The Nykur is a shape-shifting water horse that appears as a beautiful, grey stallion by the lakeside. When a weary traveler attempts to mount it, the horse's skin becomes adhesive, and it gallops straight into the deep water, drowning the rider in a cold, watery grave.

stories.name: The Maasai and the Great Lion Hunt
stories.excerpt: The lion has always held a sacred and complex place in Maasai culture — both a threat to livestock and a symbol of courage.
