stories.name: The Spirit of the Sacred Cloth
stories.excerpt: A weaver discovers that the spirit Lei inhabits the finest tais cloth, guarding the patterns that carry ancestral memory.
stories.title: The Spirit of the Sacred Cloth

stories.name: The Spring Awakening Ceremony
stories.excerpt: The most important Pawnee ceremony was the Spring Awakening, meant to awaken the earth and prepare it for planting. The timing was determined by celestial observation: the priest would track 'two small twinkling stars known as the Swimming Ducks in the northeastern horizon near the Milky Way.' When these stars appeared
stories.title: The Spring Awakening Ceremony

stories.name: The Star Husband (Arapaho)
stories.excerpt: Two Arapaho women lay outside their tipi at night. One pointed at a bright star and said she wished to marry it. The next day, a handsome young man appeared at their camp. He was the star in human form, come to claim his bride. The woman went with him to the sky world, where she lived among the star people. But she gre
stories.title: The Star Husband (Arapaho)

stories.name: The Star Woman (Blackfoot)
stories.excerpt: A Blackfoot chief's daughter married a star and went to live in the sky world. Each day she was given the task of digging roots, but she was forbidden from digging up one particular turnip. Curiosity overcame her, and when she pulled the turnip, she saw the Earth far below. Overcome with homesickness, she wove a rope o
stories.title: The Star Woman (Blackfoot)

stories.name: The Stars and Constellations
stories.excerpt: First Man, First Woman, Great Coyote, and the Holy People gathered pieces of rock-star mica to create the night sky in Navajo tradition. First Man drew a plan in the dirt to arrange stars like a woven rug. Black God placed the North Star (Sǫʼtsoh). First Man placed the Big Dipper (Náhookǫs bikąʼí) and First Woman the L
stories.title: The Stars and Constellations

stories.name: The Steadfast Tin Soldier
stories.excerpt: There were once twenty-five tin soldiers—all brothers, cast from the same old tin spoon.
stories.title: The Steadfast Tin Soldier

stories.name: The Steel Donkey of St. Lucy
stories.excerpt: A monstrous donkey of living metal haunts the northern parishes, guarding hidden treasure and trampling anyone foolish enough to dig where they should not.
stories.title: The Steel Donkey of St. Lucy

stories.name: The Stone Breaker
stories.excerpt: In the deep forests of Serbia, where the oaks grow thick enough to block the sun and the wolves howl at the edge of every village, there is a creature that haunts the nightmares of every Serbian child.
stories.title: The Stone Breaker

stories.name: The Stone City of Great Zimbabwe
stories.excerpt: The ruins of an ancient city in Zimbabwe hold secrets—and a legend about a buried treasure guarded by spirits.
stories.title: The Stone City of Great Zimbabwe

stories.name: The Stone Giant's Challenge
stories.excerpt: A heroic Iroquois warrior once issued a challenge to a fearsome Stone Giant who had been terrorizing villages. The giant accepted and the two met in battle. The warrior discovered that ordinary weapons could not pierce the giant's stone skin. Using his wits, he lured the giant onto treacherous ground where a rockslide
stories.title: The Stone Giant's Challenge

stories.name: The Stone Giant's Wife
stories.excerpt: This legend tells of a human woman who was taken captive by a Stone Giant. Against all expectations, she survived in the giant's lodge by learning his habits and discovering the secret weakness of his kind — the soft spot on the crown of the head. She eventually escaped and returned to her people with the critical know
stories.title: The Stone Giant's Wife

stories.name: The Stone Giants (Otneyarhed / Stone Coats)
stories.excerpt: The Stone Giants, also known as Stone Coats, were a race of cannibalistic giants whose skin was as hard as stone, making them nearly invulnerable to weapons. They were the mortal enemies of humans and the constant antagonists in Iroquois hero tales. According to legend, they were exterminated through the cunning and br
stories.title: The Stone Giants (Otneyarhed / Stone Coats)

stories.name: The Stone Statue
stories.excerpt: A man who blasphemed in a churchyard was turned to stone. After many parsons failed to save him, a new parson brings the statue into his study and prays daily. The statue laughs during evening prayers and explains that the parson's quarrels with his wife invite imps into the house. The parson reforms, the imps leave, a
stories.title: The Stone Statue

stories.name: The Storm-Witches of Kastelholm
stories.excerpt: Åland folklore tells of storm-witches who possessed the secret art of 'tying the wind' into knots of rope. These women could sell sailors a favorable breeze or calm at sea by selling them a knotted rope: untying one knot released a light wind, untying two filled the sails, but untying all three would awaken a devastati
stories.title: The Storm-Witches of Kastelholm

stories.name: The Story of Ablai Khan
stories.excerpt: Ablai Khan (1711-1781) was one of the greatest Kazakh khans, who united the three Kazakh zhuzes (hordes) and led the struggle against the Dzungar invaders. According to legend, as a thirteen-year-old orphan named Abulmansur, he worked as a shepherd disguised as a beggar called 'Sabalak' to avoid his father's rivals. Hi
stories.title: The Story of Ablai Khan

stories.name: The Story of Asdiwal (Tsimshian)
stories.excerpt: Asdiwal is one of the most important Tsimshian hero narratives, recorded in multiple versions by Franz Boas. The story begins with a mother and daughter dying of starvation during a winter famine in the Skeena River region. A supernatural being named Hatsenas (a bird of good omen) appears, provides food, and fathers As
stories.title: The Story of Asdiwal (Tsimshian)

stories.name: The Story of Bernardo Carpio
stories.excerpt: Bernardo Carpio is the Filipino equivalent of Hercules — a legendary giant with superhuman strength believed to be trapped between two great rocks in the mountains of Montalban (Rizal province). According to folklore, he was a Spanish-Filipino of immense size and power who single-handedly fought entire armies. When the
stories.title: The Story of Bernardo Carpio

stories.name: The Story of Ista (Nuxalk)
stories.excerpt: Ista is the name of the First Woman who descended to Nuxalknalus (King Island) in Nuxalk tradition. She came down to earth and decorated her crest on a blanket with abalone shell and danced up the coast. Ista was greatly admired for how she chose to show her connection to the Creator. Her story is part of the Nuxalk un
stories.title: The Story of Ista (Nuxalk)

stories.name: The Story of Kannagi and the Chera King — From Vengeance to Divinity
stories.excerpt: After the burning of Madurai, Kannagi left the destroyed city and journeyed west into the Chera kingdom (modern-day Kerala). The Chera king Senguttuvan, learning of her story, recognized her as a divine incarnation of chastity. He built a temple for her and established the cult of Pattini (the chastity goddess). Kannag
stories.title: The Story of Kannagi and the Chera King — From Vengeance to Divinity

stories.name: The Story of Noqoilpi the Great Gambler
stories.excerpt: In Navajo tradition, Noqoilpi was a powerful gambler who challenged and defeated all who came to him, taking their possessions and even their freedom. He was said to live at the base of Chʼóolʼį́ʼí (Great Spruce Mountain or El Capitan). Noqoilpi gambled with entire nations, winning their wealth and enslaving their peop
stories.title: The Story of Noqoilpi the Great Gambler

stories.name: The Story of Saint Yared and the Birth of Ethiopian Music
stories.excerpt: In the 6th century, a young boy named Yared was sent to study at the holy city of Axum. But he was a slow learner and often ran away to play in the fields. One day, while hiding under a tree, Yared saw a caterpillar climbing a stalk. The caterpillar fell but climbed again — and again — until it reached the top. Inspire
stories.title: The Story of Saint Yared and the Birth of Ethiopian Music

stories.name: The Story of the Girl Who Was Never Seen
stories.excerpt: A mysterious invisible girl whose presence is known only through her voice and actions.
stories.title: The Story of the Girl Who Was Never Seen

stories.name: The Story of the Moccasin Game
stories.excerpt: The Moccasin Game is a traditional Navajo story explaining the origin of a sacred winter game. In the mythological account, the animals gathered to play the moccasin game, which involves hiding a stone or yucca ball under one of four moccasins while the opposing side guesses its location. The game was played between th
stories.title: The Story of the Moccasin Game

stories.name: The Striga of the Mountain Pass
stories.excerpt: A traveling priest encounters a Striga in the High Tatras and learns that some curses cannot be broken by faith alone, only endured with courage and sacrifice.
stories.title: The Striga of the Mountain Pass

stories.name: The Stállu's Christmas Meal
stories.excerpt: A Sámi Christmas legend from Kautokeino. While parents were away at church, a Stállu came to the camp and began killing and eating children one by one. A quick-witted maid saved the youngest child, tricked Stállu with her traveling cape, and escaped on skis behind the fastest reindeer. The reindeer burst into pieces in
stories.title: The Stállu's Christmas Meal

stories.name: The Sultan of Pate and the Liongo Proclamation
stories.excerpt: When Oromo emissaries came to visit the Sultan of Pate, they heard tales of the legendary hero Liongo. Curious, they asked the Sultan about him. The Sultan sent for Liongo, who packed his bag and hung three great horns about his waist. The journey that took the messengers two days, Liongo completed in half a day. Arriv
stories.title: The Sultan of Pate and the Liongo Proclamation

stories.name: the Sumbo, Spirit of the Fallow Field
stories.excerpt: A spirit that inhabits the fields left fallow, protecting the land while it rests — and destroying anyone who plows a field before its rest is complete.
stories.title: the Sumbo, Spirit of the Fallow Field

stories.name: The Sun and the Moon
stories.excerpt: A celestial tale of sibling rivalry that explains the origin of the day and night cycle and the necessity of cosmic balance.
stories.title: The Sun and the Moon

stories.name: The Sun Dance Lodge Symbolism
stories.excerpt: The Crow Sun Dance lodge (Ashé Isée) is built as a microcosm of the universe. The central forked pole, representing God, faces east. A white flag tied to one branch represents Earth; a blue flag represents the sky. Three charcoal rings on the pole symbolize the three days of the dance and the three worlds of Crow cosmo
stories.title: The Sun Dance Lodge Symbolism

stories.name: The Sun Dance Wheel
stories.excerpt: The Arapaho Sun Dance, known as the Offerings Lodge, is a central spiritual ceremony. Unlike other Plains tribes that practiced self-torture, the Arapaho version involved donating personal items, space, or land to the community as sacrifice. The sacred Flat Pipe was central to the ceremony, symbolizing the Arapaho's co
stories.title: The Sun Dance Wheel

stories.name: The Sun Tests His Son-in-Law (Nuxalk)
stories.excerpt: In this Nuxalk myth, the daughter of the Sun married a human man known as Salmon Boy. The Sun was not pleased with his daughter's choice and subjected his new son-in-law to a series of deadly tests. The Sun took Salmon Boy to a mountain of unparalleled steepness where mountain goats climbed, commanding him to kill one.
stories.title: The Sun Tests His Son-in-Law (Nuxalk)

stories.name: The Sun's Daughter
stories.excerpt: A cycle of myths about Beaivvi nieida, the Sun's daughter, who descended from the sky to teach the Sámi people to tame reindeer, as well as beauty, handicraft, and hunting yoiks. After her death, she was buried on a mountain peak with reindeer neck hair as bedding. Her spirit wanders all of Sápmi with her reindeer herd
stories.title: The Sun's Daughter

stories.name: The Sun, Moon and Firmament
stories.excerpt: A Chukchi astral myth describing the origins and relationships of celestial bodies. The Sun is considered the most important celestial being, spoken of as an individual spirit with great power. The Moon is seen as a male figure, often described as the 'evil spirit' counterpart of the Sun. Chukchi reindeer herders still
stories.title: The Sun, Moon and Firmament

stories.name: The Sure Shot
stories.excerpt: A watchman in Göinge boasts of his marksmanship and wagers he can shoot a roe on Halland's Mountains from his doorstep. He fires into the dark and kills a magnificent stag, proving to his horrified companions that he is in league with the Evil One.
stories.title: The Sure Shot

stories.name: The Swaichen of the Salt Flats
stories.excerpt: A Bedouin herder loses his way on the salt flats of Bahrain and encounters the Swaichen, a monstrous creature that feeds on the disoriented and the desperate.
stories.title: The Swaichen of the Salt Flats

stories.name: The Sweat Lodge Origin: Seven Bison and Bones Together
stories.excerpt: Seven Bison and their male human companion fought against the angry bison Bones Together, whose pure bone armor was impenetrable. As each bison charged, they broke their legs against Bones Together. Finally the human companion, blessed by an eagle with the power to transform into a feather, faced Bones Together. The mo
stories.title: The Sweat Lodge Origin: Seven Bison and Bones Together

stories.name: The Swineherd
stories.excerpt: In the snow-covered forests of northern Japan, where the winter temperatures drop so low that your breath freezes before it leaves your lips, there is a yokai that haunts the blizzards.
stories.title: The Swineherd

stories.name: The Sword in the Stone
stories.excerpt: After the death of Uther Pendragon, the kingdom of Britain fell into turmoil. Centers on Spirit, human attempt to understand the soul, afterlife, and the unseen forces that govern existence..
stories.title: The Sword in the Stone

stories.name: The Sámi Boy Who Married a Háldi Girl
stories.excerpt: A Sámi boy falls in love with a háldi girl from the hidden underground people. Despite being from different realms, they find a way to marry. The story explores the boundaries between the visible human world and the invisible world of the háldi, a recurring theme in Sámi folklore. Such marriages come with strict taboos
stories.title: The Sámi Boy Who Married a Háldi Girl

stories.name: The Tabudo of the Motagua
stories.excerpt: A water spirit dwelling in the rivers of eastern El Salvador lures the unwary with the scent of copal incense, dragging them beneath the current to serve in its underwater kingdom.
stories.title: The Tabudo of the Motagua

stories.name: The Tale of Kagsagsuk
stories.excerpt: Kagsagsuk is a mistreated orphan boy who suffers extreme cruelty from his foster mother and the village men. Seeking strength, he journeys to the mountains to encounter the Amarok, a giant solitary wolf spirit. Through a series of grueling trials where the Amarok repeatedly throws him down, Kagsagsuk sheds his weakness
stories.title: The Tale of Kagsagsuk

stories.name: The Tale of Njunje Paggas
stories.excerpt: A Stállu tale collected by P. A. Lindholm and illustrated by John Bauer. Njunje Paggas is a Sámi hero who faces the Stállu in a battle of wits. The Stállu is a large, human-like creature who eats people. The Sámi hero wins through cleverness rather than strength. The Stállu's own knife must not be used against him, or
stories.title: The Tale of Njunje Paggas

stories.name: The Tale of the Aluxob
stories.excerpt: Small, elf-like spirits called Aluxob protect cornfields and forests, but they demand respect — and they love to dance.
stories.title: The Tale of the Aluxob

stories.name: The Tale of the Bak Bak
stories.excerpt: In the islands of the Philippines, where the coconut palms sway against turquoise skies and the sea stretches endlessly in every direction, the elders tell stories of the Bak Bak — a mysterious creature that lives in the deepest parts of the forest.
stories.title: The Tale of the Bak Bak

stories.name: The Tale of the Bamboo
stories.excerpt: A boy is born from bamboo and embarks on adventures that reveal his divine origins.
stories.title: The Tale of the Bamboo

stories.name: The Tale of the Black Duck
stories.excerpt: In the tradition of the First Nations peoples of Canada, particularly among the Algonquian and Ojibwe communities, the black duck holds a special place as a teacher of survival and adaptation.
stories.title: The Tale of the Black Duck

stories.name: The Tale of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl
stories.excerpt: A celestial weaver and a mortal cowherd fall in love, only to be separated by the Milky Way, meeting once a year on a bridge of magpies.
stories.title: The Tale of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl

stories.name: The Tale of the First Fire
stories.excerpt: In the beginning, when the world was young and the animals spoke with human voices, there was no fire on earth.
stories.title: The Tale of the First Fire

stories.name: The Tale of the Fisherman and the Little Fish
stories.excerpt: A magical golden fish grants an old fisherman's wishes, but the greed of his wife leads them back to where they started.
stories.title: The Tale of the Fisherman and the Little Fish

stories.name: The Tale of the Lost Man (Tuareg)
stories.excerpt: A classic Tuareg teaching tale from the rich Imayen oral tradition. A man becomes lost in the vast Sahara desert during a sandstorm. His water runs out, his camel collapses, and he resigns himself to death. As he lies on the sand, a mystical camel appears—a creature that seems to be made of light and shadow, with eyes
stories.title: The Tale of the Lost Man (Tuareg)

stories.name: The Tale of the Silver Salmon
stories.excerpt: A fisherman catches a shimmering silver salmon that can speak. The fish promises to grant him one wish in exchange for its freedom. The man asks for the ability to understand the language of all animals, which allows him to uncover a plot to overthrow the local chieftain.
stories.title: The Tale of the Silver Salmon

stories.name: The Tale of the Three Apples
stories.excerpt: A classic murder mystery from the Arabian Nights. Caliph Harun al-Rashid orders his vizier Jafar to solve the murder of a young woman found dismembered in a chest. The investigation leads to her husband, who confesses after returning home to find a strange apple in her possession and killed her in jealous rage. However
stories.title: The Tale of the Three Apples

stories.name: The Tale of the Three Sisters
stories.excerpt: Three sisters become corn, beans, and squash — the Three Sisters crops that sustain life.
stories.title: The Tale of the Three Sisters

stories.name: The Tale of the Two Brothers
stories.excerpt: In ancient Egypt, two brothers ruled the land. Centers on Osiris, from Egypt mythology. Known for aquatic speed and soul sight and immortality..
stories.title: The Tale of the Two Brothers

stories.name: The Tale of the Völva
stories.excerpt: A powerful Völva, or seeress, is summoned to a chieftain's court to predict the future of the land. Through a ritual of chanting and trance, she reveals a vision of coming wars and natural disasters, reminding the people that the threads of fate are woven by the Norns and cannot be undone.
stories.title: The Tale of the Völva

stories.name: The Tallow Candle
stories.excerpt: A poetic story told from the perspective of a tallow candle, reflecting on the fleeting nature of life, light, and the inevitable end.
stories.title: The Tallow Candle

stories.name: the Tanganyika Serpent, the Lake's Guardian
stories.excerpt: A massive serpent that lives in the deepest waters of Lake Tanganyika, stirring the currents that bring fish to the shore — and when it sleeps, the lake goes still and the fishermen catch nothing.
stories.title: the Tanganyika Serpent, the Lake's Guardian

stories.name: The Tashka and Walo: Brothers Who Followed the Sun (Choctaw)
stories.excerpt: Two brothers named Tashka and Walo followed the sun every day from childhood to adulthood. One day, the sun rested over a great expanse of water, and the boys swam into it, emerging in the home of the sun. The sun's wife, the moon, and the stars all lived there. The sun asked why they had followed him for so many years
stories.title: The Tashka and Walo: Brothers Who Followed the Sun (Choctaw)

stories.name: The Tell-Tale Heart
stories.excerpt: Guilt makes a man hear a heart. Centers on Spirit, human attempt to understand the soul, afterlife, and the unseen forces that govern existence..
stories.title: The Tell-Tale Heart

stories.name: the Tenga, Spirits of the Earth
stories.excerpt: The Mossi people believe the earth is alive with spirits called Tenga who must be consulted before every harvest — and those who ignore them find their fields barren and their children sick.
stories.title: the Tenga, Spirits of the Earth

stories.name: The Terror of the Yule Cat
stories.excerpt: The Yule Cat is a giant, monstrous feline that prowls the Icelandic countryside during the winter solstice. It is said that the cat eats anyone who has not received a new piece of clothing for Christmas, a legend that historically encouraged the completion of wool production before the end of the year.
stories.title: The Terror of the Yule Cat

stories.name: The Tertön (Treasure Revealer) Traditions
stories.excerpt: Tibetan legends of the tertöns — treasure revealers who discovered hidden spiritual texts and sacred objects (terma) concealed by Padmasambhava and his consort Yeshe Tsogyal in the 8th century. According to tradition, Padmasambhava foresaw the persecution of Buddhism that would occur in Tibet centuries later and hid th
stories.title: The Tertön (Treasure Revealer) Traditions

stories.name: The Theft of Daylight
stories.excerpt: In a time of eternal darkness, the world was cold and blind. Raven, the cunning trickster, discovered that a powerful being held the light of the world captured in a box. Through a series of disguises and tricks, Raven managed to steal the light and release it into the sky, creating the sun, moon, and stars, and bringi
stories.title: The Theft of Daylight

stories.name: The Theft of Light (Tsimshian - Weeget)
stories.excerpt: On Raven's first journey, Weeget (Giant/Raven) flew inland toward the east carrying a stone his father the chief had given him. When exhausted, he dropped the stone on the sea, where it became a large rock. At that time there was always darkness — no daylight existed. Weeget put on his raven skin and scattered salmon a
stories.title: The Theft of Light (Tsimshian - Weeget)

stories.name: The Three Aunts
stories.excerpt: A story about a young man who inherits a strange set of rules from his three aunts. To claim his inheritance, he must spend a year following their eccentric whims, leading to a series of surreal events and personal growth.
stories.title: The Three Aunts

stories.name: The Three Dogs
stories.excerpt: A king falls under the spell of an evil witch-queen, and only his faithful queen and three magical dogs — with powers of strength, speed, and music — can break the enchantment. From Västergötland, this tale emphasizes the magic of music against trolls.
stories.title: The Three Dogs

stories.name: The Three Little Pigs
stories.excerpt: There was once an old sow who had three little pigs, but times were lean and she could not keep them.
stories.title: The Three Little Pigs

stories.name: The Three Princesses of Whiteland
stories.excerpt: A brave youth journeys to the distant kingdom of Whiteland to win the hand of one of three princesses. He must pass three impossible tests of courage and wisdom, aided by the guidance of a mysterious forest spirit.
stories.title: The Three Princesses of Whiteland

stories.name: The Three Sisters: Corn, Beans, and Squash
stories.excerpt: In Iroquois tradition, the Three Sisters are the agricultural spirits Corn (Onatah), Beans, and Squash. They are inseparable companions who grow best when planted together. According to legend, the Creator gave these three plants to the people as a sacred gift. Corn provides a stalk for the beans to climb, beans fix ni
stories.title: The Three Sisters: Corn, Beans, and Squash

stories.name: The Thunder Beings (Aniyvdaqualosgi) (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: The Cherokee believe in the Thunder Beings, known as Aniyvdaqualosgi or Ani-Yuntikwalaski. The Great Thunder and his two sons, the Thunder Boys, live in the land of the west above the sky vault. They dress in lightning and rainbows. Unlike many tribes where thunder spirits take bird form, Cherokee Thunderers are human
stories.title: The Thunder Beings (Aniyvdaqualosgi) (Cherokee)

stories.name: The Thunderbird and the Whale
stories.excerpt: The Thunderbird, lord of the sky, wages eternal war against the Great Whale, lord of the sea — and their battle is the storm.
stories.title: The Thunderbird and the Whale

stories.name: The Thunderbird Wakinyan
stories.excerpt: Wakinyan is the great Thunderbird of Lakota mythology, a powerful sky spirit associated with thunder, lightning, and storms. His flapping wings create thunderclaps and his eyes flash lightning. When Unhcegila emerged from the primordial waters to flood the land, Wakinyan flapped his wings to dry the earth and shot ligh
stories.title: The Thunderbird Wakinyan

stories.name: The Thunderers (Hadiwennoda:dye's)
stories.excerpt: The Thunderers are powerful storm spirits who live in the sky and cause thunder and lightning. They are described as giant warriors who hunt and kill the great horned serpents and other monsters that threaten humanity. In the Seneca tradition, they are led by the great chief Hino. Their gaze can bring death to mortal m
stories.title: The Thunderers (Hadiwennoda:dye's)

stories.name: The Tickling Demon Mahaha
stories.excerpt: Mahaha is a thin, ice-blue demon who tickles victims with long nails until they die from lack of breath. However, the story concludes that Mahaha can be outwitted by the clever, who eventually trap him in a water hole.
stories.title: The Tickling Demon Mahaha

stories.name: The Tide-Keeper of Abu Dhabi
stories.excerpt: A young diver who disrespects the Gulf earns the wrath of Baba Dariah, Father of the Tide, and must learn to honor the sea before it claims him entirely.
stories.title: The Tide-Keeper of Abu Dhabi

stories.name: The Tie Snake and the Horned Serpent (Creek)
stories.excerpt: The Tie Snake and the Horned Serpent are powerful underwater serpents in Muscogee Creek mythology. The Tie Snake has immense strength and can drag humans underwater to drown. The Horned Serpent is even larger, with antlers or horns, and represents the chaotic forces of the Lower World. According to legend, these creatu
stories.title: The Tie Snake and the Horned Serpent (Creek)

stories.name: The Tiger and the Three Brothers
stories.excerpt: In an old Korean village during the Joseon dynasty, three brothers lived with their mother in a cottage at the foot of a great mountain.
stories.title: The Tiger and the Three Brothers

stories.name: The Tikoloshe in the Guest House
stories.excerpt: A visiting trader encounters the mischievous tikoloshe in a roadside inn and learns that some spirits feed on the arrogance of strangers.
stories.title: The Tikoloshe in the Guest House

stories.name: The Tinderbox
stories.excerpt: A soldier finds a magic tinderbox that allows him to summon three powerful dogs made of precious metals, leading him to wealth and a princess.
stories.title: The Tinderbox

stories.name: The Tlanuwa Bird (Natchez)
stories.excerpt: The Tlanuwa is a giant mythological bird of prey known to both the Natchez and Cherokee. This enormous raptor has feathers made of impenetrable metal that it can launch like arrows at enemies. The Tlanuwa was large enough to carry away humans and even deer. It nested in the highest cliffs and mountains. The Natchez tel
stories.title: The Tlanuwa Bird (Natchez)

stories.name: The Toad and the Snow Kachinas
stories.excerpt: In Oraibi, the Snow Kachinas were practicing for a dance in the Chórzhovi kiva. North of the village at Katcínavala lived Toad Woman with her son. The boy often went to listen to the Kachinas sing. On the dance day, the Toad Boy painted his face and wore a wildcat robe. Children laughed at him and took him to an anthil
stories.title: The Toad and the Snow Kachinas

stories.name: The Tokoloshe of the Umfolozi
stories.excerpt: A cunning water sprite terrorizes a riverside village until an elderly sangoma devises a way to banish it back to the depths.
stories.title: The Tokoloshe of the Umfolozi

stories.name: The Tomtarna
stories.excerpt: The boy Andreas has left his childhood farm to seek fortune in the city. His aging parents miss him terribly. The farm tomte takes pity on them and sets out to find the boy. Andreas works as a guard in the troll prison until a troll bites off his fingers. In despair, he runs into the forest. The tomte finds him, produc
stories.title: The Tomtarna

stories.name: The Tomte and the Christmas Porridge
stories.excerpt: A farmer learns to respect the farm spirit and the importance of keeping traditions.
stories.title: The Tomte and the Christmas Porridge

stories.name: The Tomtegubbe – Åland's Household Guardian
stories.excerpt: The tomte (or gårdstomte) is a household spirit who lives on farms and in barns, watching over the family and livestock. On Åland, as in the rest of the Swedish-speaking world, the tomte was both protector and disciplinarian: he rewarded hard work and good management with prosperity, but punished laziness, drunkenness,
stories.title: The Tomtegubbe – Åland's Household Guardian

stories.name: The Tomten's Christmas Vigil
stories.excerpt: In the deep of a winter night, the Tomten — the ancient guardian spirit of the farm — makes his silent rounds while the household sleeps, watching over all creatures and reflecting on the mysteries of life.
stories.title: The Tomten's Christmas Vigil

stories.name: The Tortoise and the Cracking Shell (Igbo)
stories.excerpt: Mbe the Tortoise was once a bird with a beautiful smooth shell, but his greed and vanity led to his downfall. When the birds of the sky were invited to a great feast in heaven, Tortoise persuaded them to lend him feathers so he could fly and join them. At the feast, he tricked the heavenly hosts into giving him the cho
stories.title: The Tortoise and the Cracking Shell (Igbo)

stories.name: The Tortoise and the Hare
stories.excerpt: In the sun-baked valleys where the dusty trails wound between olive groves and dry riverbeds, the animals of the district had gathered for their usual morning disputes.
stories.title: The Tortoise and the Hare

stories.name: The Tortoise and the Hyena
stories.excerpt: The clever tortoise tricks the greedy hyena in this traditional African folktale.
stories.title: The Tortoise and the Hyena

stories.name: The totem Pole
stories.excerpt: Animals mark family history, telling the story of a clan through carved symbols.
stories.title: The totem Pole

stories.name: The Touni Minwi of Port Louis
stories.excerpt: In the narrow streets of Port Louis, a restless spirit known as the Touni Minwi drifts through shuttered windows and locked doors, carrying a lantern that burns with a light no fire can produce.
stories.title: The Touni Minwi of Port Louis

stories.name: the Toyol and the Jeweler
stories.excerpt: A jeweler in Kampong Glam who used a Toyol to steal diamonds from his competitors, until the Toyol stole the one thing the jeweler treasured more than gold, his reflection.
stories.title: the Toyol and the Jeweler

stories.name: the Toyol, the Thief's Spirit
stories.excerpt: A small green goblin summoned by black magic to steal for its master, but the Toyol steals not just gold, but the master's humanity, one theft at a time.
stories.title: the Toyol, the Thief's Spirit

stories.name: The Transformation of Raven
stories.excerpt: An origin story explaining why the Raven is black. Originally, Raven had beautiful shimmering feathers, but through a series of mishaps and his own trickery, he was scorched by fire or covered in soot. This transformation serves as a permanent mark of his trickster nature.
stories.title: The Transformation of Raven

stories.name: The Transformer Who Became the Mountains (Coast Salish)
stories.excerpt: The Coast Salish tell of a Transformer (Xe'las) who walked through the land making the world right for the coming humans. Near Lake Chelan, he encountered people who had become corrupted by greed and selfishness. He transformed them into stone, their canoes becoming islands in the lake. Near the Fraser River, he found
stories.title: The Transformer Who Became the Mountains (Coast Salish)

stories.name: The Treasure in Säby Creek
stories.excerpt: A miserly gentleman sinks his gold-laden wagon in Saby Creek rather than let it fall to others. A farmer raises white calves on skimmed milk to drag the treasure out but one calf is weakened by watered milk. The wagon slips back as a voice taunts about the calves.
stories.title: The Treasure in Säby Creek

stories.name: The Treasure of Skógafoss
stories.excerpt: Legend tells of a wealthy man named Þrasi Þórólfsson who buried a chest filled with gold and valuables behind the curtain of water at the Skógafoss waterfall. For centuries, people have searched for the treasure, and it is said that only those with a pure heart can find the spot where the gold remains hidden.
stories.title: The Treasure of Skógafoss

stories.name: The Treasure Seekers
stories.excerpt: In Swedish folk belief, those who seek buried treasures must maintain absolute silence or the search will be in vain. Four men form a party to unearth treasures in Josäterdal. As they dig, supernatural illusions appear — an officer, soldiers firing at them, a red calf, a gallows. One digger wears a red shirt that catch
stories.title: The Treasure Seekers

stories.name: The Trial of Lovers: Maiden of Matsaki
stories.excerpt: A Zuni folk tale about the beautiful Maiden of Matsaki, desired by many suitors. After the war god Áhaiyúta and his brother courted her, they discovered she was cruel — she had let the children of Field-mice die of cold while she gambled. The gods punished her but also showed compassion for the helpless mouse children,
stories.title: The Trial of Lovers: Maiden of Matsaki

stories.name: The Trickster Hare and Bouki the Hyena (Wolof)
stories.excerpt: Leuk the Hare is the clever trickster of Wolof folklore, constantly outwitting Bouki the Hyena, who is greedy, stupid, and easily fooled. In one famous tale, Bouki and Leuk found a calabash of milk. Leuk wanted it all for himself, so he convinced Bouki that the milk was poisoned and offered to run and fetch an antidote
stories.title: The Trickster Hare and Bouki the Hyena (Wolof)

stories.name: The Trickster Scorpion and the Merchant
stories.excerpt: A greedy merchant crossing the Sahara encounters a talking scorpion who offers to guide him to a hidden caravansary in exchange for a promise he never intends to keep.
stories.title: The Trickster Scorpion and the Merchant

stories.name: The Troll Ride
stories.excerpt: Peder Lars, a farmer's son, is riding to town to buy a new jacket before courting the beautiful and wealthy Lisa that evening. He is confident she will accept his proposal. But on the way through the forest, he encounters a hideous troll-woman lying injured in a ditch. She begs him to collect resin from seven pine tree
stories.title: The Troll Ride

stories.name: The Troll Shoes
stories.excerpt: An old witch prepares to fly to Blakulla by greasing her enchanted shoes. A weary traveler accidentally puts on the witch's shoes and is dragged head-downward through the night. A passerby knocks off one shoe which instantly vanishes and the weakened witch falls into what becomes the Troll Woman's Pit.
stories.title: The Troll Shoes

stories.name: The Troll Son Who Had Sun Eyes
stories.excerpt: Humpe, the red-haired son of a troll mother, has large clear eyes with a gleam of sunlight in them, marking him as different from troll-kind. His unnatural affinity for daylight makes him an outcast. Filled with daylight's vigor, he leaves troll society and ventures into the forest. He encounters a birch maiden who, wh
stories.title: The Troll Son Who Had Sun Eyes

stories.name: The Troll Who Captured a Princess
stories.excerpt: A classic Faroese folk tale collected by Jakob Jakobsen tells of a troll who lived in a cave and captured a princess to pick lice from his hair. Three brothers set out to rescue her. The elder two brothers failed, but the youngest—helped by the princess who threw him a ball of yarn to track the cave entrance—confronted
stories.title: The Troll Who Captured a Princess

stories.name: The Troll's Daughter
stories.excerpt: A story about a human's interaction with the daughter of a troll, exploring the tension and attraction between the human and supernatural worlds.
stories.title: The Troll's Daughter

stories.name: The Trolls and the Youngest Tomte
stories.excerpt: In the world of Swedish tomtar (house gnomes), the youngest and most curious tomte listens with wonder as the older tomtar tell stories of their adventurous visits inside the trolls' mountain. The older tomtar warn of the dangers, but the youngest tomte's curiosity gets the better of him. He decides to venture into the
stories.title: The Trolls and the Youngest Tomte

stories.name: The Trolls in Resslared
stories.excerpt: Trolls in Resslared sabotage church bells until the Bishop of Skara consecrates one. The trolls then live in harmony with villagers borrowing food and repaying double. When new niggardly residents refuse a troll woman's requests their own provisions vanish and they are forced to leave.
stories.title: The Trolls in Resslared

stories.name: The Trolls of Reynisdrangar
stories.excerpt: Two trolls attempted to pull a great three-masted ship to the shore of the black sand beach of Reynisfjara. However, they were too slow, and as the sun rose over the horizon, the sunlight hit them, instantly turning them into the towering basalt sea stacks that still stand today as a warning against the power of the su
stories.title: The Trolls of Reynisdrangar

stories.name: The Trolls of the Lava Fields
stories.excerpt: The vast lava fields of the south are said to be the remains of trolls who were caught by the dawn. These creatures spent their nights carving the land and building fortresses, but the first light of the sun turned their skin to basalt, leaving them as permanent, frozen monuments in the stone.
stories.title: The Trolls of the Lava Fields

stories.name: The Trow's Fiddle
stories.excerpt: A musician is lured into the hillside by the haunting music of a Trow, learning that the beauty of the spirit world comes with a heavy price.
stories.title: The Trow's Fiddle

stories.name: The Trung Sisters Rebellion
stories.excerpt: The legend of the Trung Sisters — Trung Trac and Trung Nhi — is Vietnam's most celebrated story of female heroism and national resistance. Born in the 1st century CE to a Lac lord in Me Linh, the sisters were educated in martial arts and military strategy by their father. When Trung Trac's husband Thi Sach was brutally
stories.title: The Trung Sisters Rebellion

stories.name: The Tunche of the Jungle
stories.excerpt: Deep in the Amazon, a shape-shifting spirit called the Tunche lures the unwary into the jungle with familiar voices, and those who follow are never seen again.
stories.title: The Tunche of the Jungle

stories.name: The Twelve Brothers
stories.excerpt: A princess is born after twelve brothers who are cursed to become ravens if she speaks before her twelfth birthday. She must remain silent for twelve years to save them.
stories.title: The Twelve Brothers

stories.name: The Twelve Dancing Princesses
stories.excerpt: Twelve princesses secretly dance every night in an enchanted underground kingdom, their secret revealed by a clever soldier.
stories.title: The Twelve Dancing Princesses

stories.name: The Twelve Wild Ducks
stories.excerpt: A queen exchanges her twelve sons for a daughter, who grows up to seek her brothers. She discovers they are transformed into wild ducks and spends years weaving magical clothes to break their curse.
stories.title: The Twelve Wild Ducks

stories.name: The Two Little Ones and Their Turkeys
stories.excerpt: A Zuni story about two orphaned children who were cared for by a flock of wild turkeys. The turkeys provided them with feathers for warmth, eggs for food, and protection from danger. The children lived in harmony with the turkeys, learning the ways of the forest and the language of birds. When the children grew older,
stories.title: The Two Little Ones and Their Turkeys

stories.name: The Two Step-Sisters
stories.excerpt: A kind-hearted girl is mistreated by her cruel stepmother and step-sisters, who force her to do all the hard work. Through her perseverance and the help of magical elements, she manages to overcome their malice, proving her inner beauty and virtue, and eventually finds her rightful place of happiness and honor.
stories.title: The Two Step-Sisters

stories.name: The Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things (Coast Salish)
stories.excerpt: The Coast Salish people of the Olympic Peninsula tell of Ho-ho-e-ap-bess, the Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things, who were the brothers of the Sun and the Moon. When the world was very young, there were no people, birds, or animals — only grass and sand and creatures that were neither animal nor human. The Two-Men-Who-Changed-
stories.title: The Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things (Coast Salish)

stories.name: The Two-Mouthed Woman of Fotouni
stories.excerpt: A woman with a hidden second mouth behind her head feasts on her stepdaughter's hair each night, until the girl discovers the truth and turns the curse back upon its source.
stories.title: The Two-Mouthed Woman of Fotouni

stories.name: The Ugly Duckling
stories.excerpt: It was summertime, and the countryside was beautiful.. A mother duck was sitting on her nest, waiting for her eggs to hatch.
stories.title: The Ugly Duckling

stories.name: The Ulda's Old Mother
stories.excerpt: A Sámi story about the matriarch of the Ulda. The underground people are rich, beautiful, and well-dressed, with reindeer of exceptional colors. All gold and silver under the earth belongs to them. They care for the bear in his winter den, feeding him invisibly. They sometimes swap their children for human babies. If y
stories.title: The Ulda's Old Mother

stories.name: The Universal Basilisk
stories.excerpt: A legendary serpent or dragon, the Basilisk is known as the king of serpents, with a gaze and breath so venomous it can kill anything it encounters.
stories.title: The Universal Basilisk

stories.name: The Universal Demon
stories.excerpt: Demons are malevolent supernatural beings found in virtually every religious and mythological tradition, representing the forces of evil and chaos.
stories.title: The Universal Demon

stories.name: The Universal Dragon
stories.excerpt: The dragon is the most widespread mythical creature, appearing in cultures from Europe to Asia as a powerful serpentine being associated with elemental forces.
stories.title: The Universal Dragon

stories.name: The Universal Dwarf
stories.excerpt: Dwarfs are small, skilled humanoid beings from Germanic and Norse mythology, master craftsmen who live underground and hoard treasure.
stories.title: The Universal Dwarf

stories.name: The Universal Fairy
stories.excerpt: Fairies are nature spirits found in folklore worldwide, beings of great beauty and capricious nature who inhabit the spaces between worlds.
stories.title: The Universal Fairy

stories.name: The Universal Ghost
stories.excerpt: The ghost is a universal belief found in every culture: the spirit of a deceased person that remains among the living, usually due to unfinished business.
stories.title: The Universal Ghost

stories.name: The Universal Giant
stories.excerpt: Giants appear in the mythology of nearly every culture, representing the raw, untamed forces of nature and the primordial world.
stories.title: The Universal Giant

stories.name: The Universal Gryphon
stories.excerpt: A hybrid creature with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle, the Gryphon is a guardian of treasure and a symbol of divine power.
stories.title: The Universal Gryphon

stories.name: The Universal Kelpie
stories.excerpt: A shapeshifting water spirit that appears as a horse, the kelpie lures riders onto its back before diving into the water to drown them.
stories.title: The Universal Kelpie

stories.name: The Universal Mermaid
stories.excerpt: Half-woman, half-fish, the mermaid appears in seafaring cultures worldwide as a symbol of the ocean's beauty, danger, and mystery.
stories.title: The Universal Mermaid

stories.name: The Universal Nisse
stories.excerpt: A household spirit of Scandinavian tradition, the Nisse is a small, bearded being who helps with chores but punishes laziness or disrespect.
stories.title: The Universal Nisse

stories.name: The Universal Nix
stories.excerpt: A water spirit of Germanic and Slavic folklore, the Nix is a shape-shifting being that lures people to their deaths in rivers and lakes.
stories.title: The Universal Nix

stories.name: The Universal Phoenix
stories.excerpt: A mythical bird that cyclically regenerates by being consumed by fire and rising from its own ashes, symbolizing renewal and immortality.
stories.title: The Universal Phoenix

stories.name: The Universal Roc
stories.excerpt: A colossal bird of prey from Middle Eastern legend, the Roc is so large it can carry an elephant in its talons.
stories.title: The Universal Roc

stories.name: The Universal Selkie
stories.excerpt: A shapeshifting seal that sheds its skin to become human, the Selkie appears in the folklore of northern seafaring cultures.
stories.title: The Universal Selkie

stories.name: The Universal Sphinx
stories.excerpt: A mythical creature with a human head and a lion's body, the Sphinx is a guardian of mysteries who poses riddles to those who seek passage.
stories.title: The Universal Sphinx

stories.name: The Universal Spirit
stories.excerpt: A generic spirit that embodies the animistic belief that all things in nature possess a spiritual essence, from rocks and trees to rivers and mountains.
stories.title: The Universal Spirit

stories.name: The Universal Troll
stories.excerpt: The troll appears in folklore across cultures as a giant, brutish being that dwells under bridges and in caves, a universal symbol of the wild and untamed.
stories.title: The Universal Troll

stories.name: The Universal Vampire
stories.excerpt: Vampires are undead beings who feed on the blood of the living, appearing in the folklore of many cultures around the world.
stories.title: The Universal Vampire

stories.name: The Universal Werewolf
stories.excerpt: A human with the ability to transform into a wolf, the werewolf appears in folklore across Europe and beyond, representing the wildness within.
stories.title: The Universal Werewolf

stories.name: The Universal Witch
stories.excerpt: Witches are practitioners of magic found in folklore worldwide, wielding supernatural power for good or ill through spells, potions, and communion with spirits.
stories.title: The Universal Witch

stories.name: The Unwelcome Guest
stories.excerpt: A story exploring the laws of hospitality and the consequences of betrayal. A guest arrives unexpectedly and proceeds to cause chaos and distress, testing the patience, virtue, and generosity of the hosts in a challenging social dynamic.
stories.title: The Unwelcome Guest

stories.name: The Urko of North Wij
stories.excerpt: In the mountain of Urberg dwells the Urko a monster cow whose plowing created Lake Sommen. She is fettered by a horseshoe eating one hair from a cowhide each Christmas until the hairs run out and the world ends. If a king crosses Ydre she will break free having already killed King Frode.
stories.title: The Urko of North Wij

stories.name: The Valiant Chanticleer
stories.excerpt: A childless woman is given an egg to hatch in her bosom, but out comes a cockerel. He grows enormous, ploughs the fields with a single ox, then sets off to win the king's daughter. He gathers a fox, wolf, bear, and lake as companions, defeats the king's geese, cattle, and horses, survives being roasted, and finally the
stories.title: The Valiant Chanticleer

stories.name: The Valraven
stories.excerpt: The Valravn is a Danish supernatural raven that can transform into a knight. It appears on battlefields, feasting on the dead, and can be bound by oaths.
stories.title: The Valraven

stories.name: The Vedda Creation Myth and Kande Yakka
stories.excerpt: The Vedda people, Sri Lanka's indigenous inhabitants, trace their origin to the children of Prince Vijaya and Kuveni — a son and daughter abandoned in the wilderness who married each other and became the first Veddas. Their central deity is Kande Yakka, the chief of the ancestral spirits (Yakku), who governs hunting su
stories.title: The Vedda Creation Myth and Kande Yakka

stories.name: the Veshtitza, the Witch of the Mountain
stories.excerpt: A witch who lives in the highest mountain caves, stealing the milk from cows and the breath from children — and the only way to stop her is to leave a scissors open on the windowsill.
stories.title: the Veshtitza, the Witch of the Mountain

stories.name: The Vila of Maglić
stories.excerpt: A winged mountain spirit dances on the summit of Maglić in storms, and the shepherd who follows her song into the clouds returns with impossible knowledge — or does not return at all.
stories.title: The Vila of Maglić

stories.name: the Vila's Healing Song
stories.excerpt: A Vila who fell in love with a mortal shepherd and healed his wounds with her song — but her song could only heal the body, not the loneliness of loving someone who would grow old and die.
stories.title: the Vila's Healing Song

stories.name: the Vila, the Mountain Nymph
stories.excerpt: A beautiful winged woman who dances on the mountain peaks at dawn, her song carrying across the valleys — and the shepherd who hears her dance will never love a mortal woman again.
stories.title: the Vila, the Mountain Nymph

stories.name: The Village Magician
stories.excerpt: A traveling magician arrives in a Yorkshire village performing impossible feats, only to be revealed as a mortal man whose greatest trick is convincing others to believe.
stories.title: The Village Magician

stories.name: The Vishap on the Mountain of the Ark
stories.excerpt: A primordial dragon guards the deepest waters beneath Mount Ararat, dreaming of a second Flood that will return the world to the chaos it once commanded.
stories.title: The Vishap on the Mountain of the Ark

stories.name: The Visiting Animals
stories.excerpt: A grieving old man lives near a fjord to stay close to his son's grave. He is visited by three mysterious men of varying sizes and nose shapes. After he shows them hospitality and provides them with sole leather and walrus tusk, the visitors reveal their true natures and transform into a reindeer, a fox, and a hare, le
stories.title: The Visiting Animals

stories.name: The Vittra – The Hidden People of Åland
stories.excerpt: The vittra (singular: vitter) are an underground-dwelling people who live in a parallel civilization beneath the hills and meadows of Åland. Invisible to most humans, they have their own farms, livestock, and churches. They are known to do favors for humans who treat them with dignity and respect, but can become vengef
stories.title: The Vittra – The Hidden People of Åland

stories.name: The Vittra's Path
stories.excerpt: A hardworking farmer discovers his prosperity is tied to the unseen world when he must move his entire house to avoid blocking the ancestral path of the vittra.
stories.title: The Vittra's Path

stories.name: The Vodnik of the Mountain Stream
stories.excerpt: A fisherman who has grown too greedy learns a lesson from the Vodnik, the water spirit who guards the mountain streams and punishes those who take more than they need.
stories.title: The Vodnik of the Mountain Stream

stories.name: The Vodyanoy of the Volga
stories.excerpt: A bearded water spirit with green skin drags the unwary beneath the Volga, and the only way to escape is to throw a black rooster into the river.
stories.title: The Vodyanoy of the Volga

stories.name: The Voice of the Witz
stories.excerpt: A young Maya priest enters a sacred cave to seek a vision from the mountain spirit, but the Witz demands a price he did not expect.
stories.title: The Voice of the Witz

stories.name: The Voyages of Kiviuk
stories.excerpt: The epic adventures of Kiviuk, a supernatural hero who travels across the Arctic encountering spirits, monsters, and divine beings. His journeys involve solving riddles and completing impossible tasks. Kiviuk represents the ideal of Inuit resilience, courage, and curiosity.
stories.title: The Voyages of Kiviuk

stories.name: The Wail of Nya-Nya Bulembu
stories.excerpt: A forest monster that mimics the cries of lost children lures travelers into the deep woods, where the boundary between the living and the dead grows thin.
stories.title: The Wail of Nya-Nya Bulembu

stories.name: The Wandering Jew
stories.excerpt: A man cursed to wander the earth until the Second Coming after taunting Christ, becoming a timeless witness to human history.
stories.title: The Wandering Jew

stories.name: The Warrior Suitor of Moki (Hopi)
stories.excerpt: A Zuni story about a warrior from Zuni who traveled to the land of the Hopi (called Moki in Zuni) to win a bride. The warrior had to prove his worth through feats of strength, courage, and skill. He faced challenges set by the Hopi elders, including hunting dangerous game, competing in races and games, and demonstratin
stories.title: The Warrior Suitor of Moki (Hopi)

stories.name: The Water Dragon of Kupa
stories.excerpt: In the silver days of old Croatia, along the winding Kupa River where the waters whispered through valleys of green, there lived a family of seven children.
stories.title: The Water Dragon of Kupa

stories.name: The Water Goblin of the Vltava
stories.excerpt: An ambitious fiddler trades his soul for the secret of perfect music, only to become a permanent trophy of a river spirit.
stories.title: The Water Goblin of the Vltava

stories.name: The Water Serpent of Tornedalen
stories.excerpt: A mythical water serpent from the Tornedalen region, known in both Sámi and Meänkieli traditions as Čáhcegearpmaš. This huge serpent lives in lakes and rivers and frightens people away from fishing. It embodies the dangers of Arctic waters. The tradition is preserved in contemporary Sámi children's radio programs.
stories.title: The Water Serpent of Tornedalen

stories.name: The Waters of Aral
stories.excerpt: A young shepherd discovers that the mountain lakes harbor ancient water-spirits who guard the balance between the highland villages and the lowland deserts.
stories.title: The Waters of Aral

stories.name: The Weaving of Ix Chel
stories.excerpt: The moon goddess Ix Chel weaves the fabric of fate on her backstrap loom, but when she unravels her work in grief, the world nearly drowns.
stories.title: The Weaving of Ix Chel

stories.name: The Wee Wee Man
stories.excerpt: A traveler meets a tiny man who shows him a different world, teaching him the value of secrets.
stories.title: The Wee Wee Man

stories.name: The Weeping Nun
stories.excerpt: A nun who committed suicide now wanders a church, weeping for her unborn child—her spirit will rest only when someone acknowledges her.
stories.title: The Weeping Nun

stories.name: The Weeping Stones
stories.excerpt: In the remote Isles of the Hebrides, particularly upon the wild shores of Skye and the distant Outer Islands, there are stones that weep.
stories.title: The Weeping Stones

stories.name: The Weeping Sword
stories.excerpt: Kitsune — the fox spirit of Japanese folklore — is one of the most complex and contradictory creatures in world mythology.
stories.title: The Weeping Sword

stories.name: The Weeping Woman
stories.excerpt: A spectral woman in flowing white haunts the Danish coastline, appearing as a sorrowful omen of impending shipwrecks and oceanic tragedies.
stories.title: The Weeping Woman

stories.name: The Weeping Woman of Lake Atitlán
stories.excerpt: A Tz'utujil woman, betrayed by her husband, drowns her children in Lake Atitlán and is condemned to wander its shores forever, weeping for what she destroyed.
stories.title: The Weeping Woman of Lake Atitlán

stories.name: The Wendigo
stories.excerpt: The cannibal spirit of Algonquian legend, a gaunt creature of insatiable hunger.
stories.title: The Wendigo

stories.name: The Wendigo Hunt
stories.excerpt: A hunting party in the deep winter forest encounters a wendigo — and learns that the real monster is not the spirit, but the hunger that made it.
stories.title: The Wendigo Hunt

stories.name: The Wendigo: Cannibal Spirit
stories.excerpt: A frozen spirit of greed—it possesses humans who resort to cannibalism, turning them into monsters of hunger.
stories.title: The Wendigo: Cannibal Spirit

stories.name: The Werehyena of Bangui
stories.excerpt: In the growing city of Bangui, a man discovers his quiet neighbor is a werehyena who shifts form at the new moon, and must decide whether to expose the creature or honor the old compact that keeps the peace.
stories.title: The Werehyena of Bangui

stories.name: The Werewolf
stories.excerpt: A prince cursed to become a werewolf roams the wilderness until a princess's self-sacrificing love and courage break the spell. Rooted in the ancient Teutonic belief in werewolves, this tale from Uppland emphasizes redemption through love.
stories.title: The Werewolf

stories.name: The Werewolf Transformation
stories.excerpt: A Sámi shape-shifting legend where people are turned into wolves. The transformation can be reversed only if the werewolf does not taste the blood of a reindeer, or if they are given cooked food. This reflects Sámi beliefs about the permeability between human and animal identities, and the importance of reindeer in mai
stories.title: The Werewolf Transformation

stories.name: The Whale Who Sang the World Awake
stories.excerpt: Before the island existed, a Great Whale sang a song that called the land up from the deep, and its echo still guides fishermen home.
stories.title: The Whale Who Sang the World Awake

stories.name: The Whistle of El Silbón
stories.excerpt: A giant spirit wanders the llanos at night whistling a tune that rises and falls with the wind, carrying a sack of bones on his back and hunting the men who have wronged their fathers.
stories.title: The Whistle of El Silbón

stories.name: The White Bead Maiden's Marriage to the Sun
stories.excerpt: In this Navajo story, White Bead Maiden (Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́) was sought in marriage by the Sun. The Sun, disguised as a handsome warrior, courted the maiden. After many trials, she agreed to marry him and traveled to his house in the eastern horizon. The Sun's house was a square room of turquoise and white shell with th
stories.title: The White Bead Maiden's Marriage to the Sun

stories.name: The White Beaver Ceremony
stories.excerpt: Among the Chawi band of the Pawnee South Bands, the White Beaver ceremony served the same purpose as the Skidi's Spring Awakening ceremony—renewing life and ensuring fertility. However, instead of focusing on corn, the White Beaver ceremony revitalized hibernating animals. The white beaver was a sacred animal associate
stories.title: The White Beaver Ceremony

stories.name: The White Dove
stories.excerpt: A tale of purity, hope, and peace represented by a white dove, set within a traditional folk context of kindness and reward.
stories.title: The White Dove

stories.name: The White Mountain Apache Creation
stories.excerpt: In the White Mountain Apache creation myth from Noze (recorded in 1910), a maiden went to the top of a high mountain where the rays of the rising Sun first struck. She raised her skirt and the breath of the Sun entered her. She went up the mountain four mornings, and four times the Sun's breath entered her. This unmarr
stories.title: The White Mountain Apache Creation

stories.name: The White Snake
stories.excerpt: A white snake spirit transforms into a beautiful woman and marries a human man. A Buddhist monk discovers her true nature and traps her under Thunder Peak Pagoda.
stories.title: The White Snake

stories.name: The White Stag
stories.excerpt: In the deep forests of Hungary, where the Carpathian Mountains rose like the bones of ancient giants, there lived a white stag unlike any other.
stories.title: The White Stag

stories.name: The Wicked Prince
stories.excerpt: A tale of a prince whose inherent cruelty and lack of empathy lead to his eventual downfall and isolation from others.
stories.title: The Wicked Prince

stories.name: The Widow's Son
stories.excerpt: The youngest son of a widow is underestimated by his brothers and father, but possesses a kindness and curiosity that leads him to magical discoveries. He eventually saves his family from ruin through his generosity and bravery.
stories.title: The Widow's Son

stories.name: The Wild Swans
stories.excerpt: Far away, in a land where swallows fly when winter comes, there lived a king who had eleven sons and one daughter named Elisa.
stories.title: The Wild Swans

stories.name: The Will-o'-the-Wisp
stories.excerpt: A mysterious floating light that leads travelers astray in bogs and marshes, serving as a warning against following false promises.
stories.title: The Will-o'-the-Wisp

stories.name: The Windigo Baby
stories.excerpt: A newly married couple had a baby boy who seemed normal until one day, while still in his cradleboard, he spoke to his parents saying he would visit the Sky Spirit. That night, the baby vanished from his cradleboard. The parents found tiny tracks leading to the lake, then enormous footprints beyond. The child had trans
stories.title: The Windigo Baby

stories.name: The Wise Fool of Somali Folklore
stories.excerpt: Somali folklore features a beloved character known as the 'wise fool' — a simpleton whose apparent foolishness conceals profound wisdom. In one popular tale, a poor man was mocked by villagers for talking to rocks. 'Stupid man,' they laughed, 'rocks cannot hear!' When a terrible drought came, the wise fool walked to a
stories.title: The Wise Fool of Somali Folklore

stories.name: The Witchcraft Spirits of Lipangula
stories.excerpt: A young Makonde girl discovers that the inherited witchcraft flowing through her bloodline is not a curse but a responsibility, when the spirits of uchawi choose her to restore balance to a village torn by fear and suspicion.
stories.title: The Witchcraft Spirits of Lipangula

stories.name: The Wolf and the Seven Kids
stories.excerpt: There was once an old mother goat who lived with her seven little kids in a cozy cottage at the edge of a great forest.
stories.title: The Wolf and the Seven Kids

stories.name: The Wolf's Wedding: The Moroccan Rainbow Legend
stories.excerpt: A North African folk explanation for the rainbow that is widespread across the Maghreb, among both Arabic and Berber-speaking populations. When a rainbow appears in the sky—especially when rain falls while the sun shines—it is said to be 'the marriage of the jackal' or 'the wolf's wedding' (tameγra bbuššen in Berber, '
stories.title: The Wolf's Wedding: The Moroccan Rainbow Legend

stories.name: The Woman Who Fell from the Sky
stories.excerpt: In the Sky World above the earth, a pregnant woman named Atsi'tsaká:ion (Mature Flower) fell through a hole created when the Great Tree of Life was uprooted. As she descended, she grasped seeds from the tree. Water birds saw her falling and caught her, placing her on the back of the Great Turtle. The muskrat dove to th
stories.title: The Woman Who Fell from the Sky

stories.name: The Woman Who Married a Buffalo
stories.excerpt: A Lakota woman was picking berries when a buffalo bull approached her. To her surprise, he spoke and asked her to be his wife. She agreed and went to live with the buffalo people, where she learned their ways and language. She gave birth to a son who was half-human, half-buffalo. One day, her human brothers came huntin
stories.title: The Woman Who Married a Buffalo

stories.name: The Wonderful Horns of the Orphan Boy
stories.excerpt: A Xhosa boy whose mother had died was mistreated by his stepmothers and decided to leave home, riding on his father's ox. The ox fought and defeated a fierce bull from a passing herd. Later the ox told the boy it would die fighting another bull and instructed him to break off its horns. After the ox's death, the boy di
stories.title: The Wonderful Horns of the Orphan Boy

stories.name: The Wonderful Tar-Baby
stories.excerpt: Brer Fox fashions a doll made of tar and turpentine and sets it in the road to trap Brer Rabbit. When Brer Rabbit greets the silent Tar-Baby and receives no reply, he grows angry and strikes it, getting his paw stuck. He strikes with the other paw, then kicks, and finally butts with his head—each limb becoming hopeless
stories.title: The Wonderful Tar-Baby

stories.name: The Xan of Mountain Passes
stories.excerpt: A shepherd encounters a Xan, a restless mountain ghost, and learns why the dead sometimes refuse to leave the high places they loved in life.
stories.title: The Xan of Mountain Passes

stories.name: The Xtabai of Temptress Creek
stories.excerpt: A beautiful woman lures men into the jungle on moonlit nights, but those who follow the Xtabai discover too late that her beauty is a veil over ancient hunger, and the jungle keeps what she claims.
stories.title: The Xtabai of Temptress Creek

stories.name: The Yacumama of the Río Napo
stories.excerpt: A massive water serpent dwells in the deepest pools of the Amazon, swallowing canoes whole and guarding the jungle's hidden treasures.
stories.title: The Yacumama of the Río Napo

stories.name: The Yacuruna and the Fisherman's Wife
stories.excerpt: A water people abduct a fisherman's wife, and he must journey to their underwater city to bring her back before she forgets the surface world.
stories.title: The Yacuruna and the Fisherman's Wife

stories.name: The Yaguarón's River Curse
stories.excerpt: A cat-like river monster with glowing eyes drags livestock and children beneath the brown waters of the Paraguay River, and only the medicine man's song can release them.
stories.title: The Yaguarón's River Curse

stories.name: the Yagwanggwi, the Night Watcher
stories.excerpt: A shadowy figure that watches over sleeping villages, its glowing eyes visible from the hilltops — because in Korea, someone must guard the night.
stories.title: the Yagwanggwi, the Night Watcher

stories.name: The Yap Stone Money Origin
stories.excerpt: Yapese legend tells of the origin of rai stones, the massive stone money for which Yap is famous. According to oral tradition, a legendary navigator named Anagumang led an expedition by raft and canoe to the islands of Palau, where the Yapese discovered limestone. Anagumang had his men carve the limestone into circular
stories.title: The Yap Stone Money Origin

stories.name: The Yara-ma-yha-who: The Vampire Spirit
stories.excerpt: The Yara-ma-yha-who is a vampiric spirit from Aboriginal Australian Dreaming legends, particularly in the mythology of the Yuin people of southeastern Australia. This creature is described as a small, red-skinned being standing about four feet tall with an oversized head, large mouth, and long skinny limbs. Each of its
stories.title: The Yara-ma-yha-who: The Vampire Spirit

stories.name: The Yeti (Migoi) Legends
stories.excerpt: Tibetan legends of the Yeti (Migoi or Migyur, meaning 'wild man'), a powerful apelike creature said to inhabit the high Himalayas. In Tibetan folklore, the Yeti is not merely a physical creature but a spiritual guardian of the mountains, often associated with mountain gods like Nyenchen Thanglha. Some traditions descri
stories.title: The Yeti (Migoi) Legends

stories.name: The Yeti: Abominable Snowman of the Himalayas
stories.excerpt: The Yeti (from Sherpa 'yeh-teh', meaning 'cliff dweller') is a legendary ape-like creature said to inhabit the Himalayan mountains of Nepal, Tibet, and Bhutan. In Sherpa and Tibetan Buddhist tradition, Yetis are more than cryptids — they are spiritual beings that act as protectors of sacred valleys. Ancient Tibetan tex
stories.title: The Yeti: Abominable Snowman of the Himalayas

stories.name: The Yeti: The Abominable Snowman of the Himalayas
stories.excerpt: A mysterious ape-like creature haunts the high Himalayas, seen only by those with pure hearts.
stories.title: The Yeti: The Abominable Snowman of the Himalayas

stories.name: The Youth and His Eagle
stories.excerpt: A Zuni story about a young boy who raised an eagle and developed a deep spiritual bond with the bird. The eagle became his protector and provider, bringing him gifts from the sky world. However, jealous members of the village conspired against the boy and his eagle. The eagle, being a sacred creature connected to the S
stories.title: The Youth and His Eagle

stories.name: The Yule Lads' Mischief
stories.excerpt: Thirteen brothers, the sons of Grýla the ogress and Leppalúði, descend from the mountains each December. Each Lad has a unique personality and a specific prank, such as stealing sausages or licking windows, terrorizing children and farmers before Christmas Eve.
stories.title: The Yule Lads' Mischief

stories.name: The Yule Stállu (Juovlastállu)
stories.excerpt: A terrifying Christmas tradition from Finnmark and northern Troms. Juovlastállu is the Yule giant who punishes children who misbehave at Christmas. He drives a sled pulled by mice or lemmings. Families must sweep the area around the home clean so the sled doesn't get stuck, and must leave water outside for him. If he d
stories.title: The Yule Stállu (Juovlastállu)

stories.name: The Yumboes: The Fairy Spirits of Senegal
stories.excerpt: Small, silver-skinned fairy beings dance under the moonlight on the coast of Senegal.
stories.title: The Yumboes: The Fairy Spirits of Senegal

stories.name: The Zambur of the Valley
stories.excerpt: An ancient animal-spirit that haunts the warm valleys of southern Tajikistan teaches hunters the difference between taking what is needed and taking what is wanted.
stories.title: The Zambur of the Valley

stories.name: The Zana: Benevolent Fairies of the Albanian Mountains
stories.excerpt: Beautiful mountain fairies protect lost travelers and bless newborns with gifts of beauty and talent.
stories.title: The Zana: Benevolent Fairies of the Albanian Mountains

stories.name: The Zar of the Red Sea Coast
stories.excerpt: A woman in the coastal town of Massawa is possessed by a Zar spirit who demands music, dance, and recognition, and her family must learn that some illnesses cannot be cured by medicine alone.
stories.title: The Zar of the Red Sea Coast

stories.name: The Zar Queen of Keren
stories.excerpt: In the western city of Keren, the Zar spirits are led by a queen who selects her court from among the living, and a Tigre man who refuses her summons discovers that pride is the most dangerous offering of all.
stories.title: The Zar Queen of Keren

stories.name: The Zar Spirit Possession Cult
stories.excerpt: The Zar cult is a widespread spirit possession tradition found throughout Sudan, Egypt, and the Horn of Africa, blending pre-Islamic African beliefs with Islamic Sufi practices. According to tradition, zar spirits are invisible beings created from smokeless fire who can possess humans, causing illness, infertility, or
stories.title: The Zar Spirit Possession Cult

stories.name: the Zduhać's Battle in the Clouds
stories.excerpt: Two Zduhaći from rival villages battle above the clouds during a hailstorm, their punches becoming thunderbolts — and the villagers below can only pray and wait for the sky to choose a winner.
stories.title: the Zduhać's Battle in the Clouds

stories.name: the Zduhać, the Weather Warrior
stories.excerpt: A man who can leave his body while sleeping to fight storms in the sky, battling other Zduhaći to protect his village from hail and lightning — because in Montenegro, the weather is not natural, it is earned.
stories.title: the Zduhać, the Weather Warrior

stories.name: The Zin Who Married a Fisherman
stories.excerpt: A Songhai fisherman on the Niger River falls in love with a Zin, a water spirit of terrible beauty, and must choose between the world of water and the world of men.
stories.title: The Zin Who Married a Fisherman

stories.name: The Zombi: The Living Dead of Haitian Vodou
stories.excerpt: A bokor sorcerer raises the dead to serve as mindless slaves in Haitian folklore.
stories.title: The Zombi: The Living Dead of Haitian Vodou

stories.name: The Zombie Creation Myth of Haitian Vodou
stories.excerpt: The zombie (zonbi) originates from Haitian folklore, where it is a dead body reanimated through magic by a bokor sorcerer. In Vodou belief, a person has two souls: the ti bon ange (little good angel) and the gros bon ange (big good angel). The bokor captures the ti bon ange, the essence of personality and consciousness
stories.title: The Zombie Creation Myth of Haitian Vodou

stories.name: The Zuni People Emerge into Daylight
stories.excerpt: In Ruth Benedict's version of the Zuni emergence, people dwelt in total darkness deep in the fourth world. Awonawilona, the Sun, took pity on them. His two sons, the bow priests, located the opening to the fourth world in the southwest and led the people upward. They planted seeds that grew into pine, spruce, silver sp
stories.title: The Zuni People Emerge into Daylight

stories.name: The Älvor – Meadow Elves of the Åland Archipelago
stories.excerpt: The älvor (elves) are beautiful, otherworldly female beings who dance in the meadows and misty fields of Åland, particularly at dawn and dusk. Their dancing leaves behind 'älvringar' (fairy rings) — circles of flattened grass or mushrooms where the ground is forever enchanted. Humans who interrupt their dances may be l
stories.title: The Älvor – Meadow Elves of the Åland Archipelago

stories.name: Theyyam — The Dance of the Gods in Kerala
stories.excerpt: Theyyam is an ancient ritualistic performance tradition of northern Kerala where performers transform into living deities through elaborate makeup, costumes, and trance-dance. Each Theyyam tells a specific mythological story. Among the most famous is the legend of Muchilottu Bhagavathi, a goddess born from the fire of
stories.title: Theyyam — The Dance of the Gods in Kerala

stories.name: Thoth
stories.excerpt: In the grand hall of judgment that lies at the heart of the Duat, the Egyptian underworld, there sits a figure of profound importance.
stories.title: Thoth

stories.name: Three Billy Goats Gruff
stories.excerpt: Three billy goat brothers use their wits and varying sizes to outsmart a hungry troll guarding a bridge, proving that cleverness can overcome brute strength.
stories.title: Three Billy Goats Gruff

stories.name: Three Years without Wages
stories.excerpt: A youth serves a miserly master for three years without pay, receiving only a puppy, a kitten, and a lizard as his wages. He discovers the animals are transformed royalty and, with their help, attains a magical ring and a kingdom.
stories.title: Three Years without Wages

stories.name: Thumbelina
stories.excerpt: There once lived a woman who wanted a tiny child more than anything in the world.
stories.title: Thumbelina

stories.name: Thunderbird and Whale (Kwakwaka'wakw)
stories.excerpt: The epic struggle between Thunderbird (Tseiqami) and Whale is one of the most important myths of the Pacific Northwest, found across Kwakwaka'wakw and Nuu-chah-nulth traditions. Thunderbird is a massive supernatural bird whose wingbeats cause thunder and whose eyes flash lightning. He hunts whales for food, plunging fr
stories.title: Thunderbird and Whale (Kwakwaka'wakw)

stories.name: Ti Lobo and Chibinho
stories.excerpt: The cunning little goat Chibinho repeatedly outsmarts the greedy wolf Ti Lobo, proving that wit is more powerful than appetite.
stories.title: Ti Lobo and Chibinho

stories.name: Ti Malice and Bouki: The Trickster and the Fool
stories.excerpt: Ti Malice and Uncle Bouki are paired characters in Haitian folklore, representing the split of the Anansi trickster archetype. Ti Malice is smart, cunning, and guileful, while Uncle Bouki is hardworking but greedy and foolish. In one classic tale, Bouki hears an old woman cry 'Ay-yai!' after biting her lip, and mistake
stories.title: Ti Malice and Bouki: The Trickster and the Fool

stories.name: Tiddalik the Frog
stories.excerpt: The greedy frog who drank all the water, and had to be made to laugh to release it.
stories.title: Tiddalik the Frog

stories.name: Tiddalik the Thirsty Frog
stories.excerpt: In an Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime story attributed to the Gunaikurnai people of Gippsland, Victoria, Tiddalik the frog awoke one morning with an insatiable thirst and drank all the fresh water in the world. Lakes, rivers, and waterholes dried up, and creatures and plants everywhere began to die. The other animals c
stories.title: Tiddalik the Thirsty Frog

stories.name: Tiggak the Shaman
stories.excerpt: Tiggak is a powerful angakkoq (shaman) who becomes lazy and neglects his duties, causing friction with his brothers-in-law. During a harsh winter, the group becomes stranded on dangerous ice floes. Tiggak's supernatural foresight and magical abilities become the group's only hope for survival. By invoking charms and na
stories.title: Tiggak the Shaman

stories.name: Tikta'Liktak's Journey Home
stories.excerpt: A young hunter becomes stranded on a drifting ice floe. The story chronicles his struggle for survival and encounters with Arctic spirits. His return home is a testament to navigation skills and the spiritual connection between a hunter and his homeland.
stories.title: Tikta'Liktak's Journey Home

stories.name: Timun Mas (The Golden Cucumber)
stories.excerpt: A Javanese folktale about a childless couple who pray desperately for a child. An ogre-like giant named Buto Ijo grants their wish by giving them a magical cucumber seed, which grows into a cucumber containing a baby girl named Timun Mas (Golden Cucumber). The giant promises to return when she is seventeen to claim her
stories.title: Timun Mas (The Golden Cucumber)

stories.name: Tin Hinan, Mother of the Tuareg
stories.excerpt: Tin Hinan—meaning 'she of the tents' or 'mother of us all'—is the legendary ancestress and queen of the Tuareg people. According to oral tradition, she was a 4th-century princess who fled north Africa with her servant Takamat, riding a white camel across the Sahara. Near perishing in the wilderness, they stumbled upon
stories.title: Tin Hinan, Mother of the Tuareg

stories.name: Tin Hinan: The Queen of the Tuareg
stories.excerpt: A legendary Berber queen fled Roman persecution and established the matrilineal traditions of the Tuareg people.
stories.title: Tin Hinan: The Queen of the Tuareg

stories.name: Tippafossur and the Killing of Jógvan
stories.excerpt: A grim legend within the Ormur cycle. Jógvan, a farmer from Oyri, caught Ormur of Skála stealing his sheep and attacked him. Miraculously, Jógvan overpowered the huge Ormur and held him down, calling for his son to bring a knife. But the son, terrified of Ormur, fled and hid at the Tippafossur gorge. Ormur, pinned and
