stories.title: Tippafossur and the Killing of Jógvan

stories.name: Tiramakhan Traore Conquers Kaabu (Mande)
stories.excerpt: General Tiramakhan Traore, Sundiata Keita's greatest military commander, was sent to conquer the Senegambia region after the king of Jolof insulted Sundiata by confiscating his horses and sending him a skin to make shoes. Tiramakhan marched his army through the Gambia River valley, defeating kingdom after kingdom. The
stories.title: Tiramakhan Traore Conquers Kaabu (Mande)

stories.name: Tirawa Creates the Universe
stories.excerpt: Tirawa (Atíʼas Tirawa), 'Our Father Above,' was the supreme creator god of the Pawnee. He created the universe and placed the Morning Star in the East and the Evening Star in the West. The Morning Star, a male warrior god, was created first. The female Evening Star resisted the divine plan to create humankind, so Morni
stories.title: Tirawa Creates the Universe

stories.name: Tizan the Illness Bringer
stories.excerpt: A restless spirit called Tizan wanders the villages at dusk, laying curses of sickness on those who have wronged their neighbors or spoken ill of the dead.
stories.title: Tizan the Illness Bringer

stories.name: Tlanuwa: The Giant Raptor (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: Tlanuwa is a giant mythological bird of prey with feathers made of impenetrable metal. This massive raptor could carry off humans and even small deer in its talons. Its feathers were said to be sharp as knives and could be launched as projectiles. The Tlanuwa lived in the highest mountain peaks and remote cliffs. In Ch
stories.title: Tlanuwa: The Giant Raptor (Cherokee)

stories.name: To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu: The Twin Gods of New Britain
stories.excerpt: Two divine brothers create the world through wisdom and folly, explaining the origins of good and evil.
stories.title: To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu: The Twin Gods of New Britain

stories.name: To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu: The Wise and Foolish Brothers
stories.excerpt: In the mythology of New Britain (Papua New Guinea), the two culture hero brothers To-Kabinana (wise) and To-Karvuvu (foolish) were created when an old woman scratched her arms with pandanus strips while wading in the sea, and the two bloodied strips swelled into boys. To-Kabinana created good things for humanity while
stories.title: To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu: The Wise and Foolish Brothers

stories.name: Tobacco Society: Chief No Vitals Discovers Tobacco
stories.excerpt: The Crow people believe that tobacco was first discovered by Chief No Vitals at Devils Lake in eastern North Dakota. The Creator instructed him to seek the sacred plant, telling him that the worship of tobacco would help the Crow honor God and maintain their connection to the spirit world. Chief No Vitals found the pla
stories.title: Tobacco Society: Chief No Vitals Discovers Tobacco

stories.name: Tokoloshe: The Mischievous Water Trickster
stories.excerpt: The Tokoloshe is a dwarf-like water sprite in Zulu mythology, a small hairy humanoid summoned by witches and sorcerers to carry out evil deeds. It can become invisible at will and causes illness, bad luck, and misfortune. Many South Africans still believe in the Tokoloshe and take precautions such as raising their beds
stories.title: Tokoloshe: The Mischievous Water Trickster

stories.name: Tokoloshe: The Water Imp
stories.excerpt: A mischievous, malevolent water spirit that can only be seen by certain people—and is used to frighten children.
stories.title: Tokoloshe: The Water Imp

stories.name: Tom Thumb
stories.excerpt: In the days of the great King Arthur, there lived a poor ploughman named Thomas and his wife.
stories.title: Tom Thumb

stories.name: Tom Totherhouse
stories.excerpt: A clever youth enters into a wager with a woman who is having an affair with a neighbor while her husband is deaf. Through a series of ingenious tricks and psychological manipulations, he forces the woman to confess her infidelity, winning the wager and exposing the truth.
stories.title: Tom Totherhouse

stories.name: Tomte's Christmas Porridge
stories.excerpt: A greedy farmer attempts to steal the Christmas porridge meant for the farm's protector spirit, the Tomte, only to face the devastating consequences of his disrespect.
stories.title: Tomte's Christmas Porridge

stories.name: Tonantzin and Our Lady of Guadalupe — The Sacred Syncretism
stories.excerpt: The story of Our Lady of Guadalupe is the most profound example of indigenous-Hispanic syncretism in the Americas. According to tradition, in December 1531, the Virgin Mary appeared to Juan Diego, an Indigenous Chichimec peasant, on Tepeyac Hill in what is now Mexico City. Speaking to him in Nahuatl, she asked that a c
stories.title: Tonantzin and Our Lady of Guadalupe — The Sacred Syncretism

stories.name: Tongue-Cut Sparrow
stories.excerpt: A kind woodcutter's compassion for a wounded bird is rewarded with wealth, while his greedy neighbor's calculated kindness leads to disaster.
stories.title: Tongue-Cut Sparrow

stories.name: Torre Jeppe
stories.excerpt: A mummified corpse named Torre Jeppe sits in a church night after night until a brave sexton discovers that the ghost cannot rest because of an ancient wrong that must be righted. A ghost-story founded on the belief that wrongdoing torments the guilty even after death.
stories.title: Torre Jeppe

stories.name: Trolls in Church
stories.excerpt: In the mountains of Norway, where the trolls have their halls in the great stone halls, there live creatures who see humans as pests—annoying, but sometimes useful.
stories.title: Trolls in Church

stories.name: Trollvaskers of Dovre
stories.excerpt: A shepherd discovers the secret rhythms of the Dovre mountain trolls, who gather weekly to wash their garments in a thunderous, rhythmic display of nature.
stories.title: Trollvaskers of Dovre

stories.name: True and Untrue
stories.excerpt: Two brothers, True and Untrue, leave home. Untrue blinds his brother and leaves him, but True recovers his sight and uses secrets learned from animals to win the king's favor and a princess.
stories.title: True and Untrue

stories.name: Tróndur í Gøtu (Tróndur the Viking Chieftain)
stories.excerpt: Tróndur í Gøtu was a powerful 10th-century Viking chieftain who lived in Gøta on Eysturoy. He is the central figure in the Færeyinga Saga, which recounts his fierce opposition to the Christianization of the islands. He led pagan resistance against Sigmundur Brestisson, who was sent by King Olaf Tryggvason of Norway to
stories.title: Tróndur í Gøtu (Tróndur the Viking Chieftain)

stories.name: Trøllanes and the Troll House Party
stories.excerpt: The settlement of Trøllanes on Kalsoy Island takes its name from ancient trolls who would come ashore once a year to wreak havoc—eating all available food, drinking, dancing, and behaving like wild party-goers. Terrified villagers would flee to Mikladalur every year, leaving their homes to be ransacked. One year, a wom
stories.title: Trøllanes and the Troll House Party

stories.name: Trøllkonufingur (The Troll Woman's Finger)
stories.excerpt: A giant troll-woman from Iceland came to Vágar Island with the same plan as Risin and Kellingin: to steal the Faroe Islands and drag them to Iceland. Like the giants, she could only work at night. Caught by sunrise, sunlight turned her to stone. She toppled from the cliff into the sea—and was so enormous that her head
stories.title: Trøllkonufingur (The Troll Woman's Finger)

stories.name: Tselane and the Cannibal Dimo
stories.excerpt: A beloved Sesotho folktale about Tselane, a young girl who refused to leave her beautiful forest home when her mother wanted to migrate. They agreed that Tselane would stay, locked safely in the house, and her mother would visit daily, singing a secret call-and-response song as their code. The cannibal Dimo watched and
stories.title: Tselane and the Cannibal Dimo

stories.name: Tsichtinako Teaches the Sisters
stories.excerpt: In the Acoma Pueblo creation story, Tsichtinako (Thought Woman) appeared as a voice guiding the sisters Iatiku and Nautsiti from within the earth. She couldn't be seen because she was a spirit without a human body. Tsichtinako instructed the sisters in all aspects of life: how to plant seeds from their baskets, how to
stories.title: Tsichtinako Teaches the Sisters

stories.name: Tsui-Goab and //Gaunab: The Khoikhoi Supreme Being and the Evil One
stories.excerpt: In Khoikhoi mythology, Tsui-//goab is the supreme being, creator, and guardian of health, associated with the east, the moon, and good fortune. His eternal adversary is //Gaunab, a malevolent being who causes sickness and death. Tsui-//goab's name means 'wounded knee,' stemming from a myth where he was injured in his b
stories.title: Tsui-Goab and //Gaunab: The Khoikhoi Supreme Being and the Evil One

stories.name: Tsunki, the Water Spirit
stories.excerpt: A powerful water spirit from Shuar tradition who lives in the rivers of the Ecuadorian Amazon and controls the fish and the currents.
stories.title: Tsunki, the Water Spirit

stories.name: Tuamotu: The Voyage of Kiwa
stories.excerpt: The great navigator Kiwa sailed across the Pacific guided by the stars, discovering the Tuamotu Archipelago. According to Tuamotuan tradition, Kiwa was sent by the gods to find new lands for the growing population of the central islands. He followed the flight paths of seabirds and the patterns of ocean swells to locat
stories.title: Tuamotu: The Voyage of Kiwa

stories.name: Tunda, the Shapeshifter of the Coast
stories.excerpt: A shape-shifting spirit from Ecuador's coastal region who leads men into the wilderness and abandons them, leaving them lost and mad.
stories.title: Tunda, the Shapeshifter of the Coast

stories.name: Turtle Island: The Lenape Earth Diver
stories.excerpt: In the Lenape creation account, before land existed, all the animals lived in deep water. They grew weary of swimming and wanted dry land. One by one the animals dove to retrieve earth from the bottom — the otter, the beaver — but each failed, gasping for air. Finally the humble muskrat took his turn. He was under the
stories.title: Turtle Island: The Lenape Earth Diver

stories.name: Twigmuntus, Cowbelliantus, Perchnosius
stories.excerpt: A clever farmer's lad determines to win the king's daughter by outwitting the king and his seven learned professors. On his journey, a twig hits him (Twigmuntus), a cow bellows (Cowbelliantus), and a perch bites his nose (Perchnosius). When the professors finish their learned gibberish, he stumps them with these three
stories.title: Twigmuntus, Cowbelliantus, Perchnosius

stories.name: Two Friends: Coyote and Bull Snake Exchange Visits
stories.excerpt: Coyote and Bull Snake were friends who decided to visit each other's homes. Coyote visited Bull Snake first and found his burrow beautiful and comfortable. Bull Snake then visited Coyote's den. During the visit, Coyote played a trick on Bull Snake, or vice versa, depending on the version. The story humorously explores
stories.title: Two Friends: Coyote and Bull Snake Exchange Visits

stories.name: Tórur Rami and the Three Gifts of Mykines
stories.excerpt: A giant named Tórur Rami tried to conquer the island of Mykines. The native inhabitant Óli Rami opposed him. When the giant approached, Óli Rami used magic to split Mykineshólmur from the main island, creating the islet now reached by a narrow metal bridge. The giant jumped across and they fought. Óli Rami won and spar
stories.title: Tórur Rami and the Three Gifts of Mykines

stories.name: Udea and Her Seven Brothers
stories.excerpt: A Libyan fairy tale collected by Hans Stumme in Tripoli. A woman with seven sons gives birth to a daughter, Udea. The seven brothers are driven away from home by a rival female spirit and set out into the world. The mother promises them a sign when Udea is born: a red flag for a daughter, a white one for a son. The riv
stories.title: Udea and Her Seven Brothers

stories.name: Uekera: The Tree of Knowledge
stories.excerpt: In Kiribati legend, Uekera is a sacred tree that reaches to the heavens, known as the tree of knowledge. It was planted in Buariki village in North Tarawa by the goddess Nei Tekanuea. According to tradition, Uekera's roots extend deep into the earth while its branches reach into the sky world, making it a bridge betwee
stories.title: Uekera: The Tree of Knowledge

stories.name: Uksáhkká: Guardian of the Door
stories.excerpt: Uksáhkká (Door Woman) is one of the daughters of Máttaráhkká, living under the door of the goahti. She protects people entering and leaving the dwelling, receives the newborn child into the world during birth, and protects children as they learn to walk. Drinks were poured under the door as offerings. Christian influen
stories.title: Uksáhkká: Guardian of the Door

stories.name: Uktena: The Horned Serpent (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: Uktena is a massive horned serpent covered in shining scales, with a single blazing crystal in its forehead that grants supernatural vision. The first Uktena was once a man who attempted to kill the sun. He failed and was transformed into the monstrous serpent as punishment. Uktena dwells in deep rivers, lakes, and und
stories.title: Uktena: The Horned Serpent (Cherokee)

stories.name: Um Al Duwais, the Mother of Toes
stories.excerpt: A terrifying female jinn who steals children at night, known for leaving only a single toe behind as her signature.
stories.title: Um Al Duwais, the Mother of Toes

stories.name: Umar Marvi — The Faithful Woman of Sindh
stories.excerpt: Marvi was a beautiful peasant woman from the Thar Desert village of Malir in Sindh. The local ruler, Umar Soomro, became obsessed with her and had her kidnapped and brought to his palace. He offered her wealth, jewels, and queenship if she would marry him, but Marvi refused steadfastly, remaining faithful to her betrot
stories.title: Umar Marvi — The Faithful Woman of Sindh

stories.name: Umm Al Duwais of the Abandoned Fort
stories.excerpt: A group of children exploring an old Portuguese fort encounter the terrifying Umm Al Duwais, whose eerie laugh echoes through the ruins to this day.
stories.title: Umm Al Duwais of the Abandoned Fort

stories.name: Unhcegila the Serpent Monster
stories.excerpt: Unhcegila was a gigantic serpent monster who wreaked havoc upon the land, devouring anyone who stumbled upon her. A red crystal in the seventh spot on her head functioned as her heart and granted its bearer great power. In one version, a warrior from the Bear Clan, guided by a Weasel spirit, allowed himself to be devou
stories.title: Unhcegila the Serpent Monster

stories.name: Unkulunkulu: The First Man Who Broke from the Reeds
stories.excerpt: In the beginning there was only darkness and Uthlanga, the primordial reed bed. The god Umvelinqangi created a seed that grew into a massive reed, and at the end of one reed grew a man named Unkulunkulu, the 'old old one.' He grew so large that he snapped off from the reed and walked across the land, where he found men
stories.title: Unkulunkulu: The First Man Who Broke from the Reeds

stories.name: Urashima Taro: The Fisherman and the Sea Kingdom
stories.excerpt: A kind fisherman is rewarded with a visit to the underwater Dragon Palace, only to return to a world where centuries have passed in a heartbeat.
stories.title: Urashima Taro: The Fisherman and the Sea Kingdom

stories.name: Ursitoare, the Weavers of Destiny
stories.excerpt: Three fate-weaving spirits who appear at a child's birth to determine the course of its life, found in Moldovan and Romanian tradition.
stories.title: Ursitoare, the Weavers of Destiny

stories.name: Vasilisa and the Doll
stories.excerpt: A girl with a magical doll discovers that the love of a mother can protect her and guide her through the darkest trials.
stories.title: Vasilisa and the Doll

stories.name: Vatnsdæla Saga - The Haunted Pastures
stories.excerpt: The saga depicts a landscape where the boundary between the living and the dead is thin. It features episodes where ancestral spirits and ghosts return to warn their descendants of impending doom or to settle old scores, reflecting the deep belief in the enduring presence of the dead in the Icelandic countryside.
stories.title: Vatnsdæla Saga - The Haunted Pastures

stories.name: Viejito del Monte: The Little Old Man of the Mountain
stories.excerpt: The Viejito del Monte is a small, ancient nature-spirit of the Nicaraguan highlands who rewards those who respect the forest and punishes those who despoil it.
stories.title: Viejito del Monte: The Little Old Man of the Mountain

stories.name: Vikram and Betaal (Baital Pachisi) — The King and the Vampire
stories.excerpt: King Vikramaditya of Ujjain is challenged by a sorcerer to capture a mischievous spirit called Betaal (Vetala) who hangs from a tree in a cremation ground. Each time Vikram tries to carry Betaal back to the sorcerer, the spirit tells a riddle-like story ending with a moral question. If Vikram answers correctly (which h
stories.title: Vikram and Betaal (Baital Pachisi) — The King and the Vampire

stories.name: Vishnu
stories.excerpt: When the forces of evil threaten to overwhelm the world, when dharma—the cosmic order—crumbles and chaos threatens to consume all that is good, a presence stirs in the highest heavens.
stories.title: Vishnu

stories.name: Vodnik, the Slovenian Water Sprite
stories.excerpt: A mischievous water sprite of Slovenian folklore, Vodnik lives in rivers and lakes, drowning the unwary but also helping those he favors.
stories.title: Vodnik, the Slovenian Water Sprite

stories.name: Vorvong and Sorvong: The Two Princes of Khmer Legend
stories.excerpt: Two princes banished by their father overcome giants and treachery to reclaim their kingdom.
stories.title: Vorvong and Sorvong: The Two Princes of Khmer Legend

stories.name: Wainamoinen and Youkahainen
stories.excerpt: Youkahainen, a young and arrogant singer, challenges the elderly Wainamoinen to a singing match to prove his superiority. Wainamoinen uses his deep knowledge of the origins of things and his superior magical songs to sing Youkahainen into a swamp, demonstrating that ancient wisdom far outweighs youthful arrogance.
stories.title: Wainamoinen and Youkahainen

stories.name: Wainamoinen Finds the Lost-word
stories.excerpt: Wainamoinen seeks the 'lost words' of creation, ancient incantations that provide total mastery over nature. He journeys to the deepest parts of the ocean or the underworld to retrieve this forbidden knowledge, emphasizing the theme of knowledge as the ultimate source of power.
stories.title: Wainamoinen Finds the Lost-word

stories.name: Wainamoinen's Boat-building
stories.excerpt: Wainamoinen decides to sail to Pohjola and spends immense effort building a magnificent boat. However, he fails to complete it because he forgets a small but crucial piece, the cross-beam. This story serves as a lesson on the importance of attention to detail and the dangers of pride.
stories.title: Wainamoinen's Boat-building

stories.name: Wainamoinen's Hapless Journey
stories.excerpt: Seeking a new bride to end his loneliness, Wainamoinen sails to distant and strange lands. During his journey, he encounters numerous obstacles and faces various trials that test both his physical endurance and his magical prowess, often finding himself in precarious situations that require his ingenuity to survive.
stories.title: Wainamoinen's Hapless Journey

stories.name: Wainamoinen's Harp-songs
stories.excerpt: The songs played on the kantele are used to preserve the history of the world and the legendary deeds of the heroes. This process establishes the harp as a central tool for cultural memory and divine communication.
stories.title: Wainamoinen's Harp-songs

stories.name: Wainamoinen's Lamentation
stories.excerpt: Overcome with grief after Aino's death, Wainamoinen wanders the world, mourning the loss of the woman he loved. Through his songs, he reflects on the nature of love, the pain of loss, and the inevitability of fate, while continuing to refine his magical abilities and search for meaning in his solitude.
stories.title: Wainamoinen's Lamentation

stories.name: Wainamoinen's Rescue
stories.excerpt: While on his journeys, Wainamoinen is captured or trapped in a foreign land, often within the depths of the sea or a dark cave. Through a combination of his own magical songs and the unexpected help of allies, he is eventually rescued, continuing his endless quest for a suitable partner.
stories.title: Wainamoinen's Rescue

stories.name: Wainamoinen's Sailing
stories.excerpt: Wainamoinen organizes a final, daring voyage to retrieve the Sampo from the fortress of Pohjola. He coordinates with other heroes of Kalevala, combining their strengths for one last great effort to secure the source of prosperity.
stories.title: Wainamoinen's Sailing

stories.name: Wainamoinen's Sowing
stories.excerpt: Wainamoinen attempts to sow the earth, but the land remains barren. He is challenged by powerful winds and storms that seek to prevent the growth of life. Using his profound magical songs, he calms the elements and prepares the land for agriculture, establishing the first signs of order and sustenance in the world.
stories.title: Wainamoinen's Sowing

stories.name: Wainamoinen's Wedding-songs
stories.excerpt: Wainamoinen performs a series of magical wedding songs, using his voice to bless the union of Ilmarinen and the Daughter of Pohjola. His songs provide wisdom to the couple and attempt to instill harmony between the two conflicting nations.
stories.title: Wainamoinen's Wedding-songs

stories.name: Walu: The Sun Woman
stories.excerpt: The Sun Woman who lights the world each day — a powerful Dreamtime ancestor whose daily journey across the sky sustains all life on Earth. In the Dreamtime, Walu was chosen by the sky spirits to carry the great fire across the heavens, and her golden hair became the rays that warm the land. She rises each morning from
stories.title: Walu: The Sun Woman

stories.name: Walumbe: The Origin of Death
stories.excerpt: Walumbe, whose name means 'death' in Luganda, was the brother of Nambi who followed her and Kintu to earth when they forgot the millet. Ggulu had warned them not to return, but Walumbe insisted on accompanying them on their way back. Once on earth, Walumbe demanded one of Kintu and Nambi's children as his servant. Kint
stories.title: Walumbe: The Origin of Death

stories.name: Wandjina the Cloud Spirits
stories.excerpt: The Wandjina (also Wanjina, Wondjina) are powerful cloud and rain spirits in the beliefs of the Wanjina Wunggurr cultural bloc of northwestern Australia, including the Worrorra, Wunambal, and Ngarinyin peoples of the Kimberley region. According to Dreamtime legends, the Wandjina created the landscape and its inhabitant
stories.title: Wandjina the Cloud Spirits

stories.name: Well Done and Ill Paid
stories.excerpt: A man tricks a bear into being bound to a sledge, but the fox who helped him is betrayed by the man's own wife, who sends hounds to hunt the fox.
stories.title: Well Done and Ill Paid

stories.name: Wenebojo and the Dancing Geese
stories.excerpt: Wenebojo, hungry and lazy, saw a flock of geese dancing on the shore. He convinced them to teach him their dance, saying he had seen a more beautiful dance in his dreams. The geese agreed, and Wenebojo joined them, singing and dancing with his eyes closed as he had been instructed. As they danced, Wenebojo began to wri
stories.title: Wenebojo and the Dancing Geese

stories.name: Wenebojo Creates the Earth (After the Great Flood)
stories.excerpt: In the Algonquian creation story, the trickster-transformer Wenebojo (Nanabozho) caused a great flood through his battle with the underwater serpents who killed his brother. After the waters covered everything, Wenebojo floated on a log with the surviving animals. He asked the loon, then the otter, then the muskrat to
stories.title: Wenebojo Creates the Earth (After the Great Flood)

stories.name: Were and the Creation of the World
stories.excerpt: Were, the supreme god of the Luo, created the world from the primordial waters. First, Were created the sky and the earth, then the sun, moon, and stars to give light. He fashioned the first man and woman from clay and breathed life into their nostrils. Were gave them cattle, goats, and seeds to plant, teaching them ho
stories.title: Were and the Creation of the World

stories.name: What Shall Baby's Name Be?
stories.excerpt: A well-to-do couple's daughter Peggy finally gets a suitor, but when she goes to the cellar for beer she becomes so preoccupied with what to name her future first baby that she, her mother, and her father all become lost in thought, causing the impatient suitor to leave forever.
stories.title: What Shall Baby's Name Be?

stories.name: When Mother Troll Took in the King's Washing
stories.excerpt: Troll Mother and her son Drulle live in a forest cottage where she does laundry for travelers. When a king builds a nearby castle for his queen and newborn princess, the lady-in-waiting hires Troll Mother to wash the royal clothes cheaply so she can pocket the difference. Troll Mother becomes enchanted by the beautiful
stories.title: When Mother Troll Took in the King's Washing

stories.name: White Buffalo Calf Woman and the Sacred Pipe
stories.excerpt: During a time of great famine, two Lakota scouts encountered a mysterious woman in white buckskin. One scout approached her with lustful intent and was reduced to bones. The woman instructed the remaining scout to prepare the tribe. She gave the people the chanupa (sacred pipe) made of red stone carved with a buffalo c
stories.title: White Buffalo Calf Woman and the Sacred Pipe

stories.name: White Painted Woman and Child of the Water (Chiricahua Apache)
stories.excerpt: In Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache tradition, the creation begins not with an emergence from the underworld but with a great flood that destroyed a malevolent world. After the flood, White Painted Woman (Changing Woman) appeared. She conceived Child of the Water (also known as Killer-of-Enemies in Lipan tradition) from
stories.title: White Painted Woman and Child of the Water (Chiricahua Apache)

stories.name: Whowie: The Monster of the Murray
stories.excerpt: Long ago, before the old grandfathers' time, there lived a creature in the Murray River that was more terrible than anything that has lived since.
stories.title: Whowie: The Monster of the Murray

stories.name: Why Leaves Change Color in Autumn
stories.excerpt: According to Wyandot legend, the changing colors of autumn leaves are the result of a great battle between the summer spirits and the winter spirits. Every autumn, the giant who rules the North Wind comes down from his cold kingdom and fights with the spirit of summer. During the battle, the leaves are bruised and batt
stories.title: Why Leaves Change Color in Autumn

stories.name: Why Men Commit Evil at Night (Ashanti/Akan)
stories.excerpt: Nyame the Sky God had three sons: Esum (Darkness), Osrane (Moon), and Owia (Sun). He wanted to make Owia a chief and proposed that the son who could guess the name of a secret yam would inherit his royal stool. Anansi discovered the name 'Kintinkyi' and revealed it to Owia, who won the contest. Nyame punished Esum by d
stories.title: Why Men Commit Evil at Night (Ashanti/Akan)

stories.name: Why Mr. Possum Has No Hair on His Tail
stories.excerpt: A pourquoi tale explaining the possum's hairless tail. Brer Possum once had the most beautiful, bushy tail in the animal kingdom. He was so proud of it that he spent all his time grooming and displaying it, neglecting to gather food for the winter. When winter came, Brer Possum was starving. He went to Brer Rabbit and
stories.title: Why Mr. Possum Has No Hair on His Tail

stories.name: Why the Bear Is Stumpy-Tailed
stories.excerpt: In this origin story, a cunning fox tricks a gullible bear into believing he can catch fish by leaving his tail in a frozen pond overnight. The bear's tail freezes solid, and when he tries to pull it out, it snaps off, explaining why bears have short, stumpy tails today.
stories.title: Why the Bear Is Stumpy-Tailed

stories.name: Why the Executioner is Called Assessor
stories.excerpt: An executioner on his way to an execution discovers a robbers' den in the forest. After completing his duty, he tells the king, who disguises himself as a tramp and together they defeat twelve robbers. In gratitude, the king decrees that executioners shall be called 'Assessor' and treated with respect.
stories.title: Why the Executioner is Called Assessor

stories.name: Why the Negro Is Black
stories.excerpt: An African American origin tale explaining skin color, collected by Joel Chandler Harris. According to Uncle Remus, in the beginning, all people were the same color. The Lord was making people and set them out to bake in the sun, like bread. He planned to bake them different shades—some light, some dark, some in betwee
stories.title: Why the Negro Is Black

stories.name: Why the Ocean Is Salty
stories.excerpt: In the days when the world was young, there were two brothers. Centers on Spirit, human attempt to understand the soul, afterlife, and the unseen forces that govern existence..
stories.title: Why the Ocean Is Salty

stories.name: Why the Salt is Far Away
stories.excerpt: A Hopi legend explaining why the Hopi must travel long distances to obtain salt. Long ago, salt was close to the Hopi villages. But a woman or a group of people violated a taboo involving salt — either by being wasteful, disrespectful, or by using salt improperly during a ceremony. The Salt Woman (or salt spirits) beca
stories.title: Why the Salt is Far Away

stories.name: Why the Sea is Salt
stories.excerpt: A man possesses a magical mill capable of producing any item on command. A curious sailor steals the mill and, not knowing the command to stop it, asks for salt. The mill produces salt relentlessly, filling the ocean and explaining why the sea remains salty to this day.
stories.title: Why the Sea is Salt

stories.name: Why the Spider Has a Bald Head (Ashanti/Akan)
stories.excerpt: Anansi attended his mother-in-law's funeral wearing a fine hat made of leopard skin. During the mourning, Anansi became infatuated with the chief's daughter and boasted that he could perform a magical dance. The chief agreed, but warned that if Anansi failed to impress, he would lose his head. Anansi danced wildly, and
stories.title: Why the Spider Has a Bald Head (Ashanti/Akan)

stories.name: Wihio the Spider Trickster
stories.excerpt: Wihio is the Cheyenne trickster figure, a spider-like being similar to Iktomi of the Lakota. He is clever but greedy, often getting into trouble because of his selfishness. In one story, Wihio tried to kill some ducks for a feast by tricking them into a dance with their eyes closed. A loon peeked and exposed the trick,
stories.title: Wihio the Spider Trickster

stories.name: Will Scarlet
stories.excerpt: Will Scarlet was the most hot-tempered of Robin Hood's Merry Men, a man who wore his anger like a cloak and held a grudge like a treasured possession.
stories.title: Will Scarlet

stories.name: Wolf Clan and the Salmon (Tsimshian)
stories.excerpt: This Tsimshian legend tells of a volcanic eruption caused by disrespect for the salmon. The Wolf Clan, one of the four major Tsimshian clans, had specific protocols for harvesting and honoring the first salmon of the season. One year, a member of the Wolf Clan failed to follow the proper rituals — he did not welcome th
stories.title: Wolf Clan and the Salmon (Tsimshian)

stories.name: Wolf Spirit and the Warrior's Vision
stories.excerpt: A young Comanche warrior went on a vision quest alone in the mountains, fasting for four days without water. On the fourth night, a Wolf appeared to him in a vision. The Wolf said, 'I am your brother. I will give you strength, courage, and the ability to track your enemies. But you must never kill my kind, for we are c
stories.title: Wolf Spirit and the Warrior's Vision

stories.name: Wunzh and the Origin of Indian Corn (Mon-Daw-Min)
stories.excerpt: A young boy named Wunzh went into the forest to fast and pray for guidance, as was the custom of his people. After many days of fasting, a spirit appeared to him dressed in green and yellow, with feathers on his head. The spirit challenged Wunzh to wrestle him. Though weak from fasting, Wunzh fought with all his streng
stories.title: Wunzh and the Origin of Indian Corn (Mon-Daw-Min)

stories.name: Xnifs, the Goblin of the Megaliths
stories.excerpt: A small, hairy goblin who haunts the ancient megalithic temples of Malta, sometimes helpful and sometimes malicious.
stories.title: Xnifs, the Goblin of the Megaliths

stories.name: Yamal Creation from the Mammoth
stories.excerpt: A Nenets creation myth from the Yamal Peninsula, whose name means 'End of the Land' in the Nenets language. The legend tells that the world was formed from the body of a giant mammoth that emerged from the primordial sea. The great sky god Num sent the mammoth to create dry land for humans and reindeer. When the mammot
stories.title: Yamal Creation from the Mammoth

stories.name: Yamm, God of the Deep
stories.excerpt: The sea god who was defeated by Baal but never destroyed, because the sea cannot be destroyed — it can only be held back by the strength of the storm.
stories.title: Yamm, God of the Deep

stories.name: Yanauluha Brings Medicine and Agriculture
stories.excerpt: In Zuni mythology, Yanauluha is the benevolent culture hero who brought the arts of medicine and agriculture to the people. Unlike trickster figures in some traditions, Yanauluha is a dignified, wise teacher. After the emergence into the daylight world, the people were struggling to survive. Yanauluha appeared among th
stories.title: Yanauluha Brings Medicine and Agriculture

stories.name: Yara-ma-yha-who: The Little Red Men
stories.excerpt: In the old times, children were told: 'Do not wander alone in the bush.. Do not rest beneath the fig trees.
stories.title: Yara-ma-yha-who: The Little Red Men

stories.name: Yemayá, Mother of the Ocean
stories.excerpt: Yemayá (Yemoja) is the great mother orisha of the ocean, maternity, and the moon in Cuban Santería, syncretized with the Virgin of Regla. She is the goddess of living waters, the salt sea, and is considered the mother of all life and the protector of women and children. Her colors are blue and white, her number is 7, a
stories.title: Yemayá, Mother of the Ocean

stories.name: Yemoja and the Waters of Life (Yoruba)
stories.excerpt: Yemoja, the mother of all waters and the goddess of the Ogun River, is said to be the mother of many of the Orishas. According to legend, when her waters burst forth, they created the oceans and rivers of the world. Yemoja is the patroness of pregnancy, childbirth, and all nurturing aspects of womanhood. In one tale, w
stories.title: Yemoja and the Waters of Life (Yoruba)

stories.name: Yewe, the God of Thunder (Ewe)
stories.excerpt: Yewe (also known as So or Hevioso) is the Ewe god of thunder, lightning, and rain. Yewe is a trɔwo (lesser deity) descended from Mawu, and is considered one of the most powerful and feared spirits in the Ewe pantheon. Those who offend Yewe may be struck by lightning, and special priests (Yewe priests) are needed to int
stories.title: Yewe, the God of Thunder (Ewe)

stories.name: Ysatters-Kajsa, the Wind-Troll of Narke
stories.excerpt: A Swedish legend about Ysatters-Kajsa, a powerful troll-woman who controls the winds over Narke province. She creates storms and blizzards when angered.
stories.title: Ysatters-Kajsa, the Wind-Troll of Narke

stories.name: Yuki-Onna: The Snow Woman
stories.excerpt: A snow spirit spares a young man's life on one condition: that he never reveal the secret of their encounter, a promise that will one day be tested by love.
stories.title: Yuki-Onna: The Snow Woman

stories.name: Yuletide Specters
stories.excerpt: A woman riding to Christmas mass encounters witch-trolls at a bridge and finds the church filled with headless specters and a headless priest, barely escaping with scraps of her mantle scattered on every grave. This ghostly Christmas legend is common throughout Scandinavia.
stories.title: Yuletide Specters

stories.name: Yunwi Tsunsdi: The Little People (Cherokee)
stories.excerpt: Yunwi Tsunsdi are the Cherokee Little People — small, child-sized nature spirits who live in caves, under rocks, and in the dense forest. They are usually invisible but sometimes reveal themselves to humans they trust. They possess powerful magic and are said to have taught medicine to certain shamans. The Little Peopl
stories.title: Yunwi Tsunsdi: The Little People (Cherokee)

stories.name: Zahhak: The Serpent-Shouldered Tyrant
stories.excerpt: Zahhak (Aži-Dahāk) was a prince seduced by Ahriman (the devil) who kisses his shoulders, causing two black serpents to sprout. They demand daily sacrifices of young men's brains for sustenance. Zahhak overthrows the just king Jamshid and rules Iran for a thousand years with cruelty. The blacksmith Kaveh, having lost se
stories.title: Zahhak: The Serpent-Shouldered Tyrant

stories.name: Zanahary and Ratovantany: The Creation of Humanity
stories.excerpt: In Malagasy mythology, the supreme sky god Zanahary and the earth god Ratovantany collaborated to create humanity. Ratovantany shaped the physical bodies from clay, but they remained lifeless. Zanahary, dwelling in the sky, breathed souls into the clay forms, animating them with divine essence. This division establishe
stories.title: Zanahary and Ratovantany: The Creation of Humanity

stories.name: Zin Kibaru and the Stolen Children
stories.excerpt: When children vanish near the river at night, a Zarma grandmother confronts the Zin Kibaru, a fearsome water spirit who steals the young to serve in his underwater kingdom.
stories.title: Zin Kibaru and the Stolen Children

stories.name: Zmaj, the Kosovan Dragon
stories.excerpt: A dragon of Kosovo legend, Zmaj is a powerful serpentine being who brings rain and guards the sacred sites of the Albanian and Serbian peoples.
stories.title: Zmaj, the Kosovan Dragon

stories.name: Zmeu, the Dragon of Moldovan Skies
stories.excerpt: A great dragon-like creature with three heads that terrorizes the Moldovan countryside, often serving as the ultimate test of a hero's courage.
stories.title: Zmeu, the Dragon of Moldovan Skies

stories.name: Zmeu: The Dragon of Romanian Folklore
stories.excerpt: A dragon-like giant kidnaps maidens and battles heroes in the mountains of Romania.
stories.title: Zmeu: The Dragon of Romanian Folklore

stories.name: Zmey, the Macedonian Dragon
stories.excerpt: A dragon of Macedonian folklore, the Zmey is a wise and powerful serpent who controls the weather and protects the land from foreign invaders.
stories.title: Zmey, the Macedonian Dragon

stories.name: Zmey: The Benevolent Dragon of Bulgarian Folklore
stories.excerpt: Unlike Western dragons, the Bulgarian Zmey is a protective guardian that controls the weather and ensures good harvests.
stories.title: Zmey: The Benevolent Dragon of Bulgarian Folklore

stories.name: Zonbi of the Coconut Grove
stories.excerpt: A dead plantation worker rises as a zonbi to haunt the coconut groves, driven by unfinished labor, until a Creole healer performs the rite that finally sets him free.
stories.title: Zonbi of the Coconut Grove

stories.name: Zuleikha and the Forty Maidens
stories.excerpt: The legend of the Forty Maidens (Kirk Kiz) is a Central Asian heroic tale found among Turkmen, Kazakh, and Karakalpak peoples. A beautiful and brave maiden named Zuleikha leads a band of forty warrior women who defend their people against invading forces. Rather than submit to forced marriage to an enemy khan, Zuleikha
stories.title: Zuleikha and the Forty Maidens

stories.name: Átahsaia the Cannibal Demon
stories.excerpt: A Zuni legend about Átahsaia, a giant cannibal demon who terrorized the people. Átahsaia is described as a huge, monstrous being with burning eyes and an insatiable hunger for human flesh, especially children. The demon would descend from the mountains to raid villages, carrying off victims in a large basket on its bac
stories.title: Átahsaia the Cannibal Demon

stories.name: Čáhcerávga: The Water Wraith
stories.excerpt: Unlike the Rávga (believed real), Čáhcerávga (Water Wraith) was known to be a fictional creature used to scare children away from dangerous waters. It was described as a long-necked, scary creature that might carry a child away. It was said to appear in all bodies of water where children were not supposed to go, includ
stories.title: Čáhcerávga: The Water Wraith

stories.name: Čázevulošnieida: The Underwater Girl
stories.excerpt: A Sea Sámi legend from Unjárga on the Varangerfjord, Norway. Čázevulošnieida (the Underwater Girl) is the daughter of Čáhceháldi (the Sea Guard). She lives in a parallel underwater world. When a fisherman boy encounters her, their meeting reveals how perspectives are turned upside down when two different worlds meet.
stories.title: Čázevulošnieida: The Underwater Girl

items.name: Ade (Yoruba Beaded Crown)
items.excerpt: The ade is the beaded crown of the Yoruba oba, the king, a cone- or basket-shaped headdress whose cascading fringe of glass beads veils the wearer's face, leaving only the mouth visible as he speaks. The patterns worked in the beads are a language of their own: birds, the Ogboni eye, the royal face, and motifs recallin

items.name: Adinkra Cloth
items.excerpt: Adinkra is the stamped cloth of the Akan, dyed in dark tones and printed with the symbolic motifs that bear the same name, each one carrying a proverb and a moral lesson: the sankofa bird that looks back to learn, gye nyame, 'except God,' and dozens more that together form a written language in cloth. The dye is made f

items.name: Aegis
items.excerpt: The storm-bearing shield of Zeus, lent to Athena and sometimes Apollo, an aegis of goatskin fringed with gold tassels; in Homer it scatters armies with terror and houses the gorgoneion, the severed head of Medusa. Hephaestus forged its golden version for Zeus, and the aegis became Athena's emblem in art, worn over her

items.name: Aegis
items.excerpt: The aegis, the storm-shield of Zeus, is the awesome goatskin or bronze buckler with which the god of the Iliad terrifies armies and shakes the field of battle, and which his daughter Athena also wears in the fight; its name, from the Greek for 'goat', points to its origin as a ritual skin, though Homer treats it as a w

items.name: Agadez Cross Pendant
items.excerpt: The Agadez cross, or tanaghilt, is the best-known of the Tuareg silver pendants of Niger, a cruciform amulet with four or more arms radiating from a central square, traditionally cast by the smiths (inadan) of Agadez. Agadez and the wider Air region have their own named cross designs, and the form is sometimes said to

items.name: Ajrak
items.excerpt: The ajrak is the block-printed shawl of Sindh, stamped in deep indigo and madder red with concentric borders of geometric stars, flowers and trellis patterns, worn over the shoulder and used to cover sacred objects. The name is linked to the Arabic word for blue, and archaeologists point to indigo-dyed and resist-print

items.name: Akan Goldweight (Abrammuo)
items.excerpt: The Akan goldweight, the abrammuo, is a small cast-brass piece used from the fifteenth century onward to weigh gold dust in the trade of present-day Ghana, one of the great mercantile tools of the Atlantic world. The weights were cast by the lost-wax method, and the figurative ones depict animals, people, proverbs, obj

items.name: Aladdin's Lamp
items.excerpt: The lamp of the tale of Aladdin, added to the Thousand and One Nights by Antoine Galland from the oral telling of the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab and first printed around 1709. Rubbing it summoned a powerful jinni who granted its holder's wishes, while its twin, the old magician's lamp, drove the plot's theft and re

items.name: Alms Bowl Relic
items.excerpt: The alms-bowl relic is the bowl that the Buddha is said to have used for his daily begging round, which became a sacred object after his death together with his tooth, his staff and other personal belongings. According to a well-known legend recorded in Gandharan art and later Buddhist texts, after the enlightenment fo

items.name: Altai Komus (Jew's Harp)
items.excerpt: Jew's harp of the Altai people, usually of metal or wood with a flexible tongue, played by strumming the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The komus is widely used for personal music and to accompany songs; its voice imitates natural sounds. It belongs to the same family of Siberian mouth harps as the Yakut

items.name: Amauti
items.excerpt: The amauti is the woman's parka of the Inuit, cut from caribou skin with a large hood and a deep pouch across the back, the amaut, in which a baby rides warm against its mother's body. The pouch lets the child nurse and sleep without being lifted into the cold, while the hood shields mother and child together from the

items.name: Amber Jewelry
items.excerpt: Necklaces, pendants, and beads of Baltic amber, the fossil resin thrown up on Danish shores, worn as adornment and as protection since the Stone Age. Danish Bronze Age graves hold hundreds of amber beads, and amber amulets were believed to guard against the evil eye and sickness, while small amber figures of animals an

items.name: Ancient Egyptian Kohl Tube
items.excerpt: The kohl tube is a small cylindrical vessel used in ancient Egypt to hold kohl, the black and green eye paint worn by men and women from the Old Kingdom onward. Eye paint was prepared by grinding minerals on a slate palette and mixing the powder with fat, then applying it around the eyes with a stick; green paint from

items.name: Ancile
items.excerpt: The ancile was the sacred shield of Mars that fell from heaven in the reign of Numa Pompilius, Rome's second king, and was kept as a pledge that the city would rule the world as long as the shield was preserved. Fearing theft, Numa had the smith Mamurius Veturius make eleven identical copies, so that the twelve shields

items.name: Andvaranaut
items.excerpt: Andvaranaut is the ring at the heart of the cursed gold of the dwarf Andvari, taken from him by Loki at the waterfall Gnitaheiðr after the god caught the dwarf in the shape of a pike. When Andvari was forced to give up his treasure hoard, he kept a single ring, and when Loki wrenched that away too, the dwarf laid a cur

items.name: Ankh
items.excerpt: The ankh, the looped cross that is the Egyptian hieroglyph for 'life', is the most recognisable of Egyptian symbols, appearing on temple walls, tomb paintings, and amulets for more than three thousand years. Shaped as a cross with a looped handle, it was carried by gods and goddesses, who hold it to the nostrils of kin

items.name: Ardagh Chalice
items.excerpt: The Ardagh Chalice is a two-handled silver cup made in Ireland in the eighth century AD and found in 1868, together with a hoard of other church metalwork and a bronze pin, inside a ring-fort at Ardagh in County Limerick. The vessel is built of silver with a bronze core, and its decoration of gold filigree, glass studs

items.name: Arrows of Cupid
items.excerpt: The arrows of Cupid in Ovid's Metamorphoses are of two kinds: the golden-headed shaft that kindles love and the blunt leaden one that drives love away, and the pair together explain the passions of gods and mortals alike. When Apollo taunts Cupid about his bow, the boy shoots the golden arrow into Apollo and the leaden

items.name: Arthur's Mantle
items.excerpt: Arthur's mantle, Llen Arthur, is one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain in medieval Welsh tradition. Whoever wore the cloak became invisible, yet could still see everything about him, a power that made it a garment of spies and guardians. The treasure list, which survives in several Welsh manuscripts fr

items.name: Asson
items.excerpt: The asson is the sacred rattle of Haitian Vodou, a gourd fitted with a handle and wrapped in a beaded net threaded with snake vertebrae, held only by the houngan or the mambo, the priest and priestess who lead the congregation. Its sound opens the ceremony: as the rattle is shaken before the peristyle, the lwa, the spi

items.name: Atlatl
items.excerpt: The atlatl is the carved wooden spear-thrower that hurls darts with far greater force than an unaided arm, used across Mesoamerica from the Olmec era through the Aztec empire and beyond. Spanish accounts and Aztec codices show warriors and hunters gripping the notched end of the thrower while the dart rests in its sock

items.name: Azerbaijani Carpet
items.excerpt: The Azerbaijani carpet is the hand-knotted pile rug of Azerbaijan, woven on vertical looms in distinct regional schools - Karabakh, Shirvan, Tabriz, Baku, Gazakh and Ganja among them - each with its own palette, knot and field layout. The traditional repertoire of motifs includes the buta, the dragon, the medallion, th

items.name: Aztec Death Whistle
items.excerpt: The Aztec death whistle, sometimes called ehecachichtli or skull whistle, is a small clay whistle about three to five centimetres long, modelled as a human skull, whose internal chambers produce a shrill, wind-like and unsettling tone. The most famous examples were excavated in the late 1990s at Tlatelolco, clasped in

items.name: Baba Yaga's Mortar and Pestle
items.excerpt: Iron mortar and pestle ridden by Baba Yaga, the witch of Russian fairy tales, who flies over the forest in her mortar, sweeping away her trail with a broom and driving the mortar onward with the pestle. In Afanasyev's tales she is called 'Baba Yaga the Bone Leg' and travels in this way; the mortar, pestle and broom are

items.name: Baganda Barkcloth (Olubugo)
items.excerpt: Olubugo is the barkcloth of the Baganda of Uganda, made by stripping the inner bark of the mutuba fig tree and beating it with wooden mallets until it becomes a soft, pliable, chestnut-brown textile. The craft is usually practised by men, who peel the bark in the wet season and beat it on a log, folding and turning the

items.name: Bagua Mirror
items.excerpt: The bagua mirror is a circular mirror ringed with the eight trigrams of the Book of Changes around a central yin-yang disc, hung over doorways in Chinese feng shui practice to turn away harmful energy, sha qi, and to return an attacker's evil gaze. In domestic use it is placed above the main door or facing a threatenin

items.name: Balalaika (Russian Triangular Lute)
items.excerpt: Three-stringed Russian lute with a characteristic triangular body, plucked or strummed to accompany folk songs and dances. The balalaika became a symbol of Russian folk music in the 19th century, when Vasily Andreyev standardised its sizes into a whole family of instruments; it is played solo and in orchestras, and its

items.name: Bamileke Elephant Mask
items.excerpt: Beaded elephant masks of the Cameroon Grassfields are worn by men's societies of the Bamileke and related peoples, who dance them at the funerals of notables, the installation of chiefs, and the festivals of the kwifo, the regulatory society that enforces chiefly authority. The mask takes the shape of an elephant head,

items.name: Bamum Beaded Throne (Mandu Yenu)
items.excerpt: The Mandu Yenu is the royal throne of the Bamum kingdom of the Cameroon Grassfields, a carved wooden stool and footstool completely encased in glass beads, cowrie shells, and brass studs. Mandu Yenu means 'rich in beads', and the most famous example, made for the Bamum court in the nineteenth century, was given by King

items.name: Banarasi Sari
items.excerpt: The Banarasi sari is the handwoven silk sari of Varanasi (Banaras) in Uttar Pradesh, famous for its rich brocade, its gold and silver zari, and its intricate pictorial motifs, among them the jangla (vine), bel (creeper), kalga and jal patterns. The weaving tradition grew under the patronage of the Mughal court, which e

items.name: Bandura (Ukrainian Zither-Lute)
items.excerpt: Plucked string instrument of Ukraine combining a lute's neck with a zither-like soundboard holding up to several dozen strings, played by folk singers called bandurysts and kobzars. The kobzar tradition of singing epic dumy to the bandura is among Ukraine's most distinctive musical heritage; the instrument descends fro

items.name: Bangmangi
items.excerpt: The bangmangi is the magic club of the dokkaebi, the mischievous goblin of Korean folklore, which grants whatever a person wishes when it is struck. In the folktales the dokkaebi owns the club and uses it to summon food, gold, and servants, and clever humans trick the gullible goblin into surrendering it: a thief or a

items.name: Batá Drum
items.excerpt: The batá is the consecrated drum of Cuban Santería, an hourglass-shaped instrument with two heads of different sizes, played in a set of three, the small okónkolo, the middle itótele and the great iyá, the mother drum that speaks the lead voices. The drums descend from the Yoruba bata of West Africa, carried to Cuba by

items.name: Baule Goli Mask
items.excerpt: The goli is a round-faced, painted mask of the Baule people of the Ivory Coast, worn with a full costume during village celebrations, funerals, and the dances of the goli society. The word names a whole sequence of masks that appear in a fixed order, from the round kpan faces through animal forms to the large, frighten

items.name: Benin Bronze Plaque
items.excerpt: The Benin bronzes are the cast-brass plaques that once covered the pillars of the Oba's palace in the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Nigeria, depicting the king, his warriors, chiefs and courtiers in high relief against openwork backgrounds. They were made by the guild of the Igun quarter using lost-wax casting, a cr

items.name: Betel and Areca Tray
items.excerpt: The betel and areca tray is the lacquered brass container that carries betel leaves, areca nut, and lime, the essential offering of Vietnamese hospitality, courtship, and marriage ritual. In the founding legend two twin brothers, Cao and Lang, loved the same woman; when the woman married Cao, Lang wandered away and die

items.name: Bhutanese Festival Mask
items.excerpt: The Bhutanese festival mask is a carved and painted wooden face worn by dancers in the cham dances of Bhutanese monasteries, taking the forms of fierce deities, animals, black-hatted dancers and the skeleton guardians of the faith. The tradition of cham is said to have been brought to the Himalayan world by the teacher

items.name: Bilum (Loop String Bag)

items.name: Birchbark Canoe

items.excerpt: The great bow of Odysseus, which no other man could string and which he alone could drive an arrow through all twelve axe heads, stands at the centre of the final test of the Odyssey. items.excerpt: The spinning wheel in the Grimms' fairy tale 'Briar Rose' (Dornröschen, KHM 50) is the instrument of the sleeping curse: the princess pricks her finger on its spindle, and the whole castle falls asleep for a hundred years. items.name: Bridle of Bellerophon

items.excerpt: Brísingamen, the necklace of the goddess Freyja, is one of the great treasures of the Norse gods, forged by the dwarves. items.name: Butterfly Jigha

items.name: Bychakh (Yakut Knife)

items.name: Caduceus
items.excerpt: Hermes' herald's staff, first described as a rod wrapped with fillets or ribbons and only later twined with serpents; it charmed mortals and spirits and led the souls of the dead to the underworld. items.name: Caduceus

items.name: Caladbolg
items.excerpt: Caladbolg, the great sword of Irish legend, is carried in the Ulster Cycle by Fergus mac Róich, the strong-armed former king of Ulster, and in some traditions it is also the blade of Cú Chulainn, who is said to have wielded it in the great single combat against his foster-brother Ferdiad in the Táin Bó Cúailnge. items.name: Calumet (Peace Pipe)
items.excerpt: The calumet, or chanunpa in Lakota, is the sacred pipe of Plains peoples, a stone bowl joined to a wooden stem, smoked in ceremonies of prayer, treaty and peace. items.name: Canopic Jar
items.excerpt: Canopic jars are the four vessels in which ancient Egyptian embalmers placed the organs removed from the body during mummification, the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines being preserved separately so that the deceased could use them again in the afterlife. items.name: Chipendani Mouth Bow
items.excerpt: The chipendani is a mouth bow of the Shona of Zimbabwe, a curved wooden stave with a single fibre or wire string, held against the open mouth and plucked so that the mouth shapes the tone. items.name: Drilbu Bell
items.excerpt: The drilbu is the ritual hand bell of Himalayan Buddhism, cast in a bell-metal alloy so that it rings a long, clear note, and struck or rung during ceremonies as the companion of the dorje sceptre. The bell is held in the left hand while the dorje is held in the right, and the two together are used in most monastic rit

items.name: Drotárstvo (Wire Craft)
items.excerpt: Drotarstvo is the Slovak craft of working iron wire, born in the eighteenth century when travelling drotári from the hills of northern Slovakia walked across Europe mending cracked pottery, glass and pipes with fine wire bindings. What began as tinkering became an art: journeymen and masters built up latticework jugs,

items.name: Drómi and Leyding
items.excerpt: Leyding and Drómi are the first two fetters with which the gods tried to bind the wolf Fenrir, before the silken dwarf-made fetter Gleipnir finally held him. items.name: Duduk (Armenian Double-Reed Flute)
items.excerpt: The duduk is the double-reed woodwind of Armenia, carved from apricot wood into a short cylindrical tube fitted with a wide, flat reed, and played with circular breathing so the sound never stops. items.name: Duho
items.excerpt: The duho is the carved wooden seat of the Taíno, a low ceremonial stool of guaiacum or mahogany on which caciques and behiques sat in ritual, carved in the shape of an animal, a crouching figure or a reclining zemi with upturned chin and closed eyes. items.name: Durendal
items.excerpt: Durendal, Roland's sword in the eleventh-century Chanson de Roland, is the greatest blade of the Frankish epic, carried by the hero and given to him, according to the poem, by the emperor Charlemagne. items.name: Dvojanka
items.excerpt: The dvojanka is a double flute of North Macedonia, carved from a single piece of wood, sometimes elder or ash, as two parallel pipes joined at the mouth, with fingerholes on one pipe only. items.name: Dyrnwyn
items.excerpt: Dyrnwyn, meaning 'white-hilt', is the sword of Rhydderch Hael, the Generous, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain listed in medieval Welsh texts. items.name: Edan Ogboni Staff
items.excerpt: The edan are paired staffs of brass or iron belonging to the Ogboni, or Osugbo, the elders' society of the Yoruba, each staff topped by a seated human figure, one male and one female, joined by a short length of chain. items.name: Eglė's Dress
items.excerpt: In the Lithuanian tale 'Eglė the Queen of Serpents', the garment Eglė wore when she bathed at the lake: a coiled grass snake slipped into her sleeve and would return her clothing only if she promised to marry its king. That pledged dress drives the whole tale — the serpent bridegroom, nine years lived beneath the sea,

items.name: Ehecailacacozcatl
items.excerpt: The ehecailacacozcatl, the 'wind jewel,' is the spiral shell breast ornament of the wind god Quetzalcoatl in his aspect of Ehecatl, worn at the throat and tied to the whirlwind that sweeps the road before the rain god Tlaloc and scatters the seeds of the world. Aztec images of Quetzalcoatl-Ehecatl show the cut conch wo

items.name: Ektara
items.excerpt: The ektara is the one-stringed lute of rural Bengal, made from a gourd or a bamboo tube with a skin face and a single steel string that is plucked and struck to produce a thin, continuous drone. items.name: Eleke
items.excerpt: The eleke is the beaded necklace of Cuban Santería, strung in the colors of a particular orisha and given in ceremony to place the wearer under that spirit's protection. items.name: Elixir of Immortality
items.excerpt: The elixir of immortality is the drug of eternal life that the Queen Mother of the West, Xiwangmu, is said to have kept in her paradise of Kunlun, and it is the pivot of one of the most famous tales in Chinese mythology. The archer Hou Yi obtained the elixir as a reward for shooting down the nine suns, but his wife Cha

items.name: Estonian Kannel
items.excerpt: Estonia's plucked box zither, a small winged or trapezoid instrument carved from a single piece of wood and strung with wire or gut strings, played to accompany regilaul, the ancient runic-song tradition shared with Finland's kantele and Lithuania's kanklės. Folk songs and folk archaeology place the kannel in Baltic-Fi

items.name: Ethiopian Ketab Protective Scroll
items.excerpt: Ketab are protective prayer scrolls of the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition, strips of parchment inscribed with prayers, sacred names, and devotional images, then rolled and worn or hung as amulets. items.name: Ethiopian Processional Cross
items.excerpt: Ethiopian processional crosses are tall brass, silver, or bronze crosses carried on staffs before the clergy during the liturgy of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. items.name: Evenki Shaman's Costume
items.excerpt: Ceremonial cloak of the Evenki shaman, sewn from reindeer hide and hung with iron pendants shaped as birds, fish, deer, snakes and human figures that represent the shaman's spirit-helpers, with a fringed apron and iron rattles. items.name: Excalibur
items.excerpt: The great sword of King Arthur, given to him by the Lady of the Lake after he broke his first blade, and returned to her waters by Sir Bedivere when Arthur died at Camlann. items.name: Eye of Horus
items.excerpt: The Eye of Horus, the wedjat, is the ancient Egyptian amulet of the eye that the god Thoth healed after the falcon god Horus lost it in his contest with Set for the throne of Egypt. items.name: False Face Mask
items.excerpt: The False Face masks of the Haudenosaunee are distorted human faces carved from living basswood, painted red and black, and used by the False Face Society in curing ceremonies that drive sickness from the sick. items.name: Fijian Masi (Barkcloth)
items.excerpt: Barkcloth of Fiji, beaten by women from the inner bark of the paper mulberry into broad sheets, which are felted together on a wooden anvil and painted with geometric designs in black, brown and red. items.name: Fijian War Club
items.excerpt: Carved club of the Fijian islands, made from the dense wood of the vesi (ironwood) or Pacific casuarina and shaped in a wide range of named forms: the long-bladed ulato, the throwing club, the bulbous totokia with its blunt striking head, and ceremonial clubs inlaid with shell or whalebone. items.name: Firebird's Feather
items.excerpt: Golden feather of the Firebird (Zhar-ptitsa) of Russian fairy tales, which shines so brightly that it lights a whole dark room and is carried by heroes such as Ivan Tsarevich into the tsar's palace. items.name: Flaming Pearl
items.excerpt: The flaming pearl, huozhu, is a luminous orb wreathed in curling flame that Chinese art shows two dragons chasing or guarding, and it is one of the most common motifs of East Asian decoration. items.name: Fon Asen Altar Staff
items.excerpt: The asen is the commemorative altar staff of the Fon of Benin, a forged iron pole topped with a figurative scene, an ancestor at work, an animal, a scene of daily life, set in a base of clay or iron and placed beside the ancestor altar of the compound. items.name: Franks Casket
items.excerpt: The Franks Casket, also called the Auzon Casket, is an eighth-century Anglo-Saxon chest carved from whalebone, about 23 centimetres long, with panels bearing scenes from Germanic legend, the Bible and classical history, framed by inscriptions in runes and Latin. items.name: Frau Holle's Feather Bed
items.excerpt: Frau Holle's feather bed is the great bedding that the old woman shakes out in the Grimms' fairy tale 'Frau Holle' (KHM 24), causing its feathers to fall to earth as snow. items.name: Freyja's Falcon Cloak
items.excerpt: Freyja's falcon cloak, also called the feather cloak or fjaðrhamr, is a garment of feathers that lets its wearer fly in the shape of a falcon. items.name: Gaida
items.excerpt: The gaida is the Bulgarian bagpipe, an instrument built from a whole tanned goatskin that serves as the air bag, with a chanter pipe for the melody and a single long drone pipe that sounds a constant bass note. items.name: Ganesh Idol

items.name: Gjallarhorn

items.excerpt: The gourgui is a large earthenware water jar of Tunisia, made of porous red terracotta and fitted with a narrow neck and a pouring spout, traditionally used to store and cool drinking water. items.name: Gullinbursti
items.excerpt: Gullinbursti, the 'golden-bristled boar', is the boar of the god Freyr, forged by the dwarven brothers Brokkr and Sindri in the same wager that produced the hammer Mjölnir. items.name: Gungnir
items.excerpt: Gungnir, 'the swaying one', is the spear of Odin, the All-Father, forged by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi in the same contest of treasures that gave the gods their greatest gifts. items.name: Gákti

items.name: Harpoon

items.name: Hawaiian Feather Cloak (ʻAhuʻula)
items.excerpt: Royal cloak of the Hawaiian chiefs, built on a netted base of olonā fibre and covered with hundreds of thousands of small feathers tied in bundles by a technique called kahekahe. items.name: Hawaiian Kapa (Barkcloth)

items.name: Hawaiian Pahu (Drum)
items.excerpt: Standing drum of the Hawaiian islands, carved from a single log of coconut or breadfruit wood and headed with sharkskin or stingray skin stretched and braced with cords. items.name: Herati Carpet

items.name: Hermes’ Sandals

items.name: Hou Yi's Bow

items.excerpt: Hringhorni is the greatest of all ships, the vessel on which the gods laid the body of Baldr the Beautiful after his death by the mistletoe dart. items.excerpt: The ikenga is the carved wooden shrine figure of Igbo men, a seated human form with curving horns, a sword and a carved knife held in its hands, standing on the family altar as the image of its owner's achievement and strength. items.name: Inukshuk
items.excerpt: The inuksuk, often spelled inukshuk, is a figure of stacked stones built by the Inuit and other Arctic peoples as a landmark in landscapes where trees offer no bearings; the Inuktitut name means 'something that acts in the capacity of a human'. items.name: Jade Rabbit's Mortar
items.excerpt: The mortar and pestle with which the Jade Rabbit pounds the elixir of immortality is a fixed image in the Chinese moon, the rabbit standing beside the cassia tree on the lunar surface as the companion of the goddess Chang'e. items.excerpt: Járngreipr, the 'iron grippers', are the iron gloves of the thunder god Thor, named in the Prose Edda as one of his three great treasures beside Mjölnir and the belt Megingjörð. items.excerpt: The K'awiil scepter, often called the manikin scepter, is a short staff topped by a small figure of the Maya lightning god K'awiil, a deity shown with a mirror set in his forehead, an elongated snout and a serpent leg. items.excerpt: Kachina dolls, or katsina tihu in Hopi, are small figures carved from cottonwood root and painted with the attributes of the katsinam, the spirit beings who visit Hopi villages from the winter solstice until July. items.name: Kalfak (Tatar Women's Embroidered Cap)

items.name: Kayak

items.excerpt: A battle standard woven in the shape of a raven, carried by Viking commanders to signal the presence of a great leader. items.excerpt: Wycinanka is the Polish folk art of paper cutting, practised above all by village women from the nineteenth century, who folded and snipped dyed paper with heavy sheep shears to make flat wall decorations. items.name: Xalam Lute
items.excerpt: The xalam is a plucked five-string lute of the Wolof of Senegal, with a calabash or carved wooden bowl body, a skin head, and strings grouped into two melody and three rhythm strings. items.name: Xhosa Beadwork
items.excerpt: Xhosa beadwork of South Africa is made with imported glass beads sewn onto leather, cotton, or cloth supports to create necklaces, aprons, headdresses, and panels of dress worn at the great passages of life. items.name: Xiuhuitzolli
items.excerpt: The xiuhuitzolli is the pointed diadem of turquoise mosaic worn by the Aztec tlatoque, the supreme rulers, as the emblem of sovereignty, its name meaning 'pointed thing of turquoise.' items.name: Yap Stone Money (Rai)
items.excerpt: Large circular discs of quarried calcite used as currency on the island of Yap, some measuring several metres across and weighing many tonnes, each with a central hole for carrying on a pole. items.name: Yaranga (Chukchi Portable Dwelling)
items.excerpt: Large hemispherical tent dwelling of the coastal Chukchi, built on a wooden frame of poles and whale ribs and covered with walrus skins, with reindeer hides laid inside against the cold. items.name: Yasakani no Magatama
items.excerpt: The curved jade bead (magatama) dangled from the branch of the sacred sakaki tree beside the mirror that drew Amaterasu from her cave, and counted among the Three Sacred Treasures of Japan it symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's mandate to rule. items.name: Yata no Kagami
items.excerpt: The Eight-Fold Mirror hung from a sacred sakaki tree outside the rock-cave in which the sun goddess Amaterasu had hidden, its brilliance luring her out to illuminate the world again, in the central myth of Japanese kingship. items.name: Yeibichai Mask
items.excerpt: The yeibichai masks of the Navajo are painted buckskin masks worn by dancers in the Nightway, the great nine-night healing ceremony, so that the wearer may embody a Holy Person, or ye'i, such as Talking God (Yeibichai) or Water Sprinkler. items.name: Yeouiju
items.excerpt: The yeouiju is the wish-granting jewel of Korean lore, the glowing orb that a serpent, imugi, must grasp to climb into full dragonhood, and that grants any wish to its holder. items.name: Yule Goat
items.excerpt: The Yule goat (julbock), a goat figure of straw bound with red ribbon, made in Sweden at Christmas. items.name: Yumi Bow

items.name: Zangbeto Masquerade Costume
items.excerpt: The zangbeto is the towering masquerade of the Fon of Benin, a cone-shaped costume of plaited straw and raffia worn over the body so that only a skirt of fibers is seen, with the performer hidden inside making the figure spin, whirl and race through the streets of its own accord. items.name: Zanzibar Dhow
items.excerpt: The dhow (jahazi) of Zanzibar is a lateen-sailed wooden vessel built on the Swahili coast for fishing, cargo, and the trade that rode the monsoons across the Indian Ocean. items.name: Zemi (Taino Effigy)
items.excerpt: The zemi is the carved effigy through which the Taíno of the Greater Antilles kept their spirits close: figures of wood, stone, bone or cotton, shaped by carvers to hold a spirit and kept in the household, in the fields, or in the house of the cacique. items.name: Zulu Iwisa Knobkerrie
items.excerpt: The iwisa, often called the knobkerrie, is a Zulu club made from a single piece of hardwood, with a heavy round knob at the top of a straight or slightly curved handle. items.name: Zulu Iziqu Necklace
items.excerpt: The iziqu is the necklace of a Zulu warrior, made of carved wooden beads strung on a cord and worn across the chest as a mark of valour. items.name: Zulu Ukhamba Beer Pot
items.excerpt: The ukhamba is the clay beer pot of the Zulu, a round, low-necked vessel fired from local clay and used to brew and serve utshwala, the sorghum beer at the centre of Zulu hospitality. items.name: Ægishjálmr
items.excerpt: Ægishjálmr, the 'helm of awe' or 'helm of terror', is a protective sign of Norse and Icelandic tradition, drawn as a wheel of radiating prongs or staves. aliases: The Kettle of the Mead of Poetry
